## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## Majjhima Nikāya
## Mūlapaṇṇāsa-aṭṭhakathā (Volume I)
## Ganthārambhakathā

I pay homage to the Sugata, whose heart is cooled by compassion, who has destroyed the darkness of ignorance with the light of the lamp of wisdom of the Path of Arahantship, who is the teacher of the world of beings including devas and humans, and who is liberated from the five destinations (gati).

The Buddha, having developed and realized the state of Buddhahood, attained the unsurpassed Dhamma which is free from the stains of defilements; I pay homage to that Dhamma.

I pay homage with my head to the Ariya Saṅgha, the group of eight noble persons, who are the breast-born sons of the Sugata and the conquerors of Māra’s army.

By the power of this merit of paying homage to the Triple Gem, performed with a devoted mind, may all obstacles be entirely destroyed.

For the purpose of explaining the meaning of the noble Majjhima Nikāya, which is marked by discourses of middle length, which has been commented upon by the Buddha and the subsequent enlightened disciples, and which crushes the doctrines of others;

That commentary which was first recited by five hundred Arahants and subsequently recited again in later councils;

And which was then brought to the island of Sīhala by the Arahant Mahā Mahinda and established in the Sīhala language for the benefit of the island dwellers.

Removing the Sīhala language from that commentary, I shall present it in a faultless language that is pleasing to the wise and consistent with the method of the Tanti (Pali scriptures).
2:
Without contradicting the views of the elders of the Mahāvihāra lineage, who are the lamps of the lineage of elders and possess very subtle analytical judgment, and omitting meanings that have appeared repeatedly, I shall explain the meaning of the Majjhima Nikāya for the delight of good people and for the long endurance of the Dhamma.

Discourses on virtue (sīla), the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), all subjects of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna), the detailed explanation of meditative absorptions and attainments (jhāna-samāpatti) together with the methods of conduct, all higher knowledges (abhiññā), the analytical decisions combined with wisdom, the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), sense bases (āyatana), faculties (indriya), and the four pure Noble Truths;

As well as the teaching of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) with its very pure and subtle methods that do not deviate from the path of the Pali scriptures, and the development of insight meditation (vipassanā-bhāvana)—since all these matters have been very clearly explained by me in the Visuddhimagga, I shall not analyze them further here.

"The Visuddhimagga stands in the middle of the four Nikāyas and will explain the meaning as spoken therein." Because it was made so, take that Visuddhimagga together with this commentary to understand the meaning of the Majjhima recension.

## Nidānakathā

In that commentary, the Majjhima-saṅgīti (Majjhima Nikāya) consists of a collection of three Paṇṇāsas: the Mūlapaṇṇāsa, the Majjhimapaṇṇāsa, and the Uparipaṇṇāsa. By way of Vaggas, each Paṇṇāsa is divided into five Vaggas, making a total of fifteen Vaggas. By way of Suttas, there are one hundred and fifty suttas plus two suttas (152 suttas). By way of words (padas), there are eighty thousand, five hundred and twenty-three (80,523) words. Therefore, the ancient teachers said:

"Eighty thousand words, and five hundred more, and again twenty-three are said; thus are the words determined."
3:
By way of letters (akkharas), there are seven hundred and forty thousand, and fifty-three (740,053) letters. By way of recital sections (bhāṇavāras), there are eighty bhāṇavāras and a half-bhāṇavāra exceeding by twenty-three words. By way of connections (anusandhi), there are briefly three kinds: connection by question (pucchānusandhi), connection by inclination (ajjhāsayānusandhi), and connection by natural sequence (yathānusandhi). In detail, however, there are three thousand and nine hundred (3,900) connections in this Majjhima Nikāya. Therefore, the ancient teachers said:

"Three thousand connections, and likewise nine hundred; these methods of connection are proclaimed for the Majjhima."

Among those Paṇṇāsas, the Mūlapaṇṇāsa is the first; among the Vaggas, the Mūlapariyāyavagga is the first; among the Suttas, the Mūlapariyāyasutta is the first. Of that sutta, the prologue (nidāna) beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ," spoken by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council, is the beginning. That account of the First Great Council has been explained in detail at the beginning of the Dīgha Nikāya commentary named Sumaṅgalavilāsinī. Therefore, it should be understood exactly as detailed in that Dīgha Nikāya commentary.
4:
## 1. Mūlapariyāyavagga
## 1. Commentary on the Mūlapariyāya Sutta

There is the prologue beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" (Thus have I heard). In that prologue, the word "evaṃ" is an indeclinable (nipāta). The words beginning with "me" are nouns (nāma). In the passage "Ukkaṭṭhāyaṃ viharati," the word "vi" is a prefix (upasagga), and the word "harati" is a verb (ākhyāta); in this manner, the analysis of words should first be understood.

As for the meaning, the word "evaṃ" has many variations of meaning, such as comparison, instruction, approbation, censure, acceptance of a statement, manner, indication, and emphasis.

To illustrate this: In passages such as "Evaṃ jātena maccena kattabbaṃ kusalaṃ bahuṃ" (Thus, by a mortal being born, much merit should be performed), it occurs in the sense of comparison (upamā). In passages such as "Evaṃ te abhikkamitabbaṃ, evaṃ te paṭikkamitabbaṃ" (Thus you should advance, thus you should retreat), it occurs in the sense of instruction (upadesa). In passages such as "Evametaṃ Bhagavā, evametaṃ Sugata" (Thus it is, Blessed One; thus it is, Sugata—this word is true just as it was spoken), it occurs in the sense of approbation (sampahaṃsana). In passages such as "Evamevaṃ panāyaṃ vasalī yasmiṃ vā tasmiṃ vā tassa muṇḍakassa samaṇakassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati" (Thus indeed does this low-caste woman speak the praises of that shaveling petty recluse in whatever place), it occurs in the sense of censure (garahaṇa). In passages such as "Evaṃ bhante'ti kho te bhikkhū Bhagavato paccassosuṃ" ("Yes, venerable sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One), it occurs in the sense of acceptance of a statement (vacanasampaṭiggaha). In passages such as "Evaṃ byā kho ahaṃ, bhante, Bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi" (Venerable sir, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in this manner), it occurs in the sense of manner (ākāra).

In passages such as: "Come, young man, go to where the recluse Ānanda is. Having approached him, in my name, ask the recluse Ānanda about his freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, ease of rising, strength, and comfortable living. Say, 'The young man Subha, son of Todeyya, asks the venerable Ānanda about his freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, ease of rising, strength, and comfortable living.' And also say this: 'May the venerable Ānanda be so kind as to come to the house of the young man Subha, son of Todeyya, out of compassion,'" it occurs in the sense of indication (nidassana).

In passages such as: "What do you think, Kālāmas, are these things wholesome or unwholesome? They are unwholesome, venerable sir. Are they blameworthy or blameless? They are blameworthy, venerable sir. Are they censured by the wise or praised by the wise? They are censured by the wise, venerable sir. Being undertaken and observed, do these things lead to harm and suffering or not? How does it appear to you in this case? Being undertaken and observed, these things lead to harm and suffering; thus it appears to us in this case," it occurs in the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa). In this context, the word "evaṃ" should be understood in the senses of manner, indication, and emphasis.
5:
Among those three (evaṃ, me, sutaṃ), the word "evaṃ" in the sense of manner (ākāra) shows the following meaning: Who is capable of knowing in every aspect the speech of the Blessed One—which is subtle through various methods, arisen from many dispositions (ajjhāsaya), endowed with meaning and phrasing, possessing diverse marvels (pāṭihāriya), profound in the realization of the Dhamma and its teaching, and which reaches the path of the ear (sotapatha) according to the respective languages of all beings? However, having generated the desire to listen with all one's power, it shows: "I have heard and remembered it in this manner; I too have heard and remembered it in one particular manner."

In the sense of indication (nidassana), Ānanda frees himself from responsibility, saying, "I am not self-enlightened (sayambhū); I have not realized this Dhamma by myself," and indicates the entire sutta that is about to be spoken, saying, "I have heard and remembered it thus; I too have heard and remembered it thus."

In the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa), the Blessed One said, "Monks, among my monk disciples who are of great learning (bahussuta), who are wise, who are mindful, who are resolute, and who are attendants, this Ānanda is the foremost." Furthermore, the General of the Dhamma (Venerable Sāriputta) praised him, saying, "The venerable Ānanda is skilled in the meaning, skilled in the Dhamma, skilled in the phrasing, skilled in linguistics, and skilled in the sequence of what precedes and follows." In accordance with being so praised, Ānanda wishes to show his own power of retention and generates a desire to listen in beings, saying, "I have heard and remembered it exactly thus (as the Buddha taught); and that remembering is, whether by meaning or by phrasing, neither deficient nor excessive, exactly as the Buddha taught and not otherwise."

The word "me" is found in three senses. This is true. In passages such as "Gāthābhigītaṃ me abhojaneyyaṃ," it has the sense of "mayā" (by me). In passages such as "Sādhu me bhante Bhagavā saṅkhittena dhammaṃ desetu," it has the sense of "mayhaṃ" (to/for me). In passages such as "Dhammadāyādā me bhikkhave bhavatha," it has the sense of "mama" (of me/my). In this context, both the meanings "it was heard by me" and "my hearing" are appropriate.

Regarding "sutaṃ," this word "suta" occurs both with and without a prefix. It has many variations of meaning, such as going, being renowned, being wet (with defilements), accumulating, striving, being cognizable by ear-consciousness, and knowing by following the sound that reaches the ear-door. This is true. In passages such as "Senāya pasuto," it means "one who goes." In passages such as "Sutadhammassa passato," it means "one who has the renowned Dhamma." In passages such as "Avassutā avassutassa," it means "one who is wet (soaked) with defilements." In passages such as "Tumhehi puññaṃ pasutaṃ anappakaṃ" (By you, much merit has been accumulated)...
6:
"Pasuta" means accumulated. In phrases such as "The wise who are devoted to jhāna" (Dhp. 181), it means those who are repeatedly devoted to jhāna. In phrases such as "Seen, heard, sensed," "suta" (heard) means that which is known by ear-consciousness. In phrases such as "one who bears what is heard, one who accumulates what is heard," it means one who bears what is known by following the sound that has reached the ear-door. However, in this context (Evaṃ me sutaṃ), it means "noted" or "noting" by following the sound that has reached the ear-door. If the word "me" is taken as "mayā" (by me), it is appropriate to say, "Thus has it been noted by me by following the ear-door." If it is taken as "mama" (of me), it is appropriate to say, "Thus is the noting of me by following the ear-door."

Thus, among these three words, "Evaṃ" indicates the function of consciousness such as ear-consciousness. "Me" indicates the person endowed with the aforementioned consciousness. "Sutaṃ" indicates the noting that is neither deficient, excessive, nor distorted, by rejecting the state of not hearing. Furthermore, "Evaṃ" expresses the various ways the cognitive process (viññāṇavīthi), occurring by following the ear-door, proceeds towards the object. "Me" expresses oneself. "Sutaṃ" expresses the Dhamma. The summary here is: "By the cognitive process proceeding towards various objects, I have done no other task; I have performed only this task of hearing the Dhamma; this Dhamma has been heard."

Furthermore, "Evaṃ" expresses the Dhamma to be pointed out. "Me" expresses the person. "Sutaṃ" expresses the function of the person. The meaning is: "The sutta which I shall point out, that sutta has been thus heard and noted by me."

Furthermore, "Evaṃ" is the indication of the various modes of that mental continuum (cittasantāna) through whose various occurrences the grasping of various meanings and syllables occurs. "Evaṃ" is a designation of mode (ākārapaññatti). "Me" is the indication of the agent (kattu). "Sutaṃ" is the indication of the object (visaya). By this much, the grasping and determination regarding the agent and the object are performed by the person endowed with that mental continuum occurring in various modes.

Alternatively, "Evaṃ" is the indication of the person's function. "Sutaṃ" is the indication of the function of consciousness. "Me" is the indication of the person associated with both functions. The summary here is: "By me, the person endowed with the consciousness having the function of hearing, it has been heard and noted through the conventional expression of the function of hearing obtained by the power of consciousness."

In that sentence "Evaṃ me sutaṃ," the words "Evaṃ" and "Me" are designations of what is non-existent (avijjamānapaññatti) in terms of ultimate reality (paramattha). For what is there in ultimate reality that could receive the designation "Evaṃ" or "Me"?
7:
The designation "Suta" is a designation of what exists (vijjamānapaññatti) in terms of ultimate reality. This is because, in this hearing of the Dhamma, whatever nature of Dhamma is known by ear-consciousness, that nature of Dhamma exists undistortedly in terms of ultimate reality; therefore, it is called a designation of what exists.

Moreover, the designations "Evaṃ" and "Me" are derivative designations (upādāpaññatti) because they are spoken in dependence on the Dhamma that has become the object of such ear-consciousness. The designation "Suta" is called a comparative designation (upanidhāpaññatti) because it is spoken in comparison to "diṭṭha" (seen) and so forth. In this sentence, by the word "Evaṃ," Venerable Ānanda shows his non-delusion (asammoha). Indeed, a deluded person is not able to penetrate the various and diverse Dhammas undistortedly. By the word "Sutaṃ," he shows his non-forgetfulness (asammosa) of the Dhamma previously heard. This is because if the Dhamma heard by a person is forgotten, that person cannot claim after a long time, "I have heard it." Thus, through non-delusion, Venerable Ānanda's perfection of wisdom (paññā) is established; through non-forgetfulness, his perfection of mindfulness (sati) is established. Between these two, mindfulness preceded by wisdom is capable of bearing the words (byañjana), and wisdom preceded by mindfulness is capable of penetrating the meaning (attha). Being endowed with the power to know both the words and the meaning, he is capable of guarding the treasury of the Dhamma, which is complete in meaning and phrasing; thus, he attains the state of the Treasurer of the Dhamma (Dhammabhaṇ膽āgārika).

In another way: By the word "Evaṃ," he shows wise attention (yoniso manasikāra). This is because for one who attends unwisely, there can be no penetration of the various meanings. By the word "Sutaṃ," he shows non-distraction (avikkhepa). This is because for one with a distracted mind, there can be no hearing of the Dhamma. This statement is true. Even if the Dhamma is preached with all perfection, a person with a distracted mind says, "I did not hear it; please say it again." Here, through wise attention, he accomplishes "setting oneself in the right course" (attasammāpaṇidhi) and "having performed merit in the past" (pubbe ca katapuññatā). This is because for one who has not set himself rightly or has not performed merit in the past, such wise attention cannot occur. Through non-distraction, he accomplishes "hearing the true Dhamma" and "association with good people" (sappurisūpanissaya). Indeed, a distracted person is unable to hear, and for one who does not associate with good people, there is no hearing of the Dhamma.

In another way: It was said that the word "Evaṃ" is the indication of the various modes of that mental continuum through whose various occurrences the grasping of various meanings and syllables occurs. Such a good mode does not occur for one who has not set himself rightly or has not performed merit in the past. Therefore, by this good mode "Evaṃ," he shows his own accomplishment of the latter two wheels (pacchimacakkadwaya). By the word "Sutaṃ," which is associated with the practice of hearing, he shows his own accomplishment of the former two wheels (purimacakkadwaya). This is because for one living in an unsuitable locality or one devoid of association with good people, there is no hearing of the Dhamma. Thus, through the accomplishment of the latter two wheels, Venerable Ānanda's purity of intention (āsayasuddhi) is accomplished. Through the accomplishment of the former two wheels, his purity of effort (payogasuddhi) is accomplished. Through that purity of intention, proficiency in realization (adhigamavyatti) is accomplished, and through purity of effort, proficiency in the scriptures (āgamavyatti) is accomplished. Thus...
8:
Desiring to place the introduction in its proper place as a precursor to the words of the Blessed One—just as the dawn is the precursor to the rising sun for one pure in effort (payoga) and intention (āsaya), and endowed with mastery of the scriptures (āgama) and realization (adhigama), and just as wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) is the precursor to wholesome action—the speaker uttered the words beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" (Thus have I heard).

In another way: by the word "Evaṃ," which indicates penetration in various ways, he demonstrates his possession of the analytical insight into meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā) and the analytical insight into perspicacity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā). By the word "sutaṃ," which indicates penetration of the various types of what is to be heard, he demonstrates his possession of the analytical insight into the Dhamma (dhamma-paṭisambhidā) and the analytical insight into language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā). Furthermore, by uttering the word "Evaṃ," which indicates wise attention, he demonstrates: "These teachings have been reflected upon by my mind and well-penetrated by my vision." By uttering the word "sutaṃ," which indicates the application of hearing, he demonstrates: "Many teachings have been heard by me, retained, and practiced through speech." By both of these, while demonstrating the perfection of meaning and phrasing, he inspires respect in hearing the Dhamma. For one who does not listen respectfully to the Dhamma that is perfect in meaning and phrasing is excluded from great benefit; thus, by inspiring respect, he shows that the Dhamma should be heard with due care.

By this entire phrase "Evaṃ me sutaṃ," the Venerable Ānanda, by not claiming the Dhamma proclaimed by the Tathāgata as his own, transcends the ground of the ignoble; by professing his status as a disciple, he enters the ground of the noble. Likewise, he raises the mind from false Dhamma and establishes it in the True Dhamma. By demonstrating, "This is merely what was heard by me; it is the word of that Blessed One alone," he frees himself from blame, points to the Buddha as the Teacher, entrusts the word as the Victor's word (jinavacana), and establishes the Guide of Dhamma (dhamma-netti).

Furthermore, by saying "Evaṃ me sutaṃ," while admitting that it was not created by himself and explaining the previous statement, he declares: "This is the word I received directly from the presence of that Blessed One—the one who is courageous with the fourfold fearlessness, the possessor of the ten powers, the one who stands in the lordly place of the bull (āsabha), the one who roars the lion's roar, the supreme among all beings, the Lord of Dhamma, the King of Dhamma, the Master of Dhamma, the one who is the Lamp of Dhamma, the one who is the Refuge of Dhamma, the one who turns the noble Wheel of the True Dhamma, the Fully Enlightened One. In this, there should be no doubt or hesitation regarding the meaning, the Dhamma, the word, or the phrasing." Thus, he destroys the lack of faith in this Dhamma among all devas and humans and generates the perfection of faith. Therefore, it is said:

I, the disciple of the Great Gotama Buddha, who am skilled in various methods, mindful, and possess the eye of the Dispensation, proclaim the Dhamma with these words "Evaṃ me sutaṃ." By so proclaiming, I destroy lack of faith in the Dispensation and generate the perfection of faith. The word "Evaṃ" expresses the meaning of determining the manner. The word "samaya" expresses the meaning by way of a determined time. In that sentence (ekaṃ samayaṃ), the word "samaya" occurs in the meanings of concordance (samavāya), opportunity (khaṇa), time (kāla), assemblage (samūha), cause (hetu), and view (diṭṭhi).
9:
## 
"The disciple of Gotama, saying 'Thus have I heard,' destroys lack of faith and increases faith in the Dispensation."

The word "ekaṃ" is a designation of a specific number. The word "samayaṃ" is a designation of a determined time. "Ekaṃ samayaṃ" is an indefinite indication. In this context, the word "samaya" is seen in the meanings of concordance (samavāya), opportunity (khaṇa), time (kāla), assemblage (samūha), cause (hetu), view (diṭṭhi), attainment (paṭilābha), abandoning (pahāna), and penetration (paṭivedha).

Indeed, in passages such as "Perhaps even tomorrow we might approach, depending on the time and the concordance of causes," the meaning is concordance. In passages such as "Monks, there is only one single opportunity and moment for living the holy life," the meaning is opportunity. In passages such as "the hot time, the feverish time," the meaning is time. In passages such as "the Great Assembly in the forest," the meaning is assemblage. In passages such as "Bhaddāli, this cause also was not penetrated by you: the Blessed One is staying at Sāvatthī, and the Blessed One will know me as 'the monk named Bhaddāli is not one who fulfills the training in the Teacher's Dispensation'; Bhaddāli, this cause also was not penetrated by you," the meaning is cause. In passages such as "At that time, the wanderer Uggāhamāna, the son of Samaṇamuṇḍikā, was staying in the Mallikā Queen's park, which has a single Sal tree and is a place for debating views," the meaning is view.

In passages such as:
"The benefit that is in the present life, and the benefit that is in the life to come;
Because of the attainment of these benefits, the wise one is called a Pandit."
—the meaning is attainment. In passages such as "By the right penetration and abandoning of conceit, he made an end of suffering," the meaning is abandoning. In passages such as "the meaning of oppression, the meaning of being conditioned, the meaning of burning, the meaning of change, the meaning of penetration of suffering," the meaning is penetration.

In this context, however, its meaning is time. By that meaning of time, among the various divisions of time such as year, season, month, fortnight, night, day, morning, noon, evening, the first, middle, and last watches of the night, and moments (muhutta), it is shown as "at one time."

In this regard, although among these times such as years and so on, whichever Sutta was spoken in whichever year, season, month, fortnight, part of the night, or part of the day—all of that has been well-known and well-noted by the Elder Ānanda through his wisdom.
10:
Venerable Ānanda Thera had well understood and well-determined all those Suttas with wisdom. However, if it were said, "Thus I heard, in such a year, in such a season, in such a month, in such a fortnight, in such a part of the night, or in such a part of the day," it would not be possible to easily memorize, to recite for oneself, or to teach others; furthermore, there would be much to be said. Therefore, having combined that meaning into a single term, he said, "Ekaṃ samayaṃ" (At one time).

Alternatively, there are various times of the Blessed One which are very well-known among devas and humans, such as the time of descending into the womb, the time of birth, the time of feeling spiritual urgency (saṃvega), the time of the great renunciation, the time of practicing austerities, the time of conquering the five Māras, the time of attaining omniscience, the time of dwelling in happiness in the present life, the time of teaching the Dhamma, and the time of attaining Parinibbāna. Among those times, he shows "Ekaṃ samayaṃ" (at one time) as the time of teaching. Furthermore, between the time of the function of knowledge and the function of compassion, he refers to the time of the function of compassion; between the time of practicing for one's own benefit and the benefit of others, he refers to the time of practicing for the benefit of others; between the two duties of those assembled, he refers to the time of Dhamma talk; and between the time of teaching and the time of practice, he refers to the time of teaching by saying "Ekaṃ samayaṃ."

Why is it that in this Sutta, it is designated with the accusative case (upayoga-vacana) as "Ekaṃ samayaṃ," instead of being designated with the locative case (sattamī-vibhatta) as in the Abhidhamma, "Yasmim samaye kāmāvacaraṃ," and in other Suttas, "Bhikkhus, at the time when a bhikkhu, secluded from sensual pleasures...", or with the instrumental case (karaṇa-vibhatta) as in the Vinaya, "At that time (tena samayena) the Buddha, the Blessed One..."? It is because while it is so in the Abhidhamma and Vinaya, it is different in this Sutta due to the possibility of different meanings. In the Abhidhamma and other Suttas, the locational sense (adhikaraṇa) and the sense of characterizing an action by another action (bhāvena-bhāva-lakkhaṇa) are possible. This is because the word 'samaya,' which has the meanings of 'time' and 'assemblage,' marks the occurrence of those states such as contact (phassa) mentioned therein, through the occurrence of the 'samaya' known as the causal combination of moments (khaṇa-samavāya-hetu). Therefore, to clarify that meaning, the locative case is used in those texts.

In the Vinaya, however, the causal sense (hetu) and the instrumental sense (karaṇa) are possible. The Blessed One, desiring to prescribe the training rules (sikkhāpada) by means of that time of prescribing training rules—which is difficult to know even for great elders like Venerable Sāriputta—and considering the cause for prescribing the training rules, dwelt in various places. Therefore, to show that meaning, the instrumental case is used in the Vinaya.
11:
In this Dispensation, and in other Suttas of this nature, the sense of continuous connection (accantasaṃyogattha) is possible. For whatever duration of time the Blessed One taught this Sutta or any other Sutta, throughout that entire time, He dwelt only in the dwelling of compassion (karuṇāvihāra). Therefore, to make that meaning clear, the designation is made here using the accusative case (upayoga-vacana).

Thus it is said:

"Depending on various meanings, the word 'samaya' is stated in the locative and instrumental cases in other places; but here, it is stated in the accusative."

However, the ancient commentators (porāṇā) explain: "Whether it is said as 'Tasmiṃ samaye,' 'Tena samayena,' or 'Ekaṃ samayaṃ,' it is merely a difference in expression; in all cases, the meaning is only that of the locative." Therefore, even when "Ekaṃ samayaṃ" is said, the meaning should be understood as "Ekasmiṃ samaye" (at one time).

'Bhagavā' means 'Garu' (Teacher/Venerable). In the world, a venerable teacher is called 'Bhagavā.' And this Blessed One is the Teacher (Garu) of all beings because of His excellence in all attributes; thus He should be known as 'Bhagavā.' It was also said by the ancient teachers:

"The word 'Bhagavā' is especially praiseworthy; the word 'Bhagavā' is supreme. That Blessed One is endowed with the quality of being a venerable teacher; therefore He is called 'Bhagavā'."

Furthermore:

"Because He is fortunate (bhāgyavā), has destroyed defilements (bhaggavā), is endowed with qualities (yutto), is a classifier of the Dhamma (vibhattavā), has frequented the Dhamma (bhattavā), and has discarded wandering in the rounds of rebirth (vantagamano), the Buddha is therefore called 'Bhagavā'."

Through the power of this verse, the meaning of that word (Bhagavā) should be understood in detail. That detailed meaning has already been stated in the section on the Recollection of the Buddha (Buddhānussati-niddesa) in the Visuddhimagga.

By this sequence of words, in this preface, Venerable Ānanda, by showing the Dhamma exactly as it was heard through the words "Evaṃ me sutaṃ," makes the Dhamma-body (dhammasarīra) of the Blessed One manifest. By doing so, he consoles the people who are longing because they no longer see the Teacher, saying, "This Dispensation is not one whose Teacher has passed away; this [Dhamma] is your Teacher."

By the words "Ekaṃ samayaṃ Bhagavā," Venerable Ānanda, by showing the non-existence of the Blessed One at that time, establishes the Parinibbāna of the form-body (rūpakāya). By establishing this...
12:
"Even that Blessed One, who taught the Noble Dhamma of such a nature, who possessed the ten powers, and whose body was as firm as a diamond, has attained Parinibbāna; who else should generate a desire for life?" Thus, he causes those intoxicated with the pride of life to be stirred with spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and generates effort in the True Dhamma for them.

By saying the word "Evaṃ" (Thus), he indicates the perfection of the teaching (desanā-sampatti). By the words "me sutaṃ" (I have heard), he indicates the perfection of the disciple (sāvaka-sampatti). By the words "ekaṃ samayaṃ" (at one time), he indicates the perfection of the time (kāla-sampatti). By the word "bhagavā" (the Blessed One), he indicates the perfection of the teacher (desaka-sampatti).

In the phrase "Ukkaṭṭhāyaṃ viharati," "ukkā" means torches. That city is called "Ukkaṭṭhā" because it was built even at night while torches were lit, with the thought, "Let not the auspicious day, the good moment, and the good constellation pass by." It means it was built while handheld torches were being carried. [He dwelt] near that city of Ukkaṭṭhā. Here, the locative case is used in the sense of proximity. "Viharati" (dwells) is a general term indicating being endowed with one of the modes of dwelling, such as the postures (iriyāpatha), the divine dwelling (dibba-vihāra), the brahma-dwelling (brahma-vihāra), or the noble dwelling (ariya-vihāra). However, here it indicates being engaged in one of the postures, such as standing, walking, sitting, or lying down. Therefore, whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down, the Blessed One should be understood as "viharati" (dwelling). For the Blessed One carries on and maintains the body without it falling by interrupting the affliction caused by one posture with another posture; therefore, it is said "viharati."

In the word "Subhagavane," it is called "Subhaga" because it possesses beautiful splendor. It means because of having beautiful glory and because of the fulfillment of good desires. Due to the abundance of splendor in that forest, people take food and drink and enjoy sensual pleasures there all day long, holding festivals and gatherings. They also wish for excellent desires, saying, "May we get a son, may we get a daughter," and it happens for them just as they wish. Thus, because of having beautiful glory and the fulfillment of good desires, it is called "Subhaga." Alternatively, it is called "Subhaga" because it is beloved by many people. It is called "vana" because it causes love (vanayati). It means that by its own perfection, it causes beings to have devotion and produces affection for itself. Or it is called "vana" because it seems to entreat (vanute). It means that by the songs of birds such as cuckoos intoxicated with the scent of various flowers, and by the branches, twigs, and foliage of trees swaying in the gentle breeze, it seems to entreat all living beings, saying, "Come to me, enjoy me." Because it is both beautiful and a forest, it is called "Subhagavana." [He dwelt] in that Subhagavana. Forests are of two kinds: planted and natural. Among them...
13:
Forests such as Veḷuvana and Jetavana are planted forests. Forests such as Andhavana, Mahāvana, and Añjanavana are natural forests. This [Subhagavana] should also be known as a natural forest.

In the term "Sālarājamūle," the sal tree is also called "sāla." Just as the Blessed One taught: "Monks, suppose there were a great sal forest not far from a village or town, and it was overgrown with castor-oil plants," and "between the twin sal trees." A great tree that is the chief among forest trees is also [called sāla]. As it is said: "In your kingdom, O King, and in your park-land, there are great sal trees of straight lineage, dark-green in appearance, and delightful to the heart." Any tree whatsoever is also [called sāla]. As it is said: "Monks, then that māluva creeper seed might fall at the foot of a certain sāla tree." But in this [Sutta], the chief tree among forest trees is intended. The word "rāja" (king) clarifies the meaning of its being the chief. As it is said: "Brahmin Dhammika, of the well-established banyan-king (great banyan tree)." In that term "sālarājā," there are two ways of forming the compound: "sālarājā" because it is the king (chief) of sal trees, and "sālarājā" because it is both a sal tree and a king in the sense of being the chief. "Mūla" means proximity (nearness). This word "mūla" is seen in the sense of the root (of a tree) in passages such as: "He would pull up the roots, even down to the fibers of the usīra grass." In passages such as "Greed is the root (mūla) of the unwholesome," it is seen in the sense of an uncommon cause (hetu). In passages such as "As far as the shadow spreads at noon, and as far as the leaves fall when the wind is still, this much is called the foot of the tree (rukkhamūla)," it is seen in the sense of proximity. Here, however, the sense of proximity is intended. Therefore, the meaning should be understood as "near the great sal tree."

In that [sentence], there might be this objection: If the Blessed One was dwelling in the city of Ukkaṭṭhā, it should not be said "Subhagavane sālarājamūle" (near the great sal tree in the Subhagavana forest). If he was dwelling there [at the foot of the sal tree], it should not be said "Ukkaṭṭhāyaṃ" (in the city of Ukkaṭṭhā). For it is not possible to dwell in two places at one time. However, it should not be regarded in this way. Did we not say, "This locative case is used in the sense of proximity"? Therefore, just as herds of cattle wandering near the Ganges or Yamunā rivers are commonly said to be "wandering in the Ganges, wandering in the Yamunā," so too here, the Blessed One, who was dwelling near the great sal tree in the Subhagavana forest which is in the vicinity of the city of Ukkaṭṭhā, is said to be "dwelling in Ukkaṭṭhā, near the great sal tree in the Subhagavana forest."
14:
The mention of the word "Ukkaṭṭhā" serves the purpose of indicating the village for alms-gathering; the mention of the remaining words, "Subhagavane Sālarājamūle," serves the purpose of indicating a dwelling place suitable for those who have gone forth.

Between these two, by mentioning the city of Ukkaṭṭhā, the Venerable Ānanda shows the Blessed One’s favor towards householders; by mentioning "Subhagavana" and so forth, he shows the favor towards those who have gone forth. Similarly, by the former statement, he shows the avoidance of the devotion to self-mortification through the acceptance of the four requisites; by the latter statement, he shows the means of avoiding the devotion to sensual indulgence through the abandonment of the objects of desire. By the former, he shows the exertion in teaching the Dhamma; by the latter, the inclination towards the three kinds of seclusion (viveka). By the former, he shows the approaching of beings with compassion (karuṇā); by the latter, the withdrawing from the world with wisdom (paññā). By the former, he shows the inclination towards accomplishing the welfare and happiness of beings; by the latter, the state of being untainted while performing the welfare and happiness of others. By the former, he shows a pleasant dwelling which is the cause for not abandoning righteous happiness; by the latter, a pleasant dwelling which is the cause for the practice of superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma). By the former, he shows the state of being of great benefit to humans; by the latter, to devas. By the former, he shows the state of the Buddha, though born in the world, having grown up in the world; by the latter, the state of being untainted by the world. By the former, because of the words, "Monks, there is one person who, when arising in the world, arises for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans. Who is that one person? It is the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One," he shows the fulfillment of the purpose for which the Blessed One arose. By the latter, he shows the dwelling in accordance with the place where He arose. Indeed, the Blessed One arose first in the Lumbinī grove, and for the second time at the Bodhimaṇḍa; thus, by these mundane and supramundane births, He arose only in the forest. Therefore, he shows His dwelling only in the forest. In this way and others, the connection of meaning here should be understood.

The word "Tatra" is an indication of the place and time of the teaching. It indicates "at that time" when He was dwelling, and "at the foot of that royal Sāla tree" where He was dwelling. Or, it indicates the place and time suitable for what is to be spoken. Indeed, the Blessed One does not teach the Dhamma in an unsuitable place or at an unsuitable time. The words, "Bāhiya, it is not yet the time to teach the Dhamma," serve as evidence here. The word "Kho" is a particle used as a mere expletive, for emphasis, or in the sense of beginning. The word "Bhagavā" indicates being the Teacher respected by the world. The word "Bhikkhū" refers to the persons suitable for listening to the discourse. Furthermore, the meaning of the term should be understood in this way: "He is a bhikkhu because he begs; he is a bhikkhu because he has undertaken the practice of alms-gathering." "Āmantesi" means he addressed, he spoke, or he informed.
15:
In other Pali contexts, the word 'āmantesi' also occurs in the sense of informing. This is as He said: "Monks, I inform you; monks, I inform you." It also occurs in the sense of calling. This is as He said: "Come, monk, in my name call Sāriputta" (A. Ni. 9.11).

The word "Bhikkhavo" is an expression of the manner of addressing. That address is stated because it is established by the possession of qualities such as the habit of seeking alms. Indeed, grammarians (those who know the characteristics of words) consider that one is called a "Bhikkhu" because he is endowed with the quality of having the habit of seeking alms, or because he is endowed with the quality of the nature of seeking alms, or because he is endowed with the quality of practicing well in seeking alms. By that word, which establishes their possession of qualities such as the habit of seeking alms, He reveals a livelihood practiced by both the lowly and the noble, and thereby suppresses the state of distraction and wretchedness. With this word "Bhikkhavo," preceded by a glance from eyes and a heart cool and overflowing with compassion, He causes them to face Him. By that very word, which indicates the desire to speak, He generates in them the desire to listen. By that very word, in the sense of an address, He urges them to listen well and to apply their minds. Indeed, the perfection of the Dispensation (Sāsana) depends on listening well and proper attention.

If it is asked, "While there are other devas and humans present, why did He address only the monks?" the answer is: because they are the seniors, the most excellent, the near ones, and those constantly present. Indeed, the Buddha's Dhamma teaching is common to all assemblies. However, among the assemblies, the monks are the seniors because they were the first to arise. They are the most excellent because, starting from the state of homelessness, they follow the Teacher’s practice and are the recipients of the entire Dispensation. Among those seated there, they are the near ones because they are in the presence of the Teacher. They are constantly present because they move in the vicinity of the Teacher. Furthermore, they are the vessels for the Dhamma teaching because they practice according to the instruction. Especially, He addressed only them because this teaching was delivered with reference to certain monks only.

In that context, there might be a question: "For what purpose does the Blessed One, when teaching the Dhamma, first address the monks and not teach the Dhamma directly?" It should be answered that He addresses them to arouse mindfulness. Indeed, monks might be seated while thinking of other objects, or with distracted minds, or reflecting on the Dhamma, or attending to a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). If the Dhamma were taught without addressing them, they might not be able to discern, "By what cause, by what condition, or due to what incident was this teaching delivered?" and they might either grasp it wrongly or not grasp it at all. Therefore, to arouse mindfulness in them, the Blessed One first addresses them and only then teaches the Dhamma.
16:
The word "Bhaddante" is an expression of respect, or it is a response to the Teacher. Furthermore, the Blessed One, saying "Bhikkhavo," addresses those monks. Those monks, saying "Bhaddante," respond to the Blessed One. Thus, the Blessed One speaks, "Bhikkhavo." They respond, "Bhaddante." By the word "Bhikkhavo," He causes them to give a response; by the word "Bhaddante," they give the response. "Those monks" refers to the monks whom the Blessed One addressed. "Responded to the Blessed One" means they responded to the Blessed One's address; the meaning is that they became attentive, listened, accepted, and received it. "The Blessed One said this" means the Blessed One now spoke this entire Sutta that was to be uttered.

By this much, the Venerable Ānanda has spoken the Nidāna (prologue), which is adorned with the time, the place, the speaker, the subject matter, the assembly, and the location of the teaching, in order to make this Sutta—which is endowed with meaning and phrasing and which indicates the depth of the Buddhas' knowledge of teaching—easy to enter. It is like a landing place at a lotus pond which has pure, sweet-tasting water and is bright with red, blue, white, and night-flowering lotuses, where the landing is beautified by the elegance of a wide, clean stone slab and jeweled stairs, and has a white ground covered with sand like scattered pearl dust. It is like a staircase for ascending easily to a noble palace that is a mass of beauty, as if wishing to touch the path of the stars, surrounded by well-proportioned walls and curious railings, having smooth and soft steps made of ivory, entwined with golden creepers, and bright with the radiance of many jewels. It is like a great gateway with a well-established, grand doorframe, illuminated by the spreading radiance of gold, silver, jewels, pearls, coral, and so on, for entering easily into a great house beautified by vast wealth and power, where the household people move about with sweet voices of conversation and laughter mixed with the sound of clashing golden bracelets and anklets. The explanation of the meaning of that Nidāna is finished.

## Suttanikkhepavaṇṇanā
(Explanation of the Delivery of the Sutta)

Now, the opportunity has arrived for the explanation of the Sutta delivered by the Blessed One in the manner beginning with "Sabbadhammamūlapariyāyaṃ vo." Since that explanation of the Sutta becomes clear when the delivery (nikkhepa) of the Sutta is investigated, we shall first investigate the delivery of the Sutta. There are four types of Sutta delivery: Attajjhāsaya (by the Buddha's own inclination), Parajjhāsaya (by the inclination of others), Pucchāvasika (due to a question), and Atthuppattika (due to an incident that arose).
17:
Among those four, there are suttas which the Blessed One taught solely by his own inclination, without being requested by others. These include the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta, Vattha Sutta, Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta, Mahāsaḷāyatanavibhaṅga Sutta, Ariyavaṃsa Sutta, Sammappadhānasuttantahāraka, and Iddhipāda-indriya-bala-bojjhaṅga-maggangasuttantahāraka. The delivery of these suttas is called Attajjhāsayonikkhepa (introduction by the Buddha's own inclination).

However, there are suttas taught according to the inclinations of others, after the Buddha considered their desires, preferences, thoughts, aspirations, and capacity for understanding, such as: "The qualities of Rāhula that ripen toward liberation have matured; what if I were to lead Rāhula further toward the destruction of the taints (arahantship)?" These include the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta, Mahārāhulovāda Sutta, Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, and Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta. The delivery of these suttas is called Parajjhāsayonikkhepa (introduction by the inclination of others).

Furthermore, the four assemblies, the four castes, Nāgas, Garuḍas, Gandhabbas, Asuras, Yakkhas, the Four Great Kings, the Tāvatiṃsa deities, and Mahābrahmā approached the Blessed One and asked questions such as: "Venerable Sir, it is said, 'Factors of Enlightenment, Factors of Enlightenment'"; "Venerable Sir, it is said, 'Hindrances, Hindrances'"; "Venerable Sir, are these the five aggregates of clinging?"; or "What is a man's best wealth in this world?" To those who questioned him thus, the Blessed One taught the Bojjhaṅgasaṃyutta and others. Or he taught other suttas such as the Devatāsaṃyutta, Mārasaṃyutta, Brahmasaṃyutta, Sakkapañha Sutta, Cūḷavedalla Sutta, Mahāvedalla Sutta, Sāmaññaphala Sutta, Āḷavaka Sutta, Sūciloma Sutta, and Kharaloma Sutta. The delivery of these suttas is called Pucchāvasikanikkhepa (introduction by way of questioning).

Then there are suttas taught in connection with a specific occurrence that has arisen. These include the Dhammadāyāda Sutta, Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta, Candūpama Sutta, Puttamaṃsūpama Sutta, Dārukkhandhūpama Sutta, Aggikkhandhūpama Sutta, Pheṇapiṇḍūpama Sutta, and Pāricchattakūpama Sutta. The delivery of these suttas is called Aṭṭhuppattikanikkhepa (introduction by way of a specific occurrence).

Among these four types of introduction, the introduction of this sutta is Aṭṭhuppattikanikkhepa. This is because the Blessed One delivered this sutta because a certain cause had arisen. What was that cause? It was the arising of conceit based on learning (pariyatti). It is said that five hundred Brahmins, who had mastered the three Vedas, later heard the Buddha's teaching and, seeing the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefits of renunciation, went forth in the presence of the Blessed One. Before long, they learned the entire word of the Buddha (Buddhavacana) and, based on their learning, conceit arose in them: "Whatever the Blessed One teaches, we understand it quickly. For the Blessed One [teaches only] three..."
18:
"...[the Blessed One teaches only] three genders, four parts of speech, and seven case endings, and nothing else; and in what is taught thus, there is no such thing as a difficult word for us." Thus, they became disrespectful toward the Blessed One and, from then on, they no longer went regularly to attend upon the Blessed One or to listen to the Dhamma. The Blessed One, knowing the movement of their thoughts, considered: "These men, without removing this spike of conceit, are incapable of realizing the Path or the Fruit." Taking the conceit that had arisen in them based on their learning as the occasion, the Blessed One, being skilled in teaching, began the discourse called "Sabbadhamma-mūlapariyāya" (The Root Sequence of All Things) in order to crush their conceit.

In that phrase, "Sabbadhamma-mūlapariyāya" means the fundamental cause (mūlapariyāya) of all things (dhamma). "Sabbesaṃ" refers to all things without remainder (the phenomena of the three planes). This word "sabba" is a term denoting totality. Whenever it is connected with a word, it illustrates the exhaustiveness of that meaning. For example: "Sabbaṃ rūpaṃ aniccaṃ (All form is impermanent)"; "Sabbā vedanā aniccā (All feelings are impermanent)"; "Sabbasakkāyapariyāpannesu dhammesu (In all things included within the self-identity view)." This word "dhamma" is found in the senses of learning (pariyatti), truth (sacca), concentration (samādhi), wisdom (paññā), nature (pakati), intrinsic nature (sabhāva), emptiness (suññatā), merit (puñña), offense (āpatti), and the knowable (ñeyya). In passages such as "Here, a monk learns the Dhamma, the Sutta, the Geyya, etc.," the word "dhamma" refers to learning (pariyatti). In "One who has seen the Dhamma, known the Dhamma," it refers to the truths (sacca). In "Such was the Dhamma (concentration) of those Blessed Ones," it refers to concentration (samādhi).

"O King of Monkeys, as in you,
In whom these four qualities (dhamma) exist:
Truth, wisdom (dhamma), courage, and generosity,
He overcomes the enemy he sees."

In such passages, it refers to wisdom (paññā). In "Subject to birth (jātidhamma), subject to aging (jarādhamma), and subject to death (maraṇadhamma)," it refers to nature (pakati). In "Wholesome states (dhamma)," it refers to intrinsic nature (sabhāva). In "At that time, there are states (dhamma) [empty of a person or being]," it refers to emptiness (suññatā). In "The Dhamma (merit) well-practiced brings happiness," it refers to merit (puñña). In "There are two undetermined offenses (dhamma)," it refers to an offense (āpatti). In "All things (ñeyyadhamma) in every aspect come into the range of the knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One," it refers to the knowable (ñeyyadhamma). In this context, however, the word "dhamma" refers to intrinsic nature (sabhāva). Its derivative meaning is: "They are called dhammas because they bear their own characteristics." The word "mūla" has already been explained in detail. Here, it should be understood as the unique cause (asādhāraṇa-hetu).
19:
The word "pariyāya" occurs in the sense of 'teaching' (desanā) in such passages as: "Remember this as the Madhupiṇḍika-pariyāya (The Honeyball Discourse)" (M. i. 205). It occurs in the sense of 'cause' (kāraṇa) in such passages as: "Brahmin, there is indeed a cause (pariyāya) by which one speaking rightly of me might say: 'The ascetic Gotama is a teacher of non-action'" (Pārā. 3). It occurs in the sense of 'turn' (vāra) in such passages as: "Ānanda, whose turn (pariyāya) is it today to exhort the nuns?" (M. iii. 398). In this discourse, however, it occurs in the sense of both 'cause' and 'teaching'. Therefore, in the phrase "Sabbadhammamūlapariyāyaṃ," the meaning should be understood either as the 'cause' known as the unique root of all things, or as the 'teaching' on the cause of all things.

Since this discourse is of the type whose meaning is to be inferred (neyyattha), the "all things" (sabbadhamma) should not be understood as the ultimate realities (sabhāva-dhamma) occurring in the four planes. Rather, it should be understood without exception as the things occurring in the three planes that are included within identity (sakkāya); this is the intended meaning here.

The word "vo" is seen in the nominative, accusative, instrumental, dative, and genitive cases, as well as as a mere expletive (padapūraṇa). It is seen in the nominative case in such passages as: "Anuruddhas, are you (vo) living in concord and harmony?" (M. i. 326). In the accusative: "Go, monks, I dismiss you (vo)" (M. ii. 157). In the instrumental: "You (vo) should not stay in my presence" (M. ii. 157). In the dative: "Monks, I shall teach you (vo) the discourse on the ways of the forest" (M. i. 190). In the genitive: "Sāriputta, the speech of all of you (vo) is well-spoken" (M. i. 345). As a mere expletive: "Those noble ones who (vo) are of pure bodily conduct" (M. i. 35). In this discourse, however, this word "vo" should be understood in the dative sense.

"Bhikkhave" is a re-addressing of the monks who have turned towards him in response. "Desessāmi" is the promise to teach. This is what is meant: "Monks, I shall teach you the root cause of all things; in the second way, I shall teach you the teaching on the cause." "Taṃ suṇātha" means: "Listen to that meaning, that cause, that teaching being spoken by me." In the phrase "Sādhukaṃ manasi karotha," "sādhukaṃ" and "sādhu" have the same meaning. This word "sādhu" is seen in the senses of request, acceptance, joy, goodness, firming, and so on. It is seen in the sense of request in such passages as: "Venerable sir, may the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief" (S. iv. 95). In the sense of acceptance: "'Very well (sādhu), venerable sir,' [that monk having rejoiced and approved...]"
20:
"...that monk, having greatly rejoiced and approved of what the Blessed One said" (M. iii. 86), it occurs in the sense of acceptance. In such passages as "Good, good, Sāriputta" (D. iii. 349), it occurs in the sense of joy.

"Good is the king who loves the Dhamma, good is the man of wisdom,
Good is non-treachery towards friends, the non-doing of evil is happiness."
In such verses as these (Jā. ii. 18. 101), it occurs in the sense of goodness. In such passages as "Brahmin, if that is so, listen well (sādhukaṃ)" (A. v. 192), the word "sādhuka" itself is said to be in the sense of firming and also in the sense of command. In this discourse too, this word "sādhuka" should be understood in these very senses of firming and command. It also occurs in the sense of goodness. By the sense of firming, it means: "Listen firmly to this Dhamma, grasping it as well-apprehended." By the sense of command: "Listen according to my command." By the sense of goodness: "Listen to this good and excellent Dhamma." This is the intended meaning.

"Manasi karotha" means 'reflect' or 'bring to mind'. The intention is: "Listen with an undistracted mind and keep it in your heart." Now, the phrase "Taṃ suṇātha" is for the purpose of preventing the distraction of the ear faculty (sotindriya). The phrase "Sādhukaṃ manasi karotha" is for the purpose of preventing the distraction of the mind faculty (manindriya) by urging firm attention. The former prevents the wrong grasp of the phrasing (byañjana), while the latter prevents the wrong grasp of the meaning (attha). By the former, he encourages the listening to the Dhamma; by the latter, he encourages the retention and examination of the Dhamma that has been heard. By the former, he shows that this Dhamma is endowed with proper phrasing, and is therefore worth hearing. By the latter, he shows it is endowed with meaning, and is therefore to be attended to. Alternatively, by connecting the word "sādhuka" with both phrases: because this Dhamma is profound in text (dhamma-gambhīra) and profound in teaching (desanā-gambhīra), listen well; because it is profound in meaning (attha-gambhīra) and profound in penetration (paṭivedha-gambhīra), attend to it well in the mind. This is how the connection should be understood.

"Bhāsissāmi" means "I shall teach." In this sentence, it means that the promised teaching will not be given only in brief, but rather, I shall speak it in detail. For these words are expressive of both brevity and detail. As the Elder Vaṅgīsa said:

"He teaches in brief, and he speaks in detail,
With a voice like that of a myna bird, the Buddha,
Whose speech is endowed with the eight factors, uttered his inspired words."
(S. i. 214).
21:
Therefore, because of the depth of meaning and the depth of penetration, it should be understood in this way: 'Listen well to that Dhamma, pay close attention.' 'Bhāsissāmi' means I will teach. In the sentence 'Taṃ suṇātha' (Listen to that), it means I will teach the promised discourse not only in brief but also in detail. Indeed, these words are terms that indicate both brevity and detail. The Elder Vaṅgīsa once said: 'The Blessed One teaches in brief and speaks in detail; He teaches the word endowed with eight factors, with a voice as sweet as a sālikā bird.' When He said, 'Listen, pay attention, I will speak,' those monks, being filled with enthusiasm, replied to the Blessed One, 'Yes, Bhante,' and accepted the words of the Teacher. Then the Blessed One spoke the entire sutta to those monks, beginning with 'Monks,' which is to be spoken now. In that context, the word 'idha' (here) is an indeclinable indicating location. This word 'idha' is used in some places referring to the world, as in: 'A Tathāgata arises here in the world.' In some places, it refers to the Dispensation (Sāsana), as in: 'Monks, only here is there a recluse (samaṇa), here a second recluse.' In some places, it refers to a specific spot, as in: 'Friends, staying right here as a deva, I have regained life; know it thus.' In some places, it is used as a mere filler (padapūraṇa) without specific meaning. For example, in the sentence: 'Monks, here I have finished my meal and refused further food.' Here, however, 'idha' should be understood as referring to the world.

The address 'Bhikkhave' (O monks) is a further calling of the monks to teach the promised discourse. By both words 'idha bhikkhave,' it means 'Monks, in this world.' In the phrase 'assutavā puthujjanō' (an uninstructed worldling), 'assutavā' (uninstructed) is to be understood as the absence of learning (āgama) and attainment (adhigama). Indeed, because of being devoid of study, inquiry, and investigation regarding the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), truths (sacca), dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), etc., there is no learning (āgama) that can prohibit the imaginings (maññanā) of craving, conceit, and views. And because the supramundane Dhamma to be attained through practice has not yet been attained, there is no attainment (adhigama). Due to this absence of learning and attainment, he is known as 'uninstructed.' That worldling is called 'puthujjana' because of reasons such as generating many defilements. This being is called 'puthujjana' because he is included among the base people and because he is distinct from the many [Noble Ones]. He is a worldling because he generates various defilements. The Blessed One said: They are worldlings because they generate many defilements; they are worldlings because they have not yet abandoned many self-views (sakkāyadiṭṭhi); they are worldlings because they look up to the faces of many teachers; they are worldlings because they have not emerged from all destinations (gati); they are worldlings because they construct various volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra); they are worldlings because they are carried away by various floods (ogha); they are worldlings because they are burned by various fevers; they are worldlings because they are scorched by various heatings; they are worldlings because they are attached, greedy, infatuated, immersed, obsessed, stuck, and bound to the five cords of sensual pleasure; they are worldlings because they are obstructed, hindered, blocked, covered, and enveloped by the five hindrances.
22:
(Regarding the five cords of sensual pleasure), they are called worldlings because they are infatuated, attached, involved, entangled, and bound; and because they are obstructed, hindered, blocked, covered, and enveloped by the many five hindrances. Alternatively, they are worldlings because they are included among the many people who have exceeded the count, who have turned their backs on the Noble Dhamma, and who practice base conduct. Or, he is a worldling because this person is separate and counted as distinct from the Noble Ones (Ariyas) who are endowed with virtues such as morality and learning. Thus, by these two words 'assutavā puthujjanō'—

'The Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun, spoke of two kinds of worldlings: one is the blind worldling (andha-puthujjana), and one is the good worldling (kalyāṇa-puthujjana).'

Among these two kinds of worldlings, it should be understood that the blind worldling is meant here. In the words 'ariyanāṃ adassāvī' (not seeing the Noble Ones), 'Ariyas' (Noble Ones) refers to the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddha, because they are far from defilements, because they do not lead to harm but lead only to welfare, and because they are worthy of being approached by the world including the devas. Or, in this context, only the Buddhas are called Ariyas. As it is said: 'Monks, in the world with its devas... the Tathāgata is called an Ariya.'

In the word 'sappurisā' (true persons), Paccekabuddhas and the disciples of the Tathāgata should be understood as 'sappurisa.' They are called 'sappurisa' because they are beautiful persons (superior men) endowed with supramundane virtues. Or, all of them are referred to by both terms. For the Buddhas are both Ariyas and Sappurisas; the Paccekabuddhas and the Buddha's disciples are likewise. As it is said:

'That wise one who is indeed grateful and appreciative, who has good friends and firm devotion, and who respectfully performs duties for one in distress—such a one they call a True Person (Sappurisa).'

By the words 'having good friends and firm devotion,' the disciple of the Buddha is meant; by words such as 'gratitude,' the Paccekabuddhas and the Buddhas are meant. Now, one who is not in the habit of seeing those Noble Ones and does not act well in seeing them is to be understood as 'one who does not see the Noble Ones.' Such a person is of two kinds: one who does not see with the eye [fleshly eye] and one who does not see with knowledge [wisdom]. Among these two, the one who does not see with knowledge is intended here. For even with the fleshly eye or the divine eye...
23:
Noble Ones, even when seen (with the eye), are as if unseen. This is because those eyes grasp only the appearance (color) and cannot perceive the object that is the state of being a Noble One (the Path and Fruit). Even dogs, jackals, and so forth see Noble Ones with their eyes, yet they are not called "seers of the Noble Ones."

In this regard, there is this story: It is said that an elderly man who had ordained late in life was the attendant of an Arahant elder living on Cittalapabbata Mountain. One day, after walking for alms with the elder, he followed behind carrying the elder's bowl and robes and asked, "Venerable sir, what is a Noble One like?" The elder replied, "Friend, in this Dispensation, some who ordain late in life may carry the bowl and robes of Noble Ones, perform duties for them, and travel with them, yet they do not know the Noble Ones. Friend, Noble Ones are thus difficult to know." Even when told this, that monk did not understand. Therefore, seeing with the eye is not true seeing; only seeing with wisdom is true seeing. As the Blessed One said: "Vakkali, what is the use to you of seeing this foul body? Vakkali, he who sees the Dhamma sees me." Therefore, even if one sees with the eye, if one does not see with wisdom the characteristics such as impermanence seen by the Noble Ones, and does not attain the supramundane Dhamma attained by the Noble Ones, then because of not seeing the qualities that make one a Noble One and the state of being a Noble One, he should be known as "one who does not see the Noble Ones."

"Unskilled in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones" means one who is not proficient in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones, categorized as the foundations of mindfulness and so forth (the nine supramundane states). Regarding the phrase "undisciplined in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones":
Discipline is of two kinds, and each of these is fivefold;
Because of the absence of that (discipline), he is called "undisciplined."

This discipline is of two kinds: the discipline of restraint (saṃvara-vinaya) and the discipline of abandoning (pahāna-vinaya). In these two kinds of discipline, each is further divided into five. The discipline of restraint is fivefold: restraint by virtue (sīla-saṃvara), restraint by mindfulness (sati-saṃvara), restraint by wisdom (ñāṇa-saṃvara), restraint by patience (khanti-saṃvara), and restraint by energy (viriya-saṃvara). The discipline of abandoning is also fivefold: abandoning by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna), abandoning by suppression (vikkkhambhana-pahāna), abandoning by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna), abandoning by tranquilization (paṭippassaddhi-pahāna), and abandoning by escape (nissaraṇa-pahāna).

Among those five types of the discipline of restraint, the restraint mentioned in the sentence "He is endowed, fully endowed with this Pātimokkha restraint" is called restraint by virtue. The restraint mentioned in the sentence "He guards the eye-faculty, he practices restraint in the eye-faculty" is called restraint by mindfulness.
24:
"O Ajita, whatever streams (such as craving) there are in the world, mindfulness is their obstruction. I call it the restraint of the streams; they are shut off by wisdom" (said the Blessed One). This is restraint by wisdom. "He is one who endures cold and heat"—this is restraint by patience. "He does not tolerate (endure) an arisen sensual thought, but abandons it"—this is restraint by energy. All these forms of restraint are called "restraint" (saṃvara) because they block bodily misconduct and so forth, which ought to be restrained and disciplined according to their respective natures, and they are called "discipline" (vinaya) because they remove them. Thus, it should be understood that the discipline of restraint is first divided into five.

Similarly, just as darkness is dispelled by the light of a lamp, there is the abandoning of various disadvantages (defilements) by various insight knowledges because of their being opposites in the insight knowledges such as the discernment of mind and matter. Specifically: the abandoning of personality belief (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) by the discernment of mind and matter; the abandoning of the view of no-cause and the view of a wrong-cause by the grasping of conditions; the abandoning of doubt (vicikicchā) by the subsequent overcoming of doubt; the abandoning of the grasp of "I and mine" by the comprehension of groups (kalāpa-sammasana); the abandoning of the perception of the path in what is not the path by the discernment of path and non-path; the abandoning of the view of annihilation (uccheda-diṭṭhi) by the seeing of arising; the abandoning of the view of eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi) by the seeing of passing away; the abandoning of the perception of fearlessness in what is fearful by the seeing of fear; the abandoning of the perception of gratification by the seeing of danger; the abandoning of the perception of delight by the contemplation of disenchantment; the abandoning of the desire not to be released by the knowledge of the desire for deliverance; the abandoning of non-equanimity by the knowledge of equanimity; the abandoning of the state of being contrary to the stability of Dhamma and Nibbāna by the knowledge of conformity (anuloma-ñāṇa); and the abandoning of the grasp of the signs of formations by change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhū-ñāṇa). This is called abandoning by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna).

The abandoning of various hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and so forth by means of concentration, categorized as access concentration and absorption concentration, which prevents the occurrence of defilements—just as moss on the surface of water is pushed aside by hitting it with a pot—is called abandoning by suppression (vikkkhambhana-pahāna).

The abandoning of the group of defilements belonging to the side of the origin (samudaya), mentioned in the manner of "for the abandoning of wrong views" and so forth, in one's own continuity through the development of the four Noble Paths, by way of their absolute non-occurrence, is called abandoning by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna). The tranquilization of defilements at the moment of the Fruit is this...
25:
The calming of defilements at the moment of fruition (phala) is called abandoning by subsiding (paṭippassaddhippahāna). Nibbāna, which is free from all heat because it is released from all conditioned things, is called abandoning by escape (nissaraṇappahāna). All these forms of abandoning are called 'abandoning' (pahāna) in the sense of relinquishing, and 'discipline' (vinaya) in the sense of removing; therefore, they are called 'discipline of abandoning' (pahānavinaya). Alternatively, it is called 'discipline of abandoning' because it abandons various opposing states or because various forms of discipline arise. Thus, the discipline of abandoning should be understood as being of five kinds.

In this way, this discipline is twofold in brief and tenfold in detail. Because of the destruction of restraint (saṃvara) and because the things to be abandoned have not yet been abandoned, and because such discipline does not exist, the uninstructed worldling (puthujjana) is called 'undisciplined' (avinīta). The same method should be understood for the terms 'one who does not see the noble ones' (sappurisānaṃ adassāvī), 'one who is unskilled in the Dhamma of the good persons' (sappurisadhammassa akovido), and 'one who is undisciplined in the Dhamma of the good persons' (sappurisadhamme avinīto). In terms of meaning, all these terms are without distinction. As the Blessed One said: "Those who are noble ones (ariya) are themselves the good persons (sappurisa). Those who are good persons are themselves the noble ones. The Dhamma of the noble ones is itself the Dhamma of the good persons. The Dhamma of the good persons is itself the Dhamma of the noble ones. The discipline of the noble ones is itself the discipline of the good persons. The discipline of the good persons is itself the discipline of the noble ones. These terms—ariya, sappurisa, ariyadhamma, sappurisadhamma, ariyavinaya, sappurisavinaya—have only one meaning; they are identical, they belong to the same category, and they are of that very noble nature."

Why did the Blessed One, after saying, "Monks, I will teach you the root of all things (mūlapariyāya)," point out the worldling by saying, "Here, monks, an uninstructed worldling is one who does not see the noble ones," without first teaching that Dhamma? It was to clarify that meaning through a teaching based on the person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna). The Blessed One's teaching of the Dhamma is of four kinds based on Dhamma and person: (1) Dhamma-based teaching of Dhamma (dhammādhiṭṭhāna dhammadesanā), (2) Dhamma-based teaching of person (dhammādhiṭṭhāna puggaladesanā), (3) Person-based teaching of person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna puggaladesanā), and (4) Person-based teaching of Dhamma (puggalādhiṭṭhāna dhammadesanā).

Among these four, a teaching such as: "Monks, there are these three feelings. What three? Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling. Monks, these are the three feelings"—this should be understood as a Dhamma-based teaching of Dhamma. A teaching such as: "In this person, there are six elements, six bases of contact, eighteen mental explorations, and four foundations"—this should be understood as a Dhamma-based teaching of person. "Monks, these three persons are found existing in the world..."
26:
"...What three? The blind person, the one-eyed person, and the two-eyed person. And what, monks, is the blind person?"—this kind of teaching is called a person-based teaching of person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna puggaladesanā).

"Monks, what is the fear of the miserable realm? Here, monks, someone reflects: 'The evil result of bodily misconduct is bad in the future life...' and maintains himself in purity. Monks, this fear is called the fear of the miserable realm"—this kind of teaching is called a person-based teaching of Dhamma (puggalādhiṭṭhāna dhammadesanā).

In this sutta, because the worldling has aggregates (vatthu) that are not fully understood and causes (mūla) such as ignorance that are not fully understood, there arises 'conceiving' (maññanā—craving and views) which is the root of all things intended in this sutta. Therefore, it should be understood that the Blessed One pointed out the worldling, saying, "Here, monks, an uninstructed worldling is one who does not see the noble ones," in order to clarify that meaning through a teaching based on the person.

## Pathavīvāravaṇṇanā (Commentary on the Section on Earth)

Having thus pointed out the worldling, now, wishing to show the 'conceiving' (maññanā) produced by all things of the self-identity (sakkāyadhamma) regarding objects such as earth, the Blessed One said: "He perceives earth as earth," and so on. Therein, earth is of four kinds: characteristic earth (lakkhaṇa-pathavī), composite earth (sasambhāra-pathavī), object earth (ārammaṇa-pathavī), and conventional earth (sammuti-pathavī). Among these four, the earth described as: "Friends, what is the internal earth element? That which is internal, personal, hard, and rough is the earth element"—this is called characteristic earth. The earth described as: "He should dig the earth himself or have another dig it"—this is called composite earth. The twenty parts such as hair, etc., and external things such as iron and iron blocks also exist. Because that earth exists together with constituents (sambhāra) such as color, it is called composite earth. The earth mentioned in: "One perceives the earth-kasiṇa"—this is object earth, also called sign-earth (nimitta-pathavī). One who attains the earth-kasiṇa absorption (jhāna) and is reborn in the deva realm receives the name 'earth-deity' (pathavī-devatā) because of that origin. This should be understood as conventional earth. In this sutta, all these types of earth are included. Among those types of earth, this worldling perceives any earth through the mode of earth, perceives it as 'earth,' perceives it as a portion of earth, or taking up worldly usage, perceives it as 'earth' through the perversion of perception (saññā-vipallāsa). Or, without letting go of the mass of earth, he perceives it in such ways as 'a being' or 'a being's property.' Why does he perceive it thus? —
27:
This should not be said. For an ordinary person (puthujjana) is like a madman. That ordinary person grasps anything in any manner whatsoever. Or rather, the cause here is the lack of seeing the Noble Ones (Ariyas) and so forth. Or it is because of the reason stated later by the Blessed One himself: 'It is not fully understood by him.'

'Having perceived earth as earth' means that the ordinary person, having perceived that earth with such a distorted perception (vipariīta-saññā), then—in accordance with the words, 'Proliferations (papañca) have perception as their source'—conceives, imagines, and elaborates through the proliferations of craving (taṇhā), conceit (māna), and views (diṭṭhi), which have gained strength in the later stage and are here called 'conceivings' (maññanā). He grasps it in various ways and in a distorted manner. Therefore, it is said, 'He conceives earth.' To show the conceivings of such an ordinary person in a gross manner, internal earth (ajjhattika pathavī) is mentioned as having twenty parts, such as 'this hair of the head, hair of the body,' and so forth. In the Vibhaṅga also, external earth is described: 'Therein, what is the external earth element? That which is external, hard, rough, of a harsh nature, of a harsh state, external and not-clung-to (anupādinnaka). For example: iron, copper, tin, lead, silver, pearls, gems, cat's eye, conch, stone, coral, money, gold, ruby, variegated ruby, grass, wood, gravel, potsherd, soil, rock, and mountain.' Thus is the external earth described. This explanation is given by taking the 'sign of earth' (nimitta-pathavī) mentioned in the Triad of Internal Objects (ajjhattārammaṇa-ttika).

'He conceives earth' means that through the three conceivings, he conceives 'I am earth,' 'Earth is mine,' 'Another is earth,' or 'Earth belongs to another.' Alternatively, he conceives internal earth through the conceiving of craving, the conceiving of conceit, and the conceiving of views. How? This ordinary person generates desire and lust (chandarāga) for the hair and so forth; he relishes the hair, delights in it, speaks in praise of it ('How good is my hair!'), and remains immersed in it. He does the same with body hair, nails, teeth, skin, or any other object of lust. Thus, he conceives internal earth through the conceiving of craving. He brings craving to the hair and so forth, thinking, 'May my hair be like this in the future,' or 'Such body hair,' and so on. He directs his mind toward obtaining hair and so forth that he does not yet possess, thinking, 'By this virtue, or... by this holy life, may I have such smooth, soft, delicate, and dark hair.' In this way too, he conceives internal earth through the conceiving of craving.

Likewise, based on the excellence or defect of his own hair and so forth, he generates conceit, thinking, 'I am superior,' 'I am equal,' or 'I am inferior.' Thus—
28:
—he conceives internal earth through the conceiving of conceit. Furthermore, according to the method mentioned as 'The soul is that [body], the body is that [soul],' some people grasp the hair and so forth as 'the soul' (jīva). This same method applies to body hair and so forth. In this way, he conceives internal earth through the conceiving of views.

Alternatively, contrary to the way of occurrence stated as, 'Friends, whatever internal earth element there is and whatever external earth element there is, both are just the earth element; that is not mine, that I am not, that is not my self,' he grasps the earth consisting of hair and so forth as 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self.' In this way too, he conceives internal earth through the conceiving of views. Thus, first, he conceives internal earth through the three conceivings.

Just as with internal earth, he also conceives external earth through the three conceivings. How? This ordinary person generates strong lust for iron, copper, and so forth. He relishes iron, copper, and so forth, delights in them, praises them, and remains attached to them. He regards iron and so forth as his own, protects them, and guards them, thinking, 'My iron, my copper,' and so on. In this way, he conceives external earth through the conceiving of craving. Or he brings craving to that external earth, thinking, 'May such iron, copper, and so forth be mine in the future.' He directs his mind toward obtaining what he does not yet possess, thinking, 'By this virtue, or by this vow, or by this austerity, or by this holy life, may I be one who possesses such abundant iron, copper, and other requisites.' In this way too, he conceives external earth through the conceiving of craving.
