Likewise, based on the excellence or defect of his iron, copper, and so forth, he generates conceit, thinking, 'By this property, I am superior,' or 'I am equal,' or 'I am inferior.' Thus, he conceives external earth through the conceiving of conceit. Having the perception of a soul in iron, he grasps it, thinking, 'This iron is the soul.' This same method applies to copper and so forth. In this way, he conceives external earth through the conceiving of views.

Alternatively, as stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: 'Here, someone regards the earth kasina as the self. What is the earth kasina, that am I; what am I, that is the earth kasina—thus he regards the earth kasina and the self as non-dual,' he grasps the sign of earth (nimitta-pathavī) as 'the self.' In this way, he conceives external earth through the conceiving of views. Thus too, he conceives external earth through the three conceivings. In this manner, the three conceivings should be understood in the context of 'He conceives earth.' From here on, I shall speak only briefly.
31:
Alternatively, the discernment of mind and matter is called 'full understanding of the known' (ñāta-pariññā). The knowledge beginning from the knowledge of comprehension by groups (kalāpa-sammasana-ñāṇa) up to the knowledge of conformity (anuloma-ñāṇa) is called 'full understanding by investigation' (tīraṇa-pariññā). The knowledge occurring in the supramundane path is called 'full understanding by abandonment' (pahāna-pariññā). Whoever fully understands earth does so through these three types of full understanding. Since the uninstructed worldling does not possess these types of full understanding, because of this lack of full understanding, he conceives earth and delights in earth. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, here in this teaching, an uninstructed worldling... conceives earth, conceives in earth, conceives from earth, conceives 'earth is mine,' and delights in earth. Why is that? Because it is not fully understood by him, I say."

## The Explanation of the Earth Section is Finished.

## The Explanation of the Water Section and Others

In the phrase "āpaṃ āpato" (water as water), water is also of four kinds: by way of characteristic (lakkhaṇa), constituents (sasambhāra), object (ārammaṇa), and convention (sammuti). Among these four, the water element described in the Vibhaṅga as: "Therein, what is the internal water element? That which is internal, personal, water, watery, cohesion, cohesive, the state of binding matter, internal, and clung-to (kamma-born)," etc., is called the 'characteristic water' (lakkhaṇa-āpo). The water described in such passages as "one learning the water-kasiṇa takes up the sign in water" is called 'constituent water' (sasambhāra-āpo). All the rest is similar to what was said in the Earth Section.

Specifically, in the method of arrangement (yojanā-naya), one should understand the twelvefold internal water element described by the method of "bile, phlegm," etc., and the external water element described as: "Therein, what is the external water element? That which is external, water, watery, cohesion, cohesive, the state of binding matter, external, and not clung-to. Namely, root-juice, stalk-juice, bark-juice, leaf-juice, flower-juice, fruit-juice, milk, curd, ghee, butter, oil, honey, molasses, or waters on the earth, or waters in the atmosphere," and also the 'sign water' (nimitta-āpo) mentioned in the Triad of Internal Objects.

In this Fire Section, "tejaṃ tejato" (fire as fire), the detailed explanation should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. Here, by the method of arrangement, one should understand the fourfold internal fire element described as: "That fire element by which one is warmed, by which one ages, by which one is consumed, and by which that which is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is well digested." Therein...
32:
..."What is the external fire element? That which is external, fire, fiery, heat, heated, glow, glowing, external, and not clung-to. Namely, wood-fire, straw-fire, grass-fire, cow-dung fire, chaff-fire, rubbish-fire, lightning-fire, the heat of fire, the heat of the sun, the heat of a heap of wood, the heat of a heap of grass, the heat of a heap of grain, the heat of a heap of goods." Thus, the external fire element should be understood.

In this Air Section, "vāyaṃ vāyato" (air as air), by the method of arrangement, one should understand the internal air element described as: upward-going winds, downward-going winds, winds in the belly, winds in the bowels, winds that course through the limbs, winds that cut like a sword, winds that cut like a razor, winds that pierce the heart, in-breath and out-breath. "Therein, in that matrix, what is the external air element? That which is external, air, airy, the state of supporting matter, external, and not clung-to. Namely, winds from the east, winds from the west, winds from the north, winds from the south, winds with dust, winds without dust, cold winds, hot winds, slight winds, strong winds, black winds, high-altitude winds, winds caused by the flapping of birds' wings, the wind-force of Garuḍas, winds from a palm-leaf fan, winds from a square fan." Thus, the external air element should be understood. The remaining discourse is just as previously stated. By this much sequence of words:

"When one thing is mentioned, those things which have the same characteristic are also mentioned by that; this is called the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (lakkhaṇa-hāra)."

Thus, in the Netti-pakaraṇa, the mode called 'lakkhaṇa' is stated. By the power of that Mode of Characteristics, when the four great elements are taken, derived matter (upādā-rūpa) is also taken, because it does not transcend the characteristic of matter. Whatever is primary matter and derived matter, that is the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha). Therefore, when the Blessed One says, "The uninstructed worldling conceives earth, water, fire, and air as self," it is also stated that in effect he regards matter as self. By saying "he conceives in earth, in water, in fire, in air," it is also stated that he regards self as in matter. By saying "he conceives from earth, from water, from fire, from air," because it is established that the self is other than matter, it is also stated that he regards self as possessing matter or matter as being in the self. Thus, these four types of regarding which have matter as their object...
33:
In this way, the conceivings based on the view of self-identity (sakkāyadiṭṭhi-manyanā) having form as their object should be understood. Among those four, the one conceiving that 'one regards form as self' is called annihilationism (ucchedadiṭṭhi). The three conceivings—'one regards self as possessing form,' 'one regards form as in self,' or 'one regards self as in form'—are called eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi). Thus, it should be understood that these two types of views arise.

## Explanation of the Section on Beings (Bhūta-vāra) and Others

Having thus spoken of the conceiving based on the objects of formations (saṅkhāra) by way of form, the Teacher now speaks of 'He perceives beings as beings,' etc., wishing to point out those beings. This is because the worldling (puthujjana) performs conceiving towards those formations and those beings upon which the designation 'beings' is based. In that text, the word 'bhūta' is found in the senses of the five aggregates, non-humans (amanussa), elements (dhātu), existence (vijjamāna), Arahants (khīṇāsava), beings (satta), trees (rukkha), and so on.

In passages such as 'Bhikkhus, see this as an existing group of five aggregates,' this word 'bhūta' is evident in the sense of the five aggregates. In 'Whatever beings (bhūta) are assembled here,' it is evident in the sense of non-humans. In 'Bhikkhu, the four great elements (mahābhūta) are the causes,' it is evident in the sense of elements. In 'In what is true (existing), there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya),' it is evident in the sense of existence. In 'He who is a consumer of time, a being (bhūta),' it is evident in the sense of an Arahant. In 'All beings (bhūta) in the world shall lay aside the body,' it is evident in the sense of beings. In 'Because of destroying a group of plants (bhūtagāma),' it is evident in the sense of trees and so forth. Here, however, this word 'bhūta' refers to beings, but not without distinction (not all beings). Only those beings below the heaven of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājikā) are intended here as 'beings' (bhūta).

In that context, 'He perceives beings as beings' and so forth is just as previously explained. However, in 'He conceives [himself] in beings' and so forth, all three types of conceiving should be applied. How? This worldling, according to the method stated: 'He sees a householder or a householder’s son endowed and provided with the five cords of sensual pleasure,' takes beings to be beautiful and happy and becomes attached to them. Having seen them, he is attached; having heard, smelled, tasted, touched, or known them, [he is attached]. Thus, he conceives through the conceiving of craving (taṇhā-manyanā) regarding beings. Or, by the method: 'O, would that I might be reborn in the company of the wealthy khattiyas,' etc., he directs his mind toward obtaining what he has not yet obtained. In this way too, he conceives through the conceiving of craving regarding beings. Based on the success or failure of himself and of beings, he regards himself as superior. Among beings, he regards some being as inferior, or himself as inferior, or some being...
34:
...as superior. He regards himself as equal to a being, or a being as equal to himself. As it is said in the Vibhaṅga: 'Here, someone, by reason of birth... or by any other grounds, first regards himself as equal to others. Later, he regards himself as superior and others as inferior. Such a type of conceit is called pride and over-pride (mānātimāna).' Thus, he conceives through the conceiving of conceit (māna-manyanā) regarding beings.

Regarding beings, however, thinking 'They are permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change,' or thinking 'All beings, all breathing things, all creatures, all souls are without power, without strength, without effort; bent by the necessity of fate and circumstance, they experience pleasure and pain in the six classes of birth,' he conceives through the conceiving of views (diṭṭhi-manyanā). Thus, he conceives regarding beings through the three types of conceiving.

How does he conceive in beings (bhūtesu)? He desires his own rebirth or a happy rebirth among various beings. In this way, first, he conceives in beings through the conceiving of craving. Or, desiring rebirth among beings, he gives gifts, undertakes precepts, and performs the observance (uposatha). Such actions are also conceiving in beings through the conceiving of craving. Taking beings as a group, he regards some beings as superior, and some as equal or inferior. Thus, he conceives in beings through the conceiving of conceit. Likewise, he conceives some beings as permanent and stable, and some as impermanent and unstable, or he conceives 'I am also one among beings.' Thus, he conceives in beings through the conceiving of views.

In the phrase 'He conceives from beings' (bhūtato manyati), it should be understood that he conceives the arising of himself or others, along with their belongings, as being from some being (as a source). This is his conceiving of views. When he produces affection and conceit for that very object conceived through the conceiving of views, the conceivings of craving and conceit should also be understood. In the phrase 'He conceives [beings] as mine' (bhūte me manyati), only the conceiving of craving is obtained. This should be understood as occurring through possessiveness in such ways as 'my sons, my daughters, my goats and sheep, poultry and pigs, elephants, cattle, horses, and mares.' 'He delights in beings' (bhūte abhinandati) is just as previously explained. In the phrase 'It is not fully understood by him' (apariññātaṃ tassa), it should be understood that because the formations (saṅkhāra) upon which the designation 'beings' is based are not fully understood through the three types of full understanding (pariññā), the beings are said to be not fully understood. The connection (yojanā) should be made in the same manner as previously stated.
35:
In this way, having briefly shown the objects of conceiving (maññanā) by way of formations and beings, [the Teacher] now speaks [the words] beginning with "deve devato" in order to show them in detail by way of the distinctions of planes and so forth. In the phrase "deve devato", they are called "gods" (deva) because they sport or shine with the five cords of sensual pleasure or by their own psychic power. There are three kinds of gods: conventional gods (sammuti-deva), gods by rebirth (upapatti-deva), and gods by purity (visuddhi-deva). Kings, queens, and princes are called conventional gods. From the gods of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājikā) upwards, including the Brahma gods, they are called gods by rebirth. Arahants who have destroyed the taints (āsavas) are called gods by purity. In this context, however, only the gods by rebirth should be understood, but not all of them. By the word "deva" here, the gods of the six sensual-sphere heavens are intended, excluding Māra and his retinue in the Heaven of Gods Who Wield Power over Others' Creations (Paranimmita-vasavatti). In this section on gods (deva-vāra), all the explanations of meaning should be understood in the same way as stated in the section on beings (bhūta-vāra).

In the word "Pajāpatiṃ", Māra should be understood as "Pajāpati". Some teachers say, "This is a designation for the great kings and others who are the lords of various gods, such as the Four Great Kings." That statement is rejected in the Great Commentary (Mahā-aṭṭhakathā) as inappropriate, because those great kings are already included by the word "deva". Here, only Māra is intended as "Pajāpati" because he is the lord of the generation of beings called "creatures" (satta). Where does that Māra live? He lives in the Heaven of Gods Who Wield Power over Others' Creations. In fact, King Vasavatti rules in that heaven. It is said that Māra lives in one part of it, exercising sovereignty over his own retinue, like a rebel prince living on the border of a kingdom. It should be understood that by taking Māra here, his retinue is also included. The method of application (yojanā) in this section is as follows: A worldling, having seen or heard of Pajāpati (Māra) as being beautiful, long-lived, and full of happiness, is enamored and conceives him through craving-conceiving (taṇhā-maññanā). Or, one who aspires to attain the state of Māra which he has not yet attained, by such means as "O, that I might be reborn in the company of Pajāpati!", also conceives Pajāpati through craving-conceiving. Having attained the state of Māra, one who gives rise to conceit, thinking "I am the lord and master of beings," conceives Pajāpati through conceit-conceiving (māna-maññanā). A worldling who thinks, "Pajāpati is permanent and stable," or "He will be annihilated and perish," or "He is without power, without strength, without effort, and having reached a fixed nature, he experiences pleasure and pain in the six classes of birth (abhijāti)," should be understood as conceiving Pajāpati through view-conceiving (diṭṭhi-maññanā).

In the phrase "Pajāpatismiṃ" (in Pajāpati), only view-conceiving is appropriate. The way that view-conceiving occurs is: a certain worldling in this world conceives, "All things such as life and beauty that exist in Pajāpati (Māra) are permanent, stable, and not subject to change." Or he conceives, "There is no evil in Pajāpati; no evil deeds are found in that Māra."

In the word "Pajāpatiṃ" [as an object], all three conceivings can be obtained. How? A certain worldling in this world conceives the origin or emergence of himself or another, along with their possessions, as being from Pajāpati; this is his view-conceiving. The craving-conceiving and conceit-conceiving of a worldling who gives rise to affection or conceit regarding that very object conceived through view-conceiving should also be understood. In the phrase "Pajāpatiṃ me" (Pajāpati is mine), only craving-conceiving is obtained. How? It should be understood that this craving-conceiving occurs for a worldling who cherishes him by such means as "Pajāpati is my teacher, my master." The rest is as stated in the section on beings.

In the text "Brahmaṃ Brahmato", he is called "Brahma" because he is developed by various special qualities such as the meditative absorptions (jhāna).
36:
He conceives, "All those things such as life and beauty are permanent, eternal, stable, and not subject to change." Alternatively, he conceives, "There is no evil in Māra; evil deeds are not found in that Māra."

In the word "Pajāpatito" (from Pajāpati), all three conceivings are obtained. How? A certain person in this world conceives the arising or emergence of himself or another, along with their equipment and possessions, as being from Māra; this is his view-conceiving (diṭṭhi-maññanā). For one who gives rise to affection and pride in that very object conceived through view-conceiving, craving-conceiving (taṇhā-maññanā) and conceit-conceiving (māna-maññanā) should also be understood to occur. In the phrase "Pajāpatiṃ me" (Pajāpati is mine), only craving-conceiving is obtained. It should be understood that this craving-conceiving occurs by way of possessiveness, such as "Māra is my teacher, my master," and so forth. The rest is exactly as stated before.

In the text "Brahmaṃ Brahmato", he is called "Brahma" because he is developed by various special qualities. Furthermore, the name "Brahma" is used for Mahābrahmā, the Buddha, the Arahant, parents, and the supreme [Dhamma]. In passages such as "A Brahma with a thousand [retinue], a Brahma with two thousand," Mahābrahmā is called Brahma. In the passage, "Monks, 'Brahma' is a designation for the Tathāgata," it refers to the Buddha.

"The Buddha, the dispeller of darkness, the all-seeing,
The one who has reached the end of the world, transcended all existence,
The one without taints, who has abandoned all suffering,
Named 'Truth'—that Brahma (Arahant) has been attended by me."
In this context, "Brahma" refers to a Brāhmaṇa (an Arahant).

Parents are called "Brahma" and "First Teachers" (pubbācariya).

In the phrase "Brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti" (He turns the supreme wheel), "Brahma" means the supreme. In this Brahma-section (brahma-vāra), however, the first-born Brahma who lives for an aeon is intended. It should be understood that by taking that Brahma, the Brahma's Ministers (Brahmapurohita) and the Brahma's Retinue (Brahmapārisajja) are also included. The explanation of the meaning here should be understood in the same way as stated in the section on Pajāpati.

In the section on the Radiant Gods (ābhassara-vāra), their radiance (ābhā) spreads and streams out from their bodies as if breaking off and falling, like the flames from a torch; therefore, they are called "Ābhassara". It should be understood that by taking those Ābhassara gods, all the realms of the second jhāna—namely, Limited Radiance (Parittābha), Immeasurable Radiance (Appamāṇābha), and Radiant Lustre (Ābhassara)—are included. All those gods live in a single plane.

In the section on the Gods of Lustrous Glory (subhakiṇha-vāra), they are pervaded with a beautiful body color. They possess a glory that shines like a block of radiant gold placed in a golden casket; therefore, they are called "Subhakiṇha". By taking those Subhakiṇha gods, all the gods born in the realms of the third jhāna are included.
37:
By taking the Ābhassara Brahmas, it should be understood that all the planes of the second jhāna are included. It should be understood that all these—the Parittābha, Appamāṇābha, and Ābhassara Brahmas—are those who dwell on a single level.

In the section on Subhakiṇha, they are called Subhakiṇha because they are suffused with beautiful bodily color, and because they are solid with beautiful radiance, possessing a splendor like a mass of shining gold placed in a golden casket. By taking these Subhakiṇha Brahmas, it should be understood that all the planes of the third jhāna are included. It should be understood that all these—the Parittasubha, Appamāṇasubha, and Subhakiṇha Brahmas—are those who dwell on a single level.

In the section on Vehapphala, they are called Vehapphala because they have abundant fruit. This refers to the Brahmas of the fourth jhāna plane. The explanation of the meaning and connection in these three sections should be understood in the same way as stated in the section on beings (bhūta).

In the section on Abhibhū, one is called Abhibhū because of conquering or overcoming. What does one overcome? The four mental aggregates. This is a designation for the realm of non-percipient beings (asaññasatta). The non-percipient Brahmas dwell on the same level as the Vehapphala Brahmas, in the same space, remaining for their entire lifespan in whatever posture they were born in, being like painted figures. In this section, all non-percipient Brahmas are included by the word 'Abhibhū'. Some teachers praise the chief Brahmas in various places, saying that Abhibhū is a Great Brahma who rules over a thousand world systems and so on. However, it should be understood that this is inappropriate because that Brahma is already included by the taking of the word 'Brahma'. The method of connection here is: having heard that 'the Abhibhū Brahma is beautiful and long-lived,' one generates desire and lust for that Brahma and conceives the Abhibhū Brahma through the conceiving of craving. One who resolves his mind to attain what has not yet been attained, thinking, 'Oh, may I be reborn in the company of the Abhibhū Brahma,' also conceives the Abhibhū Brahma through the conceiving of craving. One who regards himself as inferior and the Abhibhū Brahma as superior conceives the Abhibhū Brahma through the conceiving of conceit. One who misapprehends, thinking, 'The Abhibhū Brahma is permanent and stable,' and so on, should be understood as conceiving the Abhibhū Brahma through the conceiving of views. The rest is the same as stated in the section on Pajāpati.

## The Explanation of the Section on the Sphere of Infinite Space, etc.

Thus, although the Blessed One showed the celestial worlds in order, having shown the non-percipient realm by the word 'Abhibhū', now, because in this discourse on the round of rebirth (vaṭṭakathā), the Suddhāvāsa Brahmas stand on the side of the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa)—for those devas are only Non-returners (anāgāmīs) and those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsavas)—or because...
38:
Those Suddhāvāsa Brahmas have a lifespan of many thousands of aeons and exist only during the time when a Buddha arises. When Buddhas do not arise for an incalculable number of aeons, that Suddhāvāsa plane is empty of beings. The Suddhāvāsa realm is like a royal encampment (vāsana-nagara) for the Buddhas. For that very reason, those Suddhāvāsa Brahmas are not included in terms of the stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti) or the abodes of beings (sattāvāsa); however, these conceivings (maññanā) occur at all times. Therefore, wishing to show the planes that are always present for those conceivings, He bypassed the Suddhāvāsa realm, which stands apart from the round, and spoke of the Sphere of Infinite Space (ākāsānañcāyatana) and so on. There, 'the Sphere of Infinite Space' refers to the four mental aggregates—wholesome, resultant, and functional—belonging to that plane. Those aggregates should be seen as only those arisen in that realm, as this is a discussion defining the planes of existence. This same method applies to the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness and so on. The connection of meaning in these four formless sections should be understood in the same way as stated in the section on Abhibhū. The conceiving of conceit here is also appropriate according to the method stated in the section on Pajāpati.

## The Explanation of the Sections on the Seen, Heard, etc.

Having thus shown the objects of conceiving in detail through the distinctions of specific planes and so on, now, wishing to show the things of the three planes included in the self-identity (sakkāya), which are the objects of all conceivings, by grouping them under the four names 'seen' and so on, He said 'the seen as the seen' (diṭṭhaṃ diṭṭhato) and so forth.

There, 'the seen' (diṭṭha) refers to forms seen with the physical eye and forms seen with the divine eye. This is a designation for the base of visible forms (rūpāyatana). There, 'he conceives the seen' means he conceives the seen (the base of visible forms) through the three conceivings. How? One who sees the base of visible forms with the perception of beauty (subha-saññā) and the perception of pleasure (sukha-saññā) generates desire and lust for it; he relishes it and greatly delights in it. Regarding this, the Blessed One said: 'Monks, beings are lustful, greedy, tied, infatuated, and obsessed with the forms of women; following the influence of those forms of women, they sorrow for a long time.' Thus, one conceives the seen (the base of visible forms) through the conceiving of craving. 'May my form be like this in the future,' or he brings delight to this form, or desiring the perfection of form, he gives gifts, and so on—this should be understood in detail. In this way too, one conceives the seen through the conceiving of craving. Based on the perfection or failure of one's own form or another's form, one generates conceit: 'I am superior because of this form,' or 'I am equal,' or 'I am inferior.' Thus, one conceives the seen through the conceiving of conceit. One conceives the base of visible forms as permanent, stable, and eternal; one conceives it as 'self' or 'belonging to self'; one conceives it as auspicious or inauspicious. Thus, one conceives the seen through the conceiving of views. In this way, one conceives the seen through the three conceivings. How does he conceive in the seen? An ordinary person who conceives by way of seeing in form conceives the self in the seen, just as one might conceive of wealth and grain. Thus, lust and so on arise in existence. Such an ordinary person who conceives in this way also conceives in the seen. This conceiving is called his conceiving of views. In that very object conceived through the conceiving of views, he generates affection (sineha) and conceit. For that ordinary person, those conceivings of craving and conceit should also be understood. Thus, he conceives the self in the seen. The rest should be understood in the same way as stated in the section on the element of earth. 'The heard' (suta) refers to sounds heard with the ear and sounds heard with the divine ear. This is a designation for the base of sounds (saddāyatana). 'The sensed' (muta) refers to objects apprehended by the nose and so on. It refers to those that arrive by directly striking the sense base...
39:
One who conceives by way of contemplating the self conceives in the seen. Alternatively, just as one conceives in wealth or grain, so too, one who conceives that 'lust and so forth arise in form' conceives in the seen. This is his conceiving through views (diṭṭhimaññanā). In that very object conceived through views, for one who produces affection (sineha) and conceit (māna), conceiving through craving (taṇhāmaññanā) and conceiving through conceit (mānamaññanā) should also be understood. Thus, he conceives in the seen. The rest should be understood in the same way as stated in the section on the earth (pathavīvāra).

'Suta' (the heard) means what is heard by the physical ear or the divine ear; it is a designation for the base of sound (saddāyatana).

'Muta' (the sensed) means the object known by touching or sensing. It means what is reached and struck. It refers to what is known when the faculties and objects adhere to and touch each other. This is a designation for the bases of smell, taste, and touch (gandha, rasa, phoṭṭhabbāyatana).

'Viññāta' (the cognized) means the object known by the mind (mano). It is a designation for the remaining seven bases or for the object of mental states (dhammārammaṇa). Here, however, only what is included within the personality (sakkāya) is obtained. The details should be understood in the same way as stated in the section on the seen (diṭṭhavāra).

## Explanation of the Section on Unity, etc.

Thus, having shown the entire variety of the personality (sakkāya) through the four terms beginning with 'the seen', he now says 'unity, diversity' (ekattaṃ nānattaṃ), etc., wishing to show that same personality in two ways: by way of the state of attainment (samāpannakavāra) and the state of non-attainment (asamāpannakavāra).

By the word 'ekatta' (unity), he shows the section on attainment. By the word 'nānatta' (diversity), he shows the section on non-attainment. The word-meaning of these is: a single mode is unity (ekatta); various modes are diversity (nānatta). The method of construction (yojanā) here should be understood by investigating as appropriate: dividing the section on attainment by the four [mental] aggregates and the section on non-attainment by the five aggregates, according to the method of the Teaching such as 'he regards form as self', and according to the method of the Commentaries stated in the section on the earth, etc. Some teachers say 'ekatta' refers to the method of unity (ekattanaya) and 'nānatta' to the method of diversity (nānattanaya). Other teachers say it refers to the obsession with views such as 'After death, the self is percipient of unity and healthy, or percipient of diversity'. All such views are inappropriate here as they are not intended.
40:
Having thus shown the entire personality (sakkāya) in two ways, he now says 'the all from the all' (sabbaṃ sabbato), etc., wishing to show that same personality by combining it into one. The method of construction (yojanā) here is: one who relishes the all conceives the all through conceiving by craving (taṇhāmaññanā). One who conceives that they were created by himself, in the manner of 'These beings were created by me', etc., conceives the all through conceiving by conceit (mānamaññanā). One who conceives in the manner of 'The all is due to past kamma, the all is due to creation by a Lord, the all is without cause or condition, the all exists, the all does not exist', etc., should be understood as conceiving the all through conceiving by views (diṭṭhimaññanā). How does he conceive in the all? Here, someone has such a view as 'My self is great'. He, imagining the entire world-habitation as the location for that self, conceives 'This self of mine is in the all'; this is his conceiving through views. In that very self, for one who produces affection and conceit based on that, conceiving through craving and conceiving through conceit should also be understood. The rest should be understood in the same way as stated in the section on the earth.

Having thus shown the entire personality (sakkāya) in one way, he now says 'Nirvana from Nirvana' (nibbānaṃ nibbānato), wishing to show that same personality as one in another way. There, 'Nirvana' should be understood as the five kinds of supreme Nirvana in the present life (paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbāna) that appear in the manner of: 'When, dear sirs, this self, provided and endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure, enjoys itself, to that extent, dear sirs, this self has reached the supreme Nirvana in the present life', etc. One who relishes that Nirvana conceives it through conceiving by craving. One who, based on that Nirvana, produces conceit as 'I have reached Nirvana', conceives it through conceiving by conceit. One who, while it is not Nirvana, takes it as Nirvana and as permanent, etc., should be understood as conceiving it through conceiving by views.

Furthermore, one who takes a self other than Nirvana and conceives 'This self of mine is in this Nirvana', conceives 'in Nirvana'; this is his conceiving through views. In that very self, for one who produces affection and conceit based on that, conceiving through craving and conceiving through conceit should also be understood. This same method applies to conceiving 'from Nirvana' (nibbānato). For there too, one who takes a self other than Nirvana and conceives 'This is Nirvana, this is the self, and this self of mine is other than this Nirvana', conceives 'from Nirvana'; this is his conceiving through views. In that very self, for one who produces affection and conceit based on that, conceiving through craving and conceiving through conceit should also be understood. One who conceives 'Oh, how happy is my Nirvana' should be understood as conceiving Nirvana as 'mine' (nibbānaṃ me). The rest is just as the method already stated. In this regard, there is the following concluding verse (anugītigāthā):
41:
As this identity (sakkāya) is, such is its loathsome nature. For the worldling (puthujjana) who does not know the identity of such a nature, all imaginings (maññanā)—namely craving, conceit, and view—arise regarding identity.

This identity is loathsome, fragile, suffering, and without essence. The foolish worldling, who takes it as the opposite—as permanent, pleasant, and self—grasps the imagining.

Just as a moth falls into a fire with the perception of beauty, so for one who contemplates identity as beautiful and pleasant, imagining through craving (taṇhā) arises.

Clinging to the perception of permanence, for the worldling who sees fulfillment in this unfulfilling identity, like a dung-worm in a heap of dung, imagining through conceit (māna) arises.

Just as one looking at a reflection in a mirror thinks 'this is I, this is mine,' so for the unwise worldling who contemplates this identity as 'I' and 'mine,' imagining through view (diṭṭhi) arises.

These three things called 'imagining' are the subtle bonds of Māra. Though loose, they are difficult to escape; by these bonds, the worldling is bound.

Even though struggling much, he cannot overcome identity, like a dog bound by a leather strap to a firm post.

That worldling, smeared with the filth of identity, is constantly and severely oppressed by the sufferings of birth, aging, sickness, and so forth.

O worthy ones, therefore I say to you: contemplate identity as unpleasant, as loathsome, as fragile, and as non-self (anatta).

Such is the nature of this identity. The wise one seeing it thus, having abandoned all imaginings, is released from all suffering.

## The first method of the twenty-four parts by way of the worldling is finished.

The Blessed One, having thus shown the occurrence of the worldling as the root of all identity-dhammas in objects such as earth, now wishes to show the occurrence of the trainee (sekha) in those same objects, and thus spoke the words beginning with "Monks, he who is a monk, a trainee..." In that Pali, the word "yo" is the designation of the intended meaning, and the word "so" is the specification of the meaning already designated. The word "pi" has the sense of conjunction. Worldlings are corrupt in view; in this Dispensation, trainees are perfected in view. Although there is no similarity in their nature, yet by way of the object...
42:
## Explanation of the Second Method: The Section on the Trainee (Sekha-vāra)

The Blessed One, having thus shown the occurrence of the worldling as the root of all identity-dhammas in objects such as earth, now wishes to show the occurrence of the trainee (sekha) in those same objects, and thus spoke the words beginning with "Monks, he who is a monk, a trainee..." In that Pali, the word "yo" is the designation (uddesa-vacana). The word "so" is the specification (niddesa-vacana). The word "pi" has the sense of conjunction (sampiṇḍanattha), as in "this dhamma also is uncertain," etc. By that word "pi," he connects the person by way of commonality of object, not by way of commonality of person. This is because the worldlings mentioned below are corrupt in view (diṭṭhi-vipanna), while these trainees are perfected in view (diṭṭhi-sampanna); there is no similarity in their nature. However, the object of the worldlings mentioned below is that very same object, and the object of these trainees is also that very same object. Therefore, it is said: "He connects the person by way of commonality of object, not by way of commonality of person." By this entire phrase "yo pi so," it should be understood that he shows the trainee who is now to be discussed. The words "bhikkhave bhikkhu" are just as previously explained.

In what sense is one a trainee (sekha)? One is a trainee because of obtaining trainee-dhammas (the four paths and the three lower fruits). For it was said: "To what extent, venerable sir, is one a trainee?" "Here, monks, a monk is endowed with the right view of a trainee... is endowed with the right concentration of a trainee. To this extent, monks, a monk is a trainee." Furthermore, one is a trainee because one trains (sikkhati). For it was said: "He trains, monks, therefore he is called a trainee. In what does he train? He trains in higher virtue (adhisīla), he trains in higher mind (adhicitta), and he trains in higher wisdom (adhipaññā). He trains, monks, therefore he is called a trainee."

Even a noble worldling (kalyāṇa-puthujjana) who fulfills the practice in accordance with the paths and fruits, being endowed with virtue, guarding the sense-doors, knowing moderation in eating, devoted to wakefulness, and devoted to the development of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) during the first and last watches of the night, thinking "Today or tomorrow I shall attain one of the fruits of recluseship"—he too is called a trainee because he trains. However, in this context, only the trainee who has attained penetration (paṭivedha) is intended, not the worldling.

One whose mind has not yet reached the fruition of arahantship is called "appattamānasa." "Mānasa" means lust (rāga), mind (citta), or arahantship (arahatta). In the verse: "The snare that wanders in the sky, this mānasa (lust) that wanders..." here...
43:
Lust is called *mānasa*. In the Dhammasaṅgaṇī Pāḷi, in the phrase 'Citta, mano, mānasa,' *citta* is called *mānasa*. In the Saṃyutta Nikāya Pāḷi, in the verse, 'A trainee who has not yet reached the fruit of Arahantship should perform the mind of Arahantship known by people,' the mind of the fruit of Arahantship is called *mānasa*. Here too, only the fruit of Arahantship is intended. Therefore, 'appattamānaso' means one who has not yet reached the fruit of Arahantship.

'Anuttaraṃ' means the most noble, the incomparable. 'Yogakkhemaṃ' refers to the fruit of Arahantship itself, which is security from the four yokes. Regarding 'patthayamāno,' there are two kinds of aspiring: aspiring through craving (*taṇhā*) and aspiring through desire (*chanda*). In the Sutta Nipāta Pāḷi, 'For one who aspires, there are intense longings for things desired, and there is trembling in things imagined,' aspiring through craving is meant.

In the Majjhima Nikāya Pāḷi, 'Monks, the stream of craving of the Evil One has been cut, destroyed, and made to vanish like a hollow reed. May you be full of joy; reach the security of the fruit of Arahantship,' aspiring through wholesome desire (*kusalachanda*) characterized by the wish to act is meant. Here, only this aspiring through desire is intended. Therefore, 'patthayamāno' should be understood as one who wishes to reach, wishes to attain, and is inclined, leaned, and sloped towards that fruit of Arahantship which is the security from the yokes.

'Viharati' means that one cuts off the painful feeling arising from one posture with another posture and maintains the body without it falling (dwells in balance). Alternatively, the meaning here should be noted according to the method of the Niddesa: 'He dwells with faith, being resolved that all conditioned things are impermanent.'

'Pathaviṃ pathavito abhijānāti' means he perceives earth as earth through higher knowledge; he does not perceive it with a distorted perception in every way like a worldling. Rather, he knows it with the superior knowledge of the Path. Thus, being resolved on the nature of earth, he knows it through higher knowledge as impermanent, as suffering, and as non-self. Having known it thus through higher knowledge, it means 'he should not conceive earth (as mine, etc.).' In the phrase 'maññatīti maññī,' 'maññī' cannot be said to be either conceiving or not conceiving. It should be understood that this term is used in this sense. What is the intention here? It is said: A worldling is said to 'conceive' because all conceivings (*maññanā*) have not yet been abandoned. An Arahant is said 'not to conceive' because they have been abandoned. For a trainee (*sekha*), however, conceiving through wrong view (*diṭṭhimaññanā*) has been abandoned, but the remaining conceivings (craving and conceit) have only been thinned out; therefore, that trainee cannot be said to 'conceive' like a worldling, nor can he be said 'not to conceive' like an Arahant.

'Pariññeyyaṃ tassa' means that for that trainee, the object of that conceiving is a thing to be fully understood through the three full understandings (*pariññā*), because of having entered the certainty (of the Path) and because of having the three higher Paths as his destination.
44:
It is not that it is not fully understood like a worldling, nor is it that it is a thing already fully understood like an Arahant. The rest of the text should be understood in the same way as already explained for all terms.

## The second method by way of the trainee is finished.

## Explanation of the third method, etc., on the section of the one whose taints are destroyed (Khīṇāsava)

Having thus shown the occurrence of the trainee regarding objects such as earth, now wishing to show the occurrence of the Arahant, the Blessed One said: 'Monks, whatever monk is an Arahant,' and so forth. There, in the word 'yopi,' the word 'pi' has the sense of inclusion. By that word 'pi,' it shows that in this Arahant, there is a similarity in both person and object. For a trainee is similar to an Arahant in being a Noble Person (*ariya*); thus similarity in person is obtained. Similarity in object is just as already explained. 'Arahaṃ' means one who is far from defilements, one who stands far from defilements, one who has abandoned defilements. This point was spoken by the Blessed One: 'And how, monks, is a monk an Arahant? Evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, troublesome, resulting in suffering, and leading to future birth, aging, and death are far from him. Thus, monks, a monk is an Arahant.' 'Khīṇāsavo' means the four taints: the taint of sensual desire... and the taint of ignorance. These four taints are exhausted, abandoned, cut off, subsided in the Arahant, and being incapable of arising again, they are burnt by the fire of knowledge; therefore, he is called 'one whose taints are destroyed' (*khīṇāsava*).

'Vusitavā' means he has lived and practiced in the 'heavy living' (*garusaṃvāsa*) which is practicing in the presence of teachers, in the practice of the Noble Path, and in the ten abodes of the Noble Ones (*ariyavāsa*). Because of having thus lived in the Noble Path and having practiced the conduct, he is called 'vusitavā.' 'Katakaraṇīyo' means that starting from the virtuous worldling, the seven types of trainees are said to be still performing what is to be done through the four Paths. For the Arahant, however, all things to be done have been done and brought to completion. Since there is no further task for that Arahant to perform for the sake of reaching the end of suffering, Nibbāna, he is called 'katakaraṇīyo.' This point was also spoken:
'For that monk who is rightly liberated and has a peaceful mind,
There is no accumulation of what has been done, and there is nothing further to be done.'

'Ohitabhāro' means the three burdens: the burden of the aggregates (*khandha*), the burden of defilements (*kilesa*), and the burden of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*). These three burdens have been laid down and put aside by that Arahant.
45:
The burdens have been laid down; therefore, he is called 'one who has laid down the burden' (ohitabhāro).

'Anuppattasadattho' means one who has successively reached his own goal, which is the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala). In this context, the letter 'ka' has been changed to 'da'; 'sadattha' should be understood as the fruit of Arahantship. That fruit of Arahantship is called 'one's own goal' (sakattha) because of its nature of being constantly connected to oneself, because of its nature of not being abandoned by oneself, and because of its nature of being one's own ultimate reality (paramattha) that is not subject to change.

'Parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojano' refers to the ten fetters of existence: the fetter of sensual lust (kāmarāga), ill-will (paṭigha), conceit (māna), wrong view (diṭṭhi), doubt (vicikicchā), adherence to rules and rituals (sīlabbataparāmāsa), lust for existence (bhavarāga), envy (issā), stinginess (macchariya), and the fetter of ignorance (avijjā). Indeed, these fetters bind beings to existences, or they bind one existence to another; therefore, they are called 'fetters of existence'. For the Arahant, these fetters of existence are completely exhausted and abandoned, burnt by the fire of the knowledge of the path of Arahantship; therefore, he is called 'one for whom the fetters of existence are exhausted' (parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojano).

In the phrase 'sammadanya vimutto', 'sammadanya' means having known well (knowing without distortion through the knowledge of the path of Arahantship). What is meant is: having known the nature of the aggregates (khandha) as a collection, the nature of the sense bases (āyatana) as a place of origin, the nature of the elements (dhātu) as bearing their own characteristics, the nature of suffering (dukkha) as oppression, the nature of origin (samudaya) as the source, the nature of cessation (nirodha) as peace, and the nature of the path (magga) as seeing; or, having known, investigated, weighed, clarified, and made manifest the various states such as 'all formations (saṅkhāra) are impermanent (anicca)' according to reality through the knowledge of the path of Arahantship.

'Vimutto' (liberated) refers to the two kinds of liberation: the liberation of the mind from defilements and the inclination towards Nibbāna. Because the Arahant has a mind liberated from all defilements, he is liberated through the liberation of the mind. Because he is inclined towards Nibbāna, he is also liberated in Nibbāna. Therefore, he is called 'one liberated through right knowledge' (sammadanya vimutto).

'Pariññātaṃ tassa' means that for that Arahant, the objects of conceptualization (maññanā), such as earth, have been fully understood through the three types of full understanding (pariññā). Therefore, that Arahant does not conceptualize that object, or it means he does not engage in that conceptualization; the rest is as previously explained.

In the section on Nibbāna (nibbānavāra), however, three sections beginning with 'khayā rāgassa' (through the destruction of lust) are mentioned. These sections should also be expanded in the sections on earth (pathavīvāra), etc. This section on full understanding (pariññātavāra) should also be expanded in the section on Nibbāna. When expanding, the phrase 'pariññātaṃ tassa' should be connected with all terms, and then the phrase 'khayā rāgassa vītarāgattā' (being free from lust through the destruction of lust) should also be connected. This is the method for the other sections. As for the teaching, what is said in one place is meant for all places; thus it is summarized.

Regarding the phrase 'khayā rāgassa vītarāgattā', because an outsider (one outside the Buddha's teaching) may be free from lust for sensual pleasures, but he is not free through the destruction of lust by the path. The Arahant, however, is free only through the destruction of lust; therefore...
46:
It is stated, "Because of the destruction of lust, he is free from lust" (khayā rāgassa vītarāgattā). This method applies to hatred (dosa) and delusion (moha) as well. Just as when it is said, "I declare that it is fully understood by him," it means that because it is fully understood, that Arahant does not conceptualize or perceive that object or that conceptualization; so too here, it should be understood that because he is free from lust, that Arahant does not conceptualize that object or that conceptualization.

Furthermore, this section "it is fully understood by him" (pariññātaṃ tassa) is taught to show the completion of the development of the path (maggabhāvanā). The other sections should be understood as being taught to show the completion of the realization of the fruit (phalasacchikiriyā). Alternatively, an Arahant does not conceptualize for two reasons: because the object has been fully understood and because the roots of unwholesomeness (akusalamūla) have been completely cut off. Thus, by the section on full understanding, the full understanding of the object by that Arahant is shown; by the other sections, the complete cutting off of the roots of unwholesomeness is shown.

Among those sections, this distinction should be understood in the last three sections: In the three sections, one who, seeing the danger in lust and dwelling as a contemplator of suffering (dukkhānupassī), is liberated through the desireless liberation (appaṇihita-vimokkha), becomes free from lust through the destruction of lust. One who, seeing the danger in hatred and dwelling as a contemplator of impermanence (aniccānupassī), is liberated through the signless liberation (animitta-vimokkha), becomes free from hatred through the destruction of hatred. One who, seeing the danger in delusion and dwelling as a contemplator of non-self (anattānupassī), is liberated through the emptiness liberation (suññata-vimokkha), becomes free from delusion through the destruction of delusion.

If it is argued that in such a case, since a single person cannot be liberated by all three liberations, two of the sections should not be taught, that is not so. Why? Because the teaching was given without restriction. For it was taught without restriction: "Monks, whatever monk is an Arahant." It was not specifically taught that he is liberated by the desireless liberation or by another liberation. Therefore, all sections that are appropriate for an Arahant must be taught.

Alternatively, in a general sense, although the destruction of lust, etc., is the same for any Arahant, he is called "free from lust through the destruction of lust" because of his full understanding of the suffering in change (vipariṇāma-dukkha). He is called "free from hatred through the destruction of hatred" because of his full understanding of the suffering of pain (dukkha-dukkha). He is called "free from delusion through the destruction of delusion" because of his full understanding of the suffering of formations (saṅkhāra-dukkha). Alternatively, he is free from lust because of his full understanding of pleasant objects (iṭṭhārammaṇa); free from hatred because of his full understanding of unpleasant objects (aniṭṭhārammaṇa); and free from delusion because of his full understanding of neutral objects (majjhattārammaṇa). Or, he is free from lust through the destruction of lust because the latent tendency to lust (rāgānusaya) in pleasant feeling has been completely cut off; and in the other feelings, the latent tendencies to ill-will (paṭighānusaya) and delusion (mohānusaya)...
47:
Because he has completely cut off greed, hatred, and delusion, he is one who is free from greed, free from hatred, and free from delusion. Therefore, wishing to show this distinction, [the Teacher] said: "Because of the destruction of greed, because of being free from greed... because of being free from delusion."

## The third, fourth, fifth, and sixth methods by way of the Arahant are finished.

## Explanation of the Seventh Method: The Section on the Tathāgata

Having thus shown the occurrence [of the Dhamma] in the Arahant regarding objects such as the earth element, now, wishing to show his own occurrence, [the Blessed One] said: "Monks, the Tathāgata also," and so forth. In that passage, the Blessed One is called "Tathāgata" for eight reasons: He is the Tathāgata because he has come in the same way (tathā āgato); he is the Tathāgata because he has gone in the same way (tathā gato); he is the Tathāgata because he has come to the real characteristic (tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgato); he is the Tathāgata because he has awakened to the real Dhamma as it truly is (tathadhamme yāthāvato abhisambuddho); he is the Tathāgata because of seeing correctly (tathadassitāya); he is the Tathāgata because of speaking correctly (tathāvāditāya); he is the Tathāgata because of acting correctly (tathākāritāya); he is the Tathāgata in the sense of overcoming [everything] (abhibhavanaṭṭhena).

How is the Blessed One the "Tathāgata" because he has come in the same way? Just as the previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones (Sammāsambuddhas) came, having exerted themselves for the welfare of the whole world—just as the Blessed Vipassī came, as the Blessed Sikhī, as the Blessed Vessabhū, as the Blessed Kakusandha, as the Blessed Koṇāgamana, and as the Blessed Kassapa came—so too has our Blessed One come. What is meant? By whatever aspiration (abhinīhāra) those Blessed Ones came, by that same aspiration our Blessed One also came.

Alternatively, just as the Blessed Vipassī... the Blessed Kassapa came after fulfilling the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī), the perfections of virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness, and equanimity—having fulfilled these ten perfections, ten intermediate perfections, and ten ultimate perfections, totaling thirty perfections; having sacrificed the five great sacrifices (pañca mahāpariccāga), namely the sacrifice of limbs, eyes, wealth, kingdom, and children and wife; having fulfilled the previous applications, previous conduct, preaching of the Dhamma, and conduct for the benefit of relatives, etc.; and having reached the pinnacle of the conduct for enlightenment (buddhicariyā)—so too has our Blessed One come.

And just as the Blessed Vipassī... the Blessed Kassapa came after developing and increasing the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path—so too has our Blessed One come; thus he is the Tathāgata.
48:
Just as in the world, the Sages such as Vipassī reached the state of omniscience, so too has this Sakyan Sage come. Therefore, the One endowed with the five eyes is called 'Tathāgata'. Thus, he is the Tathāgata because he has come in the same way.

How is he the 'Tathāgata' because he has gone in the same way? Just as the Blessed Vipassī, when newly born, went... [so too] the Blessed Kassapa went. And how did he go? Indeed, as soon as he was born, standing firmly on the earth with level feet, he went seven steps facing North. As it was said: 'Ānanda, as soon as he is born, the Bodhisatta stands firmly on the earth with level feet and goes seven steps facing North while a white parasol is held over him; he surveys all directions and speaks the words of the Leader: "I am the foremost in the world, I am the eldest in the world, I am the best in the world. This is my last birth; now there is no more renewed existence."' (M. Ni. 3.207).

And that going of his was real (tatha) and not false (avitatha), being a precursor for the attainment of many distinctions. That the Bodhisatta, as soon as he was born, stood firmly with level feet was the precursor for his attainment of the four bases of power (iddhipāda). His facing North was the precursor for his reaching the state of being supreme in the whole world. His taking seven steps was the precursor for his attainment of the seven jewels of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga). The waving of the fly-whisks, mentioned in the verse 'Fly-whisks with golden handles are waved' (Sn. 693), was the precursor for his crushing all heretics. The holding of the white parasol was the precursor for his attainment of the stainless white parasol of the supreme liberation of Arahantship. His surveying all directions was the precursor for his attainment of the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa) and unobstructed knowledge (anāvaraṇañāṇa). His speaking the words of the Leader was the precursor for his turning the supreme Wheel of Dhamma (dhammacakkappavattana) which cannot be turned back by others. In the same way, this Blessed One also went. And that going of his was real and not false, being a precursor for the attainment of those very distinctions. Therefore, the ancient teachers (porāṇā) said:

"Just as the Lord of the World (Gavampati), born but a moment, touched the earth with level feet, so did Gotama take seven steps, and the gods held the white parasol over him."
49:
That Bodhisatta of the Gotama lineage, having taken seven steps, looked equally in all directions. Like a lion king standing on a mountain peak, he uttered words endowed with eight qualities. Because he has gone in such a manner, he is called 'Tathāgata'.

Alternatively, just as the Blessed One Vipassī... and the Blessed One Kassapa went having abandoned sensual desire and so forth, this Blessed One likewise went having abandoned sensual desire through renunciation (nekkhamma). He went having abandoned ill-will through non-ill-will (abyāpāda), sloth and torpor through the perception of light (āloka-saññā), restlessness and remorse through non-distraction (concentration), and doubt through the discernment of phenomena (dhamma-vavatthāna); having destroyed ignorance with knowledge, dispelled discontent with joy, opened the door of the hindrances with the first jhāna, stilled the smoke of initial and sustained application with the second jhāna, faded away rapture with the third jhāna, and abandoned pleasure and pain with the fourth jhāna. He went having transcended the perception of form, the perception of impingement, and the perception of diversity through the attainment of the base of infinite space; having transcended the perception of infinite space through the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness, the perception of infinite consciousness through the attainment of the base of nothingness, and the perception of nothingness through the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

He went having abandoned the perception of permanence through the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā), the perception of pleasure through the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā), the perception of self through the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā), delight (nandi) through the contemplation of disenchantment (nibbidānupassanā), lust through the contemplation of dispassion (virāgānupassanā), origination through the contemplation of cessation (nirodhānupassanā), grasping (ādāna) through the contemplation of relinquishment (paṭinissaggānupassanā), the perception of compactness (ghana-saññā) through the contemplation of destruction (khayānupassanā), accumulation (āyūhana) through the contemplation of fall (vayānupassanā), the perception of stability (dhuva-saññā) through the contemplation of change (vipariṇāmānupassanā), signs (nimitta) through the contemplation of the signless (animittānupassanā), longing (paṇidhi) through the contemplation of the desireless (appaṇihitānupassanā), misinterpretation (abhinivesa) through the contemplation of emptiness (suññatānupassanā), the adherence to an essence through insight into phenomena through higher wisdom (adhipaññā-dhamma-vipassanā), the adherence to delusion through the knowledge and vision of things as they are (yathābhūta-ñāṇadassana), the adherence to attachment through the contemplation of danger (ādīnavānupassanā), non-reflection through the contemplation of reflection (paṭisaṅkhānupassanā), and the adherence to bondage through the contemplation of turning away (vivaṭṭānupassanā). He went having destroyed the defilements associated with wrong view through the Path of Stream-entry, abandoned gross defilements through the Path of Once-returning, uprooted subtle defilements through the Path of Non-returning, and completely cut off all defilements through the Path of Arahantship. Because he has gone in such a manner, he is called 'Tathāgata'.
50:
How is he called Tathāgata because he has arrived at the true characteristics (tatha-lakkhaṇa)? The characteristic of hardness of the earth element is true, unerring. The characteristic of flowing of the water element is true, unerring. The characteristic of heat of the fire element is true, unerring. The characteristic of supporting of the air element is true, unerring. The characteristic of non-contact of the space element is true, unerring. The characteristic of cognizing of the consciousness element is true, unerring.

The characteristic of being deformed of form, the characteristic of experiencing of feeling, the characteristic of perceiving of perception, the characteristic of constructing of formations, and the characteristic of cognizing of consciousness are also true and unerring.

The characteristic of directing onto the object of initial application (vitakka), the characteristic of examining of sustained application (vicāra), the characteristic of pervading of rapture (pīti), the characteristic of pleasantness of happiness (sukha), the characteristic of non-distraction of one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā), and the characteristic of touching of contact (phassa) are also true and unerring.

The characteristic of resolution of the faith faculty, the characteristic of exerting of the energy faculty, the characteristic of establishing of the mindfulness faculty, the characteristic of non-distraction of the concentration faculty, and the characteristic of understanding of the wisdom faculty are also true and unerring.

The characteristic of unshakability by faithlessness of the faith power, the characteristic of unshakability by laziness of the energy power, the characteristic of unshakability by forgetfulness of the mindfulness power, the characteristic of unshakability by restlessness of the concentration power, and the characteristic of unshakability by ignorance of the wisdom power are also true and unerring.

The characteristic of establishing of the mindfulness enlightenment factor, the characteristic of investigating of the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor, the characteristic of exerting of the energy enlightenment factor, the characteristic of pervading of the rapture enlightenment factor, the characteristic of calming of the tranquility enlightenment factor, the characteristic of non-distraction of the concentration enlightenment factor, and the characteristic of reflecting of the equanimity enlightenment factor are also true and unerring.

The characteristic of seeing of Right View, the characteristic of directing onto the object of Right Intention, the characteristic of embracing of Right Speech, the characteristic of originating of Right Action, the characteristic of cleansing of Right Livelihood, the characteristic of exerting of Right Effort, the characteristic of establishing of Right Mindfulness, and the characteristic of non-distraction of Right Concentration are also true and unerring.

The characteristic of non-knowing of ignorance, the characteristic of volition of formations, the characteristic of cognizing of consciousness, the characteristic of bending of name, the characteristic of being deformed of form, the characteristic of being a base of the six bases, the characteristic of touching of contact, the characteristic of experiencing of feeling, the characteristic of being a cause of craving, the characteristic of grasping of clinging, the characteristic of accumulating of existence, the characteristic of arising of birth, the characteristic of decaying of aging, and the characteristic of falling away of death are also true and unerring.
51:
The characteristic of the elements is emptiness (suññatā). The characteristic of the sense bases is the base (āyatana). The characteristic of the foundations of mindfulness is establishment (upaṭṭhāna). The characteristic of the right efforts is striving (padahana). The characteristic of the bases of power is success (ijjhana). The characteristic of the faculties is predominance (adhipati). The characteristic of the powers is immovability (akampiya). The characteristic of the factors of enlightenment is leading out (niyyāna). The characteristic of the path is cause (hetu).

The characteristic of the truths is reality (tatha). The characteristic of tranquility is non-distraction (avikkhepa). The characteristic of insight is contemplation (anupassanā). The characteristic of tranquility and insight is having a single essence (ekarasa). The characteristic of the coupled (yuganaddha) states is non-overrunning (anativattana).

The characteristic of the purification of virtue is restraint (saṃvara). The characteristic of the purification of mind is non-distraction (avikkhepa). The characteristic of the purification of view is seeing (dassana).

The characteristic of the knowledge of destruction is total cutting off (samuccheda). The characteristic of the knowledge of non-arising is tranquility (passaddhi). The characteristic of desire (chanda) is the root (mūla). The characteristic of attention (manasikāra) is origination (samuṭṭhāna). The characteristic of contact (phassa) is combination (samodhāna). The characteristic of feeling (vedanā) is meeting (samosaraṇa). The characteristic of concentration (samādhi) is being the head (pamukha). The characteristic of mindfulness (sati) is sovereignty (ādhipateyya). The characteristic of wisdom (paññā) is being furthermost (tatuttari). The characteristic of liberation (vimutti) is the essence (sāra). The characteristic of Nibbāna, which plunges into the Deathless, is the consummation (pariyosāna); these are real and not unreal. Thus, because He has arrived at the true characteristic through the course of knowledge, and has reached it without fail, He is called 'Tathāgata'. Because He has thus arrived at the true characteristic, He is called 'Tathāgata'.

How is He called 'Tathāgata' because of having fully awakened to the real Dhamma as it truly is? The real Dhammas are the Four Noble Truths. As it was said: "Monks, these four are real, not unreal, not otherwise. Which four? 'This is suffering', monks, this is real, this is not unreal, this is not otherwise," and so on in detail. The Blessed One has fully awakened to these; therefore, because of fully awakening to the real truths, He is called 'Tathāgata'. For here, the word 'gata' has the meaning of 'fully awakened' (abhisambuddha). Furthermore, the nature of aging and death arising due to birth as its condition is real, not unreal, not otherwise... [pe]... the nature of volitional formations arising due to ignorance as its condition is real, not unreal, not otherwise. Likewise, the nature of ignorance being a condition for volitional formations; the nature of volitional formations being a condition for consciousness... [pe]... the nature of birth being a condition for aging and death is real, not unreal, not otherwise. The Blessed One has fully awakened to all of that. Therefore, also because of fully awakening to the real Dhammas,
52:
He is called 'Tathāgata'. Thus, because He has fully awakened to the real Dhamma as it truly is, He is called 'Tathāgata'.

How is He called 'Tathāgata' because of seeing things as they truly are? In the world with its devas and Brahmas... [pe]... in the infinite world systems with their devas and humans, there exists what is called a visible object that comes into the range of the eye-door of infinite beings. He knows and sees that in all its aspects. Knowing and seeing thus, whether by way of the agreeable and disagreeable, or by way of the terms found among the seen, the heard, the sensed, and the cognized, that visible object—which is analyzed by many names, by thirteen cycles, and by fifty-two methods as: "What is that matter which is the base of visible form? That matter which, depending on the four great elements, is colored, bright, visible, and impingent, such as blue, yellow, etc."—is only real and not unreal. This same method applies to sounds and so on that come into the range of the ear-door and other doors. And this was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, in the world with its devas... [pe]... with its devas and humans, whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, reached, sought, and reflected upon by the mind, that I know... that I have fully understood. That is known to the Tathāgata; such an object does not manifest (with defilements) to the Tathāgata." Thus, because of seeing things as they truly are, He is called 'Tathāgata'. In this context, the origin of the word 'Tathāgata' should be understood in the sense of 'one who sees truly' (tathadassī).

How is He called 'Tathāgata' because of speaking the truth? On the night the Blessed One sat upon the Unconquered Throne at the Seat of Enlightenment, crushed the heads of the three Māras, and fully awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment; and on the night He attained Parinibbāna by the Nibbāna element without remainder between the twin Sāla trees; in this interval of forty-five years, whatever the Blessed One spoke—Suttas, Geyyas... [pe]... up to Vedallas—all of that is flawless in meaning and in phrasing, neither deficient nor excessive, complete in every aspect, and it crushes the intoxicants of lust, hatred, and delusion. In that teaching, there is not even a hair's breadth of error. All of that is only real and not unreal, as if stamped with a single seal, as if measured with a single measure, or as if weighed with a single scale. Therefore, it was said: "Cunda, on the night the Tathāgata fully awakens to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, and on the night He attains Parinibbāna by the Nibbāna element without remainder, whatever He speaks, utters, or points out in this interval, all that is just so and not otherwise. Therefore, He is called 'Tathāgata'." Thus, because of speaking the truth, He is called 'Tathāgata'. (The word 'gata' is here equivalent to the word 'gada', which means 'speaking'.)
53:
In this term 'Tathāgata', the word 'gata' has the meaning of 'gada' (utterance). Because he is one who habitually speaks the truth in this way, he is called 'Tathāgata'. Alternatively, 'āgadana' is 'āgada', meaning speech. Since the Blessed One possesses true and unerring speech (āgada), by changing the letter 'd' to 't', the formation of the word 'Tathāgata' in this sense should be understood.

How is he a 'Tathāgata' because he acts accordingly? For the Blessed One's speech conforms to his physical actions, and his physical actions conform to his speech. Therefore, as he speaks, so he acts; as he acts, so he speaks. For such a one, as his speech is, so his physical action proceeds (tathā gata). And as his physical action is, so his speech proceeds (tathā gatā). Thus he is 'Tathāgata'. Hence it was said: "Monks, as the Tathāgata speaks, so he acts; as he acts, so he speaks. Thus, because he acts as he speaks and speaks as he acts, he is called the Tathāgata" (A. IV, 23). In this way, he is the Tathāgata because he acts accordingly.

How is he a 'Tathāgata' in the sense of surpassing? From the peak of existence above to the Avīci hell below, and across the boundless world-systems, he surpasses all beings in virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. For him, there is no scale or measure. He is peerless, immeasurable, supreme, the king of kings, the god of gods, the Sakka above Sakkas, and the Brahma above Brahmas. Hence it was said: "Monks, in the world with its devas... among the generation of devas and humans, the Tathāgata is the conqueror, the unconquered, the all-seeing, the wielder of power. Therefore, he is called the Tathāgata."

In that context, the word formation should be understood as follows: he has an 'agada' (medicine) like an 'agada'. What is this 'agada'? It is the splendor of his teaching and the accumulation of his merit. By that splendor of teaching and accumulation of merit, the Blessed One, the great physician of great power, surpasses all proponents of other doctrines and the world with its devas, just as one might overcome snakes with divine medicine. Thus, in surpassing the entire world, because he possesses the 'agada' (medicine) of the true and unerring splendor of teaching and accumulation of merit, by changing the letter 'd' to 't', he should be known as 'Tathāgata'. In this way, he is 'Tathāgata' in the sense of surpassing.

Furthermore, he is 'Tathāgata' because he has known in the true way (tathāya gata) and because he has arrived at the true meaning (tathaṃ gata). 'Gata' here means known, transcended, attained, or practiced.
54:
Among those (Four Noble Truths), he is called 'Tathāgata' because he has understood the entire world unerringly through the full understanding of investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā). He is called 'Tathāgata' because he has transcended the origin of the world (samudaya-sacca) unerringly through the full understanding of abandoning (pahāna-pariññā). He is called 'Tathāgata' because he has reached Nibbāna, the cessation of the world, unerringly through realization (sacchikiriyā). He is called 'Tathāgata' because he has practiced the path leading to the cessation of the world (magga-sacca) rightly.

Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is detached from the world. Monks, the origin of the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the origin of the world has been abandoned by the Tathāgata. Monks, the cessation of the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the cessation of the world has been realized by the Tathāgata. Monks, the way leading to the cessation of the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the way leading to the cessation of the world has been developed by the Tathāgata. Monks, whatever is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized in the world with its devas... all that has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata. Therefore, he is called the Tathāgata" (A. IV, 23). The meaning of the term 'Tathāgata' should be understood in this way as well. This explanation is merely an introduction to illustrating the Tathāgata-nature of the Tathāgata. In every respect, however, only a Tathāgata could fully describe the Tathāgata-nature of a Tathāgata.

Regarding the two terms "Arahaṃ Sammāsambuddha": first, he should be known as "Arahaṃ" (the Worthy One) for these reasons: because of being remote from defilements, because of having destroyed the enemies (the defilements), because of having broken the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra, because of being worthy of requisites and offerings, and because of the absence of secrecy in doing evil. He is called "Sammāsambuddha" (the Perfectly Enlightened One) because he has rightly and by himself awakened to all phenomena. This is just a brief summary here. In detail, these two terms are explained in the Visuddhimagga under the section on the Recollection of the Buddha.

In the phrase "pariññātantaṃ tathāgatassa," the meaning should be understood as: the Tathāgata has fully understood that basis of conceiving (maññanā-vatthu). What is called 'pariññātanta' means reaching the end of full understanding, the completion of full understanding, or understanding without remainder. Although there is no difference between the Buddhas and their disciples in the abandoning of defilements through the respective paths, there is a difference in full understanding (pariññā). For disciples reach Nibbāna after investigating only a portion of the four elements. For the Buddhas, however, there is nothing among conditioned things (saṅkhāra), even as small as a speck of dust, that has not been seen, weighed, investigated, or realized by their knowledge.
55:
## Explanation of the Eighth Method of the Tathāgata Section

In the phrases such as "Nandī dukkhassa mūlaṃ" (Delight is the root of suffering), "nandī" refers to the craving (taṇhā) that occurred in a previous life. "Dukkha" refers to the five aggregates. "Mūla" means the cause. "Iti viditvā" means knowing that previous craving as "the cause of this suffering."

"Bhava" refers to the occurrence due to kamma-bhava (karmic existence). "Jāti" refers to the resultant mental aggregates (vipākakkhandhā). These resultant aggregates are called "jāti" (birth) because they arise. Alternatively, this teaching is given with birth as the primary focus. This meaning should also be understood in connection with the phrase "iti viditvā." The meaning here is: "Knowing thus that from karmic existence, rebirth-existence (upapatti-bhava) occurs."

"Bhūtassa" means of a manifest being (satta). "Jarāmaraṇa" means aging and death. The intended meaning is: Knowing thus that for a manifest being, aging and death of the aggregates occur because of that rebirth-existence.

With this sequence of words, the Buddha—while seated on the unconquered throne (aparājita-pallaṅka) at the foot of the Bodhi tree, contemplating and attaining Omniscience—shows the Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) consisting of four groups, three links, three periods, and twenty modes, in order to demonstrate the reason for the absence of imaginings (maññanā) through the penetration of that Dependent Origination.

How is it that all of Dependent Origination is shown by these words? Here, the word "nandī" is one group. Because of the word "dukkhassa," suffering is the second group. Because of the words "bhavā jāti," existence is the third group. "Jāti-jarāmaraṇaṃ" is the fourth group. Thus, the four groups (koṭṭhāsa) should be understood. The interval between craving and suffering is one link; the interval between suffering and existence is the second link; and the interval between existence and birth is the third link. Just like the spaces between four fingers, the three links between the four groups should be understood.

Among these groups, "nandī" is the past period, "jāti-jarāmaraṇa" is the future period, and "dukkha" and "bhava" are the present period; thus the three periods should be understood. In the past period, there are five modes; although only craving is mentioned by the word "nandī," ignorance (avijjā), formations (saṅkhāra), clinging (upādāna), and kamma-bhava are already included by way of being causal characteristics. By the words "jāti-jarāmaraṇa," since the aggregates in which birth, aging, and death occur are intended, consciousness (viññāṇa), mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa), the six sense bases (saḷāyatana), contact (phassa), and feeling (vedanā) which will occur in the future are also already included.

Thus, these twenty modes should be understood. In the previous karmic existence, delusion is ignorance, efforts are formations, attachment is craving, clinging is grasping, and volition is existence. These five factors...
56:
