In the previous karmic existence, delusion is called ignorance (avijjā), efforts are called formations (saṅkhāra), attachment is called craving (taṇhā), clinging is called grasping (upādāna), and volition is called karmic existence (kamma-bhava). These five factors, existing in the previous karmic existence, are the conditions for rebirth-linking in this life. In this life, rebirth-linking consciousness (viññāṇa), descending mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa), the sense bases (āyatana) which are the five sensitive matters, contact (phassa) which is touching, and feeling (vedanā) which is experiencing—these five factors in this rebirth-existence occur because of kamma performed in the past. In this life, due to the maturation of the sense bases, delusion is called ignorance, efforts are called formations, attachment is called craving, clinging is called grasping, and volition is called karmic existence. These five factors in this present karmic existence are the conditions for rebirth-linking in the future. Future rebirth-linking consciousness, descending mentality-materiality, the sense bases which are the five sensitive matters, contact, and feeling—these five factors in the future rebirth-existence occur because of the condition of kamma performed in this life. Thus, the twenty modes with these indicated characteristics should be understood here. In this way, by the sequence of words "Knowing thus that delight is the root of suffering, from existence comes birth, and for a manifest being, aging and death," it should be understood that the entire Dependent Origination with its four groups, three links, three periods, and twenty modes has been shown.

Now, in this text, "Tasmā tiha, bhikkhave... abhisambuddho ti vadāmi," I shall provide the explanation of terms not yet explained and conclude the meaning along with the word-connection. "Tasmā tiha" means simply "tasmā" (therefore). The syllables "ti" and "ha" are particles (nipāta). The word "sabbaso" means without remainder. "Taṇhānaṃ" refers to all cravings which were called "nandī." "Khayā" means due to the absolute destruction by the supramundane path. The words such as "virāga" (fading away) are merely synonyms of the word "khaya" (destruction). For when craving is destroyed, it is also faded away, ceased, given up, and relinquished. Alternatively, the word "khayā" is common to the functions of the four paths. Furthermore, it should be connected as: "virāgā" (through fading away) by the first path, "nirodhā" (through cessation) by the second path, "cāgā" (through giving up) by the third path, and "paṭinissaggā" (through relinquishment) by the fourth path. Or, through the destruction (khayā) of those cravings by which one would perceive earth as earth; through the fading away (virāgā) of those cravings by which one would conceive earth; through the cessation (nirodhā) of those cravings by which one would conceive in earth; through the giving up (cāgā) of those cravings by which one would conceive from earth; through the relinquishment (paṭinissaggā) of those cravings by which one would conceive 'earth is mine.' Or, it should be connected here as: through the destruction (khayā) of those cravings by which one would conceive earth... through the relinquishment (paṭinissaggā) of those cravings by which one would delight in earth; there is no contradiction at all.

"Anuttaraṃ" means unsurpassed, supreme among all things. "Sammāsambodhiṃ" refers to the knowledge of the Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga-ñāṇa) which penetrates and knows rightly and by itself. Alternatively, it refers to the praised and excellent knowledge of the Path of Arahantship. In the word "Bodhi," it can refer to the tree, the path, omniscience, or Nibbāna. In passages such as "Bodhirukkhamūle paṭhamābhisambuddho" (First enlightened at the foot of the Bodhi tree) and "antarā ca gayaṃ antarā ca bodhiṃ" (between Gayā and the Bodhi tree), the tree is called "Bodhi." It means he sat having first known the Four Noble Truths near the Bodhi tree, between the Gayā river and the Bodhi tree. In the passage "catūsu maggesu ဉာဏံ" (knowledge in the four paths), the path is called "Bodhi." Knowledge occurs in the four paths. In the passage "paññāyati bodhiṃ varabhūrimedho" (The one of excellent and vast wisdom reaches enlightenment), Omniscience is called "Bodhi." The Buddha, possessing excellent wisdom like the great earth, reached Omniscience. In the passage "patto bodhiṃ amataṃ asaṅkhataṃ" (Reached enlightenment, the deathless, the unconditioned), Nibbāna is called "Bodhi." It means having reached Nibbāna, which is free from death and unconditioned. In this specific text, however, the Buddha's knowledge of the Path of Arahantship is called "Bodhi."
57:
In passages such as "Between the Bodhi and Gaya" (from the Mahāvagga and Majjhima Nikāya), 'Bodhi' refers to the tree. In the passage "Knowledge in the four paths" (from the Cūḷaniddesa), it refers to the Path. In the passage "The one of excellent and vast wisdom reaches Bodhi" (from the Dīgha Nikāya), it refers to Omniscience. In the passage "Having reached Bodhi, the deathless, the unconditioned," it refers to Nibbāna. In this context, however, the Knowledge of the Path of Arahantship (Arahatta-magga-ñāṇa) of the Blessed One is intended. Other teachers also say it refers to Omniscience.

If it is asked whether the Path of Arahantship of disciples (sāvakas) is called 'Unsurpassed Enlightenment' (Anuttara Bodhi), the answer is no. Why? Because it does not bestow all qualities. For among those disciples, to some the Path of Arahantship gives only the Fruition of Arahantship; to some, the three knowledges (vijjā); to some, the six supernormal powers (abhiññā); to some, the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā); and to some, the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa). To Paccekabuddhas, it gives only the knowledge of Enlightenment for oneself (Paccekabodhi-ñāṇa). To the Buddhas, however, it gives the fulfillment of all qualities, just as the consecration of a king gives sovereignty over the entire world. Therefore, the Path of Arahantship of any other person cannot be called 'Unsurpassed Enlightenment'.

'Abhisambuddho' means having fully understood, having penetrated, having reached, or having attained. 'Thus I say' means thus I speak, declare, teach, proclaim, establish, reveal, analyze, and clarify. In this context, the connection (yojanā) is as follows: Monks, the Tathāgata also... does not conceive earth... does not delight in earth. For what reason does he not delight? Because he knows thus: "Delight (nandī) is the root of suffering; from becoming (bhava) comes birth (jāti); for the being (bhūta) there is aging and death."

In the phrase "knowing thus," the word 'iti' denotes the cause. Therefore, it means because this Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) is known and penetrated. To elaborate further: because by knowing this Dependent Origination in this way, all forms of craving called 'delight' (nandī) have been abandoned by the Tathāgata; and because of the total destruction of those cravings... the Tathāgata has fully awakened to the Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment. Therefore, it is said: "I say he does not conceive earth... does not delight in earth." It means that because of such full awakening, he does not conceive and does not delight.

Alternatively: because by knowing Dependent Origination through the method beginning with "Delight is the root of suffering," craving has reached total destruction; therefore, "Monks, I say that the Tathāgata, through the total destruction of cravings... has fully awakened." That Blessed One, in this way...
58:
Because of the state of being fully awakened, he does not conceive earth... does not delight in it. Wherever the word 'tasmā' (therefore) is stated in the Pali without 'yasmā' (because), one should bring in and connect the word 'yasmā'; this is the logical method of the Dispensation (Sāsanayutti). This method applies everywhere.

The phrase "The Blessed One said this" refers to this entire Sutta from the beginning of the introduction until the end of "I say he has fully awakened." The Blessed One, wishing to demonstrate his Omniscience, which is profoundly deep and cannot be fathomed by the wisdom of others, spoke this text (tanti) which is two recital sections (bhāṇavāra) in length. He adorned it with eight great sections (mahāvāra)—one section for worldlings (puthujjana), one for trainees (sekkha), four for those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), and two for the Tathāgata—and within each section, twenty-four intermediate sections (antaravāra) starting with earth.

Although this Sutta, endowed with such a graceful display of diverse methods, was spoken with a Brahma-voice (brahmasara) that is sweet like the song of the Karavīka bird, pleasant to the ear, and like a shower of ambrosia to the hearts of the wise, those five hundred monks did not rejoice in the Blessed One's words. Why? Because of lack of understanding (aññāṇakena). It is said that they did not understand the meaning of this Sutta, and therefore they did not delight in it. To those monks at that time, this Sutta, despite being endowed with such a graceful display of diverse methods, was like delicious food placed in front of someone whose face was bound and obstructed by a thick cloth.

Did not the Blessed One fulfill the perfections (pāramīs) for four incalculable periods and a hundred thousand eons to reach Omniscience so that others might understand the Dhamma he taught? Why then did he teach in such a way that they could not understand? It has already been stated in the discussion on the occasion for teaching (nikkhepa-vicāraṇa) of this Sutta: "He began the teaching of the Mūlapariyāya Sutta for the purpose of crushing pride (mānabhañjana)." Therefore, there is no need to repeat it here.

Upon hearing this Sutta, which was taught for the purpose of crushing pride, those monks thought: "The worldling with wrong view knows this very earth, and the trainee, the Arahant, and the Tathāgata also know it. What is this called? What is its nature?" They reflected: "Formerly, we quickly understood whatever the Blessed One taught. But now, we do not know or see the end or the limit of this Mūlapariyāya Sutta. Oh, how immeasurable and incomparable are the Buddhas!" Thus, like snakes whose fangs have been extracted, their pride vanished, and they approached to attend upon the Buddha and listen to the Dhamma with great respect.
59:
At that time, the monks were seated together in the Dhamma Hall and raised this topic: "Friends, how wonderful is the power of the Buddhas! Those monks of Brahmin birth, who were so intoxicated with the pride of their lineage, have had their pride humbled by the Blessed One through the Mūlapariyāya Discourse." While the monks' conversation was still unfinished, the Blessed One came out from the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi) and, through a miracle appropriate for the moment, sat upon the noble Buddha-seat prepared in the Dhamma Hall. He then asked the monks, "Monks, for what conversation are you gathered here now?" The monks informed the Blessed One of the matter. The Blessed One said, "Monks, it is not only now that I have made them free of pride; in the past too, I made these people, who wandered about with their heads held high in pride, free of pride." Having said this, he brought forth the past story of this incident:

Monks, in the past, there lived in the city of Bārāṇasī a world-renowned teacher (Disāpāmokkha) who was a Brahmin. He was one who had reached the further shore of the three Vedas, an expert in the Nighaṇṭu and Keṭubha glossaries, the phonology and etymology, and the Itihāsas as the fifth. He was a master of the texts, a grammarian, and fully proficient in the Lokāyata and the marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisalakkhaṇa). He taught the sacred mantras to five hundred young students. Those wise students learned many arts quickly, investigated them well, and did not forget what they had learned. That Brahmin teacher, without keeping a 'teacher's fist' (secrecy), taught them all the arts as if pouring water into a jar. After teaching them, he said to the students, "This much is the art which is for the welfare of this life and the life to come."

Then the students thought, "Whatever our teacher knows, we also know. Now we ourselves are teachers too." Becoming proud, from then on they showed no respect to the teacher and abandoned their duties toward him. The teacher, knowing this, thought, "I will humble the pride of these youths." One day, when the students came to attend to him and sat down after paying respects, he said, "Dear sons, I will ask a question. Will you be able to answer it?" Intoxicated with the pride of their learning, they immediately replied, "Ask, teacher! Ask, teacher!" The teacher then spoke this verse:

"Time consumes all beings, together with itself.
He who is the consumer of time, has cooked the cooker of beings."

He then said, "Dear sons, solve this problem."
60:
The students, though they pondered, did not know the answer and remained silent. The teacher said, "That is enough, dear sons. Go for today and answer tomorrow," and dismissed them. Whether in groups of ten or twenty, they gathered and consulted, but they could see neither the beginning nor the end of that problem. They returned to the teacher and said, "We do not know the meaning of this problem." To humble those youths, the teacher recited this verse:

"Many are the heads of men, hairy and large,
Fixed upon their necks; but only someone here has ears."

The meaning of the verse is: Many heads of men are seen; all of them are hairy, all are large, and they are merely placed on necks. They are not held in the hand like palm fruits. There is no distinction among those heads by these physical qualities. "But only someone here has ears" refers to himself. "One with ears" (kaṇṇavā) means one with wisdom. It is not that the ear-hole is absent in anyone. Hearing this, the youths were crestfallen, their shoulders slumped, they looked down, scratching the ground with their fingers, and remained silent.

Then, seeing their lack of shame, the teacher said, "Dear sons, learn the solution to the problem," and explained it. "Time" (kāla) refers to the time before the meal, the time after the meal, and so on. "Beings" (bhūtāni) is a designation for living beings. Time does not eat the skin, flesh, etc., of beings; rather, it is said to consume or eat them by exhausting their life, beauty, and strength, by crushing their youth, and by destroying their health. "Together with itself" means that in this consumption, it spares nothing and consumes everything. Not only does it consume beings, but it also consumes itself. The morning time does not reach the afternoon (the morning is consumed by the morning itself). The same applies to the afternoon and other times.

"He who is the consumer of time" is a designation for an Arahant (Khīṇāsava). Because he has exhausted and 'eaten' the time of future rebirth, he is called a "consumer of time" (kālaghasa). "He has cooked the cooker of beings" means that the Arahant has cooked, burned, and turned to ashes with the fire of knowledge (ñāṇa) that craving (taṇhā) which 'cooks' (causes suffering to) beings in the lower realms. Thus it is said, "He has cooked the cooker of beings." There is also a reading "pajaniṃ," meaning that which generates or brings forth (craving).

Then those youths, seeing the meaning of the problem clearly through the teacher's explanation—like seeing the even and uneven ground at night by the light of a thousand lamps—thought, "Now we shall live with the teacher for the rest of our lives. These teachers possess great wisdom. we have only acquired a little learning and did not even know the meaning of a single four-line verse." They humbled their pride, performed their duties toward the teacher as before, and eventually passed away to the heavenly realms.

Monks, the teacher of those youths at that time was I myself. These monks were those youths. Thus, in the past too, I humbled these monks who wandered about with pride. Having brought forth this past account and hearing this Jātaka, those monks realized, "In the past too, we suffered loss of benefit only because of pride." From then on, they became extremely humble and delighted only in their beneficial meditation subjects. Later, as the Blessed One was wandering through the countryside, he arrived at Vesālī and, while staying at the Gotamaka Shrine, knowing the maturity of the wisdom of these five hundred monks, he preached this Gotamaka Sutta.
61:
“We shall live with the teacher; these teachers are great sages. Although we were proud of our learning, we did not even know the meaning of a single four-line verse.” Thus, humbling their pride, they performed their major and minor duties toward the teacher as before, and upon death, they were reborn in a heavenly realm.

Monks, at that time, I was the teacher of those young men, and these monks were those young men. Thus, in the past too, I humbled these monks who were wandering with their heads held high in pride.

Upon hearing this Jātaka, those monks realized, “In the past too, our welfare was ruined only because of pride.” Becoming exceedingly free from pride, they became devoted solely to the meditation subjects that were beneficial to them.

Then, while the Blessed One was wandering through the countryside, he arrived at Vesālī and, while staying at the Gotamaka Shrine, he recognized that the wisdom of these five hundred monks had matured and preached this Gotamaka Sutta:

“Monks, I teach the Dhamma having known it with direct knowledge, not without direct knowledge. I teach it with a cause... Monks, I teach the Dhamma with marvels, not without marvels. Since I teach the Dhamma with direct knowledge... and not without marvels, my exhortation should be followed, and my instruction should be followed. Monks, it is fitting for you to be satisfied, fitting to be glad, and fitting to be joyful. The Blessed One is the Fully Enlightened One, the Dhamma is well-expounded, and the Saṅgha has practiced well.” Thus the Blessed One spoke. While this discourse, which does not include verses, was being preached, the ten-thousandfold world system shook.

Upon hearing this sutta, those five hundred monks attained the fruit of Arahantship along with the analytical insights right then and there. Thus, this teaching reached its conclusion at this point.

## In the Majjhima Nikāya Commentary named Papañcasūdanī,
## the explanation of the Mūlapariyāya Sutta is finished.
62:
## 2. Sabbāsava Sutta Vaṇṇanā

“Thus have I heard...” and so on. This sutta, preached in the city of Sāvatthī, is the Sabbāsava Sutta. In this Sabbāsava Sutta, the following is the explanation of new terms. Sāvatthī is the city that was the dwelling place of the sage named Sāvatthi. Grammarians say it is like the cities of Kākandī, Mākandī, and Kosambī. However, the commentators say, “It is called Sāvatthī because everything (sabba) for human use and consumption exists (atthi) here.” Also, when people gathered and were asked, “What goods are there?” the answer was “Everything exists” (Sabbaṃ atthi), and based on this, it is called Sāvatthī.

“All requisites are at all times,
gathered in the city of Sāvatthī.
Therefore, because all things are gathered,
it is called Sāvatthī.
The capital of the Kosalans is delightful,
beautiful to behold, and pleasing to the heart.
It is not silent of the ten sounds,
and is full of food, drink, and beverages.
Having reached growth and abundance,
prosperous, flourishing, and pleasant.
Like the city of Āḷakamandā of the devas,
is the noble city of Sāvatthī.”

In that city of Sāvatthī (he preached). In the word “Jetavane,” he is called “Jeta” because he conquers his enemies. Or, he is called “Jeta” because he was born when the king had conquered his enemies. Or, because of the desire for an auspicious name, the prince was given this name, hence “Jeta.” The garden of Prince Jeta is called Jetavana. That garden was planted, nurtured, and protected by Prince Jeta, and he was its owner. Therefore, it is called Jetavana. In that Jetavana monastery (he preached).

In the phrase “Anāthapiṇဍikassa ārāme,” that householder was named “Sudatta” by his parents. However, because he was endowed with all desired objects, free from the stain of stinginess, and possessed virtues such as compassion, he constantly gave alms-food (piṇḍa) to the helpless (anātha). Therefore, he came to be known as “Anāthapiṇḍika.” “Ārāma” is so called because beings, especially monks, delight (ramanti) there. It means they come from various places and live there delightfully without weariness because of the beauty of the garden's flowers and fruits, and because it is endowed with the five factors of a dwelling, such as being neither too far nor too near. Or, it is called “Ārāma” because, due to the aforementioned perfections, it draws in even those who go to various other places and makes them delight within it. In fact, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika bought that park from the hand of Prince Jeta by covering the ground with eighteen crores of gold, built monastery buildings with eighteen crores of gold, and performed the monastery dedication ceremony with eighteen crores of gold...
63:
In this way, having completed the construction by sacrificing fifty-four crores of gold, the monastery was offered to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. Therefore, it is called "Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park." In that park of Anāthapiṇḍika, [the Buddha resided].

In this context, the phrase "in Jeta’s Grove" (Jetavane) is a mention of the previous owner (Prince Jeta). The phrase "in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park" is a mention of the subsequent owner (Anāthapiṇḍika the merchant). What is the purpose of mentioning these two owners? It is for the benefit of those who wish to perform merit, so that they may follow the example they see. This is because, in the construction of the gate-towers and pinnacled buildings of that monastery, the eighteen crores of gold received from the sale of the land and the trees worth many crores were the sacrifice of Prince Jeta, while the fifty-four crores of wealth were the sacrifice of Anāthapiṇḍika. Thus, by praising and highlighting these two owners, the Venerable Ānanda, showing that "in this way, those who wish to perform merit do perform merits," encourages other seekers of merit to follow their example.

Why was this sutta, "Monks, I will [teach] you the discourse on the restraint of all taints (āsavas)," taught? It was taught to show the practice for reaching the end of taints (Nibbāna), beginning with the purification of the defilements of those monks. In that text, "Sabbāsava-saṃvara-pariyāya" refers to the cause that is the restraint of all taints, or the cause that has the nature of restraint. It refers to the cause by which those taints are restrained and blocked, and thus reach destruction—known as non-arising cessation—are abandoned, and no longer occur. In that term, they are called "āsava" because they flow in (āsavanti). It means they flow out or arise from the eye-door... and from the mind-door. Alternatively, they are called "āsava" because they flow, in terms of phenomena, up to the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū), and in terms of space, up to the highest point of existence (bhavagga). The meaning is that they occur by including these phenomena up to gotrabhū and these planes up to bhavagga. Here, the prefix "ā" expresses the meaning of inclusion. Just as spirituous liquors and so on are called "āsava" because they have been matured for a long time, these [defilements] are also called "āsava" because they have a similar nature. In the world, liquors and such that have been matured for a long time are called "āsavas." If they are to be called āsavas only because of being matured for a long time, then only these [defilements] deserve to be called āsavas. Has the Blessed One not taught: "Monks, a first beginning of ignorance is not known, such that one could say, 'Before this, ignorance did not exist'"? Alternatively, they are called "āsava" because they produce and increase the long suffering of saṃsāra. Among these meanings, the previous etymological definitions are appropriate where defilements are called āsavas. The last definition is also appropriate for karma. Not only are karma and defilements called āsavas, but various kinds of dangers (upaddava) are also called āsavas. In the suttas, it is stated: "Cunda, I do not teach the Dhamma only for the restraint of taints belonging to the present life." Here, the defilements that are the root of disputes are intended as āsavas.
65:
In this context, Pātimokkha virtue is called restraint (saṃvara). In such passages as 'he attains restraint in the eye-faculty,' it is restraint of mindfulness (sati-saṃvara). Here, mindfulness is called restraint. In the passage, 'I speak of the restraint of the streams; they are closed by wisdom,' this is restraint of knowledge (ñāṇa-saṃvara). In this context, it is called restraint in the sense of closing. By the method starting with 'he is one who endures cold... he does not tolerate (endure) arisen sensual thoughts,' restraint of patience (khanti-saṃvara) and restraint of energy (vīriya-saṃvara) are mentioned in this very sutta. Since they are included in the heading 'The Method of Restraint of All Taints' (Sabbāsava-saṃvara-pariyāya), their nature as restraint should be understood.

Furthermore, these five kinds of restraint are indeed mentioned in this sutta. Among them, restraint of patience and energy have already been mentioned. In the passage, 'that monk (avoids) unsuitable places and unsuitable resorts,' this is restraint of virtue (sīla-saṃvara). The passage, 'reflecting wisely, he dwells restrained with the restraint of the eye-faculty,' is restraint of mindfulness (sati-saṃvara). Wise reflection in all instances is restraint of knowledge (ñāṇa-saṃvara). Specifically, by way of taking up what has not yet been taken, seeing (dassana), partaking (paṭisevanā), and development (bhāvanā) are also restraint of knowledge. 'Method' (pariyāya) means that through these qualities, one reaches the arising (of the wholesome) or the cessation (of the unwholesome). By this much, all that should be said regarding the term 'The Method of Restraint of All Taints' has been said.

Now, in the words 'for one who knows, I [say],' 'for one who knows' (jānato) means for the person who knows with wisdom. 'For one who sees' (passato) means for the person who sees with wisdom. Both words have the same meaning; only the phrasing (syllables) differs. Even so, the word 'for one who knows' indicates the person by way of the characteristic of knowing of wisdom, for wisdom has the characteristic of knowing. The word 'for one who sees' indicates the person by way of the power of seeing of wisdom, for wisdom has the power of seeing. Just as a person endowed with sight sees forms with the eye, a person endowed with wisdom sees the Dhamma opened by wisdom. Alternatively, the essence here is: for one who knows so as to give rise to wise attention, and for one who sees so that unwise attention does not arise. Some teachers speak at great length, but those explanations are not suitable in this context.

'Destruction of the taints' (āsavānaṃ khaya) means the abandoning of the taints, the bringing about of the absolute destruction of the taints, the state of being destroyed, the state of non-existence. This is the meaning in this sutta and in passages such as 'through the destruction of the taints, the taintless liberation of mind.' In other places, the Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna are also called the destruction of the taints. Thus—

In passages such as 'For the trainee who is practicing, following the straight path, first knowledge arises in the destruction [of taints], and immediately after that, the higher knowledge,' the Path is called the destruction of the taints. In passages such as 'Through the destruction of the taints, one becomes a recluse,' the Fruit is called the destruction of the taints. In passages such as 'For one who habitually observes the faults of others, who is always intent on finding blame, his taints increase; he is far from the destruction of the taints,' Nibbāna is called the destruction of the taints. 'Not for one who does not know, not for one who does not see' means that for the person who does not know and does not see, I say there is no (destruction of taints). By these two terms, those who claim that purification comes through restraint alone for one who does not know or see are refuted. Alternatively, by the first two terms (knowing and seeing), of the destruction of taints...
66:
“For the trainee who is practicing, following the straight path, first knowledge arises in the destruction [of taints] (arahatta-magga), and immediately after that, the higher knowledge (arahatta-phala)” — in such passages, the Path is called the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya). “Through the destruction of the taints, one becomes a recluse” — in such passages, the Fruit is called the destruction of the taints. “For one who habitually observes the faults of others, who is always intent on finding blame, his taints increase; he is far from the destruction of the taints” — in such passages, Nibbāna is called the destruction of the taints.

“Not for one who does not know, not for one who does not see” means that for the person who does not know and does not see, I say there is no (destruction of taints). By this statement, those who claim that purification comes through restraint (saṃvara) etc. alone, even without knowing or seeing, are refuted. Alternatively, the first two terms (knowing and seeing) state the means (upāya) for the destruction of taints, while this statement rejects what is not the means (anupāya-paṭisedha). In brief, it is shown here that wisdom is the basis for the restraint of taints (āsava-saṃvara-pariyāya).

Now, desiring to show for one who knows in what way the destruction of taints occurs, he began the question: “Monks, for one who knows what (does the destruction of taints occur)?” In that context, knowing (jānanā) is of many kinds. A certain wise monk knows how to make an umbrella; another knows one of the things such as robes. If that monk performs such tasks based on his duties (vatta-sīsa), it should not be said that such knowing is not a proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for the Paths and Fruits. However, if after ordaining in the Dispensation, one knows how to perform medical work and so on, for one who knows in that way, the taints only increase. Therefore, desiring to show for one who knows and sees in what way the destruction of taints occurs, he said: “Wise attention and unwise attention” (yoniso ca manasikāraṃ ayoniso ca manasikāraṃ).

In that context, wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) means attention that is a means (upāya-manasikāra), attention that is on the right path. It is the turning of the mind, the repeated turning, the application, the attention to impermanence as impermanence, and so on, in that manner, or in accordance with the Truths. This is called wise attention.

Unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) means attention that is not a means (anupāya-manasikāra), attention that is on the wrong path. It is the attention to the impermanent as permanent, the painful as pleasant, the non-self as self, and the foul as beautiful; this is unwise attention, attention on the wrong path. Or, it is the turning of the mind, the repeated turning, in a way that is contrary to the Truths.
67:
Directing [the mind] towards an object other than the object of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), bringing it to the object, and attending to it is called unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra). Thus, for one who knows how to arouse wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) and who sees in such a way that unwise attention does not arise, there is the destruction of the taints (āsavas).

Now, wishing to show the logical reasoning for this meaning, [the Buddha] said: "Monks, for one who attends unwisely... the taints are abandoned." What is meant by this statement? Since taints arise because of unwise attention and are abandoned because of wise attention, it should be understood that for one who knows how to arouse wise attention and who sees in such a way that unwise attention does not arise, there is the destruction of the taints. This is the brief explanation here.

As for the detailed explanation: In that detail, the entire subsequent sutta is connected by these two terms: "wise" and "unwise." Indeed, the entire subsequent sutta is taught by way of the round (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa). Unwise attention is the root of the round, and wise attention is the root of the cessation of the round. How? When unwise attention increases, it fulfills two things: ignorance (avijjā) and craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā). When there is ignorance, "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise... the mass of suffering arises." When there is craving, "with craving as condition, clinging arises... the mass of suffering arises." Thus, a person who is full of unwise attention—like a boat destroyed by the force of the wind, like a herd of cattle fallen into a whirlpool in the Ganges, or like an ox yoked to a machine—revolves again and again through births, wombs, destinations, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings. This is the round rooted in unwise attention.

When wise attention increases—according to the teaching: "Monks, it is to be expected of a monk who possesses wise attention that he will develop the Noble Eightfold Path, that he will cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path"—it fulfills the Eightfold Path headed by right view (sammādiṭṭhi). That which is right view is called true knowledge (vijjā). With the arising of that knowledge, ignorance ceases. "With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease... thus there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering." In this way, the cessation of the round rooted in wise attention should be understood. Thus, the entire subsequent sutta is connected by these two terms.
68:
When it is connected in this way, it would not be appropriate in this sutta to first show the abandoning of taints and then speak of their arising. For taints that have been abandoned do not arise again. It is only appropriate to abandon taints that have arisen. Therefore, even by way of the reverse order of the summary, [the Buddha] said: "Monks, for one who attends unwisely," and so on.

In that text, "for one who attends unwisely" (ayoniso manasikaro) means for one who arouses unwise attention of the kind already described. In the phrase "unrisen taints also arise," this refers to a person who obtains a requisite such as a robe not previously obtained, or a pleasant object such as an attendant, a co-resident (saddhivihārika), or a pupil (antevāsika), and attends to that object unwisely as "beautiful" or "pleasant," whereby taints arise. Or, for one who attends unwisely in whatever way to some other object not previously experienced, taints arise. These should be understood as "unrisen taints arise." For otherwise, in the beginningless saṃsāra, there are no taints that have never arisen. Also, in the case of a previously experienced thing or object, for a person who—due to natural purity, or due to one of the factors such as recitation, inquiry, scriptural study, renovation work (navakamma), or wise attention—did not have taints arise previously, but later they suddenly arise due to such a cause; these too should be understood as "unrisen taints arise." Taints that arise repeatedly toward those very same things or objects are said to be "risen taints increase." For otherwise, there is no such thing as the "increase" of those that have arisen for the first time.

In the phrase "But, monks, for one who attends wisely," taints do not arise for a person due to natural purity—as in the case of the Venerable Mahā Kassapa and Bhaddā Kāpilānī—or due to causes such as recitation and inquiry. Such a person also knows: "My taints have not yet been eradicated by the Path; let me now practice for their eradication." Then, through the development of the Path, he eradicates them all. For that person, those taints are said to be "unrisen taints do not arise." For a practitioner who, due to a lapse of mindfulness, suddenly has taints arise, and then, being moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega), strives with wise attention and cuts off those taints; for him, it is said that "risen taints are abandoned." This is like the case of the Elder Mahā Tissa Bhūta who lived in the Maṇḍalārāma monastery. It is said that he was studying the texts in that very monastery. Then, while wandering for alms in the village, defilement arose in him regarding an unsuitable object (visabhāga-ārammaṇa). He suppressed that object with insight (vipassanā) and returned to the monastery. Even in his dreams, that object did not appear to him. He, having aroused spiritual urgency, thinking, "If this defilement increases, it will lead to the states of deprivation (apāya)," informed his teacher and left the monastery to go to the Elder Mahā Saṅgharakkhita...
69:
Having taken the meditation on foulness (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna), which is the opposite of lust, from [Mahāsaṅgharakkhita Thera], he entered a thicket, spread out his rag-robe, sat down, and by the Path of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-magga), completely cut off the lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure. Rising from his seat, he paid homage to his teacher and on the following day reached the stage of the course of recitation (uddesamagga). As for those taints (āsavas) that have arisen in the present moment, there is no such thing as abandoning them through practice.

Now, taking this very phrase, "the taints that have arisen are abandoned," the King of Dhamma, who is skilled in the divisions of teaching, wishing to clarify another cause for abandoning those taints in various ways, expanded the teaching, saying: "Bhikkhus, there are taints to be abandoned by seeing," and so forth. Therein, "to be abandoned by seeing" (dassanā pahātabbā) means they are to be abandoned by the vision [of the Path of Stream-entry]. This method applies to all terms [such as "to be abandoned by development," etc.] as well.

## Explanation of the Taints to be Abandoned by Seeing

Now, wishing to explain those terms in sequence, he asked the question: "And what, bhikkhus, are the taints to be abandoned by seeing?" and began the teaching based on the person, in the same manner as stated in the commentary on the Mūlapariyāya Sutta: "Here, bhikkhus, an uninstructed worldling..." Therein, "he does not understand the things fit for attention" means he does not understand the things that should be reflected upon and attended to. "Things unfit for attention" means the opposite of those. This method should be understood for the remaining terms as well. Because there is no fixed rule by nature that "these things are fit for attention" and "these things are unfit for attention," but there is a rule by way of mode. By whichever mode one attends, if it becomes a proximate cause for the arising of the unwholesome, by that mode one should not attend. By whichever mode one attends, if it becomes a proximate cause for the arising of the wholesome, by that mode one should attend. Therefore, he said: "Bhikkhus, for one who attends to things [unfit for attention], the unarisen taint of sensual desire arises..." and so forth.

Therein, "yassa" means for that uninstructed worldling. "For one who attends" means for one who reflects and gives attention. In the phrase "the unarisen taint of sensual desire [arises] or (vā)...", the word "vā" expresses the sense of conjunction (samuccaya), not the sense of alternative (vikalpa). Therefore, just as in the passage: "Bhikkhus, as far as there are beings, whether footless or two-footed... the Tathāgata..."
70:
"...is said to be the foremost among them" (Itivuttaka 90), it means both the footless and the two-footed. And just as in the passage: "For the support of beings that have come to be or for the assistance of those seeking birth" (Majjhima Nikāya 1.402), it means both those that have come to be and those seeking birth. And just as in the passage: "Whether by fire, or by water, or by internal dissension" (Udāna 76), it means by fire, and by water, and by internal dissension. Likewise here too, it should be understood that the unarisen taint of sensual desire arises, and the arisen taint of sensual desire increases. This applies to the remaining terms as well.

Herein, "taint of sensual desire" (kāmāsava) is lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure. "Taint of existence" (bhavāsava) is the desire and lust for existence in the fine-material and immaterial realms, the attachment to jhāna, and the lust associated with the views of eternalism and annihilation. Thus, the "taint of views" (diṭṭhāsava) is also included within the taint of existence. "Taint of ignorance" (avijjāsava) is non-knowledge regarding the Four Truths. Therein, for one who attends to the cords of sensual pleasure by way of enjoying them, the unarisen taint of sensual desire arises, and the arisen one increases. For one who attends to the sublime states (mahaggata) by way of enjoying them, the unarisen taint of existence arises, and the arisen one increases. For one who attends to the things included in the three planes as the proximate cause for the four perversions (vipallāsa), the unarisen taint of ignorance arises, and the arisen one increases. The wholesome side (sukkapakkha) should be expanded by way of the opposite of the method mentioned.

Why are only three taints mentioned here? Because they are the opposites of the liberations (vimokkha). For the taint of sensual desire is the opposite of the desireless liberation (appaṇihita-vimokkha), and the other taints are the opposites of the signless (animitta) and emptiness (suññata) liberations. Therefore, it should be understood that only three are mentioned to show that those who produce these three taints do not share in the three liberations, while those who do not produce them do share in them. Alternatively, it is explained that the taint of views is also indeed mentioned here.

"Because of his attention to things unfit for attention" means due to the cause of attention; because he attends to those things, that is what is meant. This method applies to the second term as well. "Unarisen taints arise, and arisen taints increase"—this is a conclusion without distinction of the very taints mentioned above.

By this sequence of words, the uninstructed worldling is mentioned to point out the taints to be abandoned by seeing through the teaching based on the person. Since that worldling is the locus of the taint of sensual desire, etc., which have as their cause unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra), as stated generally: "Bhikkhus, for one who practices unwise attention, unarisen taints arise..." Therefore, having shown those taints through that person, now [the taints] to be abandoned by seeing...
71:
It is also the basis for the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava) and others. Therefore, having shown those taints through that same person, now, wishing to show the taints to be abandoned by vision (dassana, the Path of Stream-entry), He spoke the words: "He attends unwisely in this way: 'Was I in the past?'" and so on. In this discourse on taints, this teaching was begun to show the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava) as well, with doubt (vicikicchā) as the head.

The meaning of that Pali is: for whichever worldling (puthujjana) taints arise in the manner mentioned, that worldling, who is described by the method starting with "uninstructed" (assutavā) and so on, attends unwisely, by the wrong way, and by the wrong path. How? "Was I in the past? ... (pe) ... Where will that person go?" What is meant is: when that worldling attends unwisely in this way, the sixteen types of doubt described by the method "Was I in the past?" and so on, arise.

In those words "Was I in the past?", he doubts his own existence or non-existence in the past, based on the aspect of eternalism (sassata) and the aspect of fortuitous origination (adhiccasamuppatti). It should not be asked why he doubts. For a foolish worldling, like a madman, acts in any way whatsoever. Alternatively, unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) itself is the cause here. What is the cause of such unwise attention? It is either the state of being a worldling itself, or the not seeing of the Noble Ones (Ariyas) and so on. One might ask: "Does not a worldling also attend wisely?" Who says they do not? However, the state of being a worldling is not the cause for such wise attention; rather, hearing the True Dhamma, having good friends (kalyāṇamitta), and so on, are the causes. Indeed, although various kinds of curries such as fish and meat do not have a fragrant smell by their own nature, they become fragrant due to the cause of preparation and seasoning.

"What was I?" means doubting based on birth, appearance, and status: "Was I a king (Khattiya)? Was I one of the brahmins, merchants, workers, householders, monks, devas, or humans?"

"How was I?" means doubting based on the aspect of physical form: "Was I tall? Was I one of those who are short, fair, dark, of certain proportions, or without proportions?" Some teachers, however, say that he doubts regarding the cause, based on creation by a Lord (Issara) and so on: "For what reason did I exist?"

"Having been what, what did I become?" means doubting one's own succession of existences based on birth and so on: "Having been a king, did I become a brahmin? ... (pe) ... Having been a deva, did I become a human?" In all places, the word "addhāna" is a term for time.
72:
"Shall I be?" means doubting one's existence or non-existence in the future, based on the aspects of eternalism (sassata) and annihilationism (uccheda). The rest of the explanation here is the same as previously mentioned.

"Or now, in the present time" means taking the entire present time, starting from rebirth and ending with death. "He is a doubter within himself" means he has doubt regarding his own aggregates (khandhas). "Am I?" means he doubts his own existence. What is the use of thinking whether such doubt is proper or improper? Furthermore, they cite this story regarding such doubt: It is said that the son of the younger mother (Cūḷamātā) had a shaved head, while the son of the elder mother (Mahāmātā) did not. The relatives shaved the head of the elder mother's son according to the family custom. When he woke up, he thought, "Am I the son of the younger mother?" In this way, the doubt "Am I?" occurs.

"Am I not?" means doubting one's own non-existence. Regarding this also, they cite this story: It is said that a certain man, while catching fish, stayed in the water for a long time; his thigh became very cold, and thinking it was a fish, he struck it. Another man, while guarding a field near a cemetery, lay curled up in fear. When he woke up, he thought his two knees were ogres (yakkhas) and struck them. In this way, the doubt "Am I not?" occurs.

"Who am I?" means even while being a king, he doubts his own status as a king. The same method applies to the remaining terms. There is no such thing as a deva who, while being a deva, does not know his status as a deva. However, even such a deva doubts in this way: "Do I have form or am I formless?" and so on. If it is asked why kings and others do not know, it is because their birth in those various families is not directly perceived by them. Even householders, like Potthalika and others, may perceive themselves as monks. Monks also, in the manner of "Is my act valid?" and so on, may perceive themselves as householders. Humans also, like kings, may perceive themselves as devas.

"How am I?" is just as previously explained. Specifically, it should be understood that one who, grasping that there is a so-called "soul" (jīva) within, and based on the shape of that soul, doubts: "Am I long, short, square, hexagonal, octagonal, sixteen-sided, or some other shape?" is doubting "How am I?". In reality, there is no one who does not know their own present physical shape.
73:
"Where did I come from? Where will he go?" Thus, one doubts the place of coming and going of the self-identity (attabhāva). Having shown the sixteen types of doubt, the Buddha now begins this teaching to show the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava) based on this doubt. To show that taint of views, he said, "six views [arise]," etc., due to that person's unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra). In that Pali text, it means that in whatever way this doubt arises for that person, because the unwise attention of that person who is possessed of doubt has reached a state of strength, one of the six views arises. In all those phrases, the word 'vā' (or) has the sense of alternative; it means either this wrong view or that wrong view arises. In the phrase "I have a self" (atthi me attā), the eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi) takes the existence of one's self at all times. "Truly and firmly" (saccato thetato) means as a reality and as something stable; it means clinging with great firmness as "this is the truth," as a reality. The view "I have no self" (natthi me attā) is the annihilationist view (ucchedadiṭṭhi), because it takes the cessation of a manifest being in various lives. Alternatively, the former view is eternalism because it takes the self to exist in the three periods of time (past, present, future), while taking only the present self to exist is annihilationism. The latter view is also annihilationism because it takes the self as non-existent in the past and future, like those who hold the view of "the sacrifice ending in ashes" (bhasmantāhutiyo). Taking the self as non-existent only in the past is eternalism, like the view of those who hold the theory of fortuitous origination (adhiccasamuppattika).

"With self I perceive self" (attanāva attānaṃ sañjānāmi) means taking the five aggregates as self, headed by the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha), and perceiving the remaining aggregates with perception; thus the view "with this self (perception) I know this self (remaining aggregates)" arises. "With self [I perceive] non-self" (attanāva anattānaṃ) means taking only the aggregate of perception as self and the other four aggregates as non-self, and knowing those other four with perception; thus this view arises. "With non-self [I perceive] self" (anattanāva attānaṃ) means taking the aggregate of perception as non-self and the other four aggregates as self, and knowing those other four with perception; thus this view arises. All these are just views of eternalism and annihilationism.

"The speaker, the experiencer" (vado vedeyyo), etc., are modes of obsession (abhinivesākāra) of the eternalist view alone. In that Pali, he is called 'vada' because he speaks; it means the doer of verbal action. He is called 'vedeyya' because he knows and experiences. What does he experience? In various births and destinations, the results of good and bad deeds...
74:
...experiences the result (vipāka). "In this and that" (tatra tatra) means in those various births (yoni), destinations (gati), stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti), and abodes of beings (sattāvāsa), or in various objects. "Permanent" (nicca) means the nature of being free from arising and passing away. "Stable" (dhuva) means firm, having essence. "Eternal" (sassata) means existing for all time. "Unchanging nature" (avipariṇāmadhamma) means the nature of not abandoning one's original state; like a chameleon, it does not change into various forms. "Equal to the eternal" (sassatisama): the moon, sun, ocean, great earth, and Mount Sineru are called 'eternal' (sassati) in worldly parlance. Because it is equal to those things, it is called 'equal to the eternal.' To one who holds that "as long as those eternal things remain, so too will this self remain," such a view arises.

"This, bhikkhus, is called a resort of views (diṭṭhigata)" etc. In this passage, the word "this" (idaṃ) is a direct indication of the wrong view that is about to be spoken. The word "idaṃ" is used in connection with the state of being obsessed with views, not just the view itself. Here, "diṭṭhigata" means the view itself is the "resort," like "gūthagata" (a heap of dung). Or, it is called "diṭṭhigata" because this vision has entered into the sixty-two wrong views. Or, "diṭṭhigata" means that which has gone to the state of a view. This view, such as "I have a self," is merely the movement of a view; it means there is no self or anything permanent here at all. That view is called a "thicket" (gahana) in the sense of being difficult to escape. It is a "wilderness" (kantāra) in the sense of being difficult to cross and being dangerous, like a wilderness of famine or a wilderness of wild beasts. It is a "contortion" (visūka) because it is pierced by right view or because it is contradictory. It is a "vacillation" (vipphandita) because it is a distorted trembling, sometimes taking the eternalist view and sometimes the annihilationist view. It is a "fetter" (saṃyojana) in the sense of binding. Therefore, it is said: "thicket of views... fetter of views." Now, wishing to show the meaning of that very binding, he said "fettered by the fetter of views," etc. The summary meaning of that statement is: the worldling (puthujjana) who is fettered by this fetter of views is not released from birth and so forth; what more is there to say, he is not released even from the entire suffering of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭadukkha).

Having thus shown the sixfold taint of views, since "clinging to rules and rituals" (sīlabbataparāmāsa) is already shown by the words "taint of sensual desire" (kāmāsava) and so on—for recluses and brahmins outside this Dispensation, overwhelmed by ignorance, cling to rules and rituals for the sake of sensual pleasure, the bliss of existence, and the purification of existence—or because it is already included under the name of "view" (diṭṭhi), he does not show it separately. Now, to show the person who abandons the taints that should be abandoned by vision (dassana) and to show the abandoning of those taints, or to show how the good worldling (kalyāṇa-puthujjana) who is free from unwise attention abandons them, after having previously shown how those taints arise in the worldling due to unwise attention, he said: "Here, bhikkhus, a well-taught noble disciple," etc. The meaning of that Pali should be understood by the method already stated in the commentary (saṃvaṇṇanā) or by the method of opposites. By the method of opposites, this noble disciple who has the great learning of the scriptures (pariyatti-bāhusacca), which is the opposite of being unskilled in the Dhamma of the Nobles and untrained in the Discipline, should be known as one skilled in the Dhamma of the Nobles and trained in the Dhamma of the Nobles. Indeed, from the peak of insight (vipassanā-ñāṇa) until the arising of change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhū-ñāṇa), in accordance with that person...
75:
Having previously shown the arising of taints in the worldling due to unwise attention, the Buddha now speaks the words beginning with "Bhikkhus, the instructed..." to show the abandoning of taints in the opposite case (of the noble worldling). The meaning of that Pali text, up to the phrase "He [understands]: This is suffering," should be understood by the method previously mentioned and by the method opposite to it. By the opposite method, this noble disciple should be understood as "The instructed noble disciple is skilled in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones, well-trained in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones," in contrast to being unskilled and untrained in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones in every way. Furthermore, from the peak of insight knowledge up to the change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhū-ñāṇa), this person should be known as a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) in the sense of being a noble one corresponding to that stage.

In the words beginning with "He wisely attends: This is suffering," the clarification of the meaning is as follows: That noble disciple, who has the meditation subject of the Four Truths, has previously learned the meditation subject of the Four Truths from a teacher, thinking: "The aggregates belonging to the three planes of existence, excluding craving, are suffering; craving is the origin of suffering; the non-occurrence of both is cessation; the path leading to cessation is the path." Later, when he has ascended to the path of insight, he wisely attends to those aggregates of the three planes as "This is suffering"; he reflects on them by way of the proper means and path, and practices insight. Here, up to the Path of Stream-entry, insight is spoken of with attention (manasikāra) as the head. He wisely attends to craving, which brings about and produces that suffering, as "This is the origin." Since suffering and its origin cease and do not occur upon reaching this Nibbāna, he wisely attends to Nibbāna as "This is the cessation of suffering." He wisely attends to the Eightfold Path, which leads to cessation, as "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering"; he reflects on it by way of the proper means and path, and practices insight.

In this context, the "proper means" (upāya) or "fixation" (abhinivesa) exists only in the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa), not in the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa). Therefore, that yogi, in the manner beginning with "In this body, there is the earth element, the water element," grasps the four great elements in his own continuity and the derived materiality based on them, and defines them as "This is the aggregate of form." For the yogi who thus defines the aggregate of form, he defines the mental states (citta and cetasika) that arise with that materiality as their object as "These are the four mental aggregates." Then he defines: "These five aggregates are suffering." Those five aggregates...
76:
In brief, there are only two groups: mind and matter. This mind and matter arise together with causes and conditions. He defines the causes and conditions such as ignorance, existence, craving, kamma, and nutriment, identifying "This is the productive cause, this is the supportive cause" of that mind and matter.

Then, having defined the actual functions and characteristics of those causes and the conditionally arisen phenomena (mind and matter), he applies the mark of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa), reflecting: "These phenomena arise without having previously existed." He applies the mark of suffering (dukkha-lakkhaṇa), reflecting: "They are suffering because they are oppressed by arising and vanishing." He applies the mark of non-self (anatta-lakkhaṇa), reflecting: "They are non-self because they do not follow one's will." Thus, applying the three marks and developing insight in sequence, he reaches the Path of Stream-entry.

At that moment of the Path of Stream-entry, he penetrates the Four Noble Truths with a single penetration; he realizes them with a single realization. He penetrates the truth of suffering through the penetration of full understanding (pariññā); the truth of origin through the penetration of abandoning (pahāna); the truth of cessation through the penetration of realization (sacchikiriyā); and the truth of the path through the penetration of development (bhāvanā). He realizes the truth of suffering through the realization of full understanding... (pe) ... he realizes the truth of the path through the realization of development, and not by different knowledges. For with a single knowledge, he penetrates and realizes cessation by way of the object, and the remaining three truths by way of function.

At that time, it does not occur to him: "I am fully understanding suffering"... (pe) ... or "I am developing the path." Nevertheless, while he is realizing cessation by way of penetration with Nibbāna as the object, that path-knowledge indeed performs the function of fully understanding suffering, the function of abandoning the origin, and the function of developing the path.

For him who thus wisely attends by the proper means, the three fetters are abandoned: identity view (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) with its twenty bases, doubt (vicikicchā) with its eight bases, and the clinging to rites and rituals (sīlabbataparāmāsa) which is the misapprehension that "purity comes through precepts, purity comes through vows." Among the four taints (āsava), identity view and clinging to rites and rituals are included in the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava), so they are both taints and fetters. Doubt is only a fetter, not a taint. However, because it is included in this Pali passage "taints to be abandoned by seeing," it is also called a taint.

To show that these, such as identity view, are the taints to be abandoned by seeing, the Buddha said: "These are called... (pe) ... to be abandoned." Alternatively, identity view is analyzed in its own form as "one of the six views arises." Referring to that analyzed identity view, the Buddha said: "Bhikkhus, these are called." And that [identity view] is abandoned along with those states that share the same abandoning and co-arise with it. For when the taint of views is abandoned, the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava) and the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava) present in the four consciousnesses associated with views, which co-arise with it...
77:
...is abandoned. However, in terms of pahānekaṭṭha (having a single sense of abandonment), the taint of existence (bhavāsava) that arises through the desire for the prosperity of Nagas, Garudas, and so forth in the four consciousnesses dissociated from wrong view is abandoned; so too is the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava) associated with that taint of existence. Likewise, the taint of ignorance that causes killing and so forth in the two consciousnesses accompanied by displeasure, and the taint of ignorance associated with the consciousness accompanied by doubt, are also abandoned. Thus, in every way, the remaining three taints are abandoned. Therefore, the meaning should be understood here as being expressed in the plural (as āsavā). This is the intention of the ancient teachers.

In the phrase "dassanā pahātabbā" (to be abandoned by seeing), "seeing" (dassana) refers to the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpattimagga). It means the taints to be abandoned by that Path of Stream-entry. Why is the Path of Stream-entry called "seeing"? Because it sees Nibbāna for the first time. If it is asked, "Does not the change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhū-ñāṇa) see it even earlier?"—it is not that it does not see it; it does see it. However, although it sees it, it cannot yet perform the necessary task because it does not abandon the fetters (saṃyojana). Therefore, it is not said to "see" (in the true sense). A villager who, despite seeing the king somewhere, has not yet completed his business by presenting a gift and says, "I have not yet seen the king to this day," is an illustration in this context.

## Explanation of Taints to be Abandoned by Restraint

Thus, having shown the taints to be abandoned by seeing, he now says, "And what, bhikkhus, are the taints to be abandoned by restraint?" in order to show the taints to be abandoned by restraint (saṃvara) mentioned immediately after that. In this way, the connection in all sentences should be understood. From here on, I shall explain only the meaning.

Is it not the case that there is no taint that cannot be abandoned by these two things: seeing (dassana) and mental development (bhāvanā)? Then why are the taints to be abandoned by restraint and so forth shown separately? The taints that are suppressed (vikkham bhita) by restraint and so forth in the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga) are utterly eradicated by the four Paths. Therefore, wishing to show the abandonment by suppression through these five modes in the preliminary stage of those Paths, he spoke thus. Hence, it should be understood that both the previously mentioned first Path of seeing and the three Paths that will now be mentioned by the name of "development" (bhāvanā)—this (restraint, etc.) is the preliminary practice (pubbabhāga-paṭipadā) for all those Paths.
78:
In that text, 'idha' means in this Dispensation (sāsana). 'Paṭisaṅkhā' means having reflected (paṭisaṅkhāya). Here, the word 'saṅkhā' is found in the senses of knowledge (ñāṇa), group (koṭṭhāsa), designation (paññatti), and counting (gaṇanā). In passages such as "saṅkhāya ekaṃ paṭisevati" (reflecting, he uses one [requisite]), it is found in the sense of knowledge (ñāṇa). In passages such as "papañcasaññāsaṅkhā samudācaranti" (the groups of perceptions of proliferation occur), it is in the sense of group (koṭṭhāsa). In passages such as "tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ saṅkhā samaññā" (the designation and name of those various phenomena), it is in the sense of designation (paññatti). In passages such as "na sukaraṃ saṅkhātuṃ" (it is not easy to count), it is in the sense of counting (gaṇanā). But here, it should be regarded in the sense of knowledge (ñāṇa).

"Paṭisaṅkhā yoniso" means having known and reflected by way of a proper means (upāya). Here, reflecting on the danger of non-restraint (asaṃvara) should be understood as "yoniso paṭisaṅkhā" (wise reflection). This reflection on the danger should be understood by the method of the Ādittapariyāya Sutta, such as: "It would be better, bhikkhus, for the eye-faculty to be struck by a red-hot iron pin, burning, blazing, and glowing, than to grasp at the signs through the features in forms cognizable by the eye." In the phrase "cakkhundriyasaṃvarasaṃvuto viharati" (he dwells restrained with the restraint of the eye-faculty), the eye itself is the faculty (indriya), hence 'eye-faculty' (cakkhundriya). It is called restraint (saṃvara) because of shutting out, because of closing off, or because of blocking. This is a synonym for mindfulness (sati). Restraint in the eye-faculty is 'eye-faculty restraint' (cakkhundriya-saṃvara). It is like the examples of the 'landing-place crow' (titthakāka), the 'puddle turtle' (āvāṭakacchapa), and the 'forest buffalo' (vanamahisa).

In that eye-faculty, there is actually no such thing as restraint (saṃvara) or non-restraint (asaṃvara). This is because mindfulness (sati) or lapse of mindfulness (muṭṭhasacca) cannot arise depending on the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda). However, when a visual object comes into the range of the eye, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) arises and ceases twice. Then, the functional mind-element (kiriya-manodhātu) performing the function of adverting (āvajjana) arises and ceases. Then, the eye-consciousness performing the function of seeing, the resultant mind-element performing the function of receiving (sampaṭicchana), the resultant rootless mind-consciousness element performing the function of investigating (santīraṇa), and the functional rootless mind-consciousness element performing the function of determining (votthabbana) arise and cease in order. Immediately after that, the impulsion (javana) impels.

Among those cognitive states, there is no restraint or non-restraint at the time of the life-continuum, nor at the time of adverting and so forth. But if at the moment of impulsion (javana), immorality (dussīlya), lapse of mindfulness (muṭṭhasacca), ignorance (aññāṇa), lack of patience (akkhanti), or laziness (kosajja) arises, this is called non-restraint (asaṃvara). Even though it occurs in the impulsion, it is called non-restraint in the eye-faculty. Why? Because when that non-restraint exists, the door is unguarded, and the life-continuum as well as the cognitive states such as adverting are also unguarded. For example...
79:
Just as when the four gates of a city are not closed but left open, even if the houses, apartments, and small rooms inside are well-closed, all the goods within the city remain unprotected and insecure. This is because thieves can enter through the city gates and do as they please. In the same way, when immorality (*dussīlya*) and so forth arise in the impulsion (*javana*), because of that lack of restraint (*asaṃvara*), the door is also insecure, and the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and process-consciousnesses (*vīthicitta*) such as adverting (*āvajjana*) and so forth are also insecure.

However, when virtue (*sīla*) and so forth arise in that impulsion, the door is secure, and the life-continuum and process-consciousnesses such as adverting and so forth are also secure. How is this? Just as when the city gates are well-closed, even if the houses and so forth inside are not closed, all the goods within the city are well-protected and well-secured. This is because when the city gates are closed, there is no entry for thieves. In the same way, when virtue and so forth arise in the impulsion, the door is well-secured, and the life-continuum and process-consciousnesses such as adverting and so forth are also well-secured. Therefore, although it arises at the moment of impulsion, it is called 'restraint of the eye-faculty' (*cakkhundriya-saṃvara*). Here, it should be understood that it is specifically this restraint by mindfulness (*sati-saṃvara*) that is intended. One who is restrained by the restraint of the eye-faculty is called 'restrained by the restraint of the eye-faculty' (*cakkhundriya-saṃvara-saṃvuta*); it means being endowed with the restraint of the eye-faculty.

This is true; in the *Vibhaṅga*, when explaining the term 'restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha' (*pātimokkha-saṃvara-saṃvuta*), it is stated: "He is endowed with this restraint of the Pātimokkha... is possessed of it." Combining all that, the meaning should be understood as 'restrained by the restraint of the eye-faculty'.

Alternatively, *saṃvarī* means closing, thus it is called *saṃvuta*; it means he closed or shut. 'Restrained by the restraint of the eye-faculty' (*cakkhundriya-saṃvara-saṃvuta*) means that at the eye-door, one closes or shuts with the door-panel of mindfulness called the restraint of the eye-faculty, just like closing a door-panel at the door of a house. This meaning is the most excellent here. Indeed, this meaning is evident in the phrases 'for one who dwells without closing the restraint of the eye-faculty' and 'for one who dwells having closed it'.

*Viharati* (dwells) means that one who is thus restrained by the restraint of the eye-faculty dwells in any of the four postures. In the phrase beginning with *yañhissa*, the meaning should be understood as 'to that bhikkhu who dwells without closing or shutting that restraint of the eye-faculty'. Alternatively, the letter *ye* is changed to *yaṃ*. The word *hi* is a mere functional particle, so the meaning should be taken as 'to that [bhikkhu]'.
80:
*Uppajjeyyuṃ* means 'they would arise'. Taints (*āsavas*) along with distress (*vighāta*) and burnings (*pariḷāha*) refer to the four taints together with other defilement-burnings that cause distress and result-burnings (*vipāka-pariḷāha*). When a pleasant object comes into focus at the eye-door, the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) arises in one who enjoys and delights in it through the power of sensual gratification. The taint of existence (*bhavāsava*) arises in one who enjoys it with a longing for existence, thinking, 'I shall obtain such an object in another happy destination (*sugati*) as well.' The taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*) arises in one who grasps it as 'a being' or 'belonging to a being'. The lack of knowledge (*aññāṇa*) that arises together with all [these taints] is the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*). Thus, the four taints arise. Other defilements associated with those taints are the distress and burnings, or they are the results of those taints that will occur in the future. These are said to 'arise' only for one who dwells without restraint.

*Evaṃsa te* should be analyzed as *evaṃ assa te* (thus of him those [taints]). It means that by this means, those taints do not occur, and not by any other way. This same method applies to the passages beginning with 'reflecting wisely, he is restrained by the restraint of the ear-faculty' and so forth.

When it is said, "Bhikkhus, these taints are to be abandoned by restraint (*saṃvara*)", it means that by taking four taints for each of the six doors, twenty-four taints are to be abandoned by restraint. In all these instances, it should be understood that restraint (*saṃvara*) refers specifically to restraint by mindfulness (*sati-saṃvara*).

## Description of Taints to be Abandoned by Using

Everything that should be said regarding the passages beginning with 'reflecting wisely, [he uses] the robe' (*paṭisaṅkhā yoniso cīvaraṃ*) has already been stated in the 'Talk on Virtue' (*Sīlakathā*) of the *Visuddhimagga*. *Yañhissa* means any one of the requisites such as the robe, alms-food, etc., that belongs to him. *Appaṭisevato* means 'for one who does not use [the requisites] with wise reflection'. The remaining words follow the method already described. However, in this section on using (*paṭisevanā*), it should be understood that the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) arises in one who longs for requisites like robes that have not yet been obtained, or in one who enjoys requisites already obtained. The taint of existence (*bhavāsava*) arises in one who enjoys them with a longing for existence, thinking, 'I shall obtain such requisites in another state of success or happy destination.' The taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*) arises in one who establishes the perception of self (*atta-saññā*), thinking, 'I obtain' or 'I do not obtain', or 'This is mine'. The arising of the four taints, including the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*) which is co-nascent with all of them, as well as the result-burnings, should also be understood through the production of new feelings.
81:
Monks, these aforementioned taints (āsavas) are said to be those that should be abandoned by partaking. By applying four to each of the four requisites, these sixteen taints are said to be abandoned by this partaking through reflection, known as restraint by knowledge (ñāṇasaṃvara).

## The Explanation of Taints to be Abandoned by Partaking is Finished.

## The Explanation of Taints to be Abandoned by Enduring

"Reflecting wisely, he is one who endures cold" (paṭisaṅkhā yoniso khamo hoti sītassa) means that by reflecting through proper means and methods, he becomes one who can endure cold. He tolerates and withstands the cold. Unlike a man lacking effort, he does not waver or tremble due to even a small amount of cold, nor does he abandon his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). Indeed, like the Elder Lomasanāgatthera, even when touched by a great amount of cold, he does not waver or tremble, but attends only to his meditation subject. It is said that while the Elder was staying in the Piyangu Cave at Cetiyapabbata, a place for meditation, during the eight days of snowfall in the interval between the months [of Māgha and Phagguna], he spent the time in the open air, reflecting on the Lokantarika hell without abandoning his meditation subject. The application of meaning for heat and so forth should be understood in this same way.

In fact, if a monk can endure even extreme heat like that Elder, he should be known as "one who endures heat." It is said that during the summer, after his meal, the Elder sat in an outdoor walkway. While attending to his meditation subject, sweat poured from his armpits. Then his pupil said, "Venerable sir, please sit here; this place is cool." The Elder replied, "Friend, it is because I fear heat that I am sitting here," and he remained sitting as he was, reflecting on the Avīci great hell. Here, "heat" should be understood as the heat of fire, but in this story, it is spoken with reference to the heat of the sun.

A monk who, even when not receiving food or water for two or three times, does not waver or abandon his meditation subject, reflecting on his own rebirth in the realm of hungry ghosts (peta) in the beginningless saṃsāra. Even when touched by the intense contact of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, and sun, he does not waver or abandon his meditation subject, reflecting on his rebirth in the animal realm. Even when touched by the contact of creeping things, he does not waver or abandon his meditation subject, like the Elder Padhāniya, reflecting on how he had many times rolled in the mouths of lions, tigers, etc., in the beginningless saṃsāra. This monk should be known as "one who endures hunger... (and so on) the contact of creeping things."
82:
It is heard that while the Elder was listening to the Ariyavaṃsa Dhamma in the Kaṇikārapadhāniyaghara at Khaṇḍacelavihāra, a snake with fierce venom bit him. Although the Elder knew he was bitten, he remained sitting with a devout mind and continued to listen only to the Dhamma. The force of the venom became intense. The Elder, reflecting on his virtue (sīla) from the time of his higher ordination (upasampadā) onwards, gave rise to joy (pīti), thinking, "I am one of pure virtue." As soon as joy arose, the venom retreated and entered the earth. The Elder attained one-pointedness of mind right there, developed insight (vipassanā), and reached Arahantship.

One who, even upon hearing pathways of speech spoken badly with the intent to abuse, which are ill-meaning because they are badly spoken, even those designated as the ultimate matter (pārājika), does not waver, reflecting only on the quality of patience (khanti) like the Elder Dīghabhāṇaka Abhaya. Such a person should be known as "one who endures badly spoken and ill-meaning pathways of speech."

It is heard that because the Elder delighted in contentment with the requisites and in meditation, he preached the Great Ariyavaṃsa practice, and the whole village came to listen. Great honor and offerings arose for the Elder. Another senior Elder, unable to endure those offerings, abused him, saying, "Dīghabhāṇaka says he will preach the Ariyavaṃsa and makes a noise all night," and so on. Both Elders, while returning to their respective monasteries, traveled together on the same path for about a gāvuta. Throughout that whole gāvuta, the senior Elder continued to abuse him. When they reached the fork where the paths to the two monasteries separated, the Elder Dīghabhāṇaka Abhaya bowed to the senior Elder and said, "Venerable sir, this is the path for you to go." The senior Elder went on as if he did not hear. Abhaya Thera also reached his monastery, washed his feet, and sat down. His pupil asked, "Venerable sir, why did you not say a single word while he was abusing you for a whole gāvuta?" The Elder replied, "Friend, patience alone is my burden, not impatience. I do not see any separation from my meditation subject even for a single step." Here, "speech" itself should be understood as the "pathway of speech" (vacanapatha).

Bodily feelings that have arisen are called "dukkha" due to the sense of suffering, "tibba" (intense) due to the sense of thickness, "khara" (harsh) due to the sense of roughness, "kaṭuka" (sharp) due to the sense of piercing, "asāta" (disagreeable) because they lack pleasure, "amanāpa" (unpleasant) because they do not please the mind, and "pāṇahara" (life-taking) because they are capable of taking life. One who endures these and does not waver, like the Elder Padhāniya of Cittalapabbata, should be known as "one who is by nature an endurer of arisen feelings... (and so on)."
83:
While the Elder was spending the night practicing meditation, a wind ailment arose in his stomach. Unable to endure that pain, he was tossing and turning.
