At that time, the Piṇḍapātika Thera, who was standing near the walkway, said, "Friend, one who has gone forth is said to be of a patient nature." The Elder replied, "Very well, Bhante," and lay still, enduring the pain. The wind split [his body] from the navel up to the heart. The Elder, suppressing the feeling and practicing insight, became an Anāgāmī (Non-returner) in a moment and attained Parinibbāna.

"Yañhissa" means if any one of the factors such as cold, etc., should arise. "Anadhivāsayato" means for one who does not endure or tolerate. The remaining words are to be understood in the same manner as previously mentioned. Here, the arising of the taints (āsavas) should be understood thus: for one who, when touched by cold, desires heat, the taint of sensual desire (kāmasava) arises; understand it in this way in all instances. For one who desires existence, thinking, "In our successful or happy rebirth, there is no cold or heat," the taint of existence (bhavāsava) arises. The grasping of "my cold, my heat" is the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava). That which is associated with all taints is the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava).

"These taints... are to be abandoned by endurance" means that by making four types for each factor such as cold, etc., many taints are to be abandoned by this endurance known as restraint through patience (khanti-saṃvara). Here, it should be understood that it is called "adhivāsanā" (endurance) because patience endures factors such as cold, etc., because it allows them to remain upon oneself, and because it does not reject them through intolerance.

## Commentary on the Taints to be Abandoned by Avoiding

"Reflecting wisely, he avoids a fierce elephant" means that one should not stand near a fierce elephant, thinking "I am a monk." Because standing there could result in death or suffering close to death, he avoids and retreats from the fierce elephant by reflecting through means, causes, and reasons. This method is the same in all instances. "Caṇḍa" means vicious, and "vāla" refers to fierce animals such as elephants and horses. "Khāṇu" refers to stumps such as khadir-stumps. "Kaṇṭakaṭṭhāna" means a place of thorns; it refers to a location where thorns are found. "Sobbha" is a pit with steep sides all around. "Papāta" is a precipice with a steep side. "Candanikā" is a place for discarding waste water, filth, and the like. "Oḷigalla" means...
84:
...a place where such filth and the like flow. That place is often filled with excrement up to the knees. Both of these places are also locations where non-humans (amanussa) may cause harm. Therefore, those places should be avoided.

In the term "anāsana," an unsuitable seat is called anāsana. In meaning, it should be understood as a seat in a secluded or hidden place with an indefinite (aniyata) basis. In the term "agocara," an unsuitable resort (for alms) is called agocara. That agocara is of five kinds, such as prostitutes and so forth.

"Pāpake mitte" refers to those who are wicked and immoral, or to false friends who pretend to be friends. "Bhajantaṃ" refers to a person who associates with or frequents them. "Viññူ sabrahmacārī" refers to wise and intelligent fellow celibates. This is a designation for monks. They are called "sabrahmacārī" (fellow celibates) because they practice this noble life together through performing the same formal acts (ekakamma), having the same recitation (ekuddesa), and having equal training. 

"Pāpakesu ṭhānesu" means in evil places. "Okkappeyyuṃ" means they would believe or suspect, thinking, "This venerable one has surely done or will do an evil deed." "Yañhissa" means any one of the things such as elephants, etc., might occur. The remaining words are to be understood in the same manner as previously mentioned.

In this context, the arising of the taints (āsavas) should be understood thus: for one who, being touched by the suffering caused by elephants and so forth, desires pleasure, the taint of sensual desire (kāmasava) arises. For one who desires existence, thinking, "In our successful or happy rebirth, there is no such suffering," the taint of existence (bhavāsava) arises. The grasping of "An elephant tramples me, a horse kicks me" is the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava). The delusion associated with all taints is the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava).

"These taints are to be abandoned by avoiding" means that by making four types for each factor such as elephants, etc., many taints are to be abandoned by this avoiding known as restraint through virtue (sīla-saṃvara).

## Commentary on the Taints to be Abandoned by Dispelling

Reflecting wisely (yoniso), he does not tolerate an arisen sensual thought (kāmavitakka). Reflecting on the danger (ādīnava) of sensual thoughts by such methods as, "This thought is unwholesome, it is blameworthy, it has a painful result, and it leads to self-affliction," he does not tolerate the sensual thought that has arisen or been produced toward various objects; he does not let it remain in the mind, nor does he let it remain within.

What does he do if he does not tolerate it? He abandons it and discards it. Is it like discarding trash with a basket? No, indeed; rather, he dispels it, prods it as if prodding an ox with a goad, and removes it.
85:
Is it like prodding an ox with a stick? Not so; rather, it makes that sensual thought come to an end, makes it disappear. It treats that sensual thought in such a way that not even a fragment, at the very least, will remain.

How does it treat it in such a way? It causes it to reach non-existence; it means it acts so that it is completely suppressed through abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna). This same method applies to the thought of ill-will (byāpāda-vitakka) and the thought of cruelty (vihiṃsā-vitakka).

Among these three types of thoughts, regarding the thought of sensual desire (kāma-vitakka), it is stated in the Vibhaṅga: "Therein, what is the thought of sensual desire? It is the thought, the thinking, the wrong intention (micchā-saṅkappa) associated with sensual lust." This same method applies to the other thoughts. 'Uppannuppanna' means those that have just arisen, or as soon as they have arisen. It does not mean that after dispelling thoughts that have arisen once, one remains indifferent the second time; even if they arise a hundred times, one dispels them every time they arise. 'Pāpake akusale' means 'evil' because of their low nature, and 'unwholesome' because of their lack of skill (being the opposite of wholesome). 'Dhamme' refers to those very thoughts such as the thought of sensual desire, or all nine great thoughts (mahā-vitakka). Among those nine, three have already been mentioned. The remaining six are: "thought concerning relatives (ñāti-vitakka), thought concerning the country (janapada-vitakka), thought concerning the amara-vikkhepa view (amara-vitakka), thought connected with sympathy for others (parānuddayatā-vitakka), thought connected with gain, honor, and fame (lābhasakkārasiloka-vitakka), and thought connected with the desire not to be despised (anavaññatti-vitakka)."

'Yañhissa' means whichever of these thoughts might arise for him; the rest is as previously explained. Among these thoughts, the thought of sensual desire is indeed the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava). The specific variety of that is the taint of existence (bhavāsava). The taint of views (diṭṭhāsava) is that which is associated with them. The delusion associated with all nine types of thoughts is called the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava). In this way, the arising of the taints should be understood.

"Ime vuccanti ...pe... vinodanā pahātabbā" means it should be understood that these taints, categorized as the thought of sensual desire etc., are to be abandoned by this dispelling (vinodana), which is known as the restraint of energy (vīriya-saṃvara) accompanied by the reflection on the danger in each of those thoughts.

## Explanation of the Taints to be Abandoned by Development

"Paṭisaṅkhā yoniso satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti" means having reflected wisely on the danger of non-development and the benefit of development through the proper means...
86:
...develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness; this method applies to all (the enlightenment factor of investigation of states, etc.). Here, although only the supramundane enlightenment factors (lokuttara-bojjhaṅga) that arise at the moment of the three higher paths are intended, I will provide an explanation of the meaning of these enlightenment factors through a mixture of the mundane and supramundane methods so that beginners (ādikammika) will not be confused regarding them. However, in this sutta, the mundane method should be set aside and only the supramundane method should be taken. Regarding the seven initial terms taught by the method beginning with 'the enlightenment factor of mindfulness' (satisambojjhaṅga), first of all:

"The wise should understand the decision
By way of meaning, characteristics, and so forth,
By way of order, and also
By way of non-deficiency and non-excess."

Therein, in the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, it is 'mindfulness' (sati) in the sense of remembering. It has the characteristic of appearing (upaṭṭhāna), or the characteristic of not floating away (apilāpana). Regarding this, it was stated in detail by the Elder Nāgasena in the Milindapañha: "O King, just as the king's treasurer reminds the king of the king's property, saying, 'O King, there is this much silver, this much gold, this much property,' even so, O King, when mindfulness arises, it reminds one of the states that are wholesome and unwholesome, blameable and blameless, low and exalted, and those that are dark and bright counterparts. These four are the foundations of mindfulness." That mindfulness has the function of reminding (apilāpana). The Elder stated this characteristic only by way of its function. Or, it has the function of non-forgetting (asammosa). It appears in the mind by way of being directed towards the object. Mindfulness itself is the enlightenment factor, thus it is the 'enlightenment factor of mindfulness'. Therein, it is called an 'enlightenment factor' (bojjhaṅga) because it is a factor of enlightenment (bodhi, the noble path) or a factor of the enlightened one (bodhi, the noble person).

What is meant by this? The noble disciple awakens by means of this concord of states (dhamma-sāmaggī) known as mindfulness, investigation of states, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity, which arises at the moment of the mundane and supramundane paths and acts as the opposite of many dangers such as sluggishness, restlessness, standing still (in defilements), striving (wrongly), devotion to sensual pleasure, devotion to self-mortification, and the adherence to annihilationism and eternalism; therefore, that concord of states is called 'Bodhi'. 'Awakens' means he rises from the sleep of the continuity of defilements, or he penetrates the Four Noble Truths, or he realizes Nibbāna. As it is said: "Having developed the seven enlightenment factors, he has perfectly awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment." It is called an enlightenment factor because it is a part of that Bodhi (the path) known as the concord of states, just like the factors of absorption (jhānaṅga) and the factors of the path (maggaṅga).
87:
Because the noble disciple knows through the harmony of these aforementioned various factors, the noble disciple is called "Bodhi". Because they are parts of that Bodhi, they are called "Bojjhaṅga" (Factors of Enlightenment), just like the factors of an army or the factors of a chariot. Therefore, the teachers of the Commentaries said: "The parts or the causes of the person who knows are called Bojjhaṅgas." Furthermore, the meaning should be understood according to the method of the Paṭisambhidāmagga: "In what sense are they Bojjhaṅgas? They are Bojjhaṅgas because they lead to enlightenment (bodhāya saṃvattanti), because they know (bujjhanti), because they know sequentially [the truths already known through insight] (anubujjhanti), because they awaken [from the sleep of defilements] (paṭibujjhanti), and because they fully know (sambujjhanti)." Because it is a praised or excellent Bojjhaṅga, it is called "Sambojjhaṅga". In this way, since mindfulness itself is a Sambojjhaṅga, it is called "Sati-sambojjhaṅga" (Mindfulness Enlightenment Factor). Thus, the decision regarding this first term should be understood through its meaning and its characteristics, etc.

In the second and subsequent terms: it is called "Dhamma-vicaya" because it investigates the Four Noble Truths. That Dhamma-vicaya has the characteristic of investigation, the function of dispelling [the darkness of delusion], and non-delusion as its manifestation. It is called "Viriya" because of the state of being heroic (vīra) and because it is to be exerted in the proper way. That Viriya has the characteristic of exertion, the function of supporting, and non-collapse as its manifestation. It is called "Pīti" because it gladdens. That Pīti has the characteristic of pervading or the characteristic of gladness, the function of refreshing the body and mind, and elation of the body and mind as its manifestation. It is called "Passaddhi" because it calms the distress of the body and mind. That Passaddhi has the characteristic of calming, the function of crushing the distress of the body and mind, and the coolness and non-wavering of the body and mind as its manifestation. It is called "Samādhi" because it places [the mind] well. That Samādhi has the characteristic of non-distraction or non-scattering, the function of unifying the mind and mental factors, and stability of mind as its manifestation. It is called "Upekkhā" because it looks on neutrally. That Upekkhā has the characteristic of looking on neutrally or the characteristic of balancing, the function of preventing deficiency and excess or the function of cutting off bias [towards pleasure and pain], and being in the middle as its manifestation. The remaining sequence of words follows the same method already mentioned. Thus, the decision regarding the remaining terms should also be understood through their meanings and characteristics, etc.

Regarding the order (kamato): In this context, according to the word, "Monks, I say that mindfulness is needed everywhere," Sati-sambojjhaṅga is mentioned first because it is helpful to all the remaining enlightenment factors. After that, the benefit of the sequential order of the remaining enlightenment factors is stated in the Sutta itself by the method: "Dwelling thus mindful, he investigates and examines that Dhamma with wisdom." Thus, the decision regarding the order should also be understood here.

Regarding being neither less nor more (anūnādhikatā): Why did the Blessed One teach exactly seven enlightenment factors, neither less nor more? It is because they are the opposites of sluggishness (līna) and restlessness (uddhacca), and because they are needed everywhere. Among these, the three enlightenment factors—Dhamma-vicaya-sambojjhaṅga, Viriya-sambojjhaṅga, and Pīti-sambojjhaṅga—are the opposites of a sluggish mind. As the Blessed One taught: "Monks, when the mind is sluggish, it is the right time to develop Dhamma-vicaya-sambojjhaṅga, it is the right time to develop Viriya-sambojjhaṅga, it is the right time to develop Pīti-sambojjhaṅga." Thus, these three enlightenment factors are the opposites of a sluggish mind. As the Blessed One taught: "Monks, when the mind is restless, it is the right time to develop Passaddhi-sambojjhaṅga, it is the right time to develop Samādhi-sambojjhaṅga, it is the right time to develop Upekkhā-sambojjhaṅga." Thus, monks, when the mind is restless...
88:
Three factors of enlightenment are the opposites of sluggishness. As the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, at the time when the mind is sluggish, it is the right time to develop the enlightenment factor of investigation of states (dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga), it is the right time to develop the enlightenment factor of energy (vīriya-sambojjhaṅga), and it is the right time to develop the enlightenment factor of joy (pīti-sambojjhaṅga)." Three factors of enlightenment are the opposites of restlessness. As the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, at the time when the mind is restless, it is the right time to develop the enlightenment factor of tranquility (passaddhi-sambojjhaṅga), it is the right time to develop the enlightenment factor of concentration (samādhi-sambojjhaṅga), and it is the right time to develop the enlightenment factor of equanimity (upekkhā-sambojjhaṅga)." However, among these, one factor—mindfulness—is desired in all circumstances. The Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, I declare mindfulness to be desired in all circumstances (sabbattha)." There is also a variant reading "sabbatthaka"; the meaning of both is that it is to be desired in every instance. Thus, because they are the opposites of sluggishness and restlessness, and because they are useful in all circumstances, the factors of enlightenment are said to be exactly seven, neither less nor more. In this way, the decision regarding their being neither less nor more should be understood.

Having thus understood the explanation of the meaning of the initial terms of the seven factors of enlightenment taught by the method beginning with "sati-sambojjhaṅga," one should now understand the words beginning with "bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ" as follows. "Bhāveti" means to increase, to repeatedly generate or produce within one's own mental continuum. "Vivekanissitaṃ" means dependent on seclusion. Seclusion (viveka) is the state of being secluded from defilements. This seclusion is of five kinds: seclusion by substitution (tadaṅga-viveka), seclusion by suppression (vikkhambhana-viveka), seclusion by eradication (samuccheda-viveka), seclusion by tranquilization (paṭippassaddhi-viveka), and seclusion by escape (nissaraṇa-viveka). The distinction between these seclusions should be understood in the same way as the method mentioned in the phrase "uninstructed in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones" (ariyadhamme avinīto). This is because these five kinds of seclusion are referred to there as "discipline" (vinaya). Thus, among these five kinds of seclusion:

"Vivekanissitaṃ" should be understood as developing the enlightenment factor of mindfulness dependent on seclusion by substitution, dependent on seclusion by eradication, and dependent on seclusion by escape. For the yogi devoted to the development of these enlightenment factors depends on seclusion by substitution by way of function at the moment of insight (vipassanā), and on seclusion by escape by way of inclination. At the moment of the Path (magga), however, he develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness dependent on seclusion by eradication by way of function, and on seclusion by escape by way of object. Some teachers say it depends on all five kinds of seclusion. This is because those teachers do not only extract the factors of enlightenment at the moments of powerful insight, path, and fruition, but also extract them during the kasina-jhāna, ānāpāna-jhāna, asubha-jhāna, and brahmavihāra-jhāna which serve as the basis for insight. This statement has not been rejected by the teachers of the Commentaries. Therefore, according to their view, at the moment of the occurrence of those jhānas, it should be said to be dependent on seclusion by suppression (vikkhambhana-viveka) by way of function.
89:
Just as it was said that at the moment of insight it is "dependent on seclusion by escape by way of inclination," so too it is proper to say that one develops it "dependent on seclusion by tranquilization." This same method applies to the terms "dependent on dispassion" (virāganissitaṃ) and so on. This is because dispassion and the others have the same meaning as seclusion.

In this context, relinquishment (vossagga) is of two kinds: relinquishment as giving up (pariccāga-vossagga) and relinquishment as entering into (pakkhandana-vossagga). Among these, relinquishment as giving up is the abandoning of defilements by way of substitution at the moment of insight, and by way of eradication at the moment of the Path. Relinquishment as entering into is the leaping into Nibbāna by way of inclination towards it at the moment of insight, and by way of making it the object at the moment of the Path. Both of these are appropriate in this method of explanation which mixes the mundane and the supramundane. For this enlightenment factor of mindfulness gives up defilements in the manner described and leaps into Nibbāna.

By the entire phrase "vossaggapariṇāmiṃ" (ripening in relinquishment), it means maturing towards the state of relinquishment, having matured, being in the process of ripening, and having ripened. What is meant is this: "The bhikkhu devoted to the development of the factors of enlightenment develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness in such a way that it matures into the state of relinquishment as giving up defilements and the state of relinquishment as entering into Nibbāna, and in such a way that it becomes fully ripened." This method applies to the remaining factors of enlightenment.

In this sutta, however, Nibbāna alone is called seclusion (viveka) because it is secluded from all conditioned things; it is called dispassion (virāga) because it is the state of being free from all things; and it is called cessation (nirodha) because it is the state of ceasing. Only the Path is that which ripens in relinquishment. Therefore, one develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness as "dependent on seclusion" because it occurs by making Nibbāna (seclusion) the object. Likewise, it is "dependent on dispassion" and "dependent on cessation." It should be understood that this enlightenment factor of mindfulness has the meaning of having matured and ripened through the state of giving up defilements by way of eradication and the state of entering into Nibbāna, due to the arising of the moment of the Noble Path. This method applies to the remaining factors of enlightenment.

"Yaṃ hissa" means whichever one of these factors of enlightenment may arise for him. The rest is exactly as already explained. Regarding the arising of the taints (āsava), since these factors of enlightenment associated with the three higher paths have not yet been developed, the three taints—the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava), the taint of existence (bhavāsava), and the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava)—might arise; but for one who develops them in this way, those taints do not occur. This is the method to be understood.

"Ime vuccanti... pe... bhāvanā pahātabbā" means it should be understood that these three taints are said to be abandoned by the development of these factors of enlightenment associated with the three higher paths.
90:
Now, the Blessed One, praising the monk who has abandoned the taints (āsavas) through these seven methods, and wishing to show the benefit of abandoning the taints, and also wishing to inspire effort in beings to abandon the taints through these very reasons, said: "Monks, when... he has made an end of suffering."

In that text, "yato kho" means "of which monk," because the suffix "-to" is used in the sense of the genitive case (sāmivacana). However, ancient teachers explain it as "at which time."

"Ye āsavā dassanā pahātabbā" means those taints that should be abandoned by vision (dassana, i.e., the Path of Stream-entry); those taints are indeed abandoned by vision alone, and one does not have the perception of having abandoned them when they are not yet abandoned. In this way, the detailed explanation should be understood in all places.

"Sabbāsavasaṃvarasaṃvuto" means closed off by the closing of all taints, or closed off by the closures of all taints. "Acchecchi taṇhaṃ" means he has cut off all craving, he has completely severed it. "Vivattayi saṃyojanaṃ" means he has also removed the ten fetters and made himself free from impurities. "Sammā" means by the proper cause or reason. "Mānābhisamayā" means due to the completion of the tasks of seeing conceit (dassanābhisamaya) and abandoning conceit (pahānābhisamaya). The Path of Arahantship sees conceit by the power of its function; this is its breakthrough of seeing (dassanābhisamaya). Conceit seen by that Path is abandoned at that very moment, just as the life of creatures is ended by venomous animals upon sight. This is its breakthrough of abandoning (pahānābhisamaya).

"Antamakāsi dukkhassa" means that because conceit has been rightly seen and abandoned by the Path of Arahantship in this way, he has made an end of the suffering of the entire round of rebirth (vaṭṭadukkha). Among the four types of "ends" (anta)—namely, the end as a final limit (antimamariyādanta) as in "the end of the waistband decays"; the end as something low (lāmakanta) as in "Monks, this living by alms-gathering is a low end"; the end as a portion (koṭṭhāsanta) as in "Identity (sakkāya) is one end"; and the end as the ultimate limit (koṭṭanta) as in "This [Nibbāna] alone is the end of suffering due to the destruction of all conditions"—he has made the end of the entire round of suffering, known as the fourth limit or the final limit. He has made a boundary, a turning away from the round. It means he has made suffering such that only the final physical body remains.

"Attamanā te bhikkhū" means they were of their own mind, of delighted mind, or possessed of a mind associated with rapture and joy. "Bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti" means they were greatly delighted, holding it above their heads, saying, "What the Blessed One has spoken is indeed true; what the Sugata has spoken is indeed true," regarding this Sabbāsava Sutta which ends with the making of an end of suffering. The remaining words in this Sabbāsava Sutta that are not commented upon are omitted because they have been explained before or because they are easy to understand. Therefore, everything should be contemplated according to the proper reasons. 

The commentary on the Sabbāsava Sutta (Sabbāsavasuttavaṇṇanā) is finished.

## Dhammadāyāda Sutta. This sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is called the Dhammadāyāda Sutta. Having shown the origin and circumstances (atthuppatti-nikkhepa) of this sutta, I shall provide the commentary on the words not yet explained.
91:
Regarding the Sabbāsava Sutta, which ends with the making of an end of suffering, spoken well and uttered well by the Blessed One, they received it respectfully with their heads and greatly rejoiced, saying, "O Blessed One, this word spoken is indeed true; O Sugata, this word spoken is thus true."

The remaining words in this Sabbāsava Sutta that were not commented upon were not mentioned because they were spoken previously and because they are easy to understand. Therefore, everything should be contemplated word by word according to the sequence of what has been spoken.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## The Commentary on the Sabbāsava Sutta is finished.
## 3. Commentary on the Dhammadāyāda Sutta

This sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is called the Dhammadāyāda Sutta. Since it has an origin for its delivery (atthuppatti), I will first show that origin and then provide the commentary on the new words in this sutta. For what reason was this sutta delivered? It was delivered concerning gains and honors (lābhasakkāra). It is said that great gains and honors arose for the Blessed One. For instance, due to the accumulation of the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī) fulfilled for four incalculables (and a hundred thousand eons), gains and honors arose for the Blessed One like a great flood resulting from a twin heavy rain falling in all directions. It was as if all the perfections combined to give their results in this final existence, producing a great flood of gains and honors.

From various places, kings, brahmins, and others came carrying food, drinks, vehicles, clothes, flowers, perfumes, and ointments in their hands, searching for the Blessed One, asking, "Where is the Buddha? Where is the Blessed One? Where is the God of gods, the Best of men, the Lion of men?" Even when they brought the four requisites in hundreds of carts, they could not find an opportunity to offer them, and they stood with the poles of their carts touching each other within an area of about one gāvuta (approx. 2 miles) around, following him continuously. This was like the case of the Brahmin Andhakavinda and others. All these details about the abundance of gains and honors should be understood as they appear in the Khandhakas (Mahāvagga and Cullavagga of the Vinaya) and in various suttas. As it was for the Blessed One, so it was for the Order of Monks (Bhikkhu Saṅgha).

And this was also said: "At that time, the Blessed One was respected, revered, esteemed, honored, and venerated, and he was a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick; the Order of Monks was also respected... (etc.) ...recipient of requisites" (as found in the Udāna). Likewise—

"Now, whatever Saṅgha or group arises in the world, I do not see any other that has reached the pinnacle of gains and the pinnacle of fame and followers like this Order of Monks," he said. When those vast gains and honors that arose for the Blessed One and the Order of Monks combined, they were as immeasurable as the confluence of two great rivers. Consequently, monks who were greedy for gains became those who prioritized the four requisites and practiced only for the abundance of the four requisites. Even when it was past noon, if people brought butter, molasses, etc., they would strike the bell and shout loudly, "Give a portion for my supporter (nissaya-dāyaka) teacher! Give a portion for my preceptor (upajjhāya)!" Such behavior of those monks was clearly known to the Blessed One.
92:
“Cunda, among the Saṅghas or groups currently existing in the world, I do not see any other single Saṅgha that has reached the pinnacle of gain, honor, and fame like this Saṅgha of bhikkhus” (Dī. Ni. 3.176).

The gain and honor that arose for the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus became united and was as immeasurable as the waters of two great rivers. Gradually, the bhikkhus became those who prioritized the four requisites and practiced to increase them. Even after noon, when ghee, honey, molasses, and so forth were brought, they would strike the wooden gong and make a very loud noise, shouting, “Give to our teacher! Give to our preceptor!” This behavior of theirs became well-known to the Blessed One. Then, the Blessed One, feeling spiritual urgency (dhamma-saṃvega) thinking “This is not appropriate,” reflected thus:

“It is not possible to prescribe a training rule stating that the four requisites are unallowable. This is because the practice of the monk's life for noble sons is connected to the four requisites. I shall teach the practice of being heirs of the Dhamma (dhamma-dāyāda-paṭipadā). This practice will be like the prescription of training rules for noble sons who desire training, and like a full-length mirror placed at a city gate. Just as the four classes of people, seeing their own reflection in a full-length mirror at a city gate, remove their flaws and become faultless; in the same way, noble sons who desire training and wish to adorn themselves with the ornament of meditation, having reflected on this teaching which is like a full-length mirror, will avoid the practice of being heirs of material things, fulfill the practice of being heirs of the Dhamma, and will quickly reach the end of birth, aging, and death.” Due to this occurrence, he spoke this sutta.

In that sutta, “Bhikkhus, be my heirs in Dhamma, not my heirs in material things” means: “Bhikkhus, be heirs of my Dhamma, not heirs of material things. Whatever Dhamma of mine there is, be the recipients of that Dhamma. Whatever material things of mine there are, do not be the recipients of those material things.” In this context, Dhamma is of two kinds: nippariyāya-dhamma (direct Dhamma) and pariyāya-dhamma (indirect Dhamma). Material things (āmisa) are also of two kinds: nippariyāya-āmisa and pariyāya-āmisa. How? The ninefold supramundane Dhamma, consisting of the Paths, Fruits, and Nibbāna, is the nippariyāya-dhamma because it is the Dhamma that is directly produced; it is not called Dhamma by any indirect means, cause, or pretext. As for the wholesome (kusala) that is based on the cessation of the round of rebirth, it is...
93:
In this Dispensation, some person, desiring Nibbāna which is the cessation of the round of rebirth, gives gifts, undertakes virtue, performs the Uposatha duties, makes offerings of objects such as perfumes and flowers, listens to the Dhamma, teaches the Dhamma, and produces meditative attainments (jhāna-samāpatti). Such a person gradually attains Nibbāna, the Deathless, which is the direct Dhamma (nippariyāya-dhamma). This practice is called indirect Dhamma (pariyāya-dhamma). Similarly, the four requisites such as robes are only direct material things (nippariyāya-āmisa); they are not material things by any other indirect means, cause, or pretext. Wholesome deeds that lead to the round of rebirth (vaṭṭagāmi-kusala) are those where a person in this world, desiring the round of rebirth and wishing for a life of prosperity, gives gifts... (pe)... and produces meditative attainments. Such a person gradually attains human and divine prosperity. This is called indirect material things (pariyāya-āmisa).

Among these, the nippariyāya-dhamma (supramundane Dhamma) belongs only to the Blessed One. It is only because it was taught by the Blessed One that the bhikkhus attain the Paths, Fruits, and Nibbāna. Thus it was said: “Brahmin, that Blessed One is the arouser of the unarisen path, the producer of the unproduced path, the declarer of the undeclared path; he is the knower of the path, the discoverer of the path, the one skilled in the path. And now his disciples live following the path and become possessed of it afterwards” (Ma. Ni. 3.79). And: “Friend, that Blessed One knows what is to be known, sees what is to be seen; he has become vision, become knowledge, become Dhamma, become Brahma; he is the sayer, the proclaimer, the bringer out of meaning, the giver of the Deathless, the Lord of Dhamma, the Tathāgata” (Ma. Ni. 1.203). The pariyāya-dhamma also belongs only to the Blessed One. It is only because it was taught by the Blessed One that they know: “One who, desiring Nibbāna, gives gifts... (pe)... and produces meditative attainments, gradually attains Nibbāna, the Deathless.” The nippariyāya-āmisa also belongs only to the Blessed One. It is only because it was allowed by the Blessed One that the bhikkhus received fine robes, starting with the case of Jīvaka. As the Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, I allow householder-robes. Let him who wishes be a rag-robe wearer; let him who wishes accept householder-robes. In either case, bhikkhus, I praise only contentment” (Mahāva. 337).

In the past, the bhikkhus did not receive fine alms-food. They ate only alms-food obtained by house-to-house collection. While they were staying in Rājagaha, the Blessed One allowed: “Bhikkhus, I allow a meal for the Saṅgha, a designated meal, an invitation, a lottery meal...” and so forth.
94:
Because the Blessed One permitted it thus: "Alms-food of the waxing and waning fortnights, alms-food of the Uposatha day, alms-food of the day before the Uposatha" (Cullavagga 325), exquisite food is obtained. Likewise, dwellings are obtained. Indeed, in the past, monks were only those who stayed in dwellings such as tree-hollows and at the roots of trees that were not constructed. Because the Blessed One permitted it thus: "Monks, I allow five [types of] dwellings" (Cullavagga 294), they obtained these dwellings: a vihāra, an aḍḍhayoga, a pāsāda, a hammiya, and a guhā. In the past, they also made medicine only with yellow myrobalan soaked in cow's urine. Because the Blessed One himself permitted it in this way: "Monks, I allow five medicines, namely: ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses" (Mahāvagga 260), they obtained various medicines.

Indirect material things (pariyāya-āmisa) also belong only to the Blessed One. Indeed, only because the Blessed One taught it, do they know: "By giving gifts, undertaking virtue... and producing attainments while aspiring for a fortunate existence, one gradually obtains heavenly bliss and human bliss, which are called indirect material things." Therefore, since direct Dhamma (nippariyāya-dhamma), indirect Dhamma (pariyāya-dhamma), direct material things (nippariyāya-āmisa), and indirect material things (pariyāya-āmisa) all belong only to the Blessed One, wishing to show his ownership over those two types of material things, he said: "Monks, be my heirs in Dhamma, not my heirs in material things."

Be heirs of the two kinds of Dhamma that are my property. Do not be heirs of that material thing which is also my property. Be masters of the portion of Dhamma, not of the portion of material things. Indeed, if a monk who has gone forth in the Conqueror's Dispensation dwells prioritizing requisites, being prominent in the four grounds for the arising of craving, and having laid down the burden in the practice of Dhamma in accordance with Dhamma, this monk is called an heir of material things. Do not be like such persons. However, if a monk dwells prioritizing practice, making use of the permitted requisites with reflection based on fewness of wishes and so forth, and being prominent in the four Noble Lineages (ariyavaṃsa), this monk is called an heir of Dhamma. "Be like such persons" is what is meant.

Now, for those who had the thought, or will have it in the future: "Does the Blessed One say this because he does not want his disciples to receive gains?", he said: "I have compassion for you... not heirs of material things" to show that "I say this because I desire for you the most exquisite gains."
95:
The meaning of that Pali text is this: "Monks, I have compassion, sympathy, and a desire for the welfare of you all. By what reason, by what means, may my disciples be heirs of Dhamma, masters of the portion of Dhamma, and not heirs of material things?" Here, the meaning is: The Blessed One sees monks who, by prioritizing material things, have stumbled and perished because of material things. He saw that in the past, during the time of Kassapa Buddha, the monk Kapila and hundreds of other evil monks, nuns, and probationers (sikkhamānā) filled the lower realms, as mentioned in the passage: "Even the outer robe burns" (Pārājika 230, Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.218). He also saw those like Devadatta, who went forth in his own Dispensation, filling the lower realms. But he saw those who prioritize Dhamma, such as the Venerable Sāriputta, Mahāmoggallāna, and Mahākassapa, obtaining virtues such as the direct knowledges (abhiññā) and the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Therefore, desiring for those monks liberation from the lower realms and the fulfillment of all virtues, he said: "I have compassion for you. How may my disciples be heirs of Dhamma, and not heirs of material things?"

One who prioritizes requisites is like a counterfeit coin or a cold ember in the midst of the fourfold assembly—without power and without luster. But one who turns his mind away from that and prioritizes Dhamma is powerful and wanders dominantly like a lion king. For that reason too, he said: "I have... not heirs of material things."

Having thus made it known that this statement, "Monks, be my heirs in Dhamma, not my heirs in material things," was spoken out of compassion by one desiring a more exquisite gain, and not by one who does not want [them to have] gains, he now said: "Monks, if you... not heirs of Dhamma" to show the danger of not following this advice. In that passage, "You would also be blameworthy because of that" means that because you are heirs of material things and not heirs of Dhamma, you would be those pointed out and blamed by the wise, those who should be set apart, and those deserving of reproach by the wise. In what way? "The disciples of the Teacher dwell as heirs of material things, not as heirs of Dhamma"—thus would they be blamed.

"I would also be blameworthy because of that" means that because you are heirs of material things and not heirs of Dhamma, I would also be blameworthy because of your being heirs of material things and not being heirs of Dhamma. In what way? "Heirs of material... [not heirs of Dhamma]." The Blessed One said this to make those monks very gentle. The meaning here is: "Monks, if you wander dwelling with frivolous greed for material things, then the wise will blame me, saying: 'How is it that, being the All-Knowing One, he cannot discipline his disciples so that they do not become heirs of material things but become heirs of Dhamma?'"
96:
The meaning here is: Monks, if you were to live greedily regarding material things, wise people would criticize me, saying, 'How is it that the Buddha, being the All-knowing One, is unable to make his own disciples heirs of the Dhamma instead of heirs of material things?' For example, seeing monks who are not endowed with proper conduct and appearance, people criticize their preceptors and teachers, asking, 'Whose co-residents are these? Whose pupils are these?' Or, seeing sons and daughters of good families who are immoral and of evil character, people criticize the parents, asking, 'Whose sons are these? Whose daughters are these?' In the same way, wise people would criticize me, saying, 'How is it that he, being the All-knowing One, is unable to make his own disciples heirs of the Dhamma instead of heirs of material things?'

Having thus shown the disadvantage of not following this instruction, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with 'Tumhe ca me,' wishing to show the advantage of following and practicing it. In understanding the intent of the Blessed One, the phrase 'I also would not be blameworthy because of that' means: for example, seeing young monks who are diligent in fulfilling their duties, endowed with the study of the Pali and Commentaries, and possessed of proper conduct and appearance like an Elder of a hundred years, when people ask, 'Whose disciples are these?' and learn, 'They are the disciples of such-and-such a teacher,' the teachers and preceptors are not blamed or criticized, but rather people say, 'It is truly fitting for the Elder; he is indeed capable of advising and instructing.' In the same way, because you are heirs of the Dhamma and not heirs of material things, when people ask, 'Whose disciples are those who practice the Nālaka-paṭipadā, the Tuvaṭṭaka-paṭipadā, the Candūpama-paṭipadā, the Rathavinīta-paṭipadā, the Mahāgosingasāla-paṭipadā, and the Mahāsuññata-paṭipadā? Those who stand as witnesses to the Ariyavaṃsa (Noble Lineage), which consists of contentment with the four requisites and delight in meditation? Those whose minds are withdrawn from greed for requisites and who live like the moon freed from clouds?' and it is said, 'They are the disciples of the Samana Gotama,' then wise people would not blame me, saying, 'The Blessed One is truly All-knowing; he is indeed able to make his disciples abandon the practice of being heirs of material things and fulfill the practice of being heirs of the Dhamma.' Having understood the meaning in this passage, the remaining parts should be understood as the opposite of the method stated in the dark side (kaṇhapakkha). Having thus shown the advantage of following this instruction, the Buddha now handed over that advice, saying: 'Tasmā tiha me, bhikkhave... no āmisadāyādā.'

Having thus handed over this instruction, the Buddha now spoke the words beginning with 'Idhāhaṃ, bhikkhave' to praise the monk who fulfills that practice of being a Dhamma-heir. For even upon hearing the praise of the Blessed One, there are those who practice for the sake of that benefit.
97:
Wise people would not be those who criticize. Having understood the Buddha's intention in this passage, the remaining words should be understood by the method opposite to what was said in the dark side (kaṇhapakkha). Having thus shown the benefit of following this Dhamma-heir instruction, the Buddha now wished to entrust that advice and said: 'Tasmā tiha me, bhikkhave... no āmisadāyādā.' After entrusting this instruction, he then spoke the words beginning with 'Idhāhaṃ, bhikkhave' to praise the monk who fulfills that practice of being a Dhamma-heir. This is because, merely by hearing the words of praise from the Blessed One, those who will practice for that benefit always arise.

In that Pali, 'idha' is merely a particle. 'Bhuttāvī' means one who has eaten, or it means one who has finished the business of the meal. 'Pavārito' means one who has refused further food after eating as much as desired (yāvadattha-pavāraṇā); alternatively, it means a satisfied person who has eaten as much as desired and has rejected further food.

Indeed, there are four types of Pavāraṇā (invitation/refusal): (1) Vassaṃvuṭṭha-pavāraṇā, (2) Paccaya-pavāraṇā, (3) Anatiritta-pavāraṇā, and (4) Yāvadattha-pavāraṇā. Among these four, the Pavāraṇā in the passage, 'Monks, I allow monks who have completed the rains-retreat to invite (pavāretuṃ) based on three grounds,' is Vassaṃvuṭṭha-pavāraṇā. The Pavāraṇā in the words, 'Venerable Sir, I wish to invite the Saṅgha with medicinal requisites for four months,' and 'except for a renewed invitation, except for a permanent invitation,' is Paccaya-pavāraṇā. The Pavāraṇā in the passage, 'What is called pavārita is when the food is evident, the meal is evident, one standing within arm's length offers it, and the refusal is evident; such a person is called pavārita,' is Anatiritta-pavāraṇā. The Pavāraṇā in the passage, 'He satisfied and invited (sampavāresi) them with his own hands with choice staple and non-staple food,' is Yāvadattha-pavāraṇā. In this context, Yāvadattha-pavāraṇā is intended. Therefore, it is said, 'Pavārito means one who has refused by way of yāvadattha-pavāraṇā.'

'Paripuṇṇo' means one who is full of food. 'Pariyosito' means one who has finished the business of eating; here, it should be understood that the subsequent word 'bhojana' (food/meal) is omitted. It means: 'I have eaten as much as should be eaten, my act of eating is finished.' 'Suhito' means one who is satisfied, or it means one who is happy because the suffering of hunger is absent. 'Yāvadattho' means: 'Whatever benefit I desired from the meal, all of it has been attained.' Among these terms, the latter three are the evidences that make the former three known. For he who has finished (pariyosito) is one who has eaten (bhuttāvī). He who is satisfied (suhito) is one who has refused by yāvadattha-pavāraṇā (pavārito). He who has as much as desired (yāvadattho) is one who is full (paripuṇṇo). Alternatively, it can be said that the former terms make the latter terms known. Because one has eaten, the act of eating is finished. Because one has refused, one is satisfied. Because one is full, one has as much as desired. All of this should be understood as being stated by considering what is appropriate.

The word 'siya' occurs in the sense of certainty (ekaṃsa) and in the sense of supposition (vikappana). In the Pali, 'The earth element may be internal (siya ajjhattikā), it may be external (siya bāhirā),' it is in the sense of certainty. In the Pali, 'There might be (siya) a transgression of an offense by a certain monk,' it is in the sense of supposition. In this context, both senses are suitable. 'Atireko' means an extra thing (atireka-dhamma). Likewise, it is a thing to be discarded (chaḍḍanīya-dhamma). It is both in excess and to be discarded; no other business is to be done with it.
98:
"It should be done" is the meaning. 'Atha' means at that time (after the Buddha had finished his meal). 'Jighacchādubbalyapareta' refers to those (monks) who have been oppressed and followed by hunger and weakness for eight or ten days. Among those monks, some are hungry but not weak; they are able to endure hunger. To show that these monks are not like those who can endure, He taught both (hunger and weakness). The term 'tyāhaṃ' should be resolved as 'te ahaṃ' (I to you). 'Sace ākaṅkhatha' means if you desire.

'Appaharite' means in a place where there is no growth of green grass, in a place where there are no grasses that could be destroyed by being covered with almsfood. By this statement, it refers to a place without grass, or a large thicket of grass where the grass would not be destroyed even if almsfood were discarded there by a cartload. In fact, this was spoken so as not to violate the training rule regarding vegetation (bhūtagāma).

'Appāṇake' means in water without living beings, or in a large body of water where there are no living beings that could die by being covered with almsfood. Indeed, if almsfood is thrown and stirred in a place with little water, subtle living beings may die, but they would not die in large tanks or rivers. This was spoken for the sake of protecting living beings. 'Opilāpessāmi' means I will immerse it.

'Tatrekassa' means of one of those two monks. This was spoken as 'vuttaṃ kho panetaṃ' (this has been said) with reference to the monk who, having well heard this Dhamma teaching, reflects on it again and again. This word 'vutta' is found in the sense of shaving hair in such passages as 'kāpaṭiko māṇavo daharo vuttasiro' (a young worker with a shaven head), etc.; in the sense of sowing in such passages as 'yathā sāradikaṃ bီjaṃ, khette vuttaṃ virūhati' (just as autumnal seed sown in a field grows), etc.; and in the sense of speaking in such passages as 'vuttamidaṃ bhagavatā' (this was said by the Blessed One), etc. Here, however, it should be understood in the sense of speaking. 'This word has indeed been spoken' is the meaning of this phrase.

'Āmisanyataraṃ' means one of the four material requisites (almsfood). 'Yadidaṃ' is an indeclinable; although it remains in that form in all genders, cases, and numbers, its meaning should be adapted according to the context. Here, it means 'that which is called this almsfood.' It means that this almsfood is one of the material requisites. 'Yannūnāhaṃ' means 'it would be good if I were to pass (the time in this way).' 'Evaṃ' means just as I pass this present moment, so too throughout the day and night. 'Vītināmeyya' means I would spend or pass (the time).

That monk, without eating that almsfood—which is worthy of being respectfully accepted with the head by the world including the devas, and which is the leftover of the Sugata—desiring to be an heir of the Dhamma...
99:
...desiring (to be an heir of the Dhamma), reflecting with the simile of one whose head is on fire, he would pass that day and night in that very state of hunger and weakness. In this section regarding the second monk, the summary is as follows: If that monk, while thinking "What if I... (pass the time)," were to also think: "Just as it is difficult for monks to find medicine in a forest infested with wild beasts, so too it is very difficult to seek almsfood in a village infested with the wild beasts of the five cords of sensual pleasure. This almsfood, however, is free from the faults of seeking and is the leftover of the Sugata; thus it is like a prince of pure birth from both parents." 

There are five reasons why almsfood should not be consumed. They are: it should not be consumed by disparaging the person, thinking "this belongs to an unconscientious person (alajjī)"; it should not be consumed because of impure origin, thinking "this was brought about by the instigation of a nun or by claiming a non-existent superhuman quality"; it should not be consumed out of compassion for the owner, thinking "the monk who owns the almsfood is himself hungry"; it should not be consumed out of compassion for pupils and others, thinking "the pupils or others connected to that monk are hungry." Even if those people are well-fed, it should not be consumed because of the owner's lack of faith, thinking "the monk who owns the almsfood has no faith." 

This almsfood is free from those reasons. The Blessed One is the pinnacle of conscientious persons (lajjī), the almsfood is of pure origin, the Blessed One is well-fed, there is no other person who would be longing for it, and the Blessed One is the foremost among those in the world who have faith. Having reflected thus, he would consume that almsfood and pass the time practicing the monk's duties. By this much, the monk who practices the monk's duties without consuming the almsfood is said to have not eaten almsfood that was fit to be eaten. The monk who practices the monk's duties after consuming it is said to have eaten almsfood that was fit to be eaten. There is no difference in the almsfood, but there is a difference in the person. Therefore, to show that special person, He said "kiñcāpi so," etc. 

In that context, "kiñcāpi" is an indeclinable in the sense of permission and praise. What does He permit? He permits that monk's blameless consumption. What does He praise? He praises the practice of the monk's duties after consuming the almsfood. This is what is meant: even if that monk, having consumed almsfood that was fit to be eaten, performs the monk's duties that should be performed, nevertheless, the first monk alone is the heir of my Dhamma. The first monk who performs the monk's duties even after rejecting that almsfood is like the more heroic of two heroes, or the wiser of two wise men. Now, to strengthen that point, He said "taṃ kissa hetu," etc. Its meaning is: "For what reason is that monk one who is exceedingly worthy of the Blessed One's honor?"
100:
## 
It means that he is exceedingly worthy of honor and praise, more so than the second monk. Now, wishing to prove this matter with a reason, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with 'For what reason?' (Taṃ kissa hetu). The meaning of that Pali is: 'For what reason would that monk be more worthy of honor and praise from the Blessed One?' This thought might occur to you. The reason is that the refusal of those leftovers will lead to that monk's fewness of wishes... and arousal of energy for a long time. How so? In the future, there might arise in that monk a desire for the requisites of others, or evil wishes, or great wishes. When that happens, he will restrain himself with this goad of refusing leftovers, reflecting: 'O monk, you refused even the leftovers of the Sugata, yet now you give rise to such desire?' In this same way, it acts as a restraint when lack of contentment and lack of effacement arise. Thus, it will lead to his fewness of wishes, contentment, and effacement.

Regarding the term 'subharatāya' (being easy to support), the explanation is: In this Dispensation, a certain monk is difficult to maintain and difficult to support, both for himself and for his supporters. Another monk is easy to maintain and easy to support, both for himself and for his supporters. How so? A monk who, having received sour food etc., seeks non-sour food; who discards food received at one donor's house at another house, wanders through the whole village, and enters the monastery to sleep with an empty bowl—this monk is difficult to maintain for himself. A monk who, even when his bowl is filled with fine rice and meat, shows a dissatisfied and unhappy face, or who disparages the donors to their faces, saying 'What is this you have given?' and gives that food to novices or laypeople—this monk is difficult to support for his supporters. Seeing this, people avoid him from afar, saying, 'This monk is difficult to support; it is not possible to maintain him.'

However, a monk who, having received whatever is coarse or fine, eats it with a contented mind, returns to the monastery, and performs his meditation task—this monk is easy to maintain for himself. And a monk who, without disparaging the gift of others, whether it be little or much, coarse or fine, eats it in the presence of the donors with a happy and clear face and then departs—this monk is easy to support for his supporters. Seeing this, people become very confident. They make a promise and support him, saying, 'Our noble lord is easy to support; he is satisfied with even a little; we alone will support him.'

In that context, if in the future a thought should arise in that monk in the manner of being difficult to support, either for himself or for his supporters, then he will restrain himself with this goad of refusing leftovers, reflecting: 'O monk, you refused even the leftovers of the Sugata...'
101:
## 
'...reflecting, "did you give rise to such a desire?" In this way, it will lead to his being easy to support. If laziness should arise in that monk, he will also restrain it with this same goad: "O monk, at that time you refused even the leftovers of the Sugata and practiced the monk's Dhamma even when overcome by the weakness of hunger; why do you now indulge in laziness?" Reflecting thus, it will lead to his arousal of energy.

In this way, this refusal of leftovers will lead to his fewness of wishes... (and so on)... and arousal of energy for a long time. Thus, when these five qualities are fulfilled, they will fulfill the ten subjects of discourse (kathāvatthu).

How so? In this very Pali of the Dhammadāyāda Sutta, three subjects appear by way of fewness of wishes (appicchatā), contentment (santuṭṭhitā), and arousal of energy (vīriyārambha). The remaining seven are included in effacement (sallekha). Indeed, "effacement" is a name for all the subjects of discourse. As the Buddha said in detail: "Ānanda, there is discourse that is extremely effacing, suitable for the removal of hindrances, and leads to absolute disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna. That is to say, discourse on fewness of wishes (appiccha-kathā)..." and so on. Thus, when these five qualities are fulfilled, they will fulfill the ten subjects of discourse. When the ten subjects of discourse are fulfilled, they will fulfill the three trainings (sikkhā).

How so? Among those ten discourses, these four—discourse on fewness of wishes, discourse on contentment, discourse on non-association, and discourse on virtue—are included in the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā). These three—discourse on seclusion, discourse on arousal of energy, and discourse on concentration—are included in the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā). These three—discourse on wisdom, discourse on liberation, and discourse on the knowledge and vision of liberation—are included in the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā). Thus, when the ten subjects of discourse are fulfilled, they will fulfill the three trainings. When the three trainings are fulfilled, they will fulfill the five aggregates of an adept (asekkha-dhammakkhandha).

How so? The fulfilled training in higher virtue is indeed the adept's aggregate of virtue. The training in higher mind is the adept's aggregate of concentration. The training in higher wisdom is the adept's aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation. Thus, when the three trainings are fulfilled, they will fulfill the five aggregates of an adept. When the five aggregates of Dhamma are fulfilled, they will fulfill the deathless Nibbāna. For example, just as a great rain cloud in the early rainy season on a mountain top...'
102:
When a heavy rain of the early rainy season falls heavily on a mountain top, it fills the mountain clefts, crevices, and gullies. When those clefts, crevices, and gullies are full, they fill the small pools. When the small pools are full, they fill the large pools. When the large pools are full, they fill the small rivers flowing down from the foot of the mountain. When the small rivers are full, they fill the large rivers. When the large rivers are full, they fill the great ocean, the vast body of water. In the same way, when these five virtues of that monk are full, they will fulfill the ten subjects of discourse (kathāvatthu), starting from the beginning up to the deathless anupādisesa-nibbāna. Seeing this matter clearly—that this monk, practicing the way of an heir of Dhamma, attains the supreme Dhamma inheritance—the Blessed One spoke these words: "Bhikkhus, for what reason is that so? That is so for that monk," and so on.

Having established the state of that monk being highly worthy of offerings and highly worthy of praise through this reason, and now wishing to urge those monks toward that state, He spoke the words: "Therefore, bhikkhus..." and so on. What is the meaning intended? It means: whichever monk would eat that alms-food and then strive in the recluse's Dhamma, that monk is outside of these five original virtues. But whichever monk would strive in the recluse's Dhamma without eating, that monk has a share in these five original virtues. Therefore, He said: "Therefore, bhikkhus... do not be heirs of material things."

"The Blessed One said this" means the Blessed One spoke this section of the sutta from the end of the introduction up to "do not be heirs of material things." Having spoken this section of the sutta, the Blessed One, who has attained the name "Sugata" because He has gone by a beautiful practice, rose from the prepared noble Buddha-seat and entered His Mahāgandhakuṭi while the assembly was not yet dispersed. Why did He enter? He entered for the sake of praising the Dhamma.

It is said that when the Buddhas enter the monastery while the teaching is not yet finished, they do so for two reasons: either to praise a person or to praise the Dhamma. When entering to praise a person, He thinks: "I have shown this summary (uddesa) in brief, but have not yet analyzed it in detail. The monks who receive the Dhamma will learn it and approach Ānanda or Kaccāna to ask about it. Those [elders] will then explain it in accordance with my wisdom. Then the monks who receive the Dhamma will ask me again. To those monks, I will say: 'Bhikkhus, it was well-spoken by Ānanda; it was well-spoken by Kaccāna. If you were to ask me this meaning, I too would explain it in this very same way.' In this way, I will praise those persons. Because of that praise, I will inspire respect for them, and the monks will approach them. They will also [guide] those monks in the meaning and in the Dhamma..."
103:
(Those elders such as Ānanda and Kaccāna) will also urge them. Those monks, being urged by those elders, will fulfill the three trainings and make an end of suffering (Nibbāna). When entering to praise the Dhamma, He thinks just as He thought in this Dhammadāyāda Sutta (and in other suttas): "When I have entered the monastery, Sāriputta, sitting in this very assembly, will criticize that material inheritance and praise the Dhamma inheritance while teaching the Dhamma. Thus, this teaching, taught with the same intention by both of us, will be supreme and highly esteemed, like a stone umbrella. It will be like a boat placed at a ferry because of its meaning of enabling one to cross the four floods, and like a thoroughbred chariot yoked with four horses because of its meaning of reaching the Path. For example, just as a King, having issued an order in the midst of the assembly saying, 'Let this punishment be given to one who acts thus,' rises from his seat and goes up to the palace, and the General remaining in that very place carries out the order issued by the King; even so, Sāriputta, sitting in this very assembly, will praise and teach the Dhamma I have established. Thus, this teaching, taught with the intention of both of us, will be very powerful and will shine like the midday sun." Thus, in this Dhammadāyāda Sutta, He rose from His seat and entered the monastery for the sake of praising the Dhamma. 

In such instances, it should be understood that the Blessed One disappears from the very seat where He was sitting and enters the monastery by mental speed (cittagati). For if He were to go by physical movement, the entire assembly would follow and surround the Blessed One. If that assembly were once dispersed, it would be difficult to reassemble them. (Reflecting thus), the Blessed One entered only by mental speed. When the Blessed One had thus entered, the Venerable Sāriputta, wishing to praise that Dhamma in accordance with the Blessed One's intention... (and so on), spoke these words. In that Pali, "Āyasmā" is a term of endearment and respect. "Sāriputto" is the name of that Elder, and that name is derived from his mother, not from his father. Because that Elder was the son of a Brahmin woman named Rūpasārī, he is called "Sāriputta". "Acirapakkantassa" means not long after he had departed. In these words "Āvuso Bhikkhave", when the Buddhas address the disciples, they say "Bhikkhave". The disciples, however, so as not to be equal with the Buddhas, first say "Āvuso" and then say "Bhikkhave". When addressed by the Buddhas, the community of monks gives the response "Bhadante"; when addressed by disciples, they respond with "Āvuso".
104:
In the phrase 'Kittāvatā nu kho, āvuso,' 'kittāvatā' is a word indicating a limit or extent; it means 'by how much of an extent?' The word 'nu' is used in a question. The word 'kho' is a mere particle. 'Satthu pavivittassa viharato' refers to the Blessed One dwelling with the three kinds of seclusion: bodily seclusion (kāya-viveka), mental seclusion (citta-viveka), and seclusion from the substrata of existence (upadhi-viveka). 'Vivekaṃ nānusikkhanti' means they do not train themselves in accordance with even one of the three kinds of seclusion, but remain only heirs in material things (āmisa-dāyāda). The Venerable Sāriputta asked the monks about this meaning. The same method should be understood for the bright side (sukka-pakkha) as well.

When this was said, the monks, wishing to hear that meaning, said 'Dūratopi kho,' and so forth. In that phrase, 'dūratopi' means from another country, from another district, or from a place counted by many leagues (yojanas). 'Santike' means nearby. 'Aññātuṃ' means to know or to understand. 'Āyasmantaṃyeva Sāriputtaṃ paṭibhātu' means 'Let it be the portion of the Venerable Sāriputta alone; let the Venerable Sāriputta make it his own portion and explain it.' The portion of the Venerable Sāriputta is the explanation of this meaning, while our portion is the hearing of it—this is the intention here, and it accords with grammatical principles. Some teachers say 'paṭibhātu' means 'let it appear in knowledge.' Others say 'upaṭṭhātu' means 'let it be established before knowledge.' 'Dhāressanti' means they will learn by heart or master it. Then the Elder, wishing to teach those monks, said 'Tena hi,' and so forth. In that phrase, 'tena' is a word indicating a reason. 'Hi' is a particle. It means 'Because you wish to hear, and because you have placed the burden upon me, therefore listen.' Those monks also accepted the Elder's words; therefore it is said, 'Evaṃ āvuso... paccassosuṃ.'

Then, the Blessed One, censuring those who are heirs in material things, said in one way: 'You too should be takers (ādiya) of that material thing.' The Venerable Sāriputta, wishing to show that meaning in three ways, said: 'Idhāvuso, satthu pavivittassa... kittāvatā kho, āvuso, satthu pavivittassa viharato sāvakā vivekaṃ nānusikkhanti.'

By this much, the meaning of the words spoken by the Blessed One while censuring the practice of being heirs in material things—'You too should be takers of that material thing'—and the meaning of the question he himself asked—'Kittāvatā nu kho... nānusikkhanti'—is well-analyzed in detail. And that meaning is analyzed without touching upon the Blessed One's state of being a 'taker' (ādiya). Indeed, it is only appropriate for the Blessed One, while showing favor to the disciples, to say 'I too will be a taker of that material thing.'
105:
To say 'I too will be a taker of that material thing' is appropriate only for the Blessed One, not for the disciples. This method applies to the bright side (sukka-pakkha) as well. This is first the connection of the sequence (anusandhi) in this context.

As for the commentary on the meaning: 'Idha' means in this Dispensation (sāsana). 'Satthu pavivittassa' means of the Teacher who is exceedingly secluded by the three kinds of seclusion. 'Vivekaṃ nānusikkhanti' means they do not train in imitation of bodily seclusion (kāya-viveka), they do not fulfill it. If it were said referring to all three kinds of seclusion, the question would have no distinction. For this is the side of the explanation (answer). Therefore, by this word [nānusikkhanti], bodily seclusion is shown; by the words 'Yesañca dhammānaṃ,' etc., mental seclusion (citta-viveka) is shown; and by the words 'Bāhulikā,' etc., seclusion from the substrata (upadhi-viveka) is shown—thus the meaning should be understood in brief.

The words 'Yesañca dhammānaṃ' are spoken referring to greed and so forth, which he will later speak of in the manner: 'Therein, friends, greed is evil,' etc. 'Nappajahanti' means they do not abandon, they do not fulfill mental seclusion. 'Bāhulikā' means those who practice for the abundance of the four requisites such as robes. Because they take the Dispensation lightly, they are called 'sāthalikā' (lax). In the phrase 'okkamane pubbaṅgamā,' 'okkamana' refers to the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa) in the sense of descending [into them]; thus it means those who make the five hindrances their precursor. 'Paviveke' means in the seclusion from substrata, which is Nibbāna. 'Nikkhittadhurā' means those who have laid down the burden, meaning they do not even make an effort to attain that Nibbāna; by this much, it is meant they do not fulfill the seclusion from substrata.

Having spoken without specific designation through this sequence of words, the Venerable Sāriputta now, wishing to define the teaching, said 'Tatra āvuso,' etc. Why? Because if it is spoken without designation as 'by three grounds,' the disciples might remain indifferent, thinking 'He is likely speaking of someone else, not us.' But when it is spoken with designation as 'Elders, new monks, middle-ranking monks,' they pay attention, thinking 'He is speaking of us.' For example, even when a king says 'The ministers must clean the city streets,' they might not clean them, wondering 'Who exactly should clean them?' But when it is announced by beat of drum that 'Each must clean the area in front of their own house,' everyone cleans and decorates it in a moment. This should be understood in the same way.

In that Pali, 'tatra' means among those disciples. 'Therā' refers to monks from ten years [of seniority] onwards. 'Tīhi ṭhānehi' means by three reasons. For this word 'ṭhāna' is seen in the senses of sovereignty, standing, moment, and reason. In such Pali passages as 'By performing what deed did Sakka, the lord of devas, reach this sovereignty (Sakka-hood)?', it is found in the sense of sovereignty.
106:
In passages such as 'By performing what meritorious deed did he reach this state of sovereignty (as Sakka)?', the word ṭhāna is found in the sense of sovereignty. In passages such as 'He is a bowman skilled in standing, who can hit a target with a flash of lightning in a short moment,' it is found in the sense of standing (posture). In passages such as 'That Tathāgata appears in an instant,' it is found in the sense of a moment. In passages such as 'He knows what is a cause as a cause, and what is not a cause as not a cause,' it is found in the sense of cause. Here, however, it is used only in the sense of cause. Because the effect resides in that cause by way of dependent existence, the cause is called 'ṭhāna'.

In the passage 'For this first reason, the elder monks are blameworthy,' the word 'gārayhā' means they should be censured. It means that although they are elders, they do not resort to secluded dwellings in the great forests; they cannot abandon dwellings near villages; they live increasing their delight in company; they do not fulfill bodily seclusion (kāyaviveka). Thus, they are to be censured, saying, 'How were they during their time as new monks and middle-level monks?' and it shows that, 'Friends, they receive this censure.' In the phrase 'For the second reason,' the connection should be understood thus: 'Friends, although these are elders, they do not abandon the unwholesome states such as greed, which the Teacher taught to be abandoned; they do not obtain one-pointedness of mind even for the duration of a finger-snap while sitting in a suitable place. How were they during their time as new monks and middle-level monks?' Thus, they are to be censured and receive this censure. In the phrase 'For the third reason,' the connection should be understood thus: 'Friends, although these are elders, they are not content with whatever requisites they receive; they live devoted to the adornment of robes, bowls, dwellings, and this foul body, without fulfilling seclusion from acquisitions (upadhiviveka). How were they during their time as new monks and middle-level monks?' Thus, they are to be censured and receive this censure. This same method applies to the sections on middle-level monks (majjhima) and new monks (nava).

This is the distinction: 'Middle-level' (majjhima) refers to monks from five to nine vassa. 'New' (nava) refers to those with less than five vassa. Just as it was said in the section on elders, 'How were they during their time as new and middle-level monks?', here in the sections for middle-level and new monks, one should connect the meaning by saying, 'How were they during their time as new monks? How will they be when they become elders? How will they be during their time as middle-level and elder monks?'

The meaning of the 'bright side' (sukkapakkha) should be understood by the method opposite to what was said in this 'dark side' (kaṇhapakkha). The summary here is as follows: These elders, though they are elders, resort to secluded dwellings in the great forests many leagues away. Even when it is appropriate to approach a village dwelling, they do not do so. Despite having such aged bodies, they strive greatly and inspire faith in the donors of requisites. For this reason, 'How did they strive during their time as new and middle-level monks?', the elders are praiseworthy and receive praise. They abandon greed and so on, and fulfill mental seclusion (cittaviveka). Although this great elder has reached an age suitable for living surrounded by saddhivihārika and antevāsika disciples, having finished his meal, he enters the forest and comes out only in the evening. If he enters a secluded place in the evening, he comes out only early in the morning. Thus, the preliminary work for the kasiṇa...
107:
The elders who have put forth effort inspire faith in the donors of requisites. For this first reason, 'What kind of striving did they have during their time as new and middle-level monks?', the elders are praiseworthy and receive praise. They abandon greed and so on, and fulfill mental seclusion (cittaviveka). Although this great elder has reached an age suitable for living surrounded by saddhivihārika and antevāsika disciples, having finished his meal, he enters the forest and comes out only in the evening; if he enters in the evening, he comes out only early in the morning. He performs the preliminary work for the kasiṇa, attains the meditative attainments (samāpatti), reaches the paths and fruits, and in every way fulfills mental seclusion (cittaviveka). For this second reason, the elder monks are praiseworthy and receive praise.

At a time when soft and light robes made of silk, fine cloth, or wool are suitable for the elder, even at such a time, this noble elder wears rag-robes (pāṃsukūla). Taking up the Dispensation without laxity, free from hindrances, entering the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), he lives fulfilling seclusion from acquisitions (upadhiviveka). For this third reason, 'What kind of striving did he have during his time as a new and middle-level monk?', the elders are praiseworthy and receive praise. This same method applies to the sections on middle-level and new monks.

In the phrase 'Tatra kho āvuso' (Therein, friends), what is the connection (anusandhi)? Having censured the practice of being heirs to material things (āmisadāyāda) through nine aspects, and having praised the practice of being heirs to the Dhamma (dhammadāyāda) through nine aspects, thus concluding the teaching with eighteen aspects, the Teacher spoke of the states to be abandoned, saying, 'They do not abandon those states which the Teacher told them to abandon.' To show those states specifically, saying 'These are those states,' he spoke the words beginning with 'Tatra kho āvuso, lobho ca' (Therein, friends, there is greed...). This is the connection.

Alternatively, the Dhamma was previously taught only figuratively (pariyāyena). Material things (āmisa), however, were taught both figuratively and literally (nippariyāyena). Now, in order to teach the literal Dhamma, the supramundane path (lokuttaramagga), he spoke these words. This is also the connection here.

In that passage, 'tatra' refers to the previous teaching. It means 'in the teaching given by the method beginning with: "While the Teacher lives in seclusion, the disciples do not train themselves in seclusion."' He shows that 'greed is evil, and anger is evil,' meaning these two states are evil and low, and they should be abandoned. Therein, greed (lobha) has the characteristic of attachment. Anger (dosa) has the characteristic of malice. Between those two, greed arises in an heir to material things when obtaining the four requisites, and anger arises when failing to obtain them.
108:
Through greed, one craves what has not yet been obtained; through hatred, one becomes distressed when not obtaining it. Greed occurs regarding the object to be given; hatred occurs toward the person who does not give, or toward the person who gives an undesirable object. Through greed, one fulfills the nine things rooted in craving; through hatred, one fulfills the five kinds of stinginess.

Now, to show the means of abandoning those base states of greed and hatred, the words beginning with "For the abandoning of greed" (lobhassa ca pahānāya) are spoken. The meaning is: for the abandoning of that greed and that hatred, the Noble Path was taught, referring to it as "There is a Middle Way" (atthi majjhimā paṭipadā). This is because the Path does not lean toward or approach these two extremes—the extreme of greed and the extreme of hatred—but is free from these extremes; therefore, it is called the "Middle Way" (majjhimā paṭipadā). It is called "Middle" (majjhimā) because it exists in the middle of those two extremes, and it is called "Way" (paṭipadā) because it should be practiced. Similarly, the devotion to sensual pleasure is one extreme, the devotion to self-mortification is one extreme, the eternalist view is one extreme, and the annihilationist view is one extreme; this should be expanded in the same manner as previously mentioned.

With the words beginning with "vision-making" (cakkhukaraṇī), he praises that very same Middle Way. It is "vision-making" because it leads to the seeing of the [Four Noble] Truths in the sense of being the leader of vision. It is "knowledge-making" (ñāṇakaraṇī) because it leads to the knowing of the Truths in the sense of making them known. It leads to "peace" (upasama) because of the subsiding of passion and so forth, and because it leads to peace.
