It leads to "direct knowledge" (abhiññā) because of seeing the state of the four Truths as things to be directly known, and because it leads to knowing through direct knowledge. "Enlightenment" (sambodha) refers to the Noble Path; it leads to "enlightenment" (sambodhāya) because it exists for the sake of that Path. Indeed, the Path itself leads to the sake of the Path because it performs the task to be done by the Path. Nibbāna is called unconditioned; it is said to lead to "Nibbāna" (nibbānāya) because it leads to the realization and direct experience of that Nibbāna. This explanation is the essence here. Any other description is merely an elaboration.

Now, wishing to show that Middle Way in its specific form, he asks "And what is that?" (katamā ca sā) and answers with the method beginning with "This very [Noble Eightfold Path]" (ayam-eva).

In that passage, the word of emphasis "this very" (ayam-eva) serves the purpose of excluding any other path and showing that it is common to Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddha. And it has been said: "This is the only path; there is no other for the purification of vision" (Dhp. 274). This path is "Noble" (ariya) because it is far from defilements, because it leads to the abandoning of enemies [defilements], because it was taught by the Noble Ones, and because it leads to the attainment of the state of a Noble One. (Because it is endowed with) eight factors (it is called Eightfold).
109:
It is called "Eightfold" (aṭṭhaṅgika) because it is endowed with eight factors; there is no path apart from its factors, unlike a five-piece musical instrument and so forth. It is called "Path" (magga) because it goes along killing the defilements, or because it seeks Nibbāna, or because it is sought by the virtuous who desire Nibbāna, or because it is practiced (reached) by those virtuous ones.

"Namely" (seyyathidaṃ) is an indeclinable; its meaning is "What is that path?" or "What are those eight factors?" In truth, each individual factor is itself the path. As it was taught: "Right view is both the path and the cause" (Dhs. 1039). The ancient teachers also say: "The path of seeing is right view, the path of application (to the object) is right intention... the path of non-distraction is right concentration."

Among these path factors such as right view: Right view (sammā-diṭṭhi) has the characteristic of seeing rightly. Right intention (sammā-saṅkappa) has the characteristic of applying (to the object) rightly. Right speech (sammā-vācā) has the characteristic of embracing rightly. Right action (sammā-kammanta) has the characteristic of originating rightly. Right livelihood (sammā-ājīva) has the characteristic of purifying rightly. Right effort (sammā-vāyāma) has the characteristic of exerting rightly. Right mindfulness (sammā-sati) has the characteristic of establishing rightly. Right concentration (sammā-samādhi) has the characteristic of placing (concentrating) rightly. The derivative meaning of these factors should also be understood in this way: "It is right view because it sees rightly."

Among those path factors, when right view arises, it abandons wrong view, the defilements opposed to right view, and ignorance. It takes Nibbāna as its object. It also sees the associated states. In seeing those associated states, it is only a seeing through non-delusion, not by taking them as an object. Therefore, it is called "right view."

Right intention abandons wrong intention and the defilements opposed to it. It takes Nibbāna as its object. It rightly applies the associated states (to the object of Nibbāna). Therefore, it is called "right intention."

Right speech abandons wrong speech and the defilements opposed to it. It takes Nibbāna as its object. It rightly embraces the associated states. Therefore, it is called "right speech."

Right action abandons wrong action and the defilements opposed to it. It takes Nibbāna as its object. It rightly originates the associated states. Therefore, it is called "right action."
110:
Right Livelihood abandons wrong livelihood and the defilements opposed to it, makes Nibbāna the object, and thoroughly purifies the associated states; therefore, it is called "Right Livelihood."

Right Effort abandons wrong effort, the defilements opposed to it, and laziness; it makes Nibbāna the object and thoroughly supports the associated states; therefore, it is called "Right Effort."

Right Mindfulness abandons wrong mindfulness and the defilements opposed to it; it makes Nibbāna the object and thoroughly establishes the associated states; therefore, it is called "Right Mindfulness."

Right Concentration abandons wrong concentration, the defilements opposed to it, and restlessness; it makes Nibbāna the object and thoroughly concentrates the associated states; therefore, it is called "Right Concentration."

Now, concluding that very practice, he said: "This, friends, is that [Middle Way]." Its meaning is: that which is spoken of as the "Eightfold Path" by combining all four supramundane paths into one—this, friends, is that... it leads to Nibbāna.

Having thus shown greed and hatred among the states to be abandoned, and the path (means) for their abandonment, he now says, "Therein, friends, what is anger?" etc., wishing to show other states to be abandoned and the path (means) for their abandonment. Among those [unwholesome states], anger (kodha) has the characteristic of being angry or the characteristic of ferocity; its function is to create ill-will (āghāta); it is manifested as malice. Resentment (upanāha) has the characteristic of repeatedly binding enmity; its function is not letting go of a grudge; it is manifested as the persistence of anger. And this has been said: "In the earlier stage it is anger (kodha); in the later stage it is resentment (upanāha)," and so forth.

Contempt (makkha) has the characteristic of denigrating others' virtues; its function is to destroy those virtues; it is manifested as covering them up. Domineering (paḷāsa) has the characteristic of rivalry; its function is to equate one's own virtues with those of others; it is manifested as measuring by the standard of others' virtues.

Envy (issā) has the characteristic of disparaging others' success, or the characteristic of being unable to endure it; its function is dissatisfaction therein; it is manifested as turning away from it. One's own...
111:
Avarice (macchera) has the characteristic of concealing one's own success; its function is not liking (unhappiness with) sharing one's success with others; it is manifested as shrinking.

Deceit (māyā) has the characteristic of hiding the evil one has done; its function is to keep that evil secret; it is manifested as covering up that evil. Hypocrisy (sāṭheyya) has the characteristic of making a display of virtues that do not exist in oneself; its function is to gather and present those virtues; it is manifested as making those virtues apparent even through bodily gestures.

Obstinacy (thambha) has the characteristic of the mind's stiffness; its function is the state of not being humble; it is manifested as lack of gentleness. Presumption (sārambha) has the characteristic of excessive action; its function is being particularly antagonistic; it is manifested as lack of respect.

Conceit (māna) has the characteristic of loftiness; its function is self-exaltation; it is manifested as being puffed up. Arrogance (atimāna) has the characteristic of excessive loftiness; its function is extreme self-exaltation; it is manifested as being extremely puffed up.

Intoxication (mada) has the characteristic of being intoxicated; its function is acting as if seized by intoxication; it is manifested as if being insane. Heedlessness (pamāda), which has the characteristic of letting the mind loose among the five cords of sensual pleasure, has the function of repeatedly giving in to that loose mind; it is manifested as the absence of mindfulness. Thus, the characteristics and so forth of these states should be understood. What has been said here is only a summary of the meaning. For details, it should be understood in the manner stated in the Vibhaṅga, starting with "Therein, what is anger?"

Particularly here, a monk who is an heir to material things (āmisa), when he does not receive material things himself, becomes angry at another monk who does receive them. That anger occurring once in that monk is called anger (kodha); beyond that, occurring repeatedly, it is called resentment (upanāha). Such a monk who is angry and resentful denigrates the existing virtues of the other monk who received [the things], and takes up rivalry, thinking, "I too have virtues like him." This is his contempt (makkha) and domineering (paḷāsa). Thus, being full of contempt and domineering, he envies and bears ill-will regarding the gains and honors, etc., of that [other monk], thinking, "What is the use of these gains and honors for this monk?" This is his envy (issā). If, however, he has some success of his own, he cannot endure sharing that success with others. This is his avarice (macchera). For the sake of gain, he hides his own existing faults; this is his deceit (māyā). He displays virtues that do not exist in him; this is his hypocrisy (sāṭheyya). A monk who practices in such a way, if he receives the desired gain, becomes stiff and hard-hearted because of that gain; he becomes one who cannot be admonished, thinking, "This should not be done in this way." This is his obstinacy (thambha). If someone says something to him, such as "This should not be done in this way," he becomes agitated in mind because of that saying, with a frowning face, [thinking] "Who...
112:
You speak oppressively, saying 'Who are you to me?'; this is called that monk's sārambha (malice/speaking oppressively). Furthermore, due to obstinacy (thambha), if he considers himself, 'I alone am superior,' he is one who has conceit (māna). Through sārambha (aggression/interference), if he despises others, thinking 'Who are these people?', he is one who has arrogance (atimāna); these are that monk's conceit and arrogance. Because of that conceit and arrogance, he generates various forms of intoxication (mada) based on birth and so forth. Being intoxicated, he is negligent (pamajjati) regarding objects such as the strands of sensual pleasure; these are that monk's intoxication (mada) and negligence (pamāda).

In this way, a monk who is an heir to material things (āmisa-dāyāda) is not liberated from these evil states (the sixteen states such as greed) and other states of such nature. Thus, first, the states to be abandoned in this Dhammadāyāda Sutta should be understood. The method of abandonment is identical in all respects, both by way of the text and the meaning.

Furthermore, in this Noble Path, for the sake of proficiency in practicing with wisdom, this distinction, this sequence, and this method of development (bhāvanā) should be understood. Among those three, the distinction should first be understood thus: this Middle Way (majjhimā paṭipadā) is sometimes the Noble Eightfold Path and sometimes a seven-factored path. When this path arises by way of the supramundane first absorption (jhāna), it is an eightfold path; when it arises by way of the remaining absorptions, it is a seven-factored path. However, by way of the excellent exposition (ukkaṭṭhaniddesa), it is said here to be eightfold. Beyond this path, there are no further path factors. Thus, first, the distinction in this path should be understood.

Because among all wholesome states, Right View (sammā-diṭṭhi) is supreme, therefore it is said: 'The wise who possess merit say that wisdom alone is supreme.' In the section on the wholesome, Right View is also the precursor, as it is understood in detail: 'And how, bhikkhus, is Right View the precursor? One understands right view as right view, and one understands wrong view as wrong view.' Furthermore, it is said: 'Bhikkhus, true knowledge (vijjā) is the precursor for the attainment of wholesome states.' The remaining path factors arise from that Right View, as it is said: 'For one of Right View, Right Intention comes to be... (pe)... for one of Right Awareness, Right Concentration comes to be.' Therefore, these path factors are taught in this sequence; thus, the sequence in this path should be understood.

Regarding the method of development (bhāvanā-naya): some develop insight preceded by tranquillity (samatha-pubbaṅgamaṃ vipassanā), and some develop tranquillity preceded by insight (vipassanā-pubbaṅgamaṃ samatha). How? Here, someone first produces access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) or attainment concentration (appanā-samādhi); this is called tranquillity (samatha). He contemplates that tranquillity and its associated states through characteristics such as impermanence; this is called insight (vipassanā). Thus, first there is tranquillity, and later insight. Therefore, it is said: 'He develops insight preceded by tranquillity.' For him who develops insight preceded by tranquillity, the path is born. He [pursues] that path...
113: (That person) frequents, develops, and practices repeatedly. For him who frequents, develops, and practices that path, the fetters are abandoned, and the underlying tendencies are eliminated. Thus, he develops insight preceded by tranquility. But here in this Dispensation, some person, without first producing tranquility of the aforementioned kind, contemplates the five aggregates of clinging as impermanent and so forth. This contemplation is called insight. For him, due to the fulfillment of insight, one-pointedness of mind arises with the peaceful (Nibbāna) as its object among the states arisen therein. This is called tranquility. Thus, first insight, then tranquility. Therefore, it is said: "He develops tranquility preceded by insight." For him who develops tranquility preceded by insight, the path arises. He frequents that path... [pe]... practices it repeatedly. For him who frequents that path... [pe]... the underlying tendencies are eliminated. Thus, he develops tranquility preceded by insight. Whether one develops insight preceded by tranquility or tranquility preceded by insight, at the moment of the supramundane path, tranquility and insight are yoked together. Thus, the method of development should be understood here. ## The Commentary on the Dhammadāyāda Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished. ## 4. Commentary on the Bhayabherava Sutta "Thus have I heard"—this sutta is the Bhayabherava Sutta. Herein, this is the explanation of terms not previously explained: The word "atha" is a particle in the sense of non-interruption. The word "kho" is a particle in the sense of emphasis. It means that the Blessed One's dwelling in Sāvatthī was indeed uninterrupted. The name "Jāṇussoṇī" is not a name given by his parents. Rather, it is a name obtained by attaining a specific rank. The rank of Jāṇussoṇī is said to be the position of the royal chaplain (purohita). The king gave that position to him. Therefore, he is called "Jāṇussoṇī". He is called a "Brāhmaṇa" because he recites the Vedas; it means he recites and chants the mantras. This is the etymological definition for brahmins by birth. However, Noble Ones (Ariyas) are called "Brāhmaṇas" because they have expelled evil.
114: In the phrase "yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami", "yena" is the instrumental case used in the sense of location (locative). Therefore, it should be understood to mean: "Where the Blessed One was, there he approached." Alternatively, it should be understood as: "For whatever reason the Blessed One should be approached by devas and humans, for that reason he approached." For what reason should the Blessed One be approached? Just as flocks of birds approach a great tree that is always fruiting with the desire to enjoy sweet fruit, so too he approached with the desire to attain various and diverse special qualities. "Upasaṅkami" means he arrived. The word "upasaṅkamitvā" indicates the completion of the approach. Alternatively, it means having gone in this way and having reached a very close place called the vicinity of the Blessed One. "Saddhiṃ sammodi" means that just as the Blessed One asked the brahmin about his health and so on, causing joy, so too the brahmin shared that joy with the Blessed One. It was like cold water becoming one when mixed with hot water. "Master Gotama, are you well? Are you healthy? Are you and your disciples free from illness, free from affliction, able to rise quickly, endowed with strength, and living in comfort?"—with such words, he spoke joyfully. These words are called "sammodanīya" (rejoicing) because they generate the joy known as zest and gladness, and because they are suitable for rejoicing. They are called "sārāṇīya" (memorable) because they are worthy of being remembered for a very long time due to the sweetness of their meaning and phrasing, worthy of being maintained continuously, and because they ought to be remembered. They are "sammodanīya" because of the happiness felt upon hearing them, and "sārāṇīya" because of the happiness felt upon recollecting them. Similarly, they are "sammodanīya" due to the purity of the phrasing and "sārāṇīya" due to the purity of the meaning. Having thus concluded and finished the conversation which was delightful and memorable in many ways, desiring to ask about the purpose for which he had come, he sat down in a suitable place. The word "ekamantaṃ" is an adverbial neuter designation (bhāvanapuṃsakaniddesa), as in the passage "visamaṃ candimasūriyā parivattanti". Therefore, it should be understood here that he sat in such a way that his sitting was "to one side" (in a suitable place). Alternatively, this word "ekamantaṃ" is an accusative case used in the sense of location. "Nisīdi" means he entered nearby and sat down. Indeed, wise men, having approached a person worthy of respect, sit to one side because of their skill in seating. This brahmin was one of those wise men; therefore, he sat to one side. How does one sit so that it is called "sitting to one side"? By sitting while avoiding the six faults of sitting. These six faults are: a place too far, a place too near, a place upwind, a place on high ground, a place directly in front, and a place directly behind. If a person sitting in a place too far wishes to speak...
115:
If one sits too far away, one must speak with a loud voice. If one sits too near, one causes physical contact. If one sits upwind, one afflicts [the other] with body odor. If one sits on a high place, it manifests a lack of respect. If one sits directly in front, one must look eye-to-eye if one wishes to see. If one sits directly behind, one must stretch the neck to see if one wishes to see. Therefore, this person also sat down avoiding these six faults of sitting; with reference to such sitting, it is said, "he sat to one side."

"Yeme" is "ye ime." There are two types of "kulaputta" (clansmen): clansmen by birth (jāti-kulaputta) and clansmen by conduct (ācāra-kulaputta). Among them, those born into high families, as mentioned in the passage: "At that time, the clansman named Raṭṭhapāla was the son of the highest family in that very village of Thullakoṭṭhika," are called clansmen by birth. However, those who are endowed with good conduct, even if born into any family, as mentioned in the passage: "Those clansmen who have gone forth from home to homelessness out of faith," are called clansmen by conduct. In this context, they are called clansmen for both reasons.

"Saddhā" means by faith (with conviction). "Agārasmā" means from the house. "Anagāriya" refers to the state of a novice and the state of a monk. In this state of a monk, there are no worldly affairs such as plowing or cattle-rearing which are for the benefit of the household; thus it is called "anagāriya" (homelessness). For a monk, there is no such house; thus he is "anagāra" (homeless), and the state of being homeless is "anagāriya." "Pabbajitā" means they have entered or approached. Therefore, in every way, it means they have entered the state of a novice or the state of a monk, which is called homelessness. "Pubbaṅgama" means the leader who goes before. "Bahukāra" means one who is very helpful by performing beneficial acts. "The Venerable Gotama is the one who makes them undertake" means that the Venerable Gotama is the one who makes those clansmen take up and trains them in the higher virtue (adhisīla) and so on. "That group of people" refers to that assembly of people. "Follows the view" means they follow the practice according to what they see; whatever view, whatever patience, and whatever preference the Venerable Gotama has, they also have that view, that patience, and that preference.

Why did he say this? It is said that this Brahmin had previously seen many clansmen living in the midst of their homes, enjoying themselves with the five cords of sensual pleasure like young devas, with well-arranged protection both inside and out. Later, having heard the sweet Dhamma of the Blessed One, they went forth from their homes out of faith and...
116:
He had seen noble sons living in the midst of houses that were well-guarded and protected both inside and out. Later, having heard the sublime Dhamma of the Blessed One, they went forth from the household life out of faith and became monks. He saw those noble sons living in forest dwellings, content with mere food and clothing, and although unprotected by anyone, they were without fear or suspicion, being exceedingly joyful and elated. Seeing this, he thought, "Depending on what has this pleasant living of these noble sons arisen?" and realized, "It has arisen depending on the ascetic Gotama," thereby gaining faith in the Blessed One. That Brahmin came to the Blessed One to declare that faith; therefore, he spoke these words.

Then the Blessed One, wishing to accept and acknowledge those words and to express appreciation, said, "Brahmin, it is so," and so on. Here, the particle 'evaṃ' has the sense of acceptance and appreciation. "Referring to me (mamaṃ uddissa)" means referring to me, the Buddha. "Faith (saddhā)" means [going forth] only out of faith. It was said with reference to not being [driven to go forth] by being oppressed by debt or by danger. The Blessed One is the leader through practice only for those who go forth out of faith, not for others. "Difficult to endure (durabhisambhavāni)" means it is very painful and difficult to complete living in that forest. It means those with little merit are unable to enter and practice there. "Forest and woodland haunts (araññavanapatthāni)" refers to forests (arañña) and woodland haunts (vanapattha). In that regard, although in the Abhidhamma it is stated without figurative language that everything outside the village threshold is "forest," here it should be understood that only a dwelling at a distance of five hundred bow-lengths, which fulfills the factor of a forest-dweller, is intended.

"Woodland haunt (vanapattha)" is a place beyond the vicinity of a village, where people do not go, and which is neither ploughed nor sown. It is also said: "Woodland haunt" is a designation for remote dwellings, for forest thickets, for terrifying places, for places that cause hair to stand on end, for bordering areas, and for places that are not the resort of people. Here, excluding the single sense of "bordering," woodland haunts should be understood by the remaining senses. "Remote (pantāni)" means bordering or very distant places. "Difficult to attain seclusion (dukkaraṃ pavivekaṃ)" means physical seclusion is difficult to obtain. "Difficult to delight in (durabhiramaṃ)" means it is not easy to find delight. "In solitude (ekatte)" means in the state of being alone. What does this show? Even if physical seclusion is obtained, it is very difficult to make the mind delight in that forest. This is because this world delights only in being in pairs. "They seem to take away (haranti manye)" means as if they carry away or as if they devour. "Mind (mano)" refers to the mind. "For one not obtaining concentration (samādhiṃ alabhamānassa)" refers to a monk who does not obtain access concentration or absorption concentration. What does this show? It shows that for such a monk, the forests seem to distract the mind with various terrifying objects such as the sounds of grass, leaves, and wild animals. All this was spoken by the Brahmin in wonder and praise of the forest-dwelling of the noble sons who went forth out of faith.
117:
## Discussion on the Section of Bodily Action

Then the Blessed One, in the same manner as before, accepted the Brahmin's words with "Brahmin, it is so," and so on, and having expressed appreciation, [spoke further]. Because such dwellings are difficult to endure for those who are devoid of grasping the object in the sixteen instances, but not for those who possess the grasping of the object, and because he himself was such a person when he was a Bodhisatta, he said, "To me also," and so on, to show the fact that such dwellings were difficult to endure for those like himself.

In that text, "Before enlightenment (pubbeva sambodhā)" means in the period before obtaining the knowledge of the Noble Path. "For one who has not fully awakened (anabhisambuddhassa)" means for one who has not yet penetrated the Four Noble Truths. "Being a Bodhisatta (bodhisattasseva sato)" means being a being worthy of knowing the things that should be fully known, or being a being worthy of attaining Right Self-Enlightenment, or being a being attached to the knowledge of the Path. Indeed, from the time the aspiration was fulfilled by the meeting of the eight factors at the feet of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, the Tathāgata was a being attached to enlightenment, coming along without letting go of the effort to attain that knowledge of the Path, thinking, "This must be attained by me." Therefore, he is called a "Bodhisatta." "To me, such a one (tassa mayhaṃ)" means to me who was such a Bodhisatta. "Whatever recluses or brahmins (ye kho keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā)" refers to all those who have gone forth or those who say "bho" (brahmins).

"Impure in bodily actions (aparisuddhakāyakammantā)" refers to those possessed of bodily actions such as killing living beings, which are not pure. "Because of the fault of impure bodily actions (aparisuddhakāyakammantasandosahetu)" means because of one's own fault called impure bodily action, or because of the cause of impure bodily action. "Indeed (have)" is a particle expressing certainty. "Unwholesome (akusalaṃ)" means blameworthy and unsafe. "Fear and dread (bhayabheravaṃ)" refers to fear and the terrifying. This is a designation for the mind's alarm and for a terrifying object. Between those two, "fear (bhaya)" should be known as unwholesome in the sense of being blameworthy, and "dread (bherava)" as unwholesome in the sense of being unsafe. "They summon (avhāyantī)" means they call out, as it were. How do they call? Having committed acts such as killing living beings, they think, "We have done what should not be done; if those whom we have wronged should know, they will now pursue us and bring us to ruin." Thinking thus, they enter the forest and sit between trees or bushes. Even if they hear the slight sound of grass or leaves, they tremble and are terrified, thinking, "Now we are ruined!" They become as if surrounded by others, or as if bound and beaten. Thus, in the sense of attributing that fear and dread to themselves, it is said that they call out, as it were.
118:
"I do not... [pe]... resort to" means "I do not resort to remote forest dwellings and lodgings, far from people, as one who has impure bodily conduct." In the phrase "Ye hi vo," "vo" is merely a particle. "Ariyas" refers to the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddha. "Parisuddhakāyakammantā" means being those who have such pure bodily conduct. "Tesamahaṃ aññataro" means "I am also one among those Buddhas and Arahants." A Bodhisatta, whether a householder or one who has gone forth, is indeed one of pure bodily conduct. "Bhiyyo" is a particle used in the sense of "excessively" (atireka). "Pallomaṃ" means the stillness of the hair (absence of horripilation), safety, and well-being. "Āpādiṃ" means "I have reached" or "attained." It means having reached an exceeding well-being, or having reached well-being through an exceeding degree. "Araññe vihārāya" means for the purpose of dwelling in the forest.

## The explanation of the section on bodily conduct (kāyakammanta) is finished.

## Explanation of the section on verbal conduct (vacīkammanta) and so forth

This method is the same in all places. However, there is this distinction: in the section on verbal conduct, "those with impure verbal conduct" refers to those endowed with verbal conduct such as impure false speech and so on. How do they summon fear and dread? They destroy the welfare of others through false speech, cause division among friends through slander, pierce the vitals of others in the midst of an assembly with harsh speech, and destroy the work of beings with frivolous talk. Thinking, "We have done what is improper; if those whom we have wronged should know of us, they might now pursue us and bring us to ruin," they enter the forest and sit in the midst of bushes or groves. Hearing even the slight sound of grass or leaves, they tremble and are terrified, thinking, "Now we are lost." They become as if surrounded by others who have arrived, as if bound, or as if being killed. Thus, they are said to summon or call forth that fear and dread in the sense of attributing it to themselves.

In the section on mental conduct, "those with impure mental conduct" refers to those endowed with mental conduct such as impure covetousness and so on. How do they summon fear and dread? They give rise to unrighteous greed, which is covetousness, regarding the goods guarded and protected by others; they become angry at others; they cause beings to hold wrong views. Thinking, "We have done what is improper... [pe]..." they are said to summon or call forth fear and dread in the sense of attributing it to themselves.
119:
In the section on livelihood, "impure livelihood" (aparisuddhājīva) refers to being endowed with livelihood consisting of the twenty-one kinds of improper search (anesana), such as medical practice, acting as a messenger, and the practice of usury. How do they summon fear and dread? While leading such a life, they hear: "It is said that the Tipiṭaka-bearing monks who purify the Sāsana have set out to purify the Sāsana; they will arrive here today or tomorrow." Then, entering the forest... [pe]... they tremble and are terrified. They become as if those [purifiers] have arrived and surrounded and captured them, and as if they have been made to wear white clothes (disrobed). The rest of the words are just as said before.

From here on, in the words such as "covetous" (abhijjhālū), although covetousness and ill-will are already included in mental conduct, it should be understood that they are mentioned again by way of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). In that text, "abhijjhālū" means one who has the habit of coveting others' property and so on. "Kāmesu tibbasārāgā" means having thick sensual passion for the objects of sensual pleasure. How do they summon fear and dread? They have unsteady (unfixed) objects of focus. For those who dwell in the forest with unsteady objects of focus, what was seen during the day appears as a fearful object at night. With agitated minds, they tremble and are terrified even at a slight cause. Seeing a rope or a vine, they perceive it as a snake. Seeing a stump, they perceive it as a demon (yakkha). Seeing a mound or a mountain, they perceive it as an elephant. They become as if they have met with ruin because of snakes and so forth. The rest of the words are just as said in the section on the covetous.

"Byāpannacittā" (malevolent mind) means having a mind that is ruined by abandoning its natural state. Indeed, a mind that follows the defilements abandons its natural state and becomes foul like old rice and curry. "Paduṭṭhamanasaṅkappā" means having corrupt mental intentions, being endowed with mental intentions that are bad and produce harm for others. How do they summon fear and dread? The summoning of fear and dread from here on should be understood in the same way as described in the section on the covetous. Where there is a distinction, we shall speak of it. In the passage "Na kho panāhaṃ byāpannacitto," [the Buddha] shows: "I have a mind of loving-kindness, I have a mind desiring welfare." Indeed, Bodhisattas are like this. Thus, in all places, the virtues of the Bodhisatta should be praised by way of being the opposite of the mentioned faults.

"Thinamiddhapariyuṭṭhitā" means being obsessed or overcome by sloth (thina), which is a sickness of the mind, and torpor (middha), which is a sickness of the remaining mental body (nāmakāya). It means they are overcome or seized. They tend to sleep a lot.
120:
The Blessed One shows this. Indeed, Bodhisattas possess minds concerned with the welfare of beings. Thus, in all matters, the virtues of the Bodhisatta are praised by way of the opposite of the aforementioned faults.

"Thinamiddhapariyuṭṭhitā" means being oppressed, overwhelmed, and obsessed by 'thina', which is the dullness and heaviness of the mind, and 'middha', which is the dullness and heaviness of the remaining mental body (nāmakāya). Those ascetics and brahmins are those who sleep excessively.

"Uddhatā" refers to those who have a restless nature and a highly agitated mind. This is because, due to restlessness (uddhacca), the mind flutters on a single object, just as a banner on a flagpole flutters in the wind. "Avūpasantacittā" (or 'appasantacittā' in the Nissaya) refers to those with unpeaceful minds; in this context, it is appropriate to take it as remorse (kukkucca).

In the phrase "Kaṅkhī Vicikicchī", this fifth hindrance (nīvaraṇa) is essentially one. It is called 'kaṅkhā' (doubt) because of doubting the object, asking, "What kind of object is this?" It is called 'vicikicchā' (wavering) because of the inability to decide, "This object is certainly of this nature." Ascetics and brahmins endowed with such wavering are called "Kaṅkhī Vicikicchī".

"Attukkaṃsanaka Paravambhī" refers to those who exalt themselves, lifting themselves up to a high position, while disparaging and blaming others, placing them in a low position. How do they summon fearful objects? When others pursue them, saying, "This person exalts himself and disparages us like slaves; catch him!", they flee and enter the forest, hiding among trees and bushes. This should be understood in detail as being similar to the results of bodily actions (kāyakammanta).

"Chambhī" refers to those endowed with stiffness, which causes bodily rigidity and the standing of hair on end. "Bhīrukajātika" refers to those who are timid by nature, being full of fear and lacking courage, like village children.

In the term "Lābhasakkārasiloka", it is called 'lābha' (gain) because it is obtained; this is a name for the four requisites. 'Sakkāra' (honor) refers to requisites that are well-prepared. Only those requisites that are prepared to be excellent among the excellent, and best among the best, are called 'sakkāra'. It also refers to the acts of respect shown by others or offerings made with flowers and such. 'Siloka' (fame) refers to the speaking of praise. The combination of gain, honor, and fame is called 'lābhasakkārasiloka'. "Nikāmayamāna" means longing for or desiring. Summoning fearful objects is just like the way of the covetous. To clarify this meaning, the story of Piyagāmika is told:

It is said that a monk named Piyagāmika, seeing the gains received by monks who practiced the dhutaṅga austerities, thought, "I too will undertake dhutaṅga and bring about gains." He undertook the cemetery-dweller's practice (sosānikanga) and lived in a cemetery. One day, an old ox that had been released from work, having grazed during the day, stood chewing its cud at night with its head tucked into a flower bush in that cemetery. The monk Piyagāmika, coming out from his walking path (caṅkamana) at night...
121:
...coming out from the walking path, that monk heard the sound of the ox's jaw moving and thought, "Surely the King of Devas, knowing that this monk lives in the cemetery because he is greedy for gain, has come to harass me." He raised his hands in salutation (añjali) before the old ox and stood praying throughout the three watches of the night, saying, "O virtuous King of Devas, please forgive me for just this one night. From tomorrow onwards, I will not do such a thing again." Then, when the sun rose and he saw the ox, he struck it with a bamboo staff and drove it away, saying, "You made me terrified all night!"

"Kusītā" refers to those who follow after indolence (kosajja). "Hīnavīriyā" refers to those with inferior energy, those devoid of effort, meaning they are without energy. Between these two, 'kusīta' individuals lack the initiation of physical effort (kāyika-vīriya). 'Hīnavīriya' individuals lack the initiation of mental effort (cetasika-vīriya). They are unable to perform even the mere defining of an object. Regarding those who cannot define an object, the entire passage is the same as previously stated.

"Muṭṭhassatī" refers to those with lost mindfulness. "Asampajānā" refers to those devoid of wisdom (paññā). Because the Buddha taught the opposite of this as "I am one with established mindfulness," this quality belongs to the category of mindfulness. However, the word 'wisdom' (paññā) is used here to show the weakness of mindfulness. Indeed, mindfulness is of two kinds: mindfulness associated with wisdom and mindfulness dissociated from wisdom. Among them, mindfulness associated with wisdom is strong. Mindfulness dissociated from wisdom is weak. Therefore, even when mindfulness arises in them, if they lack clear comprehension (asampajāna), they are still "muṭṭhassatī" (forgetful). To show this meaning—that due to weak mindfulness, the function of mindfulness cannot be performed—the term "asampajānā" was spoken. The entire passage stating that those who are thus forgetful and lacking clear comprehension cannot perform even the mere defining of an object is the same as previously stated.

"Asamāhitā" refers to those devoid of access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi). "Vibbhantacittā" refers to those with unsettled minds. Due to restlessness (uddhacca) which finds an opportunity through the absence of concentration, the minds of those lacking concentration wander among various objects. Like a forest monkey roaming among forest branches, the mind flutters on a single object due to restlessness. In the same manner as previously stated, the entire passage saying that those who are thus unconcentrated and have unsettled minds cannot perform even the mere defining of an object is the same as previously stated.

"Duppaññā" is a name for those without wisdom. As for wisdom (paññā), there is no such thing as 'bad' (duṭṭhā) wisdom. "Eḷamūgā" is derived from 'eḷamukha' (faulty mouth), where the letter 'kh' has been changed to 'g'. It means those with a driveling mouth. Indeed, when the unwise speak, saliva flows from their mouths. Saliva is also...
122:
Saliva is called "elā" because it tends to leak from the mouth; therefore, such persons are called "eḷamūga" (drooling-mutes). This is as taught in the verse: "Passela-mūgaṃ uragaṃ dujjivhaṃ." Thus, they are called "eḷamūga." There is also a variant reading "elamukha." Some read it as "eḷamūga," while others read it as "elamuka," but in all places, the meaning is "elamukha" (one with a mouth from which saliva leaks). How do they call out to fear and dread? Those eḷamūga individuals of little wisdom are unable to perform even the mere discernment of an object. For those who cannot discern objects and are living in the forest, an object seen during the day appears as something terrifying at night. Having confused minds, they are startled and terrified by even the slightest thing; seeing a rope or a vine, they perceive it as a snake; seeing a tree stump, they perceive it as a yakkha; seeing a mound or a mountain, they perceive it as an elephant. They become as if they have met with disaster and ruin due to snakes and such. In this way, they call out or summon that fear and dread by attributing it to themselves. In the phrase "I am one endowed with wisdom," the term "endowed with wisdom" does not refer to being endowed with insight wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) or path wisdom (magga-paññā), but rather it means being endowed with the wisdom that discerns objects in these sixteen bases. The remaining words are to be understood in the same manner as previously stated in all places.

## The Discernment of Objects in the Sixteen Bases is Finished.

## Description of Lodgings that Cause Fear and Dread, etc.

What is the connection of the words "tassa mayhaṃ"? It is said that while the Bodhisatta was discerning these sixteen objects, he did not encounter fear and dread, and he thought: "Fear and dread truly manifest on such nights and in such lodgings; come now, I shall search for it right there." Thus, he made a search for fear and dread. To show this matter to the brahmin now, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with "tassa mayhaṃ."

In that passage, both words "yā tā" refer only to the nights. In the word "abhiññātā," "abhi" is a prefix (upasagga) in the sense of a sign or characteristic. Therefore, "abhiññātā" should be understood as "known by signs" such as the fullness of the moon or the waning of the moon. In the word "abhilakkhitā," the "abhi" is merely a prefix; therefore, "abhilakkhitā" means days that are to be marked. It means they are to be noted, well-noted, and closely-noted for the purpose of undertaking the Uposatha, listening to the Dhamma, and performing offerings and honors.
123:
"Cātuddasī" (the fourteenth) is the fourteenth night starting from the first day of the fortnight. Likewise, the fifteenth (pañcadasī) and the eighth (aṭṭhamī). "Pakkha" (fortnight) refers to the waxing fortnight and the waning fortnight. Since there are three such days in each fortnight (8th, 14th, 15th), there are six nights in total; therefore, the word "pakkha" should be applied in every instance: "the fourteenth of the fortnight, the fifteenth of the fortnight, the eighth of the fortnight." Why was the fifth day (pañcamī) not included? Because it was not a day observed at all times. It is said that whether the Blessed Buddha had not yet appeared or had appeared but not yet attained Parinibbāna, the fifth day was not specifically marked. However, after the Parinibbāna, the Elders who were the Recorders of the Dhamma (Dhamma-saṅgāhaka) thought, "It has been a long time since the hearing of the Dhamma." Having consulted together, they established the fifth day as a day for hearing the Dhamma. From then on, it became a marked day. Thus, because it was not observed at all times, it was not included here.

"Tathārūpāsu" means on such nights (the 14th, 15th, and 8th). "Ārāma-cetiyāni": parks such as flower parks and fruit parks are themselves called "ārāma-cetiya." They are called "cetiya" in the sense of being honored; it means in the sense of being worthy of worship. "Vana-cetiyāni": forests such as those where offerings are made, Subhaga forest, and Devasāla forest are themselves called "vana-cetiya." "Rukkha-cetiyāni": trees worthy of worship at the gates of villages and market towns are themselves called "rukkha-cetiya." Worldly people, thinking "these are inhabited by deities" or having the perception of deities in them, honor and worship these parks, forests, and trees; therefore, they are all called "cetiya." "Bhīṃsanakāni" means causing fear; they generate fear in those who see or hear them. "Salomahaṃsāni" means they exist together with hair-raising (horripilation), because they cause hair-raising the moment one enters. "Appeva nāma passeyyaṃ" means "If only I might see that fear and dread." "Aparena samayena" means at another time, starting from the time he thought, "What if I were to..."

"Tattha ca me brāhmaṇa viharato" means "to me, Brahmin, dwelling there" in such lodgings. It refers to the haunts of yakkhas where humans make petitions and offerings; where the ground is scattered and moistened with flowers, incense, meat, blood, fat, marrow, spleens, lungs, and fermented spirits, appearing like a gathering place for yakkhas, rakkhasas, and pisācas; places which, when seen even by day, seem as if they would break the heart. Referring to such places, He said, "To me, Brahmin, dwelling there." "Mago vā āgacchati": a wild animal (maga) such as a gokaṇṇa, a rhinoceros, a leopard, or a boar comes, striking its horns or hooves. Here, the name "maga" refers to all four-footed animals. In some places, it also refers to a black jackal. As it was said: "O black jackal, your voice is like that of a bull, your gait is like that of a lion; King of beasts, let there be salutation to you, may we obtain some food." "Moro vā": a peacock, or the wind, causes dry leaves to shake and fall from a tree. By mentioning the peacock, all birds are intended. "Vāto vā": the wind also causes dry leaves to rustle. "Bhayaṃ āganti" means that terrifying object comes; it means the thought arises, "This is indeed a terrifying object."
124:
“Your shoulder is like that of a bull, and your gait is like that of a lion. O King of beasts, may homage be paid to you; may we receive a little food,” (it is said).

“Moro vā kaṭṭhaṃ pāteti” means a peacock (or another bird) shaking a dry branch from a tree and making it fall. By the mention of “peacock,” all birds are intended here; thus, it means any bird whatsoever. Alternatively, by the word “vā,” it means some other bird. This same method applies to the previous mention of “maga” (beast). “Vāto vā paṇṇakasaṭaṃ ereti” means the wind blowing dry leaves and rubbish. “Etaṃ nūna taṃ bhayabheravaṃ āgacchati” means (thinking), “This object that is coming is indeed fear and terror.” From this point on, the object itself should be understood as “fear and terror” (bhayabherava). Because it is the object of both slight and extreme fear, just as a visual object that is the object of happiness is like happiness itself (so too the object of fear is like fear).

“Kiṃ nu kho ahaṃ aññadatthu bhayapaṭikaṅkhī viharāမိ” means, “Why should I live as one who certainly expects and desires fear?”

“Yathābhūtaṃ yathābhūtassa” means for one who is in whatever posture, existing, occurring, or fully present. “Me” means near me. “Tathābhūtaṃ tathābhūto vā” means being in that very posture, existing, occurring, or fully present. “So kho ahaṃ... pe... paṭivinemi”: It is said that when a fearful object, such as the sound of animal horns or hooves, comes to the Bodhisatta while he is walking, the Great Being does not stand, sit, or lie down. Instead, while still walking, he investigates and reflects, and when he does not see any fear and terror—realizing it is merely the sound of horns or hooves—he knows, “This is such-and-such a thing; it is not fear and terror.” Only then does he stand, sit, or lie down. To show this meaning, he said “So kho ahaṃ” and so on. This method applies to all elisions (peyyāla). From here on, it should be understood that the postures are mentioned not in their regular order but in the order of proximity. For if fear comes while walking, he does not stand, sit, or lie down (but dispels it in that very posture); if it comes while standing, he does not walk, and so on; thus, they are mentioned in the order of proximity.

Having shown his lack of fearful objects in such terrifying places, he now says “Santi kho pana brāhmaṇa” and so on to show his living without delusion (asammohavihāra) in matters where meditators are deluded. In that Pali, “santi” means they exist, are present, are found. “Rattiṃyeva santaṃ divāti sañjānanti” means although it is night, they perceive it as “This is daytime.”
125:
## Commentary on Living without Delusion (Asammohavihāravaṇṇanā)

After showing his lack of fear and dread in such terrifying places, he now says “Santi kho pana, brāhmaṇa” and so on to show his living without delusion (asammohavihāra) in matters where meditators are deluded.

In that Pali, “santi” means they exist, are present, are found. “Rattiṃyeva samānaṃ” means although it is night, “divāti sañjānanti” means they perceive it as “This is daytime.” “Divāyeva samānaṃ” means although it is day, “rattīti sañjānanti” means they perceive it as “This is nighttime.” Why do they have such perceptions? It is either due to a lack of skill in emerging from jhāna or due to the sound of birds.

How? In this world, a certain person who has attained the white kasina (odātakasiṇa) performs the preliminary work during the day, enters the attainment, and resolves, “I shall emerge during the day.” However, he is not skilled in determining the duration of time. He passes the day and emerges during the night. Because of the pervading white kasina, the light appears clear and distinct to him. Because of his initial resolution to emerge during the day and the clarity of the white kasina’s light, he perceives it as day even though it is night.

In this world, another person who has attained the blue kasina (nīlakasiṇa) performs the preliminary work at night, enters the attainment, and resolves, “I shall emerge during the night.” However, he is not skilled in determining the duration of time. He passes the night and emerges during the day. Because of the pervading blue kasina, the light is not clear or distinct to him. Because of his initial resolution to emerge at night and the dark nature of the blue kasina, he perceives it as night even though it is day. Thus, they have such perceptions due to a lack of skill in emerging from jhāna.

Regarding the perception due to bird calls: In this world, a certain person stays inside a dwelling. Then, birds that usually cry during the day, such as crows, cry at night, thinking it is day because of the moonlight, or for other reasons. Hearing their sound, he perceives it as day even though it is night.

In this world, another person stays in a mountain cave, deep and covered by thick forest, during a seven-day period of heavy clouds when the sunlight is hidden. Then, birds that cry at night, such as owls, cry even at midday, perched in various dark places, either perceiving it as night or for other reasons. Hearing their sound, he perceives it as night even though it is day. Thus, they have such perceptions due to the sound of birds.

“Idamahaṃ” should be resolved as “idaṃ ahaṃ.” The Buddha says that he regards such people who have these perceptions as being among those who “live in delusion” (sammohavihāra). For the Bodhisatta, however, the distinction between night and day was clear. Even during a seven-day period of heavy clouds when the moon and sun were not visible, he knew, “This much time is before the meal; this much time is after the meal.”
126:
Sañjānanaṃ means perceiving (knowing). When it is cloudy for seven days in a mountain hollow and the sunlight is obscured, a person sitting there might perceive it as night, even during the day, upon hearing the cries of birds such as owls. In the statement "I speak of the dwelling in delusion," it refers to anyone who is included in or falls within such a dwelling in delusion.

In the words, "Brahmin, I... know," the Bodhisatta's discernment of the distinction between night and day is very clear. Even when the moon and sun are not visible during a seven-day period of thick clouds, he knows: "This much time has passed before the meal, this much after the meal; this much is the first watch, this much the middle watch, and this much the last watch." Therefore, he spoke thus. It is not surprising that a Bodhisatta who has fulfilled the perfections (pūritapāramī) knows in this way. Even for disciples established in partial knowledge (padesañāṇa), the distinction between night and day is clear.

It is said that at the Kalyāṇiya Mahāvihāra, Elder Godatta used to take his meal when the shadow was two fingers long and finish eating when it was one finger long. Even when the sun was not visible, he would enter his dwelling early and exit at that exact time. One day, the park attendants, thinking, "Let us observe the time the Elder exits tomorrow," prepared the meal and sat near the time-post (sundial). The Elder exited exactly when the shadow was not yet beyond two fingers. From then on, even when the sun was not visible, they would strike the drum based on the sign of the Elder's exit.

Also, at the Ajagara Vihāra, Elder Kāḷadeva used to strike the watch-drum (yāmaghaṇḍika) during the rainy season. This was the Elder's constant habit. He did not use a water clock (yantanaḷikā), though other monks did. When the first watch ended, the Elder would simply stand holding the mallet, or strike it once or twice, and the water clock would drop. After practicing the recluse's duties (samaṇadhamma) through the three watches, the Elder would enter the village for alms early in the morning, return to the monastery, take his bowl at mealtime, go to a day-rest place, and practice the recluse's duties. The monks, looking at the noon-post and not seeing the Elder, would send someone to invite him. That monk would see the Elder either coming out of his day-rest place or on the way. If the distinction between night and day is thus clear even to disciples with partial knowledge, what need is there to speak of the Bodhisattas?

In this passage, "Brahmin, whatever words... one might say," it means: "Brahmin, when a being of non-deluded nature has arisen in the world... it is for the happiness of devas and humans."
128:
In that Pali, the phrase "Brahmin, my energy was indeed exerted" means: Brahmin, this noble abiding without delusion (asammohavihāra) of mine was not attained by one who is lazy, unmindful, whose body is restless, or whose mind is distracted. On the contrary, to attain that abiding without delusion, I indeed exerted energy. While sitting at the seat of enlightenment (Bodhi-maṇḍa), I exerted energy endowed with four factors (caturangaviriya); it means the energy was upheld and continuously applied without slackening. Because that energy was exerted, my mind remained undaunted.

'Upatṭhitā sati asammutṭhā' (mindfulness was established and unconfused) means that not only was energy present, but my mindfulness was also established by being directed toward the object. Because it was so established, it was unforgetting. 'Passaddho kāyo' (the body was tranquil) means that because of the arising of tranquility in both body and mind, my body also became tranquil. In this context, since the physical body (rūpakāya) also becomes tranquil when the mental body (nāmakāya) is tranquil, it is stated as 'passaddho kāyo' (the body was tranquil) without making a distinction between the mental and physical bodies. 'Asāraddho' (not agitated) means that because the body was tranquil, it was without feverish heat; it means it was free from distress. 'Samāhitaṃ cittaṃ ekaggaṃ' (the mind was concentrated and one-pointed) means my mind was also well-placed on the object; it remained well-established as if it were fixed in absorption (appanā). Because the mind was well-concentrated, it remained one-pointed and unmoving without wavering. By this much, the preliminary practice (pubbabāgapatipadā) occurring before the actual jhana is described.

Now, wishing to show the distinction starting from the first jhana attained through this practice and ending with the three true knowledges (vijjā), the Buddha said the words beginning with "So kho ahaṃ" (I, indeed). In that Pali, regarding the passage "Secluded from sensual pleasures... I entered and dwelt in the fourth jhana," everything that should be said has already been stated in the Pathavīkasiṇa section of the Visuddhimagga. The only difference is that in the Visuddhimagga it appears as "upasampajja viharati" (he enters and dwells), whereas here it appears as "vihāsiṃ" (I dwelt). By performing what action did the Blessed One dwell having attained these jhanas? He dwelt having developed a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). Which meditation subject? He dwelt having developed the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati).

Furthermore, these four jhanas serve the purpose of one-pointedness of mind for some; for some, they serve as the basis for insight (vipassanāpādaka); for some, as the basis for supernormal knowledge (abhiññāpādaka); for some, as the basis for the attainment of cessation (nirodhapādaka); and for some, they serve the purpose of entering a new existence (bhavokkamanattha). Among them, for the Arahants, they serve the purpose of one-pointedness of mind. Thinking, "We shall dwell happily throughout the day with a concentrated mind by attaining these," they perform the preliminary work for the kasiṇa and produce the eight attainments. For the trainees (sekha) and worldlings (puthujjana), the jhanas produced with the intention, "We shall practice insight with a concentrated mind after emerging from the attainment," serve as the basis for insight. For those who, having produced the eight attainments and having entered the jhana that serves as the basis for supernormal knowledge, emerge from that attainment...
129:
...and desire supernormal knowledge (abhiññā) according to the method stated as "Being one, he becomes many," the jhanas serve as the basis for supernormal knowledge. For those who, having produced the eight attainments and entered the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), intend to dwell happily having reached Nibbāna, which is called cessation, in this very life by being without consciousness for seven days, the jhanas serve as the basis for cessation. For those who, having produced the eight attainments, intend to be reborn in the Brahma world without declining from jhana, the jhanas serve the purpose of entering a new existence.

The Blessed One, however, produced this fourth jhana at the root of the Bodhi tree. It should be understood that for the Blessed One, that fourth jhana served as the basis for insight, the basis for supernormal knowledge, the accomplisher of all tasks, and the giver of all mundane and supramundane qualities.

## Explanation of the Talk on Recollection of Past Lives

Wishing to show a portion of those qualities which the jhana provided, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with "So evaṃ samāhite citte" (When the mind was thus concentrated). In that context, the sequential explanation of the two true knowledges (vijjā) and the method of development (bhāvanā) have been detailed in the Visuddhimagga. Specifically, in that Visuddhimagga, it is stated as "So evaṃ samāhite citte... abhininnāmeti" (He thus... directs), whereas in this commentary (Papañcasūdanī), it is said as "abhininnāmesiṃ" (I directed). This section on absorption (appanāvāra) beginning with "Ayaṃ kho me brāhmaṇa" does not appear in the Visuddhimagga; this is the only distinction. In that passage, "so" means "that I." "Abhininnāmesiṃ" means "I directed forth." Because it is taught as "abhininnāmesiṃ," the meaning of the word "so" should be understood as "that I."

Since this knowledge of the recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa) is presented through the power of the Blessed One, the connection in the phrase "So tato cuto idhūpapanno" (He, having passed away from there, was reborn here) should be understood as follows: Here, "so tato cuto" (he, having passed away from there) is a reflection made by looking back. Therefore, the phrase "idhūpapanno" (reborn here) refers to the state immediately following the rebirth into this final existence. The words "amutra udapādi" (arose there) should be understood as referring to the Tusita heaven. "Tatrāpāsiṃ evaṃnāmo" means that in that Tusita heaven, I was a deity named Setaketu. "Evaṃgotto" means having the same clan as those Tusita deities. "Evaṃvaṇṇo" means having a complexion like the color of gold. "Evaṃāhāro" means having the divine ambrosia (sudhā) as food. "Evaṃsukhadukkhappaṭisaṃvedī" means experiencing divine pleasure in this way. As for suffering, it was merely the suffering of formations (saṅkhāradukkha). "Evaṃāyupariyanto" means having a lifespan limited to 570,600,000 years.
130:
‘So tato cuto’ means that I passed away from that Tusita heaven. ‘Idhūpapanno’ means being born here in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā.

In the passages beginning with ‘Ayaṃ kho me brāhmaṇa’, ‘me’ means ‘by me’ (mayā). It is called ‘vijjā’ (knowledge) in the sense of making things known. What does it make known? It makes known former dwellings (pubbenivāsa). Because it makes that former dwelling unknown, the delusion that covers it is called ‘avijjā’ (ignorance). That same delusion is called ‘tamo’ (darkness) in the sense of obscuring. That same knowledge is called ‘āloko’ (light) in the sense of illuminating. Here, ‘vijjā adhigatā’ means this very sense, and the remaining words are words of praise. The construction (yojanā) here is: ‘I have attained this knowledge; for me who has attained such knowledge, ignorance has vanished.’ Why? Because knowledge has arisen. This same method applies to the other two terms.

In the phrase ‘yathā taṃ’, ‘yathā’ is used in the sense of a simile, and ‘taṃ’ is a particle. ‘Appamattassa’ means for one who is heedful (appamatta) because of not being devoid of mindfulness. ‘Ātāpino’ means for one who is ardent (ātāpi) because of the heat of energy. ‘Pahitattassa’ means for one who is resolute (pahitatta) because of having a mind sent forth [to the goal] without regard for body or life. This is what is meant: Just as for a person who dwells heedfully, ardently, and resolutely, ignorance would vanish and knowledge would arise, and darkness would vanish and light would arise; even so, for me, ignorance has vanished and knowledge has arisen, darkness has vanished and light has arisen. I have obtained the fruit appropriate to this exertion of mine.

## The explanation of the talk on recollecting past lives is finished.

## Explanation of the Knowledge of the Divine Eye

In the talk on passing away and rebirth (cutūpapāta), because the Pali text comes by way of the power of the Blessed One in this Sutta, it is said, ‘I see, I know.’ This is the distinction. The rest is the same as what is said in the Visuddhimagga.

Here, ‘vijjā’ refers to the knowledge of the divine eye (dibbacakkhuñāṇa). ‘Avijjā’ refers to the ignorance that covers the passing away and rebirth of beings. The rest is according to the method already mentioned. Furthermore, for Great Beings (Mahāsattas) who have fulfilled the perfections, there is no such thing as preliminary preparation (parikamma). For them, just by inclining the mind...
131:
...they can recollect various former dwellings and see beings with the divine eye. Therefore, the method of meditation starting with preparation mentioned in that [Visuddhimagga] is of no use here.

## Explanation of the Knowledge of the Destruction of the Taints

In the third knowledge, ‘evaṃ samāhite citte’ (when the mind was thus concentrated) should be understood as the fourth jhāna mind which is the basis for insight. ‘Āsavānaṃ khayañāṇāya’ (for the knowledge of the destruction of the taints) means for the sake of the knowledge of the path of Arahatship. Indeed, the path of Arahatship is called ‘āsavānaṃ khaya’ (the destruction of the taints) because it destroys the taints, and this knowledge is so called because it is included in that destruction. ‘Cittaṃ abhininnāmesiṃ’ means I directed the insight-mind forward. In the sentences beginning with ‘This is suffering’, the Blessed One understood through higher knowledge, knew, and penetrated all the truth of suffering as it really is, by penetrating its individual essence, thinking, ‘Suffering is only this much; there is nothing beyond this.’ He understood through higher knowledge, knew, and penetrated the craving that produces that suffering as ‘This is the origin of suffering.’ He understood through higher knowledge, knew, and penetrated that place where both [suffering and its origin] reach and cease—that Nibbāna which is the non-occurrence of those two truths—as ‘This is the cessation of suffering.’ He understood through higher knowledge, knew, and penetrated the Noble Path that leads to that Nibbāna as ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering,’ by penetrating its individual essence as it really is. This is how the meaning should be understood.

Having thus shown the truths by their nature, now wishing to show them by way of defilements through a figurative method (pariyāya), he said ‘These are the taints,’ and so on. ‘Tassa me evaṃ jānato evaṃ passato’ means for me, knowing thus and seeing thus. This describes the Path that has reached its peak along with insight. ‘Kāmāsavā’ means from the taint of sensual desire. By the word ‘vimuccittha’ (was liberated), the moment of the Fruit (phala) is shown; for at the moment of the Path, the mind is being liberated, and at the moment of the Fruit, it is liberated. By the phrase ‘vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ’ (in the liberated [mind], the knowledge [arose] that it is liberated), the reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa) is shown. ‘Khīṇā jātī’ (Birth is destroyed) and so on show its objective field (bhūmi). The Blessed One, reviewing with that knowledge, understood through higher knowledge that ‘Birth is destroyed,’ and so on. What kind of birth of the Blessed One is destroyed, and how did he know it? First of all, his past birth cannot be destroyed, because it has already been destroyed. Future birth is not [yet] destroyed, because there is no exertion in the future. Present birth is not destroyed, because it is currently existing. However, the birth consisting of one, four, or five constituents in the one-constituent, four-constituent, or five-constituent existence, which would have arisen because the Path had not yet been developed, is now destroyed by attaining the state of non-arising (anuppādadhammatā) because the Path has been developed. The Blessed One, having reviewed the defilements abandoned by the development of the Path, knew and understood through higher knowledge: ‘Because of the absence of defilements, even the existing kamma will not result in rebirth in the future.’
132:
What kind of birth is exhausted, and how is it known? First, the birth in the past successions of the Blessed One cannot be exhausted because it has already ended in previous lives. Birth in future successions cannot be exhausted because no effort has been made yet. Birth in the present life is not yet exhausted because it is still manifest. However, because the Path has been developed, the birth consisting of one, four, or five aggregates that would have occurred in the one-constituent, four-constituent, or five-constituent realms has reached the state of non-arising and is thus exhausted. The Blessed One, reflecting on the defilements abandoned by developing the Path, and knowing that the manifest karma no longer has the nature to produce rebirth since there are no more defilements, understood that birth with penetrative insight.

'Vusitaṃ' means lived, practiced, or reached completion. 'Brahmacariyaṃ' refers to the noble practice of the Path (magga-brahmacariya). The seven types of trainees (sekha), along with the virtuous worldlings (kalyāṇa-puthujjana), are those who are living the holy life, whereas the Arahant is one who has lived it. Therefore, the Blessed One, reflecting on the completion of his own holy life, understood with penetrative insight: 'The holy life has been lived.' 'Kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ' means that the sixteen-fold tasks regarding the Four Noble Truths—by way of full understanding (pariññā), abandonment (pahāna), realization (sacchikiriyā), and development (bhāvanā) through the four Paths—have been completed. While virtuous worldlings and others are still performing these tasks, the Arahant is one who has finished what was to be done. Therefore, the Blessed One, reflecting on the completion of his own tasks, understood with penetrative insight: 'Done is what was to be done.'

'Nāparaṃ itthattāya' means he understood that there is no more task of developing the Path for the sake of these sixteen-fold Path-tasks or for the destruction of defilements. Alternatively, 'itthattāya' means that from this state, from this current continuity of aggregates, there is no further continuity of aggregates for me. These five aggregates, having been fully understood, remain like uprooted trees. He understood with penetrative insight that those aggregates, with the cessation of the final consciousness, will be extinguished like a fire without fuel.

Now, wishing to show the Brahmin the attainment of the knowledge of the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa) as grasped by the knowledge of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa), he spoke the words beginning with 'Ayaṃ kho me brāhmaṇa.' In that text, 'Vijjā' refers to the knowledge of the Path of Arahantship, and 'Avijjā' refers to the ignorance that covers the Four Noble Truths. The remaining terms are to be understood as previously explained. With this sequence of words, he encompassed all the qualities of omniscience (sabbaññuta) through the three knowledges—knowledge of the past through the recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa), knowledge of the present and future through the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), and all mundane and supramundane qualities through the destruction of taints—and thus revealed his dwelling in non-delusion to the Brahmin.

## Aranyavāsakāraṇavaṇṇanā

When this was said, it is said that the Brahmin thought: 'The ascetic Gotama claims omniscience, yet even now he does not give up living in the forest. Does this ascetic Gotama still have some other task to perform?' Then the Blessed One, knowing the Brahmin's intention, spoke the words beginning with 'Siyā kho pana te' as a connection to that intention. In that text, 'Siyā kho pana te, brāhmaṇa, evamassa' means 'Brahmin, it may be that you might have such a thought.' 'Na kho panetaṃ, brāhmaṇa, evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ' means 'Brahmin, you should not regard my living in the forest in this way.' Reflecting on his own pleasant dwelling in the present life, he said, 'Dve kho ahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, atthavase paṭicca...' In that text, 'atthavasaṃ' means reason or cause. Therefore, it means, 'Brahmin, because I clearly see two reasons...' In the phrase 'attano diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāraṃ,' 'diṭṭhadhamma' refers to this present existence, and 'sukhavihāra' refers to the comfort of the four postures. Indeed, for a monk living alone in the forest, all postures, from the simplest tasks like defecation and urination onwards, are comfortable.
133:
It should not be regarded that resorting to secluded dwellings is due to not being free from lust and so forth. Having rejected the notion that there is no reason for resorting to such secluded dwellings, and wishing to show the actual reason, the Buddha said, "Brahmin, I [see] two reasons..." and so forth. In that passage, the meaning itself is called 'atthavasa' (reason). Therefore, "Brahmin, I [see] two reasons" means "Brahmin, it is because I clearly see two benefits, two reasons."

In the phrase "a pleasant dwelling for oneself in this very life," 'diṭṭhadhamma' refers to this present existence. 'Sukhavihāra' (pleasant dwelling) means being at ease in all four postures. Indeed, for a monk living alone in the forest, all postures are comfortable, starting from the simple act of defecation and urination. Therefore, this meaning of dwelling happily in the present life should be understood.

In the phrase "out of compassion for future generations," how does living in the forest constitute compassion for future generations? When sons of good families who have gone forth out of faith see the Buddha's forest-dwelling, they will think: "Even the Blessed One, for whom there is nothing further to be fully understood, nothing to be abandoned, nothing to be developed, and nothing to be realized, does not give up forest dwellings; what then can be said of us?" Thinking thus, they will intend only to dwell in the forest. In this way, they will quickly make an end of suffering. Thus, it constitutes compassion for future generations. To show this meaning, the Buddha said, "out of compassion for future generations."

## Commentary on the Appreciation of the Teaching

Having heard those words, the Brahmin, with a delighted mind, said "anukampitarūpā" and so forth. There, "anukampitarūpā" means having a compassionate nature or a compassionate disposition. "Janatā" refers to a group of people. The meaning is: "Just as the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One, would show compassion, in that same way [these people] are of a compassionate nature."

Having spoken thus, and again greatly appreciating the Blessed One's Dhamma teaching, he said this to the Blessed One: "Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama!" In this context, the word "abhikkanta" is seen used in the senses of exhaustion (end), excellence, extreme beauty, and great appreciation. It is seen in the sense of exhaustion (end) in such passages as: "Venerable sir, the night is far spent, the first watch has ended, the community of monks has been sitting for a long time" (Cūḷavagga 383; Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.20). It is seen in the sense of excellence in such passages as: "Of these four persons, this one is the more excellent and the more sublime" (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.100).
134:
In such passages as: "Who is this that worships my feet, shining with psychic power and glory, illuminating all directions with such magnificent beauty?" (Vimānavatthu 857), the word 'abhikkanta' is used in the sense of extreme beauty. In such passages as: "Excellent, venerable sir!" (Dīgha Nikāya 1.250; Pārājika 15), it is used in the sense of great appreciation. Here too, it is used only in the sense of great appreciation. Since it is used in the sense of great appreciation, it should be understood as meaning, "Sadhu, sadhu (well said, well said), Master Gotama!"

According to the rule: "In fear, anger, praise, haste, wonder, joy, sorrow, and devotion, the wise should repeat the word twice," it should be understood that here the word 'abhikkanta' is spoken twice by way of devotion and by way of praise. Alternatively, 'abhikkanta' means extremely desirable, extremely pleasing, and extremely excellent.

Among those two instances of the word 'abhikkanta', with one he praises the teaching, and with the other he praises his own devotion. The intention here is: "Master Gotama, this Dhamma teaching of Master Gotama is excellent; and my devotion, which has arisen depending on Master Gotama's Dhamma teaching, is also excellent." Or, he praises the Blessed One's words themselves, intending two meanings for each: Master Gotama's words are excellent because they destroy faults, excellent because they lead to the attainment of virtues. Likewise, they are excellent because they generate faith, generate wisdom, are full of meaning, full of phrasing, have clear words, have deep meaning, are pleasant to the ear, are heart-touching, do not exalt oneself, do not disparage others, are cool with compassion, are pure with wisdom, are delightful upon hearing, can withstand investigation, are pleasant when heard, and are beneficial when reflected upon—thus it should be connected.

Following that, he praises the teaching itself with four similes. In those similes, 'nikkujjita' means an object placed face down or turned downwards. 'Ukkujjeyya' means to turn it face upwards. 'Paṭicchanna' means covered with grass, leaves, etc. 'Vivareyya' means to uncover it. 'Mūḷhassa' means to one who is lost (confused about directions). 'Maggaṃ ācikkheyya' means to take one by the hand and say, "This is the path." 'Andhakāre' means in the fourfold darkness caused by the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, midnight, a dense forest, and a mass of clouds. This is the initial meaning of the words that were not clear.

This is the application of the meaning: Just as someone might turn upright what was overturned, even so, by Master Gotama raising me up from the false Dhamma in which I had fallen, having turned my back on the True Dhamma; just as one might reveal what was hidden, even so, Master Gotama...
136:
"Where it is said that a gift given has great fruit, among the four pure pairs of men, these eight persons who have seen the Dhamma (are the Saṅgha); go to this Saṅgha for the sake of refuge." (Thus it is said in the Vimānavatthu).

The community of monks is called the Bhikkhu Saṅgha. With this much sequence of words, the Brahmin declared the three goings for refuge.

## Explanation of the Discourse on Going for Refuge

Now, in order to be skillful regarding those goings for refuge, the following method should be understood: the refuge (saraṇa), the going for refuge (saraṇagamana), the person who goes for refuge, the divisions of going for refuge, the fruit of going for refuge, the defilement, and the breach. To begin with, by way of the meaning of the word: it is called "saraṇa" because it destroys (hiṃsati). The meaning is that, for those who have gone for refuge, by that very act of going for refuge, it kills or destroys fear, dread, suffering, and the defilements associated with the miserable realms (duggati). This is a designation for the Triple Gem alone.

Alternatively, the Buddha is so called because he destroys the fear of beings by promoting their welfare and by turning them away from what is not beneficial. The Dhamma is so called because it destroys fear by leading beings out of the wilderness of existence (bhava-kantāra) and by providing relief. The Saṅgha is so called because it destroys fear by making even small acts of honor yield abundant fruit. Therefore, by this method also, the Triple Gem is the refuge. The arising of consciousness (cittuppāda) which has defilements suppressed by faith and reverence toward that Triple Gem, and which proceeds in the manner of having that as one's final resort, is called "going for refuge" (saraṇagamana). The being endowed with that consciousness is said to "go for refuge" (saraṇaṃ gacchati). The meaning is that, through the arising of consciousness of the aforementioned kind, one approaches thus: "These three refuges are my refuge; these are my final resort."

Thus, first of all, these three—the refuge, the going for refuge, and the one who goes for refuge—should be understood.

Regarding the divisions of going for refuge, there are two kinds: the supramundane (lokuttara) and the mundane (lokiya). Among them, the supramundane going for refuge, for noble persons who have seen the Truth, at the moment of the Path, succeeds in all the Triple Gem by way of its function, having Nibbāna as its object through the total cutting off of the defilements of going for refuge. The mundane going for refuge, for worldlings (puthujjana), succeeds by having the attributes of the Buddha and so on as its object through the suppression of the defilements of going for refuge. In terms of meaning, that mundane going for refuge is the acquisition of faith in the objects such as the Buddha; it is called "rectification of view" (diṭṭhijukamma) among the ten bases of meritorious action, being right view rooted in faith.

That mundane refuge proceeds in four ways: by self-dedication (attasanniyyātana), by having the Triple Gem as one's final resort (tapparāyaṇatā), by accepting the status of a disciple (sissabhāvūpagamana), and by veneration (paṇipāta).
