Among these, self-dedication means the surrendering of oneself to the Triple Gem such as the Buddha in this way: "From this day forward, I dedicate myself to the Buddha, I dedicate myself to the Dhamma, I dedicate myself to the Saṅgha." Having the Triple Gem as one's final resort means the state of being one who resorts only to that Triple Gem in this way: "From this day forward, please remember me as one who has the Buddha as his final resort, the Dhamma as his final resort, and the Saṅgha as his final resort." The going for refuge by accepting the status of a disciple is [the state of being a disciple of] the Buddha and so on...
137:
“From today onwards, I dedicate myself to the Buddha, I dedicate myself to the Dhamma, I dedicate myself to the Saṅgha”—this dedication of oneself to the Triple Gem, starting with the Buddha, is called *attasanniyātana*. *Tapparāyaṇatā* means: “From today onwards, may you recognize me as one who has the Buddha as my resort (refuge), the Dhamma as my resort, the Saṅgha as my resort”—this is the state of being solely reliant on those Three Jewels. *Sissabhāvūpagamana* means: “From today onwards, may you recognize me as a disciple of the Buddha, a disciple of the Dhamma, a disciple of the Saṅgha”—this is the entering into the state of a disciple. *Paṇipāta* means: “From today onwards, I shall perform acts of salutation, rising to greet, joining the palms, and respectful service only to the three objects, starting with the Buddha; may you recognize me as such”—this is the mode of supreme humility towards the Triple Gem. A person who performs any one of these four modes has indeed taken the refuge.

Alternatively, *attasanniyātana* should be understood as: “I dedicate my person (*attabhāva*) to the Blessed One, I dedicate my person to the Dhamma, I dedicate my person to the Saṅgha. I sacrifice my life; my person is indeed sacrificed, my life is indeed sacrificed. Until the end of my life, I go to the Buddha for refuge; the Buddha is my refuge, my shelter, my protection.” *Sissabhāvūpagamana* should be understood like the refuge-taking of Mahākassapa Thera: “Indeed, I would see the Teacher, I would see only the Blessed One; indeed, I would see the Sugata, I would see only the Blessed One; indeed, I would see the Sammāsambuddha, I would see only the Blessed One.”

“I shall wander from village to village, from city to city, paying homage to the Fully Enlightened One and the excellence of the Dhamma”—*tapparāyaṇatā* should be understood like the refuge-taking of Āḷavaka the Yakkha and others. *Paṇipāta* should also be understood as follows: “Then the brahmin Brahmāyu rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, fell with his head at the feet of the Blessed One, kissed the Blessed One's feet with his mouth, stroked them with his hands, and announced his name: ‘I am the brahmin Brahmāyu, O Master Gotama; I am the brahmin Brahmāyu, O Master Gotama.’”

That *paṇipāta* (veneration) is of four kinds: due to kinship, due to fear, due to being a teacher, and due to being worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*). Among these four, refuge-taking occurs only through veneration of one worthy of offerings, not through the others. For the refuge is taken by regarding [the object] as supreme, and it is broken by regarding [the object] as supreme. Therefore, if a Sakyan or a Koliyan pays homage thinking, “The Buddha is our relative,” the refuge is not taken. Or if one pays homage out of fear, thinking, “The ascetic Gotama is honored by kings and possesses great power; if I do not pay homage, he might do me harm,” the refuge is not taken. Or if one pays homage thinking, “He is my teacher,” remembering some art or science learned from the Bodhisatta in a previous life, the refuge is not taken. Only for one who pays homage thinking, “This Blessed One is the supreme person worthy of offerings in the world,” [does the refuge occur].
138:
Whether a Sakyan or a Koliyan, if they pay homage thinking, “The Buddha is our relative,” the refuge is not considered taken. Or if one pays homage out of fear, thinking, “The ascetic Gotama is honored by kings and possesses great power; if I do not pay homage, he might do me harm,” the refuge is not considered taken. Or if one pays homage thinking, “He is my teacher,” remembering some knowledge learned from the Blessed One during his time as a Bodhisatta, or having learned an instruction such as: “One portion of wealth should be enjoyed, two portions invested in business, and the fourth portion should be set aside for use in times of adversity,” the refuge is not considered taken. However, for one who pays homage thinking, “This Blessed One is the supreme person worthy of offerings in the world,” the refuge is indeed taken.

For a lay follower (*upāsaka* or *upāsikā*) who has thus established the refuge, even if they pay homage to a relative who has gone forth among other sectarians, thinking, “This person is my relative,” the refuge is not broken; much less so in the case of paying homage to a lay relative. Likewise, the refuge is not broken when paying homage to a king out of fear, because that king is honored by the country and might cause harm if not paid homage. Similarly, the refuge is not broken even when paying homage to a sectarian who teaches some art or craft, thinking, “This person is my teacher.” In this way, the distinctions of refuge-taking should be understood.

Among these, for the supramundane refuge (*lokuttara-saraṇagamana*), the four fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*) are the result as fruition (*vipāka-phala*), and the destruction of all suffering is the result as benefit (*ānisaṃsa-phala*). For it has been said by the Blessed One:

“He who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha,
sees with right wisdom the four Noble Truths:
Suffering, the origin of suffering, the overcoming of suffering,
and the Noble Eightfold Path leading to the cessation of suffering.
This indeed is the safe refuge, this is the supreme refuge;
having come to this refuge, one is released from all suffering.”

Furthermore, the benefit of this supramundane refuge should be understood through the power of not adhering to [views of] permanence (*nicca*), etc. For the Blessed One said: “It is impossible, bhikkhus, it is impossible for a person endowed with right view to regard any formation as permanent, to regard any formation as pleasurable, to regard any phenomenon as self, to deprive his mother of life, to deprive his father of life, to deprive an Arahant of life, to shed the blood of a Tathāgata with a malicious mind, to cause a schism in the Saṅgha, or to designate another teacher [as his refuge].” As for the mundane refuge (*lokiya-saraṇagamana*), its fruits are the attainment of a happy destination (*sugati*) and the attainment of wealth and prosperity. For the Blessed One said: “Those who have gone to the Buddha for refuge shall not go to a state of woe. Having discarded the human body, they shall fill the heavenly realms.” On another occasion, Sakka, the king of gods, approached the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna with eighty thousand devas and stood at one side. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said: “Sakka, the establishment of the refuge is truly excellent. Because of going to the Buddha for refuge, beings, upon the breakup of the body after death, reach a happy destination, the heavenly world. They surpass other devas in ten respects: in divine life-span, beauty, happiness, fame, and power; and in divine sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches.” Then Sakka, together with his eighty thousand followers...
139:
It is impossible for one to deprive an Arahant of life, to draw the blood of the Tathāgata with a malicious mind, to cause a schism in the Saṅgha, or to designate another as one's teacher.

The fruit of mundane refuge (lokiya-saraṇagamana) is the attainment of a happy rebirth and the attainment of wealth. Thus it was said:
"Whoever goes to the Buddha for refuge,
They will not go to a state of woe.
Having left the human body,
They will fill the ranks of the devas."

Another discourse was also taught: At that time, Sakka, the Lord of Devas, together with eighty thousand deities, approached the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna... To Sakka, the Lord of Devas, who was standing at a respectful distance, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said: "Sakka, going to the Buddha for refuge is truly good. Sakka, because of going to the Buddha for refuge, some beings in this world, after the breaking up of the body, after death, are reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world. They surpass other devas in ten respects: in divine life-span, divine beauty, happiness, fame, and sovereignty; and in divine sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches." The same should be understood for the Dhamma and the Saṅgha. Furthermore, the special fruit of going for refuge should be understood by way of the Velāma Sutta and others. In this way, the fruit of going for refuge is to be understood.

Among those two types of refuge, mundane refuge is defiled by ignorance, doubt, and wrong knowledge regarding the Three Jewels. It is not of great splendor or of great pervasiveness. Supramundane refuge (lokuttara-saraṇagamana) has no defilement. The breaking of mundane refuge is of two kinds: blameworthy and blameless. Among them, the blameworthy breaking occurs due to reasons such as dedicating oneself to other teachers. That breaking has undesirable results. The blameless breaking occurs due to death. That breaking has no result because it does not have the nature of producing a result.

Supramundane refuge has no breaking. This is because the noble disciple (ariya-sāvaka) does not designate another teacher even in a future life. In this way, the defilement and breaking of the refuge should be understood. "May [the Blessed One] remember me as a lay follower (upāsaka)" means "May the Blessed One remember and know me as 'this person is a lay follower'."
140:
## Explanation of the Regulations for Lay Followers

For the sake of proficiency in the regulations for lay followers (upāsaka-vidhi), these miscellaneous topics should be understood: Who is a lay follower? Why is one called a lay follower? What is his virtue (sīla)? What is his livelihood (ājīva)? What is his failure (vipatti)? What is his success (sampatti)?

Among those topics, who is a lay follower? Any householder who has gone for refuge to the Triple Gem is a lay follower. Thus it was said by the Blessed One: "Mahānāma, when a lay follower has gone for refuge to the Buddha, has gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha, to that extent, Mahānāma, one is a lay follower."

Why is one called a lay follower? One is called a lay follower because of attending to (upāsana) the Triple Gem. Indeed, he is a lay follower because he attends to the Buddha. He is a lay follower because he attends to the Dhamma and the Saṅgha.

What is his virtue? It is the five abstinences (veramaṇī). As the Blessed One said: "Mahānāma, when a lay follower abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, and abstains from wines, liquors, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence; to that extent, Mahānāma, a lay follower is virtuous."

What is his livelihood? It is the leading of one's life righteously and equitably, having abandoned the five types of wrong trade. Thus it was said: "Monks, these five types of trade should not be practiced by a lay follower. Which five? Trade in weapons, trade in living beings, trade in meat, trade in intoxicants, and trade in poisons. Monks, these five types of trade should not be practiced by a lay follower."

What is his failure (vipatti)? Whatever failure there is of that very virtue and livelihood, this is his failure. Furthermore, that by which he becomes an outcast (caṇḍāla), a stain (mala), and detestable (patikuṭṭha) should also be understood as the failure of that lay follower.

In terms of meaning, those states such as being an outcast are the five qualities beginning with lack of faith (assaddhiya). As the Blessed One said: "Monks, possessed of five qualities, a lay follower is an outcast lay follower, a stain of a lay follower, and a detestable lay follower. Which five? He is faithless; he is immoral; he is one who believes in superstitious omens; he relies on omens and not on Kamma; and he seeks for those worthy of offerings outside of this Dispensation and performs his primary service there."
141:
What is success (sampatti)? It is the lay follower's accomplishment in virtue (sīla-sampadā) and accomplishment in livelihood (ājīva-sampadā). That lay follower also possesses the five qualities such as faith (saddhā), which make one a 'jewel'. As it is said: "Monks, a lay follower endowed with five qualities is a jewel of a lay follower, a lotus of a lay follower, a white lily of a lay follower. What are the five? He has faith; he has virtue; he is not superstitious about omens; he believes in kamma and not in omens; he does not seek for those worthy of gifts outside of this Dispensation; and he performs his first service here [within the Dispensation]."

In the word 'ajjatagge', this word 'agga' is seen in the senses of beginning, end (tip), portion, and best. In passages such as "From today onwards (ajjatagge), friend doorkeeper, I close the door to the Nigaṇṭhas and Nigaṇṭhīs," it is seen in the sense of beginning. In passages such as "He should touch that fingertip with that same fingertip (aṅgulagge), the tip of the sugarcane, the tip of the bamboo," it is seen in the sense of end (tip). In passages such as "the sour portion (ambilaggaṃ), the sweet portion, or the bitter portion," or "Monks, I allow you to distribute by the portion of the monastery (vihāragge) or the portion of the precinct," it is seen in the sense of portion. In passages such as "Monks, as far as there are beings, whether footless... the Tathāgata is declared the best (agga) among them," it is seen in the sense of best. Here, however, it should be understood in the sense of beginning. Therefore, 'ajjatagge' means 'having made today the beginning'; this is how the meaning should be understood. 'Ajjataṃ' means the state of today. There is also a reading 'ajjadagge', where the 'd' is a phonetic euphonic particle (padasandhikara), meaning 'having made today the beginning'.

'Pāṇupetaṃ' means 'endowed with life', as long as my life-faculty (jīvitindriya) continues. May the Blessed Gotama accept me as a lay follower, an attendant (kappiyakāraka), who has gone for refuge through the three refuges, having no other teacher. Even if my head were cut off with a sharp sword, I would never say of the Buddha, "He is not the Buddha," or of the Dhamma, "It is not the Dhamma," or of the Saṅgha, "It is not the Saṅgha." Having thus gone for refuge by dedicating himself, and having invited [the Buddha] with the four requisites, he rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated Him three times keeping Him to his right, and departed.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## the Explanation of the Bhayabherava Sutta is finished.
142:
## 5. Anaṅgaṇasutta-vaṇṇanā

The sutta taught by the Venerable Sāriputta beginning with "Thus have I heard" is the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta. In that sutta, there is the following explanation of terms not yet clear (anuttānapada-vaṇṇanā). Just as the connection of sequences (anusandhi) is stated in all suttas, from here on, without stating any such connection, I shall only provide the explanation of the meanings of terms not previously explained.

"Cattāro" (four) is a delimitation of number. "Puggalā" (persons) means beings, men, individuals. By this sequence of words, the Great Elder Sāriputta should not be taken as a 'Puggalavādī' (Personalist) who holds that a person truly exists. This is because this Venerable One is the foremost among the sons of the Buddha, and he teaches without contradicting the teaching of the Buddha, the Blessed One.

## Explanation of the Discourse on Conventional and Ultimate Truth

The teaching of the Buddha, the Blessed One, is twofold: conventional teaching (sammuti-desanā) and ultimate teaching (paramattha-desanā). Therein, teaching in terms of person, being, woman, man, noble, brahmin, deva, or Māra is conventional teaching. Teaching in terms of impermanence (anicca), suffering (dukkha), non-self (anattā), aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), sense-bases (āyatana), and foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) is ultimate teaching.

Between these two types of teaching, the Blessed One teaches the conventional teaching to those who, by hearing the teaching through the medium of convention, are able to penetrate the meaning, abandon delusion, and attain distinction. However, He teaches the ultimate teaching to those who, by hearing the teaching through the medium of the ultimate, are able to penetrate the meaning, abandon delusion, and attain distinction.

In this regard, there is this analogy: Just as a teacher who is skilled in regional languages and an expositor of the three Vedas teaches in the Tamil language to those who understand the meaning when spoken in Tamil. To those who understand in another language such as the Andhra language, he teaches in those respective languages. In this way, those young men, depending on the skilled and proficient teacher, learn the craft quickly. 

In this analogy, the Buddha, the Blessed One, should be understood as the teacher. The three Piṭakas, which stand as that which is to be taught, are like the three Vedas. The Buddha's proficiency in convention and the ultimate is like the proficiency in regional languages. The veneyya beings (beings to be guided) who are capable of penetrating the conventional and ultimate teachings are like the young men of various regional languages. The Blessed One's teaching by way of convention and the ultimate should be understood as the teacher's instruction in Tamil and so on. And it is said in this regard:

"The Fully Enlightened One, the best of speakers, declared two truths: the conventional and the ultimate; a third is not found.

Conventional speech is true because it is the cause of convention. Ultimate speech is true because it has the characteristic of the actual nature of things. For one who uses common usage, there is no false speech," so He taught.

The Fully Enlightened One, the best of speakers, declared two truths: the conventional and the ultimate; a third is not found. Conventional speech is true because it is the cause of convention. Ultimate speech is true because it has the characteristic of the actual nature of things. Therefore, even though the Blessed One, who is skilled in usage and the refuge of the world, teaches by way of convention, there is no false speech.

Furthermore, the Blessed One teaches the discourse on persons (puggala-desanā) for eight reasons. What are they? To demonstrate shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa); to demonstrate that kamma is one's own (kammassakatā); to demonstrate the individual deeds performed by various persons; to demonstrate the five crimes with immediate result (ānantariya-kamma); to demonstrate the divine abidings (brahmavihāra); to demonstrate the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussati); to demonstrate the purity of gifts...
143: Conventional speech is true because it is the basis of worldly convention. Ultimate speech is true because it is the actual nature of phenomena. Therefore, for the Teacher, the Lord of the World, who is skilled in worldly usage, even when speaking in terms of convention, no false speech occurs. ## In another way, the Blessed One speaks in terms of personal designation (puggala-kathā) for eight reasons. They are: to illustrate moral shame and moral dread (hiri-ottappa), to illustrate the ownership of kamma (kamma-ssakatā), to illustrate the individual effort of various persons, to illustrate heinous crimes (ānantariya-kamma), to illustrate the divine abodes (brahma-vihāra), to illustrate past lives (pubbe-nivāsa), to illustrate the purity of offerings (dakkhiṇā-visuddhi), and for the sake of not discarding worldly convention. ## Indeed, if it were taught that 'the aggregates, elements, and sense bases feel shame and dread,' the masses would not understand; they would fall into great confusion and become like an enemy, asking, 'What is this that is called the aggregates, elements, and sense bases feeling shame and dread?' However, when it is taught that 'a woman, a man, a king, a brahmin, a deva, or Māra feels shame and dread,' they understand; they do not fall into confusion, nor do they become like an enemy. Therefore, the Blessed One speaks in terms of personal designation to illustrate moral shame and dread. ## The same method applies when teaching that 'the aggregates, elements, and sense bases are the owners of their kamma.' Therefore, the Blessed One speaks in terms of personal designation to illustrate the ownership of kamma (kamma-ssakatā). ## The same method applies when teaching that 'the great monasteries such as Veḷuvana were caused to be built by the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.' Therefore, the Blessed One speaks in terms of personal designation to illustrate the individual effort of various persons. ## The same method applies when teaching that 'the aggregates kill the mother, kill the father, kill the Arahant, cause the shedding of the Buddha's blood, or cause a schism in the Saṅgha; the elements and sense bases do likewise.' Therefore, the Blessed One speaks in terms of personal designation to illustrate heinous crimes (ānantariya-kamma). The same method applies when teaching that 'the aggregates, elements, and sense bases develop loving-kindness.' Therefore, the Blessed One speaks in terms of personal designation to illustrate the divine abodes (brahma-vihāra). ## The same method applies when teaching that 'the aggregates, elements, and sense bases remember the sequence of former dwellings.' Therefore, the Blessed One speaks in terms of personal designation to illustrate past lives (pubbe-nivāsa). When it is taught that 'the aggregates, elements, and sense bases receive offerings,' the masses do not understand; they fall into confusion and become like an enemy, asking, 'What is this that is called the aggregates, elements, and sense bases receiving offerings?' However, when it is taught that 'persons who are virtuous and of good conduct receive offerings,' they understand; they do not fall into confusion, nor do they become like an enemy. Therefore, the Blessed One speaks in terms of personal designation to illustrate the purity of offerings (dakkhiṇā-visuddhi).
144: The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not discard worldly convention (loka-sammuti); they teach the Dhamma while standing on the worldly designations, worldly language, and worldly expressions. Therefore, the Blessed One speaks in terms of personal designation (puggala-kathā) also for the sake of not discarding worldly convention. Thus, this venerable one [Sāriputta], being skilled in worldly usage and not contradicting the teaching of the Buddha, the Blessed One, said 'Friends, there are these four persons' while standing on worldly convention. Therefore, in this context, a 'person' should be understood by way of convention, not by way of ultimate reality. ## 'Existing and found' (santo saṃvijjamānā) means those who exist and are found by way of worldly designation. 'In the world' (lokasmiṃ) means in the world of sentient beings. In the passages beginning with 'being one with blemishes' (sāṅgaṇova samāno), the word 'blemish' (aṅgaṇa) is in some places said to be the defilements. Thus, it was taught: 'Among those, what are the three blemishes? Lust is a blemish, hatred is a blemish, delusion is a blemish.' In some places, it refers to any dirt or mud. Thus, it was taught: 'He strives for the abandoning of that dust or blemish.' In some places, it refers to a certain piece of ground; this should be understood by way of the courtyard of the Bodhi tree (bodhiyaṅgaṇa), the courtyard of a stupa (cetiyaṅgaṇa), and so on. In this context, however, various intense defilements are intended by 'blemish.' Thus, it will be taught later: 'Friends, blemish is a designation for those evil, unwholesome states that roam in desires (icchāvacara).' Because it is together with blemishes, it is called 'with blemishes' (sāṅgaṇa). ## 'Being one with blemishes' means being one who has defilements. 'He does not understand as it really is that "there is a blemish within me"' means he does not even know that there is a defilement in his own mental continuum. He also does not know according to its true nature and function that 'these defilements are coarse and fierce, they should be abandoned and not held onto, and they are like poisoned arrows.' One who knows that they exist and knows in this manner is said to be 'one who understands as it really is that "there is a blemish within me."' For one whose defilements have not yet been eradicated by the Noble Path, but do not arise because they are suppressed by some means (such as learning the scriptures or undertaking ascetic practices), he is intended here as 'one without blemishes' (anaṅgaṇa). 'He does not understand as it really is that "there is no blemish within me"' means he does not know that 'my defilements are absent only because they are suppressed by some means, not because they have been eradicated by the Path.' He also does not know according to its true nature and function that 'if those defilements arise, they will cause great harm; they are coarse, fierce, and like poisoned arrows.' However, one who knows that 'they are absent due to this reason' and knows in this manner is said to be 'one who understands as it really is that "there is no blemish within me."'
145:
"Tatra" means among those four individuals or among those two individuals with blemishes. "Yvāyam" should be analyzed as "yo ayaṃ". There is also a reading "yāyam".

"Friend Sāriputta, what is the cause, what is the condition?"—by both [terms], he asks only for the reason. "Yenimesaṃ" means: by what cause and by what condition is one of these two individuals called a superior person and the other an inferior person? What is that cause and what is that condition? Thus the connection of meaning here should be understood. In that context, although it is said "does not know" and "knows," both knowing and not knowing are themselves the cause and the condition.

The Elder [Sāriputta], in order to make that point clearer through his own diverse and brilliant analytical wit, spoke again starting with "Tatrāvuso." In that speech, "tassetam pāṭikaṅkhā" means this is only to be expected for that person. It should be understood that this person will reach only this state and no other; it means it is something that will inevitably happen. It is spoken with reference to the non-arising of desire, etc., mentioned in the manner of "he will not generate desire," and so on.

In that context, "he will not generate desire" means that because he does not know he has blemishes, he will not generate the desire to act (kattukamyatā-chanda) in order to abandon those blemishes. "He will not strive" means he will not make an effort stronger than that desire. "He will not initiate energy" means he will not start or produce vigorous energy. "Sāṅgaṇa" (with blemishes) means being together with these blemishes such as lust (rāga), etc. "One with a defiled mind" means having a mind that is extremely defiled, soiled, afflicted, and tormented by those very blemishes. "Will pass away" (kālaṃ karissati) means he will die.

"Seyyathāpi" means "just as if." "Bronze bowl" (kaṃsapāti) is a vessel made of bronze. "Brought" (ābhatā) means carried. "From a shop or from a smith's house" means brought either from a shop or from the house of smiths who make bronze bowls. "By dust" (rajena) means by adventitious dust such as soil, etc. "By dirt" (malena) means by the tarnish of the metal arising right there [on the vessel]. "Covered" (pariyonaddhā) means completely enveloped. "Neither would they use it" means they would not use it for purposes such as putting in water or food. "Nor would they clean it" means they would not have it purified by washing, scrubbing, etc. "In a dusty place" (rajāpathe) means in a place where there is dust. Alternatively, there is a reading "rajapatha." It means a place where dust comes, or where it rises or does not rise, such as under a bed, in a chaff-barn, or among other vessels—wherever it is strewn with dust. In the phrase "it would be more defiled and covered with dirt," it means it becomes more defiled due to being placed in a dusty place.
146:
It means that due to non-use, non-washing, and non-scrubbing, dirt clings to it even more. This is also a question asked back by the Elder Sāriputta. Therefore, the meaning of that Pali should be understood thus: "Friend Moggallāna, if that bronze bowl is treated in this way, would it not, after some time, become more defiled and more covered with dirt, so that it would be difficult to know whether it is a clay bowl or a bronze bowl?" When asked, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, acknowledging that statement, said, "Even so, friend." Again, the Captain of the Dhamma, the Elder Sāriputta, wishing to connect the simile with the thing illustrated, spoke the words starting with "Evameva kho." The comparison of that simile should be understood thus: The person with blemishes is like the defiled bronze bowl. Just as leaving the defiled bronze bowl in a dusty place without using it, the receiving of ordination by that person is like receiving ordination in the presence of a person who is devoted to wrong livelihoods such as medical practice, etc. Just as the defiled bronze bowl becomes even more defiled, the person who practices by following the example of his teachers and preceptors is like performing medical practice, etc. One should understand the death with blemishes of one established in such failure of livelihood (ājīva-vipatti). Or, it refers to the death with blemishes of a monk established in the successive commission of Dukkaṭa and Dubbhāsita offenses. Or, it refers to the death with blemishes of a person established in the successive commission of Pācittiya, Thullaccaya, Saṅghādisesa, and Pārājika offenses, or the commission of ānantariya-kamma such as matricide, etc.—established in such major and minor offenses and ānantariya-kamma.

"Saṅkiliṭṭhacitto kālaṃ karissati" (he will die with a defiled mind), in this phrase, the meaning should not be taken as "he will die with an unwholesome consciousness." Indeed, all beings die with the natural consciousness, which is the life-continuum (bhavaṅga-citta). However, it should be understood that this is said with reference to the meaning that this person will die without having purified his mental continuum (citta-santāna).

In the second turn, "pariyodapeyyuṃ" (would clean it) means they would make it as pure as a mirror-surface by washing, scrubbing, and rubbing with fine ash, etc. "Na ca naṃ rajāpathe" means instead of placing it in a dusty place as previously described, they would keep it in a casket or a box, or wrap it in cloth and hang it on an ivory peg. The remaining words should be taken according to the previously stated method.

The comparison of the simile here should also be understood thus: The capable (bhabba) person who has blemishes is like the defiled bronze bowl. Just as using the defiled bronze bowl and placing it in a clean place, the receiving of ordination by that person is like receiving ordination in the presence of virtuous monks (pesala-bhikkhu). Those teachers and preceptors first admonish and then instruct; seeing even a slight negligence, they impose a penalty and make them train repeatedly. Just as the defiled bronze bowl later reaches purity and brightness, that person who practices by following the example of his teachers and preceptors gradually develops good conduct (vatta-paṭipatti), virtue (sīla), and so on. One should understand the death without blemishes of one established in this conduct. Alternatively, it refers to being established in gradually purified virtue, learning the word of the Buddha suitable for oneself, undertaking ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), taking up a suitable meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), and leaving a village-monastery to live in a forest-monastery. One should understand the death without blemishes of a monk established in such qualities. Alternatively, it refers to gradually performing the preliminary work for kasiṇa, causing the eight attainments (samāpatti) to arise and thereby removing blemishes; or arising from the jhāna which is the basis for insight (vipassanā) and abandoning blemishes through insight-knowledge by way of substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna), reaching the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala), and thus realizing the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala). One should understand the death without blemishes of a person established in such extraordinary qualities.
147:
In a later time, as if reaching a state of pure and radiant cleanliness, that person, by following and practicing the instructions of their teachers and preceptors, gradually stands in right conduct and passes away without blemish (anangaṇakālakiriyā). Alternatively, by gradually standing in pure virtue, learning the words of the Buddha appropriate for oneself, undertaking ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), taking up a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) suitable for oneself, and abandoning living in a village monastery to live in a forest monastery, while standing in that practice, one passes away without blemish. Alternatively, by gradually performing the preliminary work for kasiṇa meditation and attaining the eight attainments (samāpatti), one suppresses the defilements; then, emerging from the jhāna that serves as the basis for insight (vipassanā), one abandons the defilements through the insight of 'abandoning by substitution' (tadaṅga-pahāna); and from the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) until the realization of the fruit of arahantship (arahatta-phala), for the person standing in that extraordinary Dhamma, it is indeed a passing away with defilements permanently removed.

In the third case, 'subhanimitta' refers to an agreeable object (iṭṭhārammaṇa) that is a cause for lust (rāga). 'Will attend to' means that, being devoid of mindfulness regarding that object which causes lust, one will reflect upon and contemplate that sign. 'Because of attending to that beautiful sign' means that due to that person's attention to the beautiful sign, (the defilement) will destroy, harass, and overwhelm them. Indeed, it should be understood that when lust arises, it cuts off the opportunity for the wholesome, and becoming an unwholesome impulsion (akusala-javana) itself, it remains and destroys the wholesome mind. The remaining terms should be understood according to the method already mentioned.

The comparison with the simile here should be understood thus: A person without blemish (anangaṇa), who by nature has few defilements, is like a clean bronze bowl. Just as a clean bronze bowl, if not used and instead thrown onto a dusty road, the case of that person who has received ordination should be understood from here on as being similar to the first case.

In the fourth case, 'will not attend to the beautiful sign' means that because there is no lack of mindfulness regarding that object, one will not reflect upon that sign. The rest should be understood according to the second case. The passage beginning with 'Ayaṃ kho, āvuso' is also according to the method mentioned in the passage beginning with 'Ko nu kho, āvuso'.

Now, because the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna wished to make that blemish (aṅgaṇa) clear through various aspects, he asked in the manner beginning with 'Aṅgaṇaṃ, aṅgaṇaṃ,' and when the Venerable Sāriputta answered, he said the words beginning with 'Pāpakānaṃ kho etaṃ, āvuso.' In that context, 'icchāvacarānaṃ' means the various causes of anger and discontent that follow the will of desire and arise within the mental continuum through the power of desire. 'Yaṃ idhekaccassa' means that for a certain person in this Dispensation, there exists the cause for such an evil desire to arise. 'Āpanno' means one who has fallen into an offense. What is the longing, 'If only the monks did not know that I have fallen into an offense'? It is simply the state of being greedy (lobhikkhatā). Indeed, a monk who desires greed...
148:
...means it exists. 'Āpanno assaṃ' means 'I might be one who has fallen into an offense.' 'Na ca maṃ bhikkhū jāneyyuṃ' means 'If only the monks did not know me (as having an offense).' What is the reason here? It is the state of desiring gain (lābhatthikatā). Truly, a monk who desires gain, even if he naturally has merit from past wholesome deeds and is respected and honored by people, thinks thus: 'The Elders, knowing a monk who has fallen into an offense, inform the middle-seated monks; they inform the juniors; the juniors inform the scavengers and others in the monastery; they inform the nuns who come for exhortation; thus, in sequence, the fourfold assembly comes to know. If they know thus, it becomes an obstacle to that monk's gain. May I fall into an offense, but may the monks not know that I have fallen into it.'

'Yaṃ taṃ bhikkhuṃ bhikkhū jāneyyuṃ' means that the reason by which other monks would know that monk indeed exists; it is not that it does not exist. The Elders, having known, inform the middle-seated monks. Thus, that monk becomes well-known among the fourfold assembly by the method mentioned before. Being thus well-known and overwhelmed by ill-repute, even if he enters a hundred villages and seeks alms at a hundred doorsteps, he comes out with only a washed empty bowl. Then, thinking, 'The monks know that I have fallen into an offense; they have destroyed me in this way,' that monk becomes angry and dissatisfied. Because of that reason, he is both angry—being overwhelmed by anger—and dissatisfied—being overwhelmed by displeasure (domanassa).

'Friend, both this anger (kopa) and this discontent (appaccaya) are called blemishes (aṅgaṇa).' This is how the meaning should be understood here: anger, which is included in the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), and discontent, which is included in the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha), both of these are blemishes. This statement is made with reference to such persons. Greed (lobha) is taken by way of its occurrence in the preliminary stage of this blemish, and delusion (moha) is taken by way of its association (sampayoga).

'Anuraho maṃ' means he desires to be admonished by taking that same monk mentioned before to the edge of the monastery, putting him inside, and closing the door. 'Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ' means there is the possibility that skilled and disciplined monks might bring that monk who has committed an offense into the midst of the fourfold assembly and admonish him in this manner: 'You have performed medical practice (vejjakamma) in such and such a place.' That monk becomes well-known among the fourfold assembly. The entire passage 'Being thus well-known and overwhelmed by ill-repute' is just the same as what was mentioned before.
150:
...like a post. When will the monks who perform legal acts (dhammakammika) bring this old elder to an unsuitable state and expel him? If he were not in this monastery, the Blessed One would surely converse with me." In this way, he is angry with the elder.

'Purakkhatvā purakkhatvā' means placing in front and surrounding. This monk is also one who seeks gain. For he sees learned monks entering the village with a large retinue or worshipping a stupa, and seeing their success, he sees lay followers showing devotion and performing acts of faith. Therefore, he longs for such a retinue.

'Kupito' means that this monk also becomes angry in two instances: toward the monks and toward the elder. How toward the monks? He thinks: "These monks take and consume the robes or alms-food that arise for me, but there is no one who even follows behind me carrying my bowl and robes." In this way, he is angry with the monks. How toward the elder? He thinks: "This great elder is famous by himself in various places. When will the monks who perform legal acts expel him? In his absence, they will surely surround only me."

'Bhattagge' means in the refectory. 'Aggāsana' is the seat of the Sangha elders. 'Aggodaka' is the water of donation (dakkhiṇodaka) given as the best. 'Aggapiṇḍa' is the alms-food offered to the Sangha elders. In all contexts, the word 'agga' is a designation for what is excellent.

Among these three, the desire "May I alone receive them" is not a very great fault, but the desire "May no other monk receive them" is a very grave fault. This monk who seeks gain appears inspiring (pāsādika) in his manner of wearing robes and so on; sometimes he ordains, and sometimes he returns to the lay life. Because of such behavior, when he later fails to receive the priority seats and so on that he used to receive before, he thinks in this way.

"May that monk not receive" means that the monk seeking gain does not receive the priority seats of the elders according to the sequence of those great elders, but instead sometimes receives whatever low seat is available among the middle-seated or junior monks. 

'Kupito' means that this monk also becomes angry in two instances: toward the people and toward the elders. How toward the people? He thinks: "These people obtain monks for auspicious ceremonies and so on by depending on me. They used to say, 'Venerable sir, please take this many monks and show us compassion.' Now, they have taken the great elder whom they have only just seen and departed. Let it be for now; I shall see when their business arises." In this way, he is angry with the people. How toward the elders? He thinks: "If only these elders were not here, the people would surely invite only me." In this way, he is angry with the elders.
151:
"He should give a blessing (anumodeyya)" means he should perform the thanksgiving. This monk, desirous of gain, knows some fragmentary blessing and thinks, "Many women (mātugāma) come to the place where the blessing is given; they will recognize me and from then on will give me bowls of alms-food (thālakabhikkha)," thus aspiring and thinking in this way. "Occasion (ṭḥāna)" refers to the turn or responsibility of the learned monks (bahussuta) to give the blessing; therefore, it means a learned monk should give the blessing. "He becomes angry" means this monk also becomes angry in three instances: with the people, with the elder, and with the Dhamma preacher (dhammakathika). How does he become angry with the people? He thinks: "In the past, these people used to approach only me and request, 'May our Elder Nāga, our Elder Sumana, give the blessing'; but today they did not say so." In this way, he is angry with the people. How is he angry with the elder? "This Elder of the Sangha does not say, 'Approach your family teacher, Elder Nāga or Elder Sumana; he will give the blessing.'" In this way, he is angry with the elder. How is he angry with the Dhamma preacher? "As soon as the elder speaks, he crows (preaches) hurriedly like a cock that has been struck; there is no one to drive this person out; if this person were not here, I myself would give the blessing." In this way, he is angry with the Dhamma preacher.

"To those who have come to the monastery" means to those assembled in the monastery. This monk, desirous of gain, knows some fragmentary Dhamma talk and sees monks who have assembled from two or three leagues away in such places listening to the Dhamma throughout the night, and with delighted minds, the young monks and novices giving a great shout of "Sādhu, Sādhu." Then, on the following day, when the monks enter the village, the lay devotees ask, "Venerable sirs, who preached the Dhamma?" They reply, "It was such and such an elder." Hearing this, the people, being inspired, make great offerings and honors to the Dhamma preachers. Desiring those honors, he thinks in this way. "Occasion (ṭḥāna)" refers to the turn of the learned monks who are skilled in decision-making to preach the Dhamma; therefore, it means a learned monk should preach. "He becomes angry" means that because of his own dullness, not getting the opportunity to speak even a single four-line verse, he becomes angry, thinking, "I am dull and without wisdom; how shall I get the chance to preach?"

"To the Bhikkhunī s" means to the nuns who have come and assembled at the monastery for the sake of exhortation (ovāda), or for recitation (uddesa), or for inquiry (paripucchā), or for making offerings. This monk, desirous of gain, has this thought: "These Bhikkhunī s are ordained from noble families; when they enter and sit in those family houses, people will ask, 'In whose presence do you receive exhortation, recitation, or inquiry?' Then they will say, 'Such and such a venerable one is very learned.'" This is what he desires. "Occasion (ṭḥāna)" means that giving exhortation is the responsibility of learned monks; therefore, it means a learned monk should preach. "He becomes angry" means this monk becomes angry in three instances; he is also angry with the Bhikkhunī s. "In the past, these Bhikkhunī s depended on me for the Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, and so on; but now, they go to the presence of the elderly elder who has just been seen..."
152:
“This venerable one is learned (bahussuta); give to him, attend to him”—because of such words, such a desire arises in that monk. “Occasion” (ṭhāna) means that responsibilities such as giving advice belong to those who are learned; therefore, it is meant that only a learned person should teach. “Angry” (kupita) means that this monk also becomes angry on two grounds. Regarding those bhikkhunīs, he is angry, thinking: “In the past, these bhikkhunīs obtained the observance (uposatha) and the invitation (pavāraṇā) etc., by depending on me; but now they have gone to the presence of an old elder (Mahallaka Thera) who has only just been seen.” Regarding the Dhamma-preacher, he is angry, thinking: “This Dhamma-preacher has already given advice to these bhikkhunīs so quickly.”

“To the lay followers” (upāsakānaṃ) refers to the male lay followers who have come to the monastery. Those who have relinquished their business affairs are the great lay followers; they entrust their work to their sons and brothers and wander about listening to the Dhamma. This monk desires to preach to them. For what reason? (He thinks:) “These people, having gained faith, will also tell the female lay followers; then, together with the female lay followers, they will bring gains and honor only to me.” “Occasion” (ṭhāna) should be understood only in connection with being learned. “Angry” (kupita) means that this monk also becomes angry on two grounds. Regarding the lay followers, he is angry, thinking: “These people listen to the Dhamma elsewhere; they do not come to listen in the presence of a family-associated monk (kulūpaka) like us. Let it be for now; I will see when a need arises for them.” Regarding the Dhamma-preacher, he is angry, thinking: “This person is preaching to them.”

“To the female lay followers” (upāsikānaṃ) refers to those who have come to the monastery. Female lay followers are those who have gathered either to perform seat-offerings and so on, or to listen to the Dhamma on the observance day. The rest is exactly as said in the section on male lay followers.

“They should honor” (sakkareyyuṃ) means they should act respectfully and they should act well. By this, he desires that the honor shown to him be done respectfully and well. “They should respect” (garuṃ kareyyuṃ) means they should treat him as important. By this, he desires that the monks place him in a position of respect. “They should cherish” (māneyyuṃ) means they should hold him dear. “They should offer” (pūjeyyuṃ) means that while honoring, respecting, and cherishing him in this way, they should offer him the four requisites; thus, he desires the offering of requisites. “Occasion” (ṭhāna) means that only a person who is learned and virtuous, described as “dear, respected, and inspiring,” is worthy of this treatment; therefore, it is meant that monks should treat such a person in this way. “Angry” (kupita) means that this monk also becomes angry on two grounds. Regarding the monks, he is angry, thinking: “These monks are honoring this person.” Regarding the elder, he is angry, thinking: “If this elder were not here, they would honor only me.” In this same way, it should be understood in the subsequent three sections.
153:
Excellent robes refer to robes made of silk, fine cloth, wild silk, pure silk, and so forth, which are of great value, delicate, and pleasant to the touch. Regarding the wearing of these robes, the desire 'May I alone be the one to receive it' is not a very great fault. However, the desire 'May no other monk receive it (may I alone receive it)' is a great fault.

Excellent alms-food refers to superior alms-food enriched with ghee, oil, honey, sugar, and so forth. Excellent lodgings refer to superior requisites such as couches and chairs that are worth hundreds of thousands. Excellent medicinal requisites for the sick refer to noble medicines such as ghee, oil, honey, molasses, and so forth. In all these instances, the meaning should be understood in relation to monks of great learning (bahussuta) and monks of great merit (puññavanta).

'He is angry' means that he becomes angry in two instances regarding all these matters. Towards people, he feels anger thinking: 'These people have no intimacy with me; though I have lived with them for a long time, and have wandered from house to house for the sake of refuse-rag robes, or for alms-food, or for reasons such as ghee and oil, they do not offer me even a single day of excellent requisites. Yet, upon seeing a visiting elder, they offer him whatever he desires.' Towards the elder, he feels anger thinking: 'This old monk wanders about merely showing himself to these people; when will the monks who perform legal acts of the Dhamma (dhammakammika) expel him? If he were not here, I alone would be the one to receive these excellent requisites.'

'Friends, these things' refers to these evil desires (icchāvacara) preached below in nineteen rounds.

'They are both seen and heard' means that since evil desires are objects of the mind-consciousness (manoviññāṇa), they cannot be seen with the eye nor heard with the ear. However, when one sees the bodily actions of a person who has not yet abandoned evil desires, which occur by the power of those desires, it is as if they are seen; and when one hears their vocal actions, it is as if they are heard. Therefore, it is said, 'They are both seen and heard.' They are seen in one's presence, and they are heard in one's absence, as in 'That monk of such a name is of such a nature.' The word 'even if' (kiñcāpi) is a term used for both praise and censure. By that word, the Buddha praises the practice of forest-dwelling (āraññika) but censures the failure to abandon evil desires.

In this context, the connection of the meaning is: even if that monk rejects lodgings near a village and is a forest-dweller, living in a lodging far from the vicinity of people, yet these many evil desires of his are not yet abandoned. Even if that monk rejects excessive gains...
154:
...he is an alms-food seeker (piṇḍapātika). Even though that monk avoids improper wandering and practices wandering from house to house for alms; even though that monk rejects robes given by householders and is a wearer of refuse-rag robes (paṃsukūlika).

In the phrase 'wearer of coarse robes' (lūkha-cīvara-dhara), coarseness should be understood through three reasons: coarseness due to cutting with a weapon, coarseness due to sewing with thread, and coarseness due to dyeing with dye-potency. Among these three, a robe cut into small pieces with a small weapon is called coarse due to the weapon; that robe is diminished in value. A robe sewn with coarse, long threads is called coarse due to the thread; that robe is diminished in its feel and has a rough touch. A robe dyed with dye-potency is called coarse due to the dye; that robe is diminished in color and becomes ill-colored. Even if that monk is a wearer of robes that are coarse due to the weapon, the thread, and the dye, if these many evil desires are not yet abandoned and are both seen and heard, then wise fellow-monks will not respect him... (pe)... nor honor him. In the phrase 'For what reason is that?' (taṃ kissa hetu), 'taṃ' is merely a particle, and 'kissa hetu' means for what reason. It means that those evil desires of his are both seen and heard because he has not yet abandoned these evil desires.

Now, wishing to make that meaning clear with a simile, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with 'Just as if' (seyyathāpi). In that passage, 'carcass' (kuṇapa) refers to a dead body. The carcass of a snake is a snake-carcass. The others are the same. It should be understood that only these three carcasses are mentioned because they are extremely repulsive and loathsome. Indeed, people may prepare and consume other carcasses such as those of rabbits or pigs by seasoning them with ginger, bay leaves, and so forth. But they loathe the carcasses of these snakes and so on even when they are fresh; what more need be said when they are putrid with the passing of time? 'Racayitvā' means arranging in layers or filling; it means taking the carcass and putting it into a bronze bowl. 'Aññissā' means with another bronze bowl. 'Paṭikujjitvā' means having covered it. 'Antarāpaṇa' refers to the main street crowded with people between the shops. 'Paṭipajjeyyuṃ' means if they should go. 'Jaññajaññaṃ viya' means like an extremely sightly object, or like an extremely cherished object; alternatively, it means like a wedding gift given to a new bride. 'Vadhukā' refers to a daughter-in-law (bride); the gift given to that new bride is called 'jañña'. In both senses, the repetition is due to respect or praise. There is also a reading 'jaññajaññaṃ byā'.

'Apāpuritvā' means having opened. 'Disgust would be established in him simultaneously with the seeing' means that as soon as he sees that carcass, a state of being displeased would be established in that person. The name 'displeasure' (amanāpatā) is the name of the mental factors (cetasika) that arise thinking, 'This does not make the mind prosper.' In the state of being repulsive and loathsome...
155:
Disagreeableness (amanāpatā) refers to the name of the mind and mental factors that arise as 'this is disagreeable.' The same method should be applied to loathsomeness and repulsiveness. 'To those who are hungry' means to those who are famished. 'Would have no desire to eat' means the absence of the wish to eat. For those who have eaten well, it means they would have no desire to eat from the very beginning.

To compare this simile—the monk's appearance is like a pure bronze bowl. Not abandoning evil desires is like putting a carcass inside. Concealing those evil desires with practices such as the forest-dweller's practice (āraññikanga) is like covering it with another bronze bowl. Just as people are displeased when they open the bowl and see the carcass, it should be understood that when fellow celibates (sabrahmacārī) see the evil desires without regarding the forest-dweller's practice, lack of respect and such arise.

On the bright side (sukkapakkha), the word 'kiñcāpi' expresses support and praise. Through that word, it supports the state of being a forest-dweller and praises the abandoning of evil desires. 'Nemantanika' refers to one who accepts invited alms. 'Removed impurities' means selecting and removing black spots such as unhusked grains and gravel. In the phrase 'many curries, many condiments,' 'sūpa' refers to curry that is taken by hand. 'Byañjana' refers to various side dishes such as meat and fish. Therefore, it means having many curries like fish, meat, and green gram soup, and many condiments like various types of meat. The rest should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.

In comparing the simile—abandoning evil desires is like excellent hill-paddy rice. Concealing that abandonment of desires by living in a village monastery and such, which arise from fewness of wishes, is like covering with another bronze bowl. Just as people are pleased when they open the bowl and see the excellent rice, it should be understood that when fellow celibates see the abandonment of desires without regarding the village-dwelling and such, respect and such arise.

'Friend Sāriputta, a simile occurs to me' means 'I wish to speak a simile.' 'Let it occur to you (speak)' means 'Please speak.' In the phrase 'Once I,' 'idā' is a mere particle. In the phrase 'living in Giribbaja at Rājagaha,' 'Rājagaha' is the name of that city. It is called 'Giribbaja' because it is surrounded by mountains like a cattle pen. It means living in that city, or living depending on that city.
156:
It means 'I live.' 'Atha khvāhaṃ' means 'Then I.' Here, the word 'atha' is a particle used at the beginning of a new topic. 'Kho' is a mere expletive. 'Pubbaṇhasamayaṃ' means the morning time, the first part of the day. It can also be interpreted as 'in the morning.' Or, in saying 'pubbaṇhe vā samayaṃ pubbaṇhasamayaṃ,' it refers to a moment in the morning. Thus, the accusative case is used in the sense of continuous duration (accantasaṃyoga). 'Nivāsetvā' means dressing. This should be understood as changing clothes, or as dressing properly for the purpose of entering the village, for he was not without clothes before that.

'Taking bowl and robe' means taking the bowl with the hand and the robe with the body. 'For alms' means for the sake of alms-food. 'Samīti' is his name. 'Yānakāraputta' is the son of a cartwright. 'Paṇḍuputta' is the son of Paṇḍu. 'Ājīvaka' is a naked ascetic. 'Purāဏယာနကာရပုတ္တော' (purāṇayānakāraputta) is a son of a former cartwright family. 'Paccupaṭṭhita' means standing near. 'Vaṅka' refers to being crooked on one side. 'Jimha' refers to a crook similar to a snake's path. 'Dosa' refers to defects such as sapwood, unevenness, and knots. 'Yathā yathā' is a particle in the sense of time, meaning 'whenever.' 'Tathā tathā' is also in the sense of time, meaning 'at those times.' That Paṇḍuputta thinks according to his own string-line. The other (the cartwright) carves the spot exactly as thought at the very moment of thinking. 'Attamano' means one's mind is delighted, overwhelmed by rapture and joy. 'Uttered words of delight' means uttering words out of delight, or uttering words suitable for a state of delight. 'Knowing heart with heart' means as if knowing the mind with the mind.

'Faithless' (assaddhā) are those lacking faith in the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha. 'Seeking a livelihood' (jīvikatthā) are those who come to seek a livelihood in this Dispensation because they are oppressed by the fear of debt and such, and are unable to live outside. 'Not out of faith' means not because of faith. 'Deceitful and hypocritical' (saṭhā māyāvino) are those endowed with hypocrisy and deceit. 'Ketabino' means those with practiced deceit, or those whose deceit has reached full strength. Deceit (sāṭheyya) is called 'kerāṭiya' because it shows non-existent qualities, similar to showing the qualities of non-existent goods. 'Unnaḷā' means those who are haughty, having vain pride.
157:
Capalā refers to those who are frivolous, being characterized by unsteadiness in such things as decorating the bowl and robes. Mukharā means talkative, or one who has harsh speech. Vikiṇṇavācā refers to those with unrestrained speech, who are prone to speaking useless and vain words all day long. Indriyesu aguttadvārā refers to those who have unrestrained doors of action in the six sense faculties. Bhojane amattaññuno refers to those who do not know the proper measure to be known in seeking, receiving, and consuming food. Jāgariyaṃ ananuyuttā refers to those who are not devoted to wakefulness. Sāmaññe anapekkhavanto refers to those who have no regard for the state of a recluse, meaning they are devoid of practice in accordance with the Dhamma. Sikkhāya na tibbagāravā refers to those who do not have great respect for the training rules, or who frequently commit offenses. The terms beginning with bāhulikā have been explained in the Dhammadāyāda Sutta; the terms beginning with kusītā have been explained in the Bhayabherava Sutta. Dhammapariyāyena means by way of the Dhamma teaching.

Saddhā agārasmā refers to those who have natural faith and who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith. Pivanti maññe ghasanti maññe means as if drinking, as if devouring. Those who utter pleasant words are as if drinking with their speech; those who greatly rejoice are as if devouring with their minds. Sādhu vata means "Excellent indeed." In the term sabrahmacārī, both the short vowel and the long vowel are appropriate. If the short vowel is used, the meaning applies to the Venerable Sāriputta; if the long vowel is used, the meaning applies to the fellow practitioners. When it applies to the Venerable Sāriputta, it means "the fellow practitioner Sāriputta, having raised us from unwholesome states." When it applies to the fellow practitioners, it means "the fellow practitioners, having raised us from unwholesome states."

Daharo means young. Yuvā means one who is in the prime of youth. Maṇḍanakajātiko means one who is by nature fond of ornaments. Among them, some may be young but not in the prime of youth, such as those who are extremely young. Some may be in the prime of youth but not fond of ornaments, such as those who are of a peaceful nature, or those overcome by laziness, misfortune, and so on. In this illustration, however, one who is young, in the prime of youth, and fond of ornaments is intended. Therefore, it is said in this way.

The blue lotus (uppala) and others are mentioned because they are recognized as excellent in the world. Itiha te means "thus they." Ubho mahānāgā refers to those two great elephants. These two chief disciples are also called "Mahānāga." The etymology of the word Mahānāga is as follows: they are called Nāga because they do not go (na gacchanti) by way of bias such as desire (chanda) and so on; they are called Nāga because they do not return (na āgacchanti) to the defilements abandoned by each respective path; they are called Nāga because they do not commit (na karonti) various kinds of evil (āgu). This is the summary here. The detailed explanation should be understood according to the method stated in the Mahāniddesa. Furthermore—
158:
“He does no evil (āgu) in the world,
Having abandoned all fetters and bonds;
He is not attached anywhere, being liberated,
Such a one is called a Nāga because of being thus.” (Mahāniddesa 80).

Thus the meaning should be understood here. Mahānāgā means great Nāgas, meaning they are more venerable and more praiseworthy than other Arahant-Nāgas. Aññamaññassa means one Elder to another. Samanumodisuṃ means they rejoiced together. In that context, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna rejoiced with this illustration, and the General of the Dhamma (Venerable Sāriputta) said, “Friend, may this Dhamma be clear to you.” Therefore, it is said, “They rejoiced together in each other's well-spoken words.”

## The Commentary on the Anangaṇa Sutta
## in the Papañcasūdanī, the Middle Length Discourses Commentary, is finished.
## 6. Commentary on the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta

“Evaṃ me sutaṃ” and so forth is the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta. There, in the term “sampannasīlā,” there are three kinds of perfection: by way of being complete (paripuṇṇa), being endowed (samangi), and being sweet or excellent (madhura). Among those three—

“O Brahma of the Kosiya clan, the parrots eat the perfected (sampannaṃ) rice field; I inform you, O Brahmin, I cannot stop them.” In this verse, the word sampanna means complete (paripuṇṇa-sampanna).

“He is possessed of, fully possessed of, attained to, fully attained to, endowed with, perfected in (sampanno), and characterized by this Pātimokkha restraint.” In this Pali passage, the word sampanna means endowed (samangi-sampanna).

“Venerable Sir, the lower surface of this great earth is perfected (sampannaṃ) with a sweet taste, just like pure honey from small bees.” In this Pali passage, the word sampanna means sweet or excellent (madhura-sampanna).

In this sutta, however, both “complete” and “endowed” are appropriate. Therefore, “sampannasīlā” should be understood as meaning those who have complete virtue, or those who are well-endowed with virtue. Why is it called “sīla”? It is called sīla in the sense of composing (sīlana) [the bodily and verbal actions]. The detailed explanation of that virtue has been stated in the Visuddhimagga.

Between those two (complete and endowed), perfection in this sense is like the perfection of a field defined by its excellence and being free from defects. Virtue is also said to be perfected by being free from defects. To illustrate, for example, a field is not perfected if it is affected by four defects: failure of seeds to sprout, improper growth, damage by water, and salinity of the soil. Among those four, failure of seeds (bījuppatti) means a field where the seeds are broken or rotten in between. When those seeds are sown, the crops do not grow in that field, and the field is ruined. Improper growth (vaḍḍhana) means a field where an unskilled farmer sows seeds with gaps in between...
159:
In the term 'Sampannasīla', the meaning of 'Paripuṇṇasီlā' (those with fully complete virtue) implies the completeness of virtue through the absence of defects, just as a field is complete when free from faults. Indeed, for example, a field is incomplete if it possesses four defects: deficiency in seeds, deficiency in sowing, deficiency in water, and deficiency due to salinity.

Among these four, 'Bījakhaṇḍa' (seed-deficiency) refers to a field where seeds are broken or rotten in various places; when such seeds are sown, crops do not grow, making the field 'broken'. 'Vappakhaṇḍa' (sowing-deficiency) refers to an unskilled farmer who, while sowing, leaves gaps in between. Because of this, crops do not grow everywhere, making the field 'broken'. 'Udakakhaṇḍa' (water-deficiency) refers to a field where there is either too much water or none at all. In such a field, crops cannot grow, making the field 'broken'. 'Ūsakhaṇḍa' (salinity-deficiency) refers to a field where a farmer plows too deeply—four or five times in one spot—causing salt (ūsa) to rise; there too, crops do not grow, making the field 'broken'. Such a field is not of great fruit or great benefit; even if much is sown, little is harvested. Only when free from these four defects is a field complete. Such a field is of great fruit and great benefit. Similarly, virtue that possesses the four defects—being broken, perforated, spotted, or mottled—is incomplete. Such virtue is not of great fruit or great benefit. Only when free from these four defects is the 'field of virtue' complete. Such virtue is of great fruit and great benefit.

By the term 'Sīlasamaṅgino', it means 'live as those who are endowed with virtue, united with virtue, and possessed of virtue'. One becomes possessed of virtue (Sampannasīla) through two reasons: seeing the danger in the failure of virtue and seeing the benefit in the accomplishment of virtue. Both of these are explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga.

Regarding the term 'Sampannasīlā', Elder Sumana, a resident of Dīpavihāra, stated that the Blessed One referred to the fourfold purification virtue (Catupārisuddhisīla), and by the phrase 'Pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutā', He elaborated on the Pātimokkha restraint, which is the chief among those four. However, his pupil, Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga, said: In both the summary (uddesa) and the explanation (niddesa), the Blessed One spoke only of the Pātimokkha restraint; for Pātimokkha restraint alone is 'virtue'. He disagreed that the other three are called 'virtue' in the Pali texts, stating: Restraint of the senses (Indriyasaṃvara) is merely guarding the doors; purification of livelihood (Ājīvapārisuddhi) is merely seeking requisites in accordance with the Dhamma; and virtue concerning requisites (Paccayasannissita) is merely reflecting while using the four requisites. In the primary sense, only Pātimokkha restraint is called virtue. If that Pātimokkha restraint is destroyed for a monk, he becomes like a man whose head is cut off; how then can he protect the other limbs? If that Pātimokkha restraint remains intact for a monk, he is like a man whose head is not cut off, who can repair and protect his life and his other major and minor limbs; likewise, he can fulfill and protect the other three virtues. Therefore, by the term 'Sampannasīlā', only the Pātimokkha restraint is intended.
160:
Restraint of the senses (indriya-saṃvara-sīla) is merely the guarding of the six sense-doors. Purity of livelihood (ājīva-pārisuddhi-sīla) is merely the obtaining of requisites in accordance with the Dhamma and justice. Virtue dependent on requisites (paccaya-sannissita-sīla) is merely the use of the obtained requisites after reflecting on their purpose. It is said directly that only the restraint of the Patimokkha (pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla) is truly virtue. If that Patimokkha restraint is broken for a monk, it cannot be said that he, like a man with his head cut off, will protect his hands, feet, and the rest of his limbs. However, if that Patimokkha restraint is healthy and complete for a monk, he, like a man whose head is not cut off, can protect his life and restore his other limbs to their normal state; similarly, he can restore and protect the other three types of virtue. Therefore, the Blessed One, referring to the restraint of the Patimokkha with the term 'sampannasīlā' (perfect in virtue), and having spoken its synonym 'sampannapātimokkhā' (perfect in the Patimokkha), spoke the words beginning with 'pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutā' (restrained by the restraint of the Patimokkha) to explain that perfection in the Patimokkha in detail.

In that passage, 'pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutā' means those who are endowed with the restraint of the Patimokkha. 'Ācāragocarasampannā' means those monks who are endowed with proper conduct (ācāra) and proper resort (gocara). 'Aṇumattesu' means in the slightest. 'Vajjesu' means in unwholesome states. 'Bhayadassāvī' means those who are accustomed to seeing danger even in the slightest fault. 'Samādāya' means having properly and respectfully undertaken. 'Sikkhatha sikkhāpadesu' means 'train yourselves by undertaking each of those training rules among the collection of training rules.' Alternatively, 'samādāya sikkhatha sikkhāpadesu' means 'train yourselves by undertaking all the training rules pertaining to the doors of body and speech that should be practiced among the groups of training.' This is the summary; in detail, all these terms such as 'pātimokkhasaṃvara' and so on have been explained in the Visuddhimagga.

Why was this teaching beginning with 'Ākaṅkheyya ce' (If he should desire) started? It was started for the purpose of showing the benefits of virtue. If newly ordained monks or those of little wisdom should think, 'The Blessed One says, "Fulfill virtue"; what indeed is the benefit in fulfilling virtue? What is the distinction? What is the growth?', then this was spoken to show them the seventeen benefits. Indeed, it was spoken with the intention that, having heard the benefits starting from being dear and pleasing to fellow practitioners and ending with the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya), they might fulfill their virtue. It is like the merchant of Visakaṇṭaka. The merchant of Visakaṇṭaka refers to a merchant of molasses.

That merchant, it is said, took molasses, syrup, sugar-chunks, granulated sugar, and so on by cart to a border village and proclaimed, 'Take Visakaṇṭaka! Take Visakaṇṭaka!' Hearing that proclamation, the villagers thought, 'Poison (visa) is harsh; he who eats it dies. A thorn (kaṇṭaka) also kills by piercing. Both of these are harsh. What benefit is there in this?' and they closed their house doors and made their children run away. Seeing that behavior, the merchant...
161:
Thinking, “These villagers are not skilled in trade; I will make them buy by means of a stratagem,” he proclaimed, “Take what is very sweet, take what is very delicious; molasses, syrup, and sugar are available in equal measure; they can be obtained even with counterfeit coins (kūṭamāsaka, kūṭakahāpaṇa), and so forth.” Hearing that proclamation, the villagers came joyfully and bought them, paying a high price. In that metaphor, the Buddha’s words, “Monks, dwell possessed of virtue... undertake and train in the training rules,” should be understood as being like the merchant’s proclamation, “Take the poison-thorn.” Just as the villagers thought, “Both of these are harsh; what benefit is there here?” when the Buddha said, “Dwell possessed of virtue,” the monks’ thought should be understood as, “This thing called virtue is harsh and rough, being the opposite of play and amusement; what benefit or advantage is there for those possessed of virtue?” Then, like the merchant’s words, “Take what is very sweet,” and so forth, the Buddha’s words beginning with “If he should desire” should be understood as being for the purpose of revealing the seventeen benefits, starting from being dear and agreeable and ending with the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya).

In those words, “Ākankheyya ce” means if he should desire, if he should wish. “Piyo ca assa” means he should be one who is looked upon with dear eyes, one who is the proximate cause for the arising of affection. “Manāpo” means one who increases their mind, or one who is to be reached by their mind, or one who is to be pervaded with a mind of loving-kindness. “Garu” means one who is a position of respect for them, like a stone parasol. “Bhāvanīyo” means one who is estimable in this way: “Indeed, this venerable one knows what should be known, sees what should be seen.” “Sīlesvevassa paripūrakārī” means he should be one who fulfills the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla) completely; he should be endowed with the manner of one who has fulfilled them without deficiency. “Ajjhattaṃ cetosamatham-anuyutto” means one who exerts effort in his own serenity of mind (samatha). Here, whether it is “ajjhattaṃ” or “attano,” the meaning is the same, only the phrasing differs. The accusative case “samathaṃ” is used in the sense of the locative (in). It is formed in conjunction with the prefix “anu.” “Anirākatajjhāno” means one whose meditation (jhāna) is not discarded externally, or one whose meditation is not destroyed; for this word “nirākaraṇa” has the meaning of discarding or destroying. Its usage should also be understood in such passages as “Having discarded stiffness, he is of humble conduct” (thambhaṃ niraṅkatvā nivātavuttī).

“Vipassanāya samannāgato” means one who is endowed with the seven types of contemplation (anupassanā). The seven types of contemplation are: contemplation of impermanence, contemplation of suffering, contemplation of non-self, contemplation of disenchantment, contemplation of dispassion, contemplation of cessation, and contemplation of relinquishment. These have been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. “Brūhetā suññāgārānaṃ” means one who fosters empty places. A monk who, having taken up a meditation subject through the power of serenity and insight, enters and sits in empty places day and night, should be known as a “fosterer of empty places.” It should be noted that even if he is walking on ninety-nine islands, he is still one who fosters empty places. By this sequence of words—just as the teaching of the Taṇhāvicarita Sutta was first undertaken by the power of craving, but because it is the proximate cause for the underlying tendency of craving, it entered into conceit and views and gradually became a teaching on the three proliferations (pappañca)—likewise, this teaching of the Ākankheyya Sutta was first undertaken by the power of the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), but because virtue is the proximate cause for serenity and insight, it entered into serenity and insight and gradually became a teaching on the three trainings.
162:
A fosterer of empty places means, in this Dispensation, a monk who, having taken up a meditation subject through the power of serenity and insight, enters and sits in an empty place day and night; he is to be known as a “fosterer of empty places.” However, one who is performing (meditation) in a single-storied mansion or similar places should not be regarded as a fosterer of empty places.

By this much of the sequence of words—just as the teaching of the Taṇhāvicarita was first undertaken by the power of craving, but because craving is the supporting cause, it entered into conceit and views and gradually became a teaching on the three proliferations (pappañca)—likewise, this teaching of the Ākankheyya Sutta was first undertaken by the power of the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), but because virtue is the supporting cause, it entered into serenity and insight and gradually became a teaching on the three trainings.

Indeed, in this teaching, the training in higher virtue is spoken of by the phrase, “one who fulfills the virtues.” The training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā) is spoken of by the phrase, “devoted to internal serenity of mind, not neglecting meditation.” The training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā) is spoken of by the phrase, “endowed with insight.” By the phrase “fosterer of empty places,” both trainings are included: the training in higher mind in the sense of fostering empty places through serenity, and the training in higher wisdom through the power of insight. Among these phrases, by the words “devoted to internal serenity of mind, not neglecting meditation,” one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā) which protects virtue is spoken of. By the phrase “with insight,” the comprehension of formations (saṅkhārapari-ggaha) which protects virtue is spoken of.

How does one-pointedness of mind protect virtue? If a monk lacks one-pointedness of mind, he is distressed when illness arises. Being oppressed by illness and having a distracted mind, he might even destroy his virtue to bring about the subsiding of the illness. But if a monk possesses one-pointedness of mind, he suppresses the pain of that illness and enters into a meditative attainment (samāpatti). At the moment of attainment, the pain is far removed, and a very powerful bliss arises. In this way, one-pointedness of mind protects virtue.

How does the comprehension of formations protect virtue? If a person lacks the comprehension of formations, he has a strong sense of possessiveness toward the individual existence (attabhāva), thinking, “My form, my consciousness.” When such things as famine or the fear of disease arrive, he might even destroy his virtue to nourish his own existence. But if a person possesses the comprehension of formations, he has no strong possessiveness or affection for the individual existence. When such things as famine or the fear of disease arrive, even if his entrails were to come out...
163:
Even if the body dries up, withers, breaks into pieces, or shatters into hundreds or thousands of fragments, one should not be a person who nourishes the physical body by destroying virtue (sīla). Thus, the comprehension of formations (saṅkhāra) protects virtue.
