By the words "brūhetā suññāgārānaṃ" (cultivator of empty dwellings), the development, growth, and continuous practice of both are shown.

Thus, the Blessed One said that a monk who desires these four qualities—"May I be dear, pleasing, respected, and venerable to my fellow practitioners (sabrahmacārī)"—has no other task to perform; indeed, he must be endowed with virtues such as sīla. For only such a monk is dear, pleasing, respected, and venerable to his fellow practitioners. Regarding this, it has been said:

"The person who is perfect in virtue and insight, established in Dhamma, truthful, and who attends to his own business—him the people hold dear." (Dhp. 217).

Therefore, having said, "If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should desire: 'May I be dear, pleasing, respected, and venerable to my fellow practitioners,' he should be a perfect fulfiller of the virtues... (etc.) ...he should cultivate empty dwellings," now, because a monk who desires the acquisition of the four requisites (paccaya) and so forth should also perform only this fulfillment of virtue and no other task, the Blessed One said, "If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should desire: 'May I be a recipient of gains,'" and so forth. It should be understood that the Blessed One does not speak here of fulfilling virtue for the sake of gains. For the Blessed One has cut off talk related to seeking (gains) and does not speak words used with ulterior motives; thus he admonishes his disciples. How could that Blessed One speak of fulfilling virtue for the sake of gains? In fact, this was said according to the disposition (ajjhāsaya) of the individual. For those who might have the disposition: "If we were not troubled by the four requisites, we would be able to fulfill virtue and so forth," the Blessed One spoke thus according to their disposition. Furthermore, these four requisites are the natural benefit (sarāsanisaṃsa) of virtue. For wise people take out wealth stored in granaries and so forth, and without giving it to their children or consuming it themselves, they offer it to those possessed of virtue. Thus, this was said to show the natural benefit of virtue.

In the third turn (vāra), "yesāhaṃ" is the term "yesaṃ ahaṃ". "Tesaṃ te kāရာ" refers to those acts of offering requisites performed for me by those devas or humans. For not only humans give; devas also give requisites to those endowed with virtues like sīla, just as Sakka gave to the Venerable Mahākassapa. "Mahapphalā mahānisaṃsā"—these two terms are identical in meaning and differ only in phrasing. Or, because they yield great mundane happiness as fruit (they are called mahapphala)...
164:
...they are of great fruit (mahapphala). Because they are the cause of great supramundane happiness, they are of great benefit (mahānisaṃsa). For to one endowed with virtues like sīla, even an offering of a mere spoonful of alms-food, or a leaf-roofed hut built on a piece of land the size of five jewels (ratana), protects one from falling into states of misery (duggati) for many thousands of aeons. In the end, it becomes a cause for the deathless element of Nibbāna. In this regard, stories such as "I gave milk-rice" and so forth, as well as the entire Petavatthu and Vimānavatthu, serve as evidence. Therefore, just as donors of requisites desire the greatness of the fruit of the meritorious deeds they have performed, so too the monk who desires (their welfare) must be one endowed with virtues like sīla; this is what is shown.

In the fourth turn, "ñātī" refers to relatives from the side of the parents-in-law. "Sālohita" refers to blood relations such as father, grandfather, great-grandfather, etc. "Petā" refers to those who have gone to the afterlife. "Kālaṅkatā" refers to those who have died. "Tesaṃ taṃ" refers to their state of having a confident mind toward me or their recollection with a confident mind. For if the deceased parents of a monk, with a confident mind, recollect that monk, thinking, "Our relative, the Elder, is virtuous and of good character," even that mere mental clarity and recollection becomes of great fruit and great benefit for them. It is indeed capable of preventing them from states of misery for many hundreds of thousands of aeons and leading them to the deathless in the end. For this was said by the Blessed One: "Bhikkhus, I say that even the sight of those monks who are accomplished in virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation is of great benefit. I say that even the hearing, the recollection, the following in renunciation, the approaching, and the attending upon those monks is of great benefit." (Itivuttaka 104). Therefore, it is shown that the monk who desires the greatness of the fruit of his relatives' mental clarity and recollection toward him must be one endowed with virtues like sīla.

In the fifth turn, "aratiratisaho assaṃ" means "if only I could be one who overcomes and masters dissatisfaction (arati) and delight (rati)". Here, "arati" is dissatisfaction with higher wholesome states and secluded dwellings. "Rati" is delight in the five strands of sensual pleasure. "May dissatisfaction not overcome me" means may dissatisfaction not master, crush, or overwhelm me. "Uppannaṃ" refers to the dissatisfaction and delight that have arisen. For a monk endowed with virtues like sīla stands having crushed and mastered both dissatisfaction and delight. Therefore, it is shown that the monk who desires such a state for himself must be one endowed with virtues like sīla.
165:
In the sixth cycle (chaṭṭhavāra), 'bhaya' (fear) refers to both the agitation of the mind and the object. 'Bherava' (terror), however, refers only to the terrifying object itself. The remaining terms are as explained in the fifth cycle. Indeed, one endowed with virtues such as morality (sīla) can endure, overcome, and remain firm by crushing fear and terrifying objects, just like the Elder Mahādatta who resided at Ariyakoṭi.

It is said that while traveling, the Elder Mahādatta saw a certain pleasant forest and thought, 'I will go after practicing the recluse's dhamma right here today.' He stepped off the path, spread his double robe (saṅghāṭi) at the foot of a tree, and sat down cross-legged. At that time, the young children of the tree-deity were unable to remain in their natural state due to the power of the Elder's virtue, and so they made terrifying noises. The deity also shook the tree. The Elder, however, sat unmoved. Although the deity produced smoke and flames, she could not make the Elder stir. Finally, she approached in the guise of a lay follower (upāsaka), paid homage, and stood there. When asked, 'Who is this?', she replied, 'Venerable sir, I am the deity residing in this tree.' When asked, 'Did you cause these disturbances?', she replied, 'Yes, venerable sir.' When asked why, the deity said, 'Venerable sir, because of the power of your virtue, my children could not remain in their natural state and made terrifying noises. Therefore, I did this wanting to make you flee.'

Then the Elder said, 'If so, why did you not say from the beginning, "Venerable sir, do not stay here; it is not comfortable for me"? Now, do not say anything further. I would be greatly ashamed to hear the words, "The Elder Mahādatta from Ariyakoṭi fled because of fear of a non-human." Therefore, I will continue to stay right here; you should go and stay wherever is convenient for just this one day.' Thus, one endowed with virtues such as morality is one who can endure fear and terrifying objects. Therefore, it is shown that one who desires such a state for oneself should be one endowed with virtues such as morality.

In the seventh cycle (sattama-vāra), in the word 'ābhicetasikānaṃ', 'abhiceto' refers to the exalted, pure mind or 'adhicitta' (higher mind). Those states that arise in that 'abhiceto' or depend on 'abhiceto' are called 'ābhicetasika'. 'Diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānaṃ' refers to the jhānas which are the cause of dwelling happily in the present life. 'Diṭṭhadhamma' refers to the visible individual existence (the body), and it means the states that are the cause of dwelling happily in that body. This is a designation for the rūpāvacara jhānas (fine-material sphere jhānas). This is because meditators who sit having attained those jhānas experience the uncorrupted bliss of renunciation, which is the escape from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), in this very existence; therefore, they are called 'diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra'. 'Nikāmalābhī' means one who obtains according to one's desire, or one who can enter [the attainment] as one wishes.
166:
It means being able to enter the attainment at any desired moment. 'Akicchalābhī' means being able to enter the attainment by easily suppressing the opposing states, the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). 'Akasiralābhī' means obtaining the jhānas that have extensive objects without fatigue, and being able to emerge exactly as determined.

Indeed, some people are merely obtainers [of jhāna] but are unable to enter it at any desired moment. Some are able to enter it as desired but suppress the opposing obstacles with difficulty. Some can enter it thus and suppress obstacles without difficulty, but are unable to emerge exactly as determined, like a mechanical timer. If a person desires these three types of perfection, that person must also be one who fulfills the moralities (sīla).

Thus, having spoken of the jhānas which are the basis for supernormal powers (abhiññā), although the cycle for supernormal powers has arrived, the Blessed One did not take up that cycle yet. Because the benefits of morality are not only the basis-jhānas and the supernormal powers, but also the four immaterial jhānas (āruppa) and the three lower noble paths (magga), He desired to show all of them comprehensively and thus spoke the words beginning with 'ye te santā'.

In that text, 'santā' (peaceful) means peaceful because of the peacefulness of the factors and the peacefulness of the object. 'Vimokkhā' (liberations) are so called because of being liberated from opposing states and because of being fully intent on the object. 'Atikkamma rūpe' means having transcended the rūpāvacara jhānas. The words should be connected as 'ye te vimokkhā atikkamma rūpe santā'. Otherwise, it would not be clear what one does after transcending form. 'Āruppā' (immaterial) means being devoid of form both in terms of object and result (vipāka). 'Kāyena phusitvā' (touching with the body) means attaining and realizing with the mental body (nāmakāya). The remaining words are as already explained. This is the meaning: 'If a bhikkhu desires to dwell having touched these liberations, he too must be one who fulfills the moralities.'

In the ninth cycle, 'of the three fetters' (tiṇṇāṃ saṃyojanānaṃ) means of the three bonds known as personality belief (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), skeptical doubt (vicikicchā), and adherence to rules and rituals (sီlabbataparāmāsa). These are called 'saṃyojana' (fetters) because they bind the aggregates (khandha), destinations (gati), and existences (bhava), or because they bind kamma with its fruit; the meaning is 'bonds'. 'Parikkhayā' means by the destruction [of them] through the Path of Arahantship. 'Sotāpanno' (Stream-enterer) means...
167:
(A Stream-enterer is) one who has reached the stream, which is the Noble Path. 'Stream' (sota) is a designation for the Path, and 'Stream-enterer' (sotāpanna) is a designation for the person endowed with that Path. As it is said: 'Sāriputta, it is said, "The stream, the stream." Sāriputta, what is the stream?' 'Venerable sir, this Noble Eightfold Path is the stream; that is, right view ... right concentration.' 'Sāriputta, it is said, "A stream-enterer, a stream-enterer." Sāriputta, who is a stream-enterer?' 'Venerable sir, whoever is endowed with this Noble Eightfold Path is called a stream-enterer, this venerable one of such a name and such a clan.' However, in this context, the name of the Path is given to the Fruit; therefore, one established in the Fruit should be understood as a 'Stream-enterer.'

'Not subject to downfall' (avinipātadhamma) means one who does not have the nature of falling into the states of misery (vinipāta). It means one does not have the nature of casting oneself into the lower worlds. Why? Because the states leading to the lower worlds have been abandoned. 'Destined for enlightenment' (sambodhiparāyaṇa) means one whose destination and final goal is the three higher paths. It means one who will certainly reach the three higher paths. Why? Because the first path has been attained. 'Only in virtues' (sīlesveva) means that even one who wishes to be like such a person should be one who fully perfects and practices the virtues.

In the tenth turn, the three fetters already destroyed by the first path are mentioned again to praise the excellence of the path of the Once-returner. 'Due to the thinning of greed, hatred, and delusion' means by their becoming thin or by the act of making them thin. This thinning should be understood in two ways: by the infrequency of their arising and by the weakness of their obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna). For a Once-returner, the defilements do not arise constantly as they do for the worldlings who follow the round of rebirth; they arise only occasionally and sparsely, like sprouts in a field that has been sown thinly. Even when they do arise, they do not arise by crushing, spreading, covering, or creating darkness as they do for worldlings; they arise very weakly and thinly, like a thin layer of cloud or a fly's wing.

In this matter, some elders say: 'Although the defilements of a Once-returner arise after a long time, they arise thickly; for this reason, his sons and daughters are seen.' However, this is not a standard to be accepted. For sons and daughters can be born even by the mere touching of limbs. The thinning of that person's defilements should be understood only by the two reasons: the infrequency of arising and the weakness of obsession.
168:
'Once-returner' (sakadāgāmī) means one who has the nature of coming back once. 'Having come to this world only once' (sakiṃ deva imaṃ lokaṃ āgantvā) means having come back to this human world through rebirth only one more time. For one who develops the path of Once-returning here and attains Parinibbāna right here is not included in this category. Also, one who develops the path here, is reborn among the devas, and attains Parinibbāna there; one who develops the path in the deva world and attains Parinibbāna there; and one who develops the path in the deva world, is reborn here in the human world, and then attains Parinibbāna—these are also not included. But the person who develops the path here in the human world, is reborn in the deva world, stays there for the full life-span, and then is reborn once more in this human world to attain Parinibbāna—this is the one to be understood as included here. 'Would make an end of suffering' (dukkhassantaṃ kareyya) means one would make an end to the suffering of the round of rebirth. 'Only in virtues' (sīlesveva) means that one who wishes to be such a person should be one who fully perfects the virtues.

In the eleventh turn, 'of the five' (pañcannaṃ) is a numerical limitation. 'Of the lower [fetters]' (orambhāgiyānaṃ) means those belonging to the lower part; the meaning is those which are the causes for arising in the sense-sphere world (kāmāvacara loka). 'Of the fetters' (saṃyojanānaṃ) means of the bonds. These should be understood as the previously mentioned fetters along with the fetters of sensual desire (kāmarāga) and ill will (byāpāda). For whoever has not abandoned these, even if he is born in the highest plane of existence (bhavagga), he will certainly be reborn in the sense-sphere when his life-span is exhausted. Such a person should be understood as being like a fish that has swallowed a hook, or like a bird tied by its leg with a long string. The mention of the previously stated fetters here is only for the purpose of praising the excellence (of the path of Non-returning). 'One of spontaneous birth' (opapātiko) is a term that excludes the other modes of birth. 'Attaining Parinibbāna there' (tattha parinibbāyī) means attaining Parinibbāna right there in the Brahma world. 'One who does not return from that world' (anāvattidhammo tasmā lokā) means one who has the nature of not returning from that Brahma world by way of rebirth. 'Only in virtues' (sīlesveva) means that one who wishes to be such a Non-returner should be one who fully perfects the virtues.

When the path of Non-returning has been thus described, although the turn for the fourth path (the path of Arahatship) has arrived, the Blessed One did not take it up yet. This is because the benefit of virtues is not only the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya-abhiññā), but also the five mundane supernormal knowledges (lokiya-abhiññā) are benefits of virtue; therefore, he wished to show those as well. Furthermore, if the destruction of taints were taught immediately, the discourse would be finished; in that case, because these qualities (the mundane supernormal knowledges) would remain unmentioned, this discourse would be called a 'shorn discourse on supernormal knowledges' (muṇḍābhiññākathā). Therefore, to show the fulfillment of the supernormal knowledges, and because one established in the path of Non-returning has completely abandoned sensual desire and ill will—which are the opposites of concentration—and can thus easily perform various transformations (vikubbana), and because a Non-returner is one perfected in virtue and concentration, the Blessed One taught the words beginning with 'If he should wish... in many ways' (ākaṅkheyya... anekavihitaṃ) in the proper sequence to show the mundane supernormal knowledges. This is the connection of the preceding and following words (anusandhi). In those words beginning with 'in many ways' (anekavihitaṃ)...
169:
Because sensual desire and ill-will, which are obstacles to concentration, have been completely eradicated, psychic transformation (iddhividha) is successful. Since a Non-returner (Anāgāmī) is one who fully practices virtue (sīla) and concentration (samādhi), the Buddha taught, "If he should wish... manifold..." and so forth, to demonstrate mundane superknowledges (abhiññā) only at the appropriate occasion; this is the connection (anusandhi) of this discourse.

The Pali explanation of the five mundane superknowledges that appear in the manner of "manifold kinds of psychic power" and so forth, along with the method of meditation (bhāvanā), has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga.

Regarding the sixth superknowledge, "destruction of the taints" (āsavānaṃ khayā) means the exhaustion of all defilements through the Path of Arahantship. "Taintless" (anāsavaṃ) means being free from taints. In the terms "liberation of mind" (cetovimutti) and "liberation by wisdom" (paññāvimutti), "mind" (ceto) refers to the concentration associated with the Fruit of Arahantship, and "wisdom" (paññā) refers only to the wisdom associated with that Fruit. Among these two, concentration is called "liberation of mind" because it is liberated from lust (rāga), and wisdom is called "liberation by wisdom" because it is liberated from ignorance (avijjā). This was stated by the Blessed One: "Bhikkhus, whatever concentration he has, that is his faculty of concentration. Whatever wisdom he has, that is his faculty of wisdom. Thus, bhikkhus, through the fading away of lust there is liberation of mind; through the fading away of ignorance there is liberation by wisdom." Alternatively, it should be understood here that the fruit of serenity (samatha) is liberation of mind, and the fruit of insight (vipassanā) is liberation by wisdom.

"In this very life" (diṭṭhe va dhamme) means in this very existence. "Having realized it for himself through direct knowledge" means knowing it personally through one's own wisdom without depending on others. "Having attained and completed it, may I dwell" means dwelling while having attained and fulfilled it. "Only in virtues" means that even one who wishes to abandon all taints and attain liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom must be one who fully practices virtue.

Thus, the Blessed One, having taught the benefits of virtue up to the Fruit of Arahantship, now wishing to summarize all those benefits of virtue, spoke the concluding words: "Bhikkhus, be possessed of virtue... it was said in reference to this." The summary of that conclusion is: "Bhikkhus, dwell possessed of virtue... undertake and train in the training rules." All these words previously spoken by me mean that a bhikkhu possessed of virtue is dear and pleasing to his fellow practitioners, respected and esteemed, a recipient of the four requisites, one who makes the gifts of the donors highly fruitful, one who makes the merit of the relatives' mindful intentions great, one who can overcome dissatisfaction and delight, one who can overcome fear and dread, a recipient of the fine-material sphere jhānas and immaterial sphere jhānas, and one who, through his own direct knowledge, [realizes] these qualities: the three lower fruits of recluseship, the five mundane superknowledges, and the knowledge of the destruction of taints...
171:
He shows the first simile to those persons. This method applies to all suttas. Because he has thoroughly penetrated that Dhamma-element, he has attained the elegance of teaching; that Dhamma-element is well-penetrated by the Blessed One. Therefore, the Blessed One, who has attained the elegance of teaching, the Lord of Dhamma, the King of Dhamma, teaches the Dhamma just as he wishes. Thus, it should be understood that he shows this either through the disposition of the person or through the elegance of teaching.

In that simile, 'vatthaṃ' means a naturally pure cloth. 'Saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ malaggahitaṃ' means a cloth defiled by adventitious impurities such as dust and dirt, and stained because it has gathered grime such as sweat and body-filth. In the phrase 'raṅgajāte', the dye itself is called 'raṅgajāta'. 'Upasaṃhareyya' means he would apply (or put into). 'Yadi nīlakāya' means for the purpose of making it blue, or for the sake of a blue color. This method applies to all terms. For when a dyer applies it for the sake of a blue color, he puts it into blue dyes such as bronze-blue or leaf-blue. When applying it for the sake of a yellow color, he puts it into yellow dyes similar to the Kaṇikāra flower. When applying it for the sake of a red color, he puts it into red dyes similar to the Bandhujīvaka flower. When applying it for the sake of a crimson color, he puts it into slightly red dyes similar to the Kaṇavīra flower. Therefore, it was said: "If for the purpose of blue... if for the purpose of crimson."

'Durattavaṇṇamevassa' means that cloth would have a poorly dyed color. 'Aparisuddhavaṇṇamevassa' means that even its blue color would not be pure, nor would the other colors. For such a cloth, even if cast into a blue vat, does not become a good blue; even if cast into other vats, it does not take on colors like yellow, but becomes only like the color of a withered blue-kuranda, kaṇikāra, bandhujīvaka, or kaṇavīra flower. 'Taṃ kissa hetu' is a question: For what reason does that cloth become like this, or for what reason does the dye in that cloth have such a poorly dyed and impure color? Since the defiled state of that cloth is the only cause here and there is no other cause, he said: "Bhikkhus, because the cloth is impure."

'Evameva kho' is the completion of the comparison of the simile. 'Citte saṃkiliṭṭhe' means when the mind is defiled. Why did the Blessed One make a simile with a defiled cloth? It is to show that effort has great fruit. Just as a cloth defiled by adventitious stains, being naturally white, becomes white again when washed—unlike effort being fruitless as in the case of naturally black sheep's wool—so too the mind is defiled by adventitious defilements. But naturally, that mind is radiant in all instances of rebirth-linking and the life-continuum. Thus it was said: "Bhikkhus, this mind is radiant..."
172:
"...and it is defiled by adventitious defilements" (Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.51). If that mind is cleansed, it can be made even more radiant; effort in such cleansing is not fruitless. Thus, it should be understood that he made the simile with the defiled cloth to show that effort has great fruit.

'Duggati pāṭikaṅkhā' means if such a mind exists, only a bad destination is to be expected; it means he will surely reach a bad destination and nowhere else; thus a bad destination is certain to occur. This so-called 'duggati' is of two kinds: bad destination of practice (paṭipatti-duggati) and bad destination of rebirth (gati-duggati). Paṭipatti-duggati is also of two kinds: the bad practice of householders (agāriya-paṭipatti-duggati) and the bad practice of monastics (anagāriya-paṭipatti-duggati).

A householder, having a defiled mind, kills living beings, takes what is not given, and fulfills all ten unwholesome courses of action; this is his bad practice of a householder. Established in that practice, with the breakup of the body after death, he goes to hell, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts; this is his bad destination of rebirth.

One who has gone forth in this Dispensation, having a defiled mind, performs the work of a messenger, practices medicine, strives for the schism of the Saṅgha or the destruction of a cetiya, makes a living by wrong livelihoods such as giving bamboo, and fulfills all forms of improper conduct and improper resort; this is his bad practice of a monastic. Established in that practice, with the breakup of the body after death, he goes to hell, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts; he becomes an ascetic-yakkha or an ascetic-peta (monk-ghost), wandering about with a body burning with flaming robes and such, crying out in terror; this is his bad destination of rebirth.

With the word 'Seyyathāpi', he begins to show the bright side (sukkapakkha). The meaning of the bright side should be understood by the opposite of what was said in the dark side (kaṇhapakkha). Here too, 'sugati' is of two kinds: good destination of practice (paṭipatti-sugati) and good destination of rebirth (gati-sugati). Paṭipatti-sugati is also of two kinds: the good practice of householders and the good practice of monastics. A householder, having a pure mind, abstains from killing living beings, abstains from taking what is not given, and fulfills all ten wholesome courses of action; this is his good practice of a householder. Established in that practice, with the breakup of the body after death, he is reborn into the state of a great human or a great deva; this is his good destination of rebirth.
173:
A monk, having gone forth in this Dispensation, with a completely purified mind, purifies the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla), undertakes the thirteen ascetic practices (terasa dhutaṅga), takes up a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) suitable for himself from among the thirty-eight objects, and while dwelling in a secluded lodging, performs the preparatory work for kasiṇa and brings about the meditative attainments of jhāna. He develops the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga) ... develops the path of non-returning (anāgāmimagga). This is called his 'happy destination resulting from the practice of the homeless life' (anagāriyapaṭipattisugati). Established in that practice, after the breaking up of the body, he is reborn either in the human world among the three great families, or in the six sensual-sphere deva realms, or in the ten Brahma realms, or in the five Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa), or in the four formless realms (āruppa). This is called his 'happy destination in the course of existence' (gatisugati).

Having said that if the mind is defiled, a miserable destination is to be expected, and if the mind is undefiled, a happy destination is to be expected, the Buddha now, wishing to show those defilements by which the mind is defiled, said: "Monks, what are the defilements of the mind? Covetousness and unrighteous greed (abhijjhā-visamalobha) are defilements of the mind..." and so forth.

In that passage, strong attachment to one's own property is called 'covetousness' (abhijjhā); strong attachment to another's property is called 'unrighteous greed' (visamalobha). Alternatively, whether it be one's own property or another's, strong attachment in a proper situation is abhijjhā, and strong attachment in an improper situation is visamalobha. However, the Elder Mahāsaṅgharakkhita said: "Why do you make a distinction? Whether it be proper or improper, because it was taught that 'Greed is uneven (visama), hatred is uneven, delusion is uneven,' there is no greed that is not uneven. Therefore, greed itself is called abhijjhā in the sense of coveting, and visama in the sense of being uneven. These two are one in meaning, differing only in name." That covetousness and unrighteous greed, having arisen, corrupts the mind and does not allow it to shine. Therefore, it is called a 'defilement of the mind' (cittassa upakkilesa).

Just like this greed, there is ill will (byāpāda) arising from the nine grounds for resentment, anger (kodha) arising from the ten grounds for resentment, hostility (upanāha) which repeatedly binds the mind, and denigration (makkha) which destroys the recognition of favors done by others, whether for a layperson or a monk. Indeed, a layperson, being poor, might be placed in a high position by some compassionate person; at a later time, saying "What favor have you done for me?", he destroys the recognition of that person's good deed. A monk also, from the time he was a novice, being supported by a teacher or a preceptor with the four requisites and by the teaching of the Pali texts and commentaries...
174:
...from the time he was a novice, having been supported by a teacher or a preceptor with the four requisites and by the teaching of the Pali texts and commentaries, and having been trained to be proficient in the methods of Dhamma discourse and the scriptures; at a later time, when he is honored, respected, and revered by kings, royal ministers, and so forth, he wanders about without showing respect to his teachers and preceptors. When it is said, "We supported and nurtured this person in his youth like this, but now he has become devoid of affection," he says, "What favor have you done for me?", thus destroying the recognition of their well-performed service. For him, that makkha (denigration), which destroys the recognition of favors done by others, arises and corrupts the mind, not allowing it to shine. Therefore, it is called a 'defilement of the mind' (upakkilesa).

Just as this greed was described, domineering (paḷāsa) arises by overwhelming even a learned person, in such a way as: "The destination of even such a learned person is not certain; what is the difference between you and me?" Envy (issā) is the disparaging of others' honors and so forth. Stinginess (macchariya) is the inability to bear sharing one's own success with others. Deceit (māyā) is the nature of deceptive behavior. Hypocrisy (sāṭheyya) is the state that arises through craftiness. Indeed, a crafty person is like a 'shrine-fish' (āyatanamaccha). It is said that a shrine-fish shows its tail to fish and its head to snakes to make them think, "I am like you." In the same way, a crafty person approaches whichever monk is an expert in the Suttas or the Abhidhamma and says: "I am your constant attendant; you are my compassionate benefactors; I will not leave you." He thinks, "If I say this, they will think, 'This person is respectful and deferential toward us.'" For him, that hypocrisy (sāṭheyya) arising from craftiness arises and corrupts the mind, not allowing it to shine. Therefore, it is called a 'defilement of the mind' (upakkilesa).

Just as this hypocrisy was described, obstinacy (thambha) is the state of being stiff like a leather bag filled with air, not being humble, and holding one's head high. Presumption (sārambha) is the act of doing twice or thrice as much as another. That presumption is found in two ways: by way of the unwholesome and by way of the wholesome. Among these, for a layperson, seeing the ornaments and so forth made by another and doing twice as much as that person is unwholesome presumption. For a monk, seeing how much another learns or recites, and doing twice as much as that person out of conceit, is unwholesome. On the other hand, for a layperson, seeing another give one ticket-meal (salākabhatta) and wishing to give two or three himself, the presumption that arises is wholesome. For a monk, seeing another...
175:
Seeing another learning a different Nikāya, one who overcomes their own laziness and desires to learn two Nikāyas without relying on pride—this sārambha (rivalry/striving) is wholesome. However, in this context, unwholesome sārambha is intended. When this arises, it defiles the mind and does not allow it to shine. Therefore, it is called an 'impurity of the mind' (upakkilesa).

Just like this sārambha, māna (pride) which occurs through the elevation of the mind based on birth etc., atimāna (arrogance) which occurs through excessive elevation, mada (intoxication) in the form of vanity, and pamāda (negligence) which arises through the letting go of the mind in the strands of sensual pleasure—these also, when they arise, defile the mind and do not allow it to shine. Therefore, they are called 'impurities of the mind'.

Why does the Blessed One, when showing the impurities, show them starting with greed (lobha)? It is because that greed arises first. For all beings born anywhere, even in the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa), greed arises first of all through attachment to existence (bhavanikanti). Thereafter, the remaining defilements arise according to their respective causes and conditions. These sixteen factors are not the only impurities of the mind; it should be understood that all defilements are included by this method.

Having shown the defilement (saṅkilesa) to this extent, the Buddha, now wishing to show the purification (vodāna), said "Sa kho so, bhikkhave" and so on. Therein, "knowing thus" means having understood in this way. "Abandons" means abandoning by the Noble Path through the power of abandonment by eradication (samucchedappahāna). In that abandonment, it should be understood in two ways: by the sequence of defilements and by the sequence of paths.

First, by the sequence of defilements: these six defilements—covetousness and unrighteous greed (abhijjhā-visamalobha), obstinacy (thambha), rivalry (sārambha), pride (māna), arrogance (atimāna), and intoxication (mada)—are abandoned by the Path of Arahantship (Arahattamagga). These four defilements—ill-will (byāpāda), anger (kodha), malice (upanāha), and negligence (pamāda)—are abandoned by the Path of Non-returning (Anāgāmimagga). These six defilements—contempt (makkha), domineering (palāsa), envy (issā), avarice (macchariya), deceit (māyā), and hypocrisy (sāṭheyya)—are abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpattimagga).

By the sequence of paths: by the Path of Stream-entry, these six—contempt, domineering, envy, avarice, deceit, and hypocrisy—are abandoned. By the Path of Non-returning, these four—ill-will, anger, malice, and negligence—are abandoned. By the Path of Arahantship, these six—covetousness and unrighteous greed, obstinacy, rivalry, pride, arrogance, and intoxication—are abandoned.
176:
In this context, whether these defilements such as covetousness and unrighteous greed are to be abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry or by the remaining paths, it should be understood that the Buddha spoke the words "he abandons covetousness and unrighteous greed, an impurity of the mind" etc., specifically intending the abandonment by the Path of Non-returning (Anāgāmimagga). What has been stated here is the traditional sequence (paveṇimagga) handed down through teachers. That sequence is also appropriate because it is shown above only for the fourth path (Arahattamagga). For, the abandonment of the remaining unrighteous greed etc., which were not abandoned by the third path, occurs through that Path of Arahantship, while the rest are abandoned by this aforementioned method. Even those defilements abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry are only fully abandoned by the Path of Non-returning, because the minds that originate those defilements have not yet been completely abandoned. Some teachers explain the abandonment here as being by the first path, but that does not harmonize with the preceding and following statements. Some say it is abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhanappahāna), but that is merely their own opinion.

In the phrase "Yato kho bhikkhave", "yato" means at which time. "Pahīno hoti" is said specifically intending the abandonment at the moment of the Path of Non-returning.

The statement "So buddhe aveccappasādena" should be connected word by word thus: "O monks, when covetousness and unrighteous greed have been abandoned, that monk becomes possessed of unshakeable confidence in the Buddha." For this monk, supramundane confidence (lokuttara-pasāda) arrives through the Path of Non-returning; thereafter, at another time, mundane confidence (lokiya) arises as he recollects the qualities of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. Wishing to show all his confidence, which is a mixture of mundane and supramundane, the Blessed One said "with unshakeable confidence in the Buddha" and so on.

Therein, "aveccappasādena" means with confidence that is immovable and unwavering because of knowing the qualities of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha as they really are. Now, wishing to show the procedure by which that unshakeable confidence arose for that monk as he was recollecting, the Buddha expanded on the three subjects of recollection by the method starting with "Itipi so bhagavā". The complete explanation of the meaning of those recollections is stated in the Visuddhimagga, in the chapter on Recollections (Anussatikathā).

Having thus shown the monk's confidence, which is a mixture of mundane and supramundane, now for one who reflects on the abandonment of defilements and the possession of unshakeable confidence, there arises...
177:
Wishing to show the benefits beginning with joy (somanassa), the Buddha spoke the words beginning with "Yathodhi kho panassa." Just as a king living in a great city feels strong joy when reflecting on the suppression of a bandit uprising that had arisen in a border province, so too does an Anāgāmī (Non-returner) feel strong joy when reflecting on the abandonment of his own defilements, thinking, "Such and such defilements of mine have been abandoned." Wishing to show that joy, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with "Yathodhi kho panassa."

The meaning of those words is: For that Anāgāmī monk who is thus "endowed with unwavering confidence in the Buddha... in the Dhamma... in the Saṅgha, the incomparable field of merit for the world," there is defilement that has been relinquished and completely renounced according to their respective limits. It is indeed relinquished by the power of their respective limits. That collection of defilements is something vomited, released, abandoned, and completely renounced. "By the power of their respective limits" means there are two kinds of limits: the limit of defilements (kilesodhi) and the limit of the path (maggodhi). Among those two, by the power of the limit of defilements, those defilements which are to be destroyed by a specific path are abandoned by their own limit, without being mixed with defilements to be destroyed by other paths. By the power of the limit of the path, only those defilements that are to be abandoned by a specific path are indeed abandoned by that path. Thus, by the power of their respective limits, that collection of defilements is indeed relinquished and completely renounced. Having reflected on those abandoned defilements and gained joy, that Anāgāmī monk further gains the inspiration of the meaning (atthaveda), thinking, "I am endowed with unwavering confidence in the Buddha." This is how the connection should be understood.

There is also a variant reading "Yatodhi kho." According to that reading, the meaning is: For this monk, defilements have been relinquished and completely renounced because of the limit of the three lower paths. In that text, "Yato" is a word denoting cause, meaning "because of which." "Odhi" refers to the three lower paths. Why? Because those three paths abandon defilements by making a limit or a portion, leaving aside the defilements to be abandoned by the higher path; therefore, they are called "odhi" (limited). The Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga), however, abandons defilements without leaving any remainder, and is therefore called "anodhi" (without limit). For this Anāgāmī monk, defilements have been relinquished by the three lower paths. Therefore, it is said, "Yatodhi kho panassa cattaṃ hoti." In that text, "kho pana" are merely particles. This is the summary of the meaning: Because this Anāgāmī monk has defilements that have been relinquished and completely renounced according to a limit, he reflects on those defilements and gains joy; and further, he gains the inspiration of the meaning (atthaveda), thinking, "I am endowed with unwavering confidence in the Buddha." This should be understood in accordance with the Pali.

In that text, the word "cattaṃ" (relinquished) is spoken in the sense of giving up one's own nature. The word "vantaṃ" (vomited) is spoken in the sense of showing the state of not taking back. The word "muttaṃ" (released) is spoken in the sense of being freed from the continuity [of mind]. The word "pahīnaṃ" (abandoned) is spoken in the sense of showing that even what is released does not remain anywhere. The word "paṭinissaṭṭhaṃ" (renounced) is spoken in the sense of [renouncing] what was previously...
178:
...showing the renunciation of what was previously taken, or showing the state of being sent away, or showing the state of being sent away by overcoming through the power of meditation (bhāvanā)—this is what is meant by "paṭinissaṭṭha." In the phrase "he gains the inspiration of the meaning (atthaveda), he gains the inspiration of the Dhamma (dhammaveda)," unwavering confidence (aveccappasāda) in the Buddha and so on is called "attha" because it is the objective to be attained, meaning it is to be approached. It is called "dhamma" because it upholds, meaning it does not allow one to fall into the lower realms. "Veda" refers to scripture, knowledge, and joy (somanassa). In passages such as "one who has reached the far shore of the three Vedas," scripture is called "veda." In passages such as "that brahmin whom one should know as a 'vedagū' (knower of veda), who is possessionless and unattached to the realm of desire," knowledge is called "veda." In passages such as "those who wander in the world with veda (joy) arisen," joy is called "veda." In this context, however, both joy and the knowledge associated with joy are intended. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: "he gains the joy that has unwavering confidence as its object, and he gains the knowledge consisting of joy."

Alternatively, "atthaveda" refers to the aforementioned veda arising for one who reflects on unwavering confidence. "Dhammaveda" refers to the aforementioned veda arising for one who reflects on the abandonment of defilements according to their limits, which is the cause of unwavering confidence. This is how the meaning should be understood here. Indeed, it has been said: "Knowledge of the cause is the discrimination of the Dhamma (dhammapaṭisambhidā); knowledge of the result of the cause is the discrimination of the meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā)." "Gladness connected with the Dhamma (pāmojja)" is the gladness that arises for one who reflects on that meaning, that cause, and the veda which is the benefit of the meaning and the Dhamma. That gladness is said to be connected with the Dhamma which proceeds in the manner of reflection characterized by faultlessness. "For one who is glad, rapture (pīti) arises" means that for one who is glad through this gladness, unworldly rapture arises. "One with a rapturous mind" means one whose mind is satisfied by that rapture. "The body becomes tranquil" means the body is also tranquil, with distress subsided. "One with a tranquil body feels happiness" means one whose bodily distress has thus subsided experiences mental happiness (cetasika sukha). "The mind becomes concentrated" means the mind is well-established, remaining unshakable like an attainment (appanā).

Thus, having shown the benefits beginning with joy that arise for one who reflects on the abandonment of defilements and the possession of unwavering confidence, [the Buddha] now reveals the manner in which that reflection occurs through the section "Yathodhi kho pana me"...
179:
Wishing to show the fruit (phala) that indicates the power of the path of non-returning (anāgāmimagga) of that bhikkhu, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with, "Bhikkhus, that bhikkhu..."

In that passage, "is of such virtue" (evaṃsīlo) shows the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) associated with the path of non-returning of that person. "Is of such nature, is of such wisdom" (evaṃdhammo evaṃpañño) shows the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha) and the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha) which are also associated with that path. "Sālīnaṃ" refers to many kinds of hill rice, such as lohitasāli and gandhasāli. "Piṇḍapātaṃ" refers to almsfood (cooked rice). "Vicitakāḷakaṃ" refers to almsfood from which black grains (such as gravel and unhusked rice) have been removed.

"That almsfood does not become an obstacle for that bhikkhu" means that for a bhikkhu of such a nature, the eating of the aforementioned almsfood is not a cause for an obstacle to either the path or the fruit. For how could that food cause an obstacle to an Anāgāmi bhikkhu who has already attained such qualities? Even for one who has begun insight (vipassanā) to attain the fourth path (arahattamagga) and fruit which he has not yet attained, that food does not become an obstacle; it is simply incapable of causing an obstacle. Why? Because his mind is purified by the path that encompasses the aforementioned virtue, Dhamma, and wisdom.

Since this purity of mind is the primary cause, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with, "For example..." wishing to show a simile appropriate to that cause. In that simile, "acchaṃ" means especially clear. "Parisuddhaṃ" means free from impurities. "Pariyodātaṃ" means emitting a brilliant radiance. "Ukkāmukhaṃ" is the mouth of a goldsmith's furnace (crucible). Here, the goldsmith's furnace is called "ukkā." In other places, torches and so on are also called "ukkā." In the passage "ukkāsu dhārīyamānāsu," a torch is called "ukkā." In the passage "ukkaṃ bandheyya, ukkaṃ bandhitvā ukkāmukhaṃ ālimpeyya," a charcoal brazier (pot) is called "ukkā." In the passage "kammārānaṃ yathā ukkā," a smith's furnace is called "ukkā." In the passage "evaṃvipāko ukkāpāto bhavissati," the force of the wind is called "ukkā." However, in this context and other similar contexts such as "taking the gold with tongs and putting it into the furnace mouth," the goldsmith's furnace (crucible) should be understood as "ukkā."

The comparison with that simile is as follows: Like a soiled cloth or impure gold, the mind of this bhikkhu during his time as a worldling (puthujjana), which was followed by impurities such as sensual lust, should be understood. Like the very clear water or the furnace mouth, the path of non-returning should be understood. That water...
180:
Relying on the furnace mouth, just like the purity of cloth and gold, the state of having a pure mind should be understood as relying on the path of non-returning (anāgāmimagga) which encompasses the various types of virtue, Dhamma, and wisdom already mentioned.

"That bhikkhu, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness..."—this teaching comes by way of natural connection (yathānusandhi). There are three kinds of connections (anusandhi): connection by question (pucchānusandhi), connection by inclination (ajjhāsayānusandhi), and natural connection (yathānusandhi). Among these three, the connection by question should be understood by way of a sutta preached to those who ask questions, such as: "When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One, 'Venerable Sir, could there be agitation regarding non-existent external things?' 'There could be, bhikkhu,' the Blessed One said."

The connection by inclination should be understood by way of a sutta preached after knowing the desires of others, such as: "Brahmin, the thought might occur to you, 'Even now, the ascetic Gotama is not free from lust.'"

The natural connection should be understood by way of those suttas where the teaching follows in the upper part of the discourse based on a quality that is either similar to or opposite to the quality with which the teaching began in the lower part. For example: In the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta, the teaching begins with virtue (sīla) in the lower part, and the six higher powers (abhiññā) come in the upper part. In the Kakacūpama Sutta, it begins with impatience in the lower part, and the Advice on the Simile of the Saw comes in the upper part. In the Alagaddūpama Sutta, it begins with the explanation of views (diṭṭhi) in the lower part, and the declaration of the three-fold round of emptiness comes in the upper part. In the Cūḷa-assapura Sutta, it begins with the explanation of defilements in the lower part, and the divine abidings (brahmavihāra) come in the upper part. In the Kosambiya Sutta, it begins with quarreling in the lower part, and the principles of cordiality (sāraṇīyadhamma) come in the upper part. In this Vattha Sutta also, it begins with the explanation of defilements in the lower part, and the divine abidings come in the upper part. Therefore, it is said, "The teaching comes by way of natural connection."

Regarding the divine abidings, the word-by-word commentary and the entire method of meditation have been explained in every aspect in the Visuddhimagga.

Thus, the Blessed One, having shown the meditation on the divine abidings of that Non-returner—which is the opposite of the defilements such as covetousness, and which has gained a proximate cause because its enemies have been destroyed by the total abandoning of sensual lust and ill-will—now, in order to show insight (vipassanā) for the sake of his Arahatship and to show the attainment of Arahatship, spoke the words beginning with, "He [knows], 'There is this...'"

The meaning of that passage is: That Non-returner, who has developed the divine abidings, having emerged from any one of those divine abidings, [contemplates] those very divine abiding states...
181:
Having emerged from the Brahma-vihāra (Divine Abidings) and having delimited those very Brahma-vihāra states by way of mentality (nāma), and then delimiting the heart-base (hadayavatthu) which is the support of those Brahma-vihāras, as well as the great elements (mahābhūta) which depend on that heart-base, by way of materiality (rūpa) through the method of primary matter and derived matter (bhūtarūpa and upādārūpa), one knows specifically: "This mentality-materiality (nāma-rūpa) exists." By this extent of delimiting mentality-materiality, this Anāgāmī (Non-returner) has accomplished the delimitation of the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca). After delimiting the Truth of Suffering, when investigating the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca) which is the cause of that suffering, one knows: "The inferior Truth of the Origin exists." By this extent of delimiting craving (lobha), this Anāgāmī has accomplished the delimitation of the Truth of the Origin.

After delimiting the Truth of the Origin, when investigating the means for the abandonment of that Truth of the Origin, one knows: "The noble Truth of the Path (magga-sacca) exists." By this extent of knowing the Truth of the Path, this Anāgāmī has accomplished the delimitation of the Truth of the Path. After delimiting the Truth of the Path, when investigating the state to be attained by that Path, one knows: "There is Nibbāna, which is beyond this suffering of the round (vaṭṭa-dukkha) and is the escape from all suffering of the round." The meaning is that one knows specifically: "Beyond this state which has reached the object of the Brahma-vihāra perception (saññā) attained by me, there is Nibbāna, the escape." By this extent of delimiting Nibbāna, that person has accomplished the delimitation of the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca).

Regarding the phrase "tassa evaṃ jānato evaṃ passato" (for him who thus knows and thus sees): for that person who knows the Four Noble Truths in these four ways through insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā), and who thus sees through the wisdom of the Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga-paññā), the mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava) in the same manner as stated in the Bhayabherava Sutta... up to... one knows: "itthattāyāti pajānāti" (there is no more of this state of being).

Having thus led the teaching up to the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala), the Blessed One knew that at that time, a Brahmin who believed in purification through bathing was sitting in the assembly, and that upon hearing the virtues of purification through bathing being spoken of in this way, he would go forth and attain Arahantship. Therefore, to give that Brahmin an opportunity, He spoke this separate connection (anusandhi): "Monks, this bhikkhu is called one who has bathed with the internal bathing." In that text, "antarena sinānena" (by internal bathing) means by the most excellent bathing of the Noble Path (ariya-magga) which purifies the stains of defilements (kilesa) that arise within the mental continuum.

Regarding "Sundarikabhāradvājo": that Brahmin was named Bhāradvāja by way of his lineage. However, he held the wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi) that for one who bathes in the Sundarikā River, there is the abandonment of evil. Therefore, he is called "Sundarika Bhāradvāja." Upon hearing those words of the Blessed One, the Brahmin thought: "We praise purification through bathing, and the ascetic Gotama also praises it in the same way; now this ascetic Gotama has the same desire as we do." Then, imagining the Blessed One as if He had gone to the Bāhuka River, washed away evil in that river, and returned, he asked: "Does the Venerable Gotama go to the Bāhuka River to bathe?" The Blessed One, without saying "I go" or "I do not go," but wishing to uproot the Brahmin's wrong view, said: "Brahmin, what can the Bāhuka River do?" The meaning of that Pali is...
182:
Regarding the river (and bathing), He said: "What can the Bāhuka River do?" The meaning is: What benefit is there in the Bāhuka River? What can that river do? Since it is not capable of providing any benefit to anyone, why go to that river?

Then the Brahmin, wishing to praise that river, spoke the words beginning with "lokkhasammatā." In that context, "lokkhasammatā" means it is regarded as giving the nature of purity (cokkha-bhāva), thus it is said to be "regarded as having the nature of purity (lūkha-bhāva-sammatā)." There is also a reading "lokayasammatā," meaning it is regarded as leading to the noble world. "Puññasammatā" means it is regarded as merit (puñña). "Pavāheti" means it causes to go or it purifies. "Gāthāhi ajjhabhāsī" means he addressed specifically with verses. Verses are spoken either to clarify the meaning mentioned before, or for those who delight in verses, or to show a special meaning. Here, it should be understood that they were spoken to show both of those meanings.

Only this word "Bāhukaṃ" clarifies the meaning mentioned below. The remaining words clarify special meanings. Just as the multitude of people go to the Bāhuka River to wash away evil through bathing, they also go to the fords (tittha) such as Adhikakka to purify evil. Among them, those who are near those places bathe three times a day. Those who are far bathe in sequence: twice, once, every other day, and so on up to once a year. Those who cannot go at all have water brought from there in jars and bathe. All of this is useless. Therefore, to show this special meaning, He said "adhikakkādīnipi" (Adhikakka and so on).

In that Pali, "Adhikakka" refers to a certain ford named so because of the structures for bathing equipment. "Gayā" also refers to a ford that has the shape of a circular pond. "Payāga" is also a ford of the Ganges River, located opposite the stairs of the palace of King Mahāpanāda which is submerged in the Ganges. Bāhuka, Sundarikā, Sarassatī, and Bāhumatī are four rivers. "Bāla" means a person without wisdom. "Pakkhanda" means one who enters. "Na sujjhati" means one does not reach the purification of defilements (kilesa), but only washes away physical dust and dirt.

"What can the Sundarikā River do?" means what can the Sundarikā River do in the purification of defilements? The intention is that it is not capable of doing anything. This same method applies to the Payāga ford and the Bāhuka River. By these three words mentioned—Sundarikā, Payāga, and Bāhuka—the other four such as Adhikakka are also already mentioned by the method of the conveyance of characteristics (lakkhaṇahāra-naya). Therefore, the Sundarikā River...
183:
The Payāga ford and the Bāhukā river cannot effect any purification of defilements; likewise, it should be understood that fords such as Adhikakka and others cannot do so either. 'Vērī' refers to a person endowed with the fivefold enmity, such as killing living beings. 'Katakibbisaṃ' refers to one who has committed wicked and evil deeds. The meaning is that the Sundarikā river, the Payāga ford, or the Bāhukā river cannot cleanse or purify such a person. 'Pāpakammī' refers to a person endowed with evil and cruel kammic actions that bring danger, or a person endowed with even minor evils that have not yet reached the state of being cruel dangers but are still base actions.

'Suddhassa' refers to a person without defilements. 'Sadā Phaggū' means always being conjoined with the Phaggunī constellation. It is said that in the month of Phagguna, on the day conjoined with the Uttara-phaggunī constellation, the Brahmin held the view that 'whoever bathes [then] purifies the evil committed throughout the year.' Therefore, desiring to dispel that Brahmin's view, the Blessed One said, 'For the pure, it is always Phaggū.' For one free from defilements, it is always the Phaggunī constellation; how could anyone else be pure? 'Uposatho sadā' means that for the pure person, even if they do not formally undertake the factors of the Uposatha on days such as the 14th or 15th, they are constantly in a state of Uposatha. 'Suddhassa sucikammassa' refers to a person who is pure due to being free from defilements and is endowed with pure actions of body, speech, and so on. 'Sadā sampajjate vataṃ' means that for such a person, the undertaking of practices associated with wholesome states is always fulfilled. 'Idheva sināhi' means 'bathe only in this Dispensation of mine.' What is meant? It means: 'If you desire the washing away of the stain of internal defilements, bathe only in this Dispensation of mine with the water of the Noble Eightfold Path; for this water of the Path does not exist elsewhere.'

Now, wishing to show the purification in the three doors by the power of a teaching suitable for that Brahmin, [the Buddha] spoke the words beginning with 'Sabbabhūtesu karohi khemaṃ.' Therein, 'khemaṃ' means fearlessness and the state of welfare; it refers to the development of loving-kindness (mettā). By this statement, the purification of the mind-door is shown for that Brahmin. By the words 'Sace musā na bhaṇasi,' the purification of the speech-door is shown. By the words 'Sace pāṇaṃ na hiṃsasi, sace adinnaṃ nādiyasi,' the purification of the body-door is shown. By the words 'Saddahāno amaccharī,' he urged the Brahmin, who thus had purified doors, toward the fulfillment of faith and the fulfillment of generosity. The verse 'Kiṃ kāhasi gayaṃ gantvā, udapānopi te gayā' is a half-verse. If you practice fearlessness toward all beings, do not speak lies, do not kill living beings, do not take what is not given, and are endowed with faith and free from stinginess, what will you do by going to the Gayā ford? Even the well [at your home] is Gayā for you.
184:
Whether in the Gayā river or in a well, how could purification of internal defilements be achieved for one who bathes by means of this practice? However, the purification of external dirt is the same in both places; thus it should be connected. And because in the world Gayā is highly esteemed as a purifying river, even though the Blessed One was asked, 'Does Master Gotama go to the Bāhukā?' he did not say, 'What will you do by going to the Bāhukā?' but said, 'What will you do by going to the Gayā?'—this should be understood.

The words beginning with 'Evaṃ vutte' are quite clear as they have been spoken in the Bhayabherava Sutta. In the phrases beginning with 'Eko vūpakaṭṭho,' 'eko' means being alone through physical seclusion (kāya-viveka). 'Vūpakaṭṭho' means withdrawing to a secluded place through mental seclusion (citta-viveka). 'Appamatto' means being diligent by not abandoning mindfulness of the meditation subject. 'Ātāpī' means having the ardor called physical and mental energy that burns up defilements. 'Pahitatto' means having a resolute mind that has been sent forth without concern for body or life. 'Viharanto' means dwelling in one or another of the postures. The phrase 'Nacirasseva' (not long after) is said starting from the time of ordination. Regarding 'Kulaputtā' (sons of good family), there are two kinds: sons of good family by birth (jāti-kulaputta) and sons of good family by conduct (ācāra-kulaputta); this Brahmin Sundarika Bhāradvāja is a son of good family in both ways. 'Agārasmā' means from the house. The work beneficial to the house is called 'agāriya,' referring to household maintenance such as plowing and cattle-rearing. Since in this monkhood there is no such household benefit, it is called 'anagāriya' (homelessness). This is a designation for the monkhood. 'Pabbajanti' means they go forth, they approach. 'Tadanuttaraṃ' refers to that unsurpassed, supreme goal. 'Brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ' refers to the fruit of Arahantship, which is the culmination of the holy life of the Path. For the sake of that fruit of Arahantship, sons of good family go forth. 'Diṭṭheva dhamme' means in this very present existence. 'Sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā' means realizing for oneself through one's own wisdom and knowing without depending on others. 'Upasampajja vihāsī' means having attained and fulfilled it, he dwelt. While dwelling thus, 'Birth is destroyed... and so on... he knew.' By this word 'abbhaññāsi,' the object of the reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa) of that Arahant is shown.

If it is asked, 'Which birth of that Arahant is destroyed? And how did he know that birth?' the answer is given. Although this matter has been stated in the Bhayabherava Sutta, it is briefly stated here again to show the method of connection in the third person (pathama-purisa). It cannot be said that his past birth is destroyed, because it was already destroyed previously. It is not future birth, because there is no effort toward that future existence. It is not present birth, because it is currently manifest. But the birth that would have arisen in the one-constituent, four-constituent, or five-constituent existences with the divisions of one, four, or five aggregates because the Path had not yet been developed—that birth, because the Path has been developed, has been destroyed by reaching the state of non-arising. That Arahant, having reviewed the defilements abandoned by the development of the Path, knows that because of the absence of defilements, even the existing kamma will not produce rebirth in the future.
185:
"Vusitaṃ" means lived, lived repeatedly, done, practiced, and brought to completion. "Brahmacariyaṃ" refers to the noble practice of the Path. "Kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ" means that the sixteen-fold task—by way of the functions of full understanding (pariññā), abandoning (pahāna), realization (sacchikiriyā), and development (bhāvanā) through the four Paths regarding the four Noble Truths—has been completed. "Nāparaṃ itthattāya" means that now there is no more of this state (the sixteen-fold task of the Path) as in the present life, nor is there any further development of the Path for the destruction of defilements. Alternatively, "itthattāya" means there is no further continuity of the aggregates beyond this current continuity of the aggregates. He understood that these five aggregates, which have been fully understood, remain like a tree with its roots cut. "Aññataro" means a certain person. "Arahataṃ" means he became one among the Arahants, the disciples of the Blessed One.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## the Explanation of the Vattha Sutta is finished.
## 8. Explanation of the Sallekha Sutta

The sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Sallekha Sutta. Therein, "Mahācunda" is the name of that Elder. "Sāyanhasamayaṃ" means in the evening. In the phrase "paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito," "paṭisallānaṃ" means turning back from the various formations of beings and dwelling in seclusion, being alone, or solitude. One who has arisen from that seclusion is called "one who has arisen from seclusion." Since this Venerable Mahācunda arose from the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti), which is the highest form of seclusion, he is said to have "arisen from seclusion."

"Bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā" means respectfully saluting the Blessed One with his head adorned by the brilliant light of his ten fingers joined together, or having performed the salutation, causing the words "Cunda, may you be happy" to be spoken. It is said that when the Blessed One is saluted, he raises his neck, which is like a golden drum, and utters the Brahma-voice (brahmaghosa), which is pleasant to the ear, endearing, and like an aspersion of nectar, saying "May you be happy," calling the person by name. This is the custom of the Tathāgatas. The following sutta is evidence for this: "Venerable Sir, Sakka, the lord of devas, together with his ministers and followers, salutes the Blessed One's feet with his head." (When the celestial musician Pañcasikha reported this), the Buddha replied, "Pañcasikha, may Sakka, the lord of devas, together with his ministers and followers, be happy; for devas, humans, asuras, nāgas, and gandhabbas desire happiness. Those who..."
186:
"...and there are many other beings." (Thus he said). In this way, the Tathāgatas address such powerful yakkhas (devas) with the knowledge of compassion.

The phrase "yā imā" is spoken as if bringing the words to be said into the present. "Anekavihitā" means of various kinds and varieties. "Diṭṭhiyo" means wrong views. "Loke uppajjanti" means they manifest among beings. "Attavādappaṭisaṃyuttā" means those connected with the doctrine of self, occurring in the manner of "one regards form as self," etc.; there are twenty such views. "Lokavādappaṭisaṃyuttā" means those connected with the doctrine of the world, occurring in the manner of "the self and the world are eternal," etc.; there are eight such views. They are eight because they occur as: the self and the world are eternal; not eternal; both eternal and not eternal; neither eternal nor not eternal; finite; infinite; both finite and infinite; and neither finite nor infinite.

In the words "ādimeva" etc., the following meaning should be understood: "Venerable Sir, for a monk who attends [to things] at the very beginning (through serenity and insight), even if he has not yet reached the Path of Stream-entry, can the abandoning and relinquishing of these wrong views occur merely by this much means of the first attention mixed with insight?" This should be understood as the Elder asking as if he were one possessed of overestimation (adhimāna), although he himself was not, in order to remove the overestimation of those who are. Others, however, say: "Among the Elder's pupils, there were some who thought that the abandoning of views by way of eradication (samuccheda-pahāna) occurs through initial attention alone, and some who thought that the dwelling in attainment (samāpatti-vihāra) is the dwelling in effacement (sallekha-vihāra). He asked the Blessed One for their benefit."

Then the Blessed One, wishing to show him the means of abandoning those views, spoke the words beginning with "yā imā." Therein, the passage "yattha cetā diṭṭhiyo uppajjanti" etc., is spoken with reference to the five aggregates. For it is in these five aggregates that these views arise. As he said: "Bhikkhus, when there is form, by clinging to form and misinterpreting it, such a view arises: 'That self is that world; after death I shall be permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change,'" and so on in detail. However, by way of the object, he spoke in the singular as "yattha ca," meaning in whatever object they arise. Here, the distinction between these three terms—"uppajjanti," "anusenti," and "samudācaranti"—should be understood. Views that have not yet arisen but are arising by way of birth (jāti) are said to "arise" (uppajjanti). Defilements that have gained strength through repeated cultivation and have not yet been abandoned by the Noble Path are said to "underlie" (anusenti). Wrong views that have reached the doors of body and speech and have become manifest are said to "obsess" or "be active" (samudācaranti). This is the distinction between these three.

In the passages beginning with "netaṃ mama," the meaning is: "This object, such as the five aggregates, is not mine; this collection of the five aggregates is not I; this collection of the five aggregates is not my self." In the passage "evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ," the meaning of the words should first be understood in this way. This is because, among these three, the clinging "this is mine" is the clinging of craving (taṇhā-gāha), which has eighteen varieties of mental wandering.
187:
Defilements that have reached a state of strength, which have not yet been removed by the Noble Path and lie latent repeatedly, are called 'anusenti'. Their arising upon reaching the doors of body and speech is called 'samudācaranti'. This is the distinction between these terms. For one who sees according to reality with right wisdom that 'This object, consisting of the five aggregates, is not mine; this collection of the five aggregates I am not; this collection of the five aggregates is not my self,' the meaning of the words should first be understood in this way.

Because in this context, the grasping of 'This is mine' is the grasping of craving (taṇhāgāha). One who grasps in this way grasps the proliferation of craving (taṇhāpapañca) consisting of the eighteen types of mental wandering. The grasping of 'This I am' is the grasping of conceit (mānagāha). One who grasps in this way grasps the nine types of the proliferation of conceit (mānapapañca). The grasping of 'This is my self' is the grasping of views (diṭṭhigāha). One who grasps in this way grasps the sixty-two types of the proliferation of views (diṭṭhipapañca). Therefore, by saying 'This is not mine,' the Blessed One rejects the aforementioned proliferation of craving. By saying 'This I am not,' He rejects the proliferation of conceit. By saying 'This is not my self,' He rejects the proliferation of views. In this regard, craving and conceit should be understood as having the same basis as views.

'In this way, these five aggregates' refers to the five aggregates in the manner of 'This is not mine,' and so forth. 'According to reality' (yathābhūtaṃ) means according to their nature, as they truly exist in the manner of being impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul. The five aggregates exist only in that manner. The intention is that although they are grasped as 'mine' and so forth, they do not exist in that manner. 'For one who sees with right wisdom' refers to one who sees clearly with insight wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) culminating in the wisdom of the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga-paññā). 'In this way, of these things' means by this method, of these proliferations. Both 'abandoning' (pahāna) and 'relinquishing' (paṭinissagga) are synonyms for abandonment by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna).

Thus, when the Venerable Mahā Cunda asked a question concerning those with overestimation (adhimānika), inquiring whether the abandoning of views occurs through non-attention (amanasikāra) alone, the Blessed One showed the abandoning of views through the Path of Stream-entry. Now, wishing to distinguish the meditative states of those with overestimation, He said, 'Monks, there is such a case,' and so forth. In that context, those with overestimation (adhimānika) are those in whom overestimation arises by perceiving that they have attained what they have not yet attained. This overestimation does not arise in foolish worldlings (bāla-puthujjana) who follow the round of existence, nor does it arise in Noble Disciples (ariya-sāvaka). Indeed, overestimation does not arise in a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna) thinking 'I am a Once-returner (sakadāgāmī),' nor in a Once-returner thinking 'I am a Non-returner (anāgāmī),' nor in a Non-returner thinking 'I am an Arahant.' It only tends to arise in a practitioner (kāraka) who has suppressed the defilements through the power of serenity (samatha) or insight (vipassanā), who is constantly devoted to the practice, and who has begun insight. Because such a person does not see the manifestation of defilements suppressed by serenity or insight, overestimation arises thinking, 'I am a Stream-enterer, a Once-returner, a Non-returner, or an Arahant.'

This is like the case of the Elders who lived under the instruction of the Elder Dhammadinna, a resident of Talangaratissabbata. It is said that many monks attained distinction by following the instruction of that Elder Dhammadinna, even though he had not been ordained for long. Hearing of this, the Saṅgha of monks residing at Tissamahāvihāra said, 'This Elder is not one who encourages without reason; bring that Elder here,' and they sent many monks. Those monks went and said, 'Friend Dhammadinna, the Saṅgha of monks calls for you.' The Elder asked, 'Venerables, are you seeking yourselves or another?' When they replied, 'Good man, we are seeking ourselves,' the Elder gave them a meditation subject, and they all attained Arahantship. The Saṅgha of monks sent other monks again. In this way, up to the third time, all the monks who were sent attained Arahantship right there and remained.
188:
The overestimation (adhimāna) of thinking 'I am a Non-returner' or 'I am an Arahant' occurs to practitioners, just as it happened to the Elders who received the instruction of the Elder Dhammadinna residing at Talangaratissabbata.

It is heard that although the Elder Dhammadinna had not been ordained for long, many monks attained distinction by following his instruction. When the Saṅgha of monks residing at Tissamahāvihāra heard of this, they said, 'This Elder is not one who encourages without reason; bring that Elder here,' and they sent many monks. Those monks went and said, 'Friend Dhammadinna, the Saṅgha of monks calls for you.' Then the Elder Dhammadinna asked, 'Venerables, are you seeking yourselves or are you seeking another?' When they said, 'Good man, we are seeking only ourselves,' the Elder gave them a meditation subject, and all of them reached the fruit of Arahantship. The Saṅgha of monks sent other monks again. In this way, all the monks sent up to the third time reached the fruit of Arahantship right there and remained.

Then the Saṅgha, noting that 'all who go do not return,' sent another elderly ordained monk. That monk went and said, 'Venerable Dhammadinna, the Saṅgha of monks residing at Tissamahāvihāra has sent for you three times; do you not respect the authority of the Saṅgha and refuse to come?' The Elder said, 'Is it so?' and without even entering his dwelling, he had his bowl and robes taken and departed immediately. On the way, he entered Hiṅkanavihāra. In that monastery, there was a Great Elder over sixty years of age (vassa) who, through overestimation, claimed to have attained Arahantship. The Elder Dhammadinna approached him, paid respects, and after exchanging greetings, asked about his attainment. The Great Elder said, 'Yes, Dhammadinna, what should be done by a monk has been done by me; it has been done for a long time; I am now over sixty years of age.' When asked, 'Venerable, can you also exercise psychic power?' he replied, 'Yes, Dhammadinna.' The Elder said, 'It is well, Venerable; please create an elephant coming towards you.' Saying 'Very well, friend,' the Great Elder created a great elephant, entirely white, endowed with seven points of contact, with its tail raised in three ways, its trunk placed in its mouth, and coming forward as if to gore with its two tusks. When the Great Elder saw the elephant he himself had created, he became terrified and began to flee. At that moment, realizing 'I am not an Arahant,' he sat on his haunches at the feet of the Elder Dhammadinna and said, 'Friend Dhammadinna, be my refuge.' The Elder Dhammadinna comforted him, saying, 'Venerable, do not grieve; do not be displeased; such overestimation occurs only to practitioners,' and he gave him a meditation subject. The Great Elder, following that instruction, practiced and reached the fruit of Arahantship.
189:
At Cittalapabbata, there lived another elder similar to the previous one. The Elder Dhammadinna approached him as well and questioned him in the same manner. That elder also answered just like the former one. Then, Elder Dhammadinna asked, "Venerable Sir, do you also make use of psychic powers (iddhi)?" "Yes, friend Dhammadinna, I have used them," he replied. "It would be good, Venerable Sir, if you could create a lotus pond," he requested, and the elder created it. "Venerable Sir, please create a thicket of lotuses in this pond," he requested, and he created that too. "Venerable Sir, please create a large lotus flower in that thicket," he requested, and he created that too. "Venerable Sir, please create the figure of a woman standing on that lotus flower, singing and dancing with a sweet voice," he requested, and he created that too.

Elder Dhammadinna said, "Venerable Sir, please contemplate this female figure again and again," and then he himself entered the monastery building. As the elder contemplated the female figure, the defilements that had been suppressed for sixty years began to stir. At that moment, the elder realized he was still a worldling (puthujjana). Just like the previous elder, he took a meditation subject from Elder Dhammadinna and, through practice, attained the fruit of Arahatship.

Elder Dhammadinna then proceeded in due course and arrived at Tissamahāvihāra. At that time, the elders there had finished sweeping the courtyard of the stupa and were sitting, generating joy (pīti) with the Buddha as their object. It is said that this was their regular duty. Because they were fulfilling this duty, not a single elder among them spoke to Elder Dhammadinna or asked, "Please place your bowl and robes here." However, realizing that this must be Elder Dhammadinna, they asked him questions.
