Elder Dhammadinna answered the questions asked of him clearly and decisively, like cutting a bundle of lotus stalks with a sharp sword, and then struck the great earth with his big toe. "Venerable sirs, even this insentient great earth knows the virtue of Dhammadinna, but you do not know it," he said, and uttered this verse:

"This insentient earth knows virtue and non-virtue;
But you, venerable sirs, though sentient, do not know virtue and non-virtue."

Immediately after, he flew into the air and went to Talangaratissa Mountain. It is only to a monk who strives in this way that the overestimation (adhimāna) "I have attained the Noble Dhamma" arises. Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to distinguish jhāna for the sake of such monks, spoke the words beginning with "Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ" (This is a possibility).

The meaning of those words is as follows: This reason exists; it is not that it does not. By which jhāna a certain monk in this Dispensation, secluded from sensual pleasures associated with external wanderers... [pe]... enters and dwells in the first jhāna. To that monk, the thought might occur, "I am dwelling in effacement (sallekha)." The thought "I am dwelling by that practice which scrapes away defilements" is not appropriate.
190:
For a monk with overestimation (adhimānika), jhāna is neither effacement (sallekha) nor the practice of effacement. Why? Because it is not the foundation for insight (vipassanā). Such a monk, having entered jhāna and emerged from it, does not contemplate formations (saṅkhāra). That jhāna merely produces one-pointedness of mind for him and is a dwelling in happiness in the present life (diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra). Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to show this meaning, said: "Cunda, these are not called 'effacement' in the Noble One's Discipline; these are called 'dwellings in happiness in the present life' in the Noble One's Discipline." In that text, the word "ete" (these) should be understood as plural due to the factors of jhāna; it means "these factors of the first jhāna." Or, it is plural due to the attainments (samāpatti), because even a single first jhāna becomes many through repeated attainments. Or, it is plural due to the objects (ārammaṇa), because even a single first jhāna becomes many by occurring in the earth-kasiṇa and so on. This same method applies to the second, third, and fourth jhānas. In the formless (āruppa) jhānas, however, since there is no diversity of objects, the plural should be understood only by the first two reasons mentioned above.

Because the factors and objects of those jhānas are peaceful, free from the heat of defilements, and subtle, it should be understood that they are called "these peaceful dwellings" (santa-vihāra). This is the general explanation for all four jhānas. The specific explanation should be stated according to the words beginning with "sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ" (with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form). That explanation has already been given in every aspect in the Visuddhimagga. Thus, because the dwelling in jhāna of a monk with overestimation is not the foundation for insight, it is not a dwelling in effacement. That monk, having emerged from jhāna, does not contemplate formations but merely experiences a dwelling in happiness in the present life that produces one-pointedness of mind. Therefore, wishing to show this meaning, after distinguishing the fine-material jhānas and the immaterial jhānas, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with "Idha kho pana vo" (Here, however, for you...) to show the basis and the effacement that should be practiced in forty-four ways.

Why are non-violence (avihiṃsā) and so on called "effacement" through the eight attainments? Because they are the foundation for the supramundane (lokuttara). The eight attainments of those outside the Dispensation are only foundations for the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa). Within the Dispensation, even taking refuge is a foundation for the supramundane, let alone non-violence and the rest. By this very sutta, it should be understood that "compared to the gift given to one outside the Dispensation who has attained the eight attainments and five superknowledges, [the gift given] in the Dispensation..."
191:
“A gift given to one who is endowed with the Three Refuges in the Dispensation is of great fruit.” Indeed, with reference to this statement, it was said in the Dakkhiṇāvisuddhi Sutta: “Having given a gift to a recluse who is free from lust (vītarāga) for external sensual pleasures, a hundred-thousand-fold reward is to be expected. Having given a gift to a person practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, an incalculable and immeasurable reward is to be expected; what then to say of a stream-enterer?” (M. Ni. 3.379). It should be understood that in that Sutta, from the time of taking the refuges onwards, the “person practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry” is intended. This is the word-by-word grammatical explanation (atthayojanā) of the Pali text here.

In the sequential commentary (anupadavaṇṇanā), the word “idha” (here) is an indication of the subject matter such as harming (vihiṃsā) and so on. “Kho pana” is merely a particle. “Vo” is the genitive case used in the sense of the instrumental (karaṇattha). This is the summary of the meaning: We shall speak of the subject of harming and so on in the manner beginning with “Others will be harmful.” “Cunda, in this Dispensation, effacement (sallekha) should be practiced by you.”

Having thus spoken in brief, now wishing to elaborate, he said: “Others will be harmful; we shall be non-harmful here—thus effacement should be practiced,” and so forth.

In that Pali, “pare” (others) refers to any others who do not follow this practice of effacement. “Vihiṃsakā bhavissanti” means they will be harmers of beings by means of hands, clods of earth, and so on. “Mayamettha avihiṃsakā bhavissāma” means that in whatever matter others will be harmful in such a way, we shall be non-harmful in that very matter; we shall dwell having aroused non-harming. “Iti sallekho karaṇīyo” means thus effacement should be practiced by you. And here, “sallekha” (effacement) should be understood as non-harming (avihiṃsā) itself. For non-harming scrapes away (sallekhati) harming, it cuts it off; therefore, it is called “sallekha.” This method applies everywhere. However, this is the distinction: In the phrase “pare micchādiṭṭhī” (others are of wrong view), it should be understood that “diṭṭhi” is spoken of by combining the wrong view that is the end of the courses of action (kammapatha) and the wrong view that is the beginning of the wrongnesses (micchatta). Likewise, in the place where it is said “mayamettha sammādiṭṭhī,” right view should be understood. Here, the discussion on the courses of action will become clear in detail in the Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta. Regarding the wrongnesses, wrong view and so on will become clear in the Dvedhāvitakka Sutta.

The summary in this section is: Because they kill living beings, they are called “pāṇātipātī” (killers of beings). Because they take what belongs to others, they are called “adinnādāyī” (takers of what is not given). Because they practice the ignoble and low practice of sexual intercourse, they are called “abrahmacārī.”
192:
“Methunadhamma-paṭisevakā” means those who indulge in sexual intercourse. Because they practice the noble conduct, they are called “brahmacārī,” which means those who refrain from sexual intercourse. Here, “brahmacariya” (the holy life) should be understood as “sallekha” (effacement). This is because the holy life scrapes away unchastity. Because they speak words that are not true, they are called “musāvādī,” which means those who speak empty, false words that destroy the welfare of others. Because they have speech that creates discord, they are called “pisuṇavācā.” Because they have harsh speech that cuts the heart of others, they are called “pharusavācā.” Because they talk nonsense that has no substance, they are called “samphappalāpī.” Because they have the habit of covetously planning for the goods of others, they are called “abhijjhālū,” which means those who have a nature of longing for the belongings of others. Because they have a mind that is ruined and putrid, they are called “byāpannacittā.” Because they have a base view censured by the wise, they are called “micchādiṭṭhī.” This means they are endowed with the view beginning with “natthi dinnaṃ” (there is no result of giving) which is included in the courses of action (kammapatha), and with the non-emancipating view (aniyyānika-diṭṭhi) included in the wrongnesses (micchatta). Because they have a good view praised by the wise, they are called “sammādiṭṭhī.” This means they are endowed with the view of the ownership of deeds (kammassakatā-diṭṭhi) beginning with “atthi dinnaṃ” (there is result of giving) included in the courses of action, and with the path-view (magga-diṭṭhi) included in the rightnesses (sammatta).

“Micchāsaṅkappa” (wrong intention) refers to unwholesome intention that is incorrect and not a cause for liberation from the round of suffering. The same method applies to “micchāvācā” and so forth. However, the distinction here is that, unlike wrong intention and so on, there is no separate ultimate reality (dhamma) called “micchāsati” (wrong mindfulness). It is merely a designation for the four unwholesome aggregates occurring in one who thinks about the past. As for what was said by the Blessed One—“Monks, this mindfulness (anussati) exists, I do not say it does not exist; it exists for one who remembers the gain of a son, monks, or the gain of wealth, or the gain of fame”—this should be understood as being said with reference to the occurrence of something resembling mindfulness in one who thinks about those various objects. In the term “micchāñāṇī,” “micchāñāṇa” (wrong knowledge) should be understood as the delusion (moha) that arises by way of planning the means when performing an evil deed, and by way of reviewing after having done evil, thinking “I have done well.” One endowed with that delusion is a “micchāñāṇī.” In the term “sammāñāṇī,” the nineteen types of reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇāñāṇa) are called “sammāñāṇa.” One endowed with that knowledge is a “sammāñāṇī.” “Micchāvimutti” (wrong liberation) refers to those who, while not yet liberated from the round, perceive themselves as “we are liberated,” or those who perceive liberation in that which is not a cause for liberation. The word-definition (vacanattha) there is: because they have a wrong, base, and perverted liberation, they are “micchāvimutti.” And “micchāvimutti” is a designation for the unwholesome aggregates occurring in the manner stated above. Apart from the eight factors such as right view that are associated with the fruit (phala), the remaining associated states should be understood as “sammāvimutti” (right liberation). Because it stands having scraped away wrong liberation, it is called “sallekha.”
193:
It should be known as sallekha (effacement). Desiring to encourage that right practice (sammapatipatti), [the Buddha] said: "Effacement (sallekha) should be practiced, thinking, 'We will be those who possess right liberation (sammāvimutti) in this Dispensation (sāsana).'"

The following three terms are taught by way of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). Since 'covetous' (abhijjhālu) and 'ill-willed' (byāpannacitta) are taught in the paths of action (kammapatha), it should be understood that the first two hindrances are not taught here. In that context, those who are oppressed and overwhelmed by sloth and torpor are called 'overwhelmed by sloth and torpor' (thinamiddhapariyuṭṭhita). Those possessed of restlessness are called 'restless' (uddhata). Those who are weary in investigating a certain matter and are unable to reach a decision are called 'doubters' (vicikicchī).

The ten qualities beginning with 'angry' (kodhana) are taught by way of the defilements of the mind (upakkilesa). Whatever needs to be said regarding those qualities like anger has already been stated in the Dhammadāyāda Sutta and the Vatthu Sutta. Here, the word-meaning (vacanattha) is as follows: 'Angry' (kodhana) refers to those who have the nature of getting angry. 'Grudging' (upanāhī) refers to those who have the nature of bearing a grudge or those who possess a grudge. The same applies to 'contemptuous' (makkhī) and 'domineering' (palāsī). Those who are envious are called 'envious' (issukī). Those who are stingy or possess stinginess are called 'stingy' (maccharī). Those who are deceitful are called 'deceitful' (saṭha); it means they do not speak truthfully. This is a designation for those who possess a deceitful nature. Those who possess hypocrisy are called 'hypocritical' (māyāvī). Those who are stubborn due to being endowed with a hardened nature are called 'stubborn' (thaddha). Those who are arrogant due to being associated with excessive pride are called 'arrogant' (atimānī). The bright side (sukkapakkha) should be understood by the method of opposites.

'Difficult to admonish' (dubbaca) refers to those who are hard to speak to; when something is said to them, they cannot endure it. Those who are the opposite are called 'easy to admonish' (suvaca). Those who have evil friends similar to Devadatta and others are called 'having evil friends' (pāpamitta). Those who have good friends similar to the Buddha or Venerable Sāriputta and others are called 'having spiritual friends' (kalyāṇamitta). Those who are negligent (pamatta) are so called because they let their minds loose in bodily misconduct and so on. Those who are the opposite are called 'heedful' (appamatta). These three are taught by way of miscellaneous items (pakiṇṇaka).

The seven qualities beginning with 'faithless' (assaddha) are taught by way of unwholesome qualities (asaddhamma). Among them, those who have no faith in the Three Jewels are called 'faithless' (assaddha). Those who believe in the bright side or those who possess faith are called 'faithful' (saddha). Those who have no shame are called 'shameless' (ahirika); this is a designation for those who do not loathe the attainment of unwholesome states. Those who have shame in their minds or whose minds are associated with shame are called 'shameful' (hirimana). Those who do not dread [evil] are called 'fearless of wrongdoing' (anottappī); it means they do not fear the attainment of unwholesome states. Those who are the opposite are called 'dreading wrongdoing' (ottappī). Those of little learning are called 'of little learning' (appassuta). Here, 'little' (appa) should not be taken as 'a small amount' but as 'none'. Indeed, those who are devoid of learning are called 'of little learning' (appassuta). Those of great learning are called 'of great learning' (bahussuta); this is a designation for those who, having correctly understood even a single verse spoken by the Tathāgata, practice accordingly. Those who sink in a censurable manner are called 'lazy' (kusīta); this is a designation for those of inferior energy.
194:
Those who have aroused energy are called 'of aroused energy' (āraddhavīriya); this is a designation for those endowed with right efforts (sammappadhāna). Those who have muddled mindfulness are called 'of muddled mindfulness' (muṭṭhassatī); it means their mindfulness is lost. Those who have established mindfulness are called 'of established mindfulness' (upaṭṭhitassatī); this is a designation for those whose mindfulness is always directed towards the object. Those who have corrupted wisdom are called 'unwise' (duppañña); it means their wisdom is lost. Those who are endowed with wisdom are called 'endowed with wisdom' (paññāsampannā). Here, wisdom should be understood as insight wisdom (vipassanā-paññā). Since the fulfillment of the requisites of insight is mentioned in this context, the instruction of the ancient teachers is that this is indeed insight wisdom.

Now, desiring to show the wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) which causes obstacles to supramundane qualities and does not lead out of the round of suffering, by way of three aspects, [the Buddha] said the words beginning with 'adhering to one's own views' (sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī). In that text, one is called 'adhering to one's own views' (sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī) because they grasp their own views. One is called 'gripping firmly' (ādhānaggāhī) because they grasp tightly; ādhāna means firm, thus it means 'one who grips firmly'. One who relinquishes their view upon seeing a proper reason is called 'relinquishing' (paṭinissaggī). One who cannot relinquish even when shown many reasons with great difficulty and hardship is called 'difficult to make relinquish' (duppaṭinissaggī). This is a designation for those who, having firmly grasped the view that has arisen in them as 'this alone is the truth', do not relinquish it even when told by wise ones such as the Buddha who show them reasons. Such persons, whatever doctrine (dhamma) or non-doctrine (adhamma) they grasp, they hold it all, saying, 'Thus it was told by our teachers, thus we have heard,' and just as a tortoise withdraws its limbs into its own shell, or like the grip of a crocodile, they grasp and do not let go. The bright side (sukkapakkha) should be understood by the opposite method.

Having thus shown effacement (sallekha) by way of forty-four aspects, now, to show the great benefit of the arising of thought (cittuppāda) in that effacement, [the Buddha] said the words beginning with 'Cunda, I say that even the arising of thought...' (cittuppādam pi kho ahaṃ).

The meaning is: 'Cunda, I say that even the arising of thought regarding wholesome states is of great benefit.' If that is so, what need is there to speak of the compliance through body and speech—such as performing those qualities with the body just as the thought first arose, or commanding with the speech, 'Do [this],' or learning and questioning? He shows that such compliance is indeed extremely beneficial. Why is even the arising of thought of great benefit here? Because it brings about absolute welfare and happiness, and because it is the cause of compliance through body and speech.
195:
The arising of the thought (cittuppāda) 'I shall give' itself certainly brings about welfare and happiness, and it is also the cause for the subsequent practices (anuvidhiyanā) of body and speech. Indeed, because such a thought 'I shall give' has arisen, on the second day, one clears the main road, builds a great pavilion, and gives alms to a hundred or a thousand monks. One commands the attendants, 'Invite the Saṅgha of monks, honor them, and serve them with food.' Similarly, the arising of the thought 'I shall offer robes, dwellings, and medicine to the Saṅgha' itself certainly brings about welfare and happiness, and is the cause for subsequent practices of body and speech. Because such a thought has arisen, one prepares robes and so forth, and gives them oneself or causes others to give. This same method applies to taking refuge and so on.

Only after giving rise to the thought 'I shall go for refuge' does one later take refuge by body or speech. Likewise, only after giving rise to the thought 'I shall undertake the five, eight, or ten precepts' does one undertake them by body or speech. After giving rise to the thought 'I shall ordain and establish myself in the fourfold purity of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla),' one fulfills the virtue to be fulfilled by body and speech. Only after giving rise to the thought 'I shall learn the word of the Buddha (buddhavacana)' does one learn one, two, three, four, or five Nikāyas by speech. In this same way, it should be understood extensively by way of undertaking the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), learning meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna), performing the preliminary work for kasiṇas, and through jhāna, attainment (samāpatti), insight (vipassanā), the path (magga), the fruit (phala), the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha (paccekabodhi), and the supreme enlightenment (sammāsambodhi).

The arising of the thought 'I shall become a Buddha' itself certainly brings about welfare and happiness, and is the cause for subsequent practices. Indeed, because such a thought has arisen, at a later time, for four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand aeons, one fulfills the perfections (pāramīs) by body and speech, and wanders about saving the world together with the devas from suffering. Thus, in all matters, the arising of thought is of great benefit. However, it should be understood that the subsequent practice (anuvidhiyanā) by body and speech is of even greater benefit.

Having thus shown the great benefit of the arising of thought in wholesome states, now, wishing to exhort one toward those wholesome states, the Teacher spoke the words beginning with 'Tasmā tiha Cunda.' The meaning of those words is quite clear.

Having shown the great benefit of the arising of thought in the effacement (sallekha) shown by way of forty-four modes, now, wishing to show the nature of the path for the attainment of welfare through that very effacement, the Teacher spoke the words beginning with 'Seyyathāpi.' The meaning of that Pali is: For example, there might be an uneven path with thorns, stumps, and so forth. Just as there might be another path, an even one like a well-prepared piece of ground, for the purpose of bypassing and avoiding that path with thorns and stumps. Or, there might be an uneven landing place (ford) disturbed by tree roots, stones, precipices, and so forth. For the purpose of bypassing and avoiding that dangerous landing place, there might be another even landing place, which is gradually deep and like a flight of steps.
196:
Cunda, the meaning of those words is this: For example, there might be an uneven path with stumps, thorns, stones, and so forth. To bypass and avoid that uneven path, there might be another even path like a well-prepared piece of ground. Similarly, there might be an uneven landing place (ford) that is dangerous and disturbed by tree roots, stones, precipices, crocodiles, sea-monsters (makaras), and so forth. To bypass and avoid that dangerous landing place, there might be another landing place that is not uneven, but is gradually deep and like a flight of steps. One who has entered that landing place could easily descend into that river or lake to bathe or to cross over to the other side. Even so, Cunda, for a person who is harmful, being possessed of harmfulness (vihiṃsā) which is like the uneven path and the uneven landing place, harmlessness (avihiṃsā), which is like the even path and the even landing place, is for the purpose of bypassing. Just as an even path and landing place are prepared to avoid an uneven path and landing place, so harmlessness is prepared to avoid harmfulness. One who follows that path of harmlessness would easily reach the human realm or the deva realm and enjoy prosperity, or would transcend the world. In this same way, all the other terms should be applied and understood.

Having thus shown how that practice of effacement is the path for the attainment of welfare, now, wishing to show its quality of leading to the higher states, the Teacher spoke the words beginning with 'Seyyathāpi.'

The meaning of those words is: Cunda, for example, whether they generate rebirth or not, and whether they generate results after rebirth has been given or not, all unwholesome states (akusala dhamma) are called 'downward-leading' (adhobhāgaṅgamanīya) by their nature, because they produce undesirable and disagreeable results at the time of fruition. Similarly, whether they generate rebirth or not, and whether they generate results after rebirth has been given or not, all wholesome states (kusala dhamma) are called 'upward-leading' (uparibhāgaṅgamanīya) by their nature, because they produce desirable and agreeable results at the time of fruition. Even so, Cunda, for one who is harmful... (and so forth), harmlessness is for the purpose of going to the higher states. In this matter, the comparison between the simile and the thing illustrated is: Just as all unwholesome states lead to the lower states, so the single act of harmfulness of a harmful person leads to the lower states. And just as all wholesome states lead to the higher states, so the single act of harmlessness of a harmless person leads to the higher states. In this way, the unwholesome should be compared with the unwholesome, and the wholesome with the wholesome. This is the intended meaning here.

Having thus shown that the practice of effacement leads to the higher states, now, to show its ability to bring about total extinguishing (of defilements), the Teacher spoke the words beginning with 'So vata Cunda.'
197:
In that passage, 'so' (he) refers to the person of the type already described. In relation to that word 'so', this introductory statement 'yo' (who) should be brought in and the connection in all instances should be understood as: 'Cunda, that one who is himself sunk in the mire will indeed pull out another who is sunk in the mire—this is not possible.' 'Palipapalipanna' refers to one who is submerged in deep mud; however, this is not the case in the Discipline (Vinaya) of the Noble Ones. In the Discipline of the Noble Ones, 'palipa' (mire) refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure. 'Palipanna' (sunk) refers to the foolish worldling who is submerged in those five strands of sensual pleasure. Therefore, the construction of the meaning here should be understood in this way.

Cunda, for example, it is not possible for a man who is himself submerged in deep mud up to the tip of his nose to pull out another person submerged in that same mud by grabbing them by the hand or the head. This is because there is no basis by which he could pull that person out and place them on dry ground. In the same way, it is not possible for one who is himself sunk in the mire of the five strands of sensual pleasure to pull out another who is likewise sunk in the mire.

In that case, if it were said, "This is incorrect, for even worldling monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen, having heard the Dhamma teaching, do become those who realize the Dhamma; therefore, one sunk in the mire does pull out another," that statement should not be regarded in that way. For in that instance, it is the Blessed One himself who pulls them out. The Dhamma preachers, however, receive only praise, like a reader of a letter sent by a king. For example, when a king sends a letter to a border region, the people there, not knowing how to read the letter, have someone who knows how to read it read it to them. Upon hearing the contents, they respectfully fulfill it, saying, "It is the king's command." They do not think, "This is the command of the letter-reader." The letter-reader, however, receives only praise, such as, "He read it with a clear and faultless voice." In the same way, although Dhamma preachers such as the Venerable Sāriputta preach the Dhamma, they are like the reader of the written letter. That Dhamma teaching is the teaching of the Blessed One alone, like the king's command. It should be understood that the Blessed One himself pulls out those who, having heard that Dhamma, realize it. The Dhamma preachers, however, receive only praise, such as, "They preach the Dhamma with a clear and faultless voice." Therefore, that statement (that only one not sunk can pull out another) is indeed appropriate. By the opposite of what has been said, the bright side (sukkapakkha) should be understood.

In the phrase 'adanta, avinīta, aparinibbūta': he is 'adanta' (untamed) because he is not free from the poison (of defilements). He is 'avinīta' (undisciplined) because he has not trained in the discipline. He is 'aparinibbūta' (unextinguished) because his defilements are not yet extinguished. It should be understood that such a person will tame another, [make them] free from poison...
198:
It is not possible that (one who is possessed by the poison of defilements) will discipline another, will make another free from the poison of defilements, will discipline them, will make them practice the three trainings, or will extinguish their defilements. The bright side (sukkapakkha), which is the opposite of what was previously stated, should also be understood. 

'Cunda, in the same way, for one who is cruel... (pe)... it leads to the extinguishing of defilements'—in this context, the meaning should be understood as follows: How? Just as it is possible that one who is not himself stuck in the deep mud of sensual pleasures will pull out another who is stuck in the mud; one who is himself tamed will tame another; one who is himself disciplined in the Vinaya will make another disciplined; one who has himself extinguished defilements will extinguish the defilements of another—this is possible. What is the reason for that? It is the state of not being stuck, the state of being tamed, the state of being disciplined, and the state of having extinguished defilements. 

Cunda, in the same way, for a person who is cruel, non-cruelty (avihimsā) leads to the extinguishing of defilements. What does this mean? The non-cruelty of one who is himself non-cruel serves to extinguish the cruelty of another who is cruel. For it is possible that one who is himself non-cruel will extinguish the intention of cruelty in another. What is the reason for that? It is simply the state of being non-cruel. If one has attained a quality oneself, one is able to establish another in that same quality for their benefit. 

Alternatively, just as it is possible that one who is not stuck, is tamed, disciplined, and extinguished will pull out, tame, discipline, and extinguish another who is stuck, untamed, undisciplined, and unextinguished; in the same way, for a person who is cruel, the non-cruelty that arises when developing the path (magga) for the abandoning of cruelty leads to the extinguishing of defilements. Just as one who is extinguished can extinguish one who is not, the intention of non-cruelty alone is capable of extinguishing the intention of cruelty. To show this meaning, the words 'Even so, Cunda,' etc., were spoken; this is how the meaning should be understood here. As in this case, the meaning should be understood in all other terms such as killing (pāṇātipāta), etc. Fearing it would be too lengthy, the word-by-word connection is not made. 

Having thus shown the capability to extinguish the defilements of that being, now, concluding the teaching and to urge them toward the practice of the Dhamma, the words 'Thus, Cunda,' etc., were spoken. In that Pali, 'sallekhapariyāya' means the cause of effacement (sallekha). This method applies everywhere. Here, non-cruelty and so on are the causes of effacement because they scrape away cruelty and so on. Because they cause the mind to arise through their power, they are called the cause of the arising of thought (cittuppādakāraṇa). Because they are the cause for avoiding cruelty and so on, they are called the cause of avoidance (parikkamanakāraṇa). Because they bring about the higher stages, they are called the cause of the higher part (uparibhāgakāraṇa). Because they extinguish cruelty and so on, they are called the cause of extinguishing (parinibbāpanakāraṇa). 

'Anukampaka' (compassionate) refers to one who constantly pities beings by seeking their welfare. 'Anukampāṃ upādāya' (out of compassion) means taking hold of or grasping with a mind associated with compassion. 'Taṃ mayā' (that by me) means 'I, the Buddha, by showing these five causes, have performed this teaching for you.' The unerring Dhamma teaching of the compassionate Buddha exists; with this much, the Buddha's task is complete. After this, what is called 'practice' (paṭipatti) is the task of the disciples. 

Having thus shown the Buddha's task, now, wishing to command the disciples' task, the words 'These are the roots of trees,' etc., were spoken. In some versions, the word 'roots of trees' (rukkhamūlāni) shows the dwelling at the foot of a tree. The word 'empty huts' (suññāgārāni) shows a place secluded from people. By both terms, he points out and assigns a dwelling suitable for the practice of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna). 'Jhāyatha' (meditate) means by way of jhāna, which is the close contemplation of an object...
199:
Because it is the cause for the upper part, it is called uparibhāga-kāraṇa; because it causes the extinguishment of cruelty and so forth, it is known as parinibbāpana-kāraṇa. Hitesinā refers to one who is compassionate by seeking welfare (hita). Anukampaka refers to one who possesses compassion. Anukampā upādāya means having embraced or taken up compassion with a mind associated with pity. Katā vo taṃ mayā means 'I, the Buddha, by showing these five methods, have performed that teaching of the Dhamma for you.' The duty of a compassionate Teacher is only this much: the teaching of the Dhamma that is unerring. Beyond this, what is called practice (paṭipatti) is the duty of the disciples. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Cunda, these are the roots of trees... this is our instruction.'

In that passage, by the word 'rukkhamūlāni', He shows the dwelling at the roots of trees. By the word 'suññāgārāni', He shows places secluded from people. By both words, He points out dwellings suitable for meditation and hands over the inheritance. Jhāyatha means: by means of meditation that contemplates the object (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna), contemplate the thirty-eight meditation objects (excluding space and light); and by means of meditation that contemplates the characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna), contemplate the aggregates, sense bases, etc., by way of impermanence and so forth. It means: develop tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). Mā pamādattha means: do not be negligent. Mā pacchā vippaṭisārino ahuvattha means: those monks who, in the past—during the time of youth, the time of health, the time of being endowed with the seven suitable factors, and the time of being in the presence of the Teacher—being devoid of wise attention (yoniso manasikāra), spent day and night with a gloomy face, enjoying the pleasure of sleep and the pleasure of drowsiness, and were negligent. Those monks, later—at the time of old age, the time of sickness, the time of death, the time of ruin, and the time after the Teacher has attained Parinibbāna—remembering that former life of negligence and seeing the grave danger of death that leads to rebirth, become remorseful. Showing this meaning, 'Do not be such persons,' He said: 'Do not be regretful later.' Ayaṃ vo amhākaṃ anusāsanī means: 'This instruction from us to you, "Meditate, do not be negligent," is the advice (ovāda).'

## In the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, Papañcasūdanī,
## The Explanation of the Sallekha Sutta is finished.
## 9. Sammādiṭṭhisutta-vaṇṇanā

The Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta. 'Thus have I heard' and so forth is the Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta. In that sutta, 'Friends, "Right View, Right View" it is said; to what extent, friends...' or 'What is the unwholesome?'—thus the Elder Sāriputta spoke with the desire to explain the entire commentary. In this regard, even those who do not know wisdom say 'Right View.' Those outside the dispensation and those within the dispensation say it, either by way of hearsay or by personal realization. Therefore, based on that speech of many, and wishing to examine it twice, he said 'Right View, Right View.' Indeed, this following...
200:
'Friends, "unwholesome"'—to this extent, whatever questions were spoken by the Elder, they were all questions asked with the desire to explain. In those questions, because even those who know say 'Right View,' and those who do not know, those outside the dispensation, those within the dispensation, by way of hearsay, or by personal realization also say it; therefore, based on the speech of many, the Elder, considering it twice, said: 'Friends, it is said, "Right View, Right View."' The meaning here is: 'Right View' is spoken of by some, and 'Right View' is spoken of by others. Based on the meaning and characteristics of that which is so called, [the question is]: 'Friend, to what extent is a noble disciple one of Right View?'

In that passage, 'Sammādiṭṭhi' refers to a person endowed with beautiful and praiseworthy wisdom. When this word Sammādiṭṭhi refers only to the Dhamma, then beautiful and praiseworthy wisdom should be understood as the meaning of 'Right View.' This Right View is of two kinds: mundane (lokiya) and supramundane (lokuttara). Among these, the knowledge of the ownership of kamma (kammassakatā-ñāṇa) and the knowledge in conformity with the truths (saccānulomika-ñāṇa or insight knowledge) are called mundane Right View. Or, in brief, all wisdom that is the object of taints (sāsava) is mundane Right View. Wisdom associated with the Noble Path and Fruit is called supramundane Right View.

A person is of three kinds: a worldling (puthujjana), a trainee (sekha), and one beyond training (asekha). Among them, a worldling is of two kinds: one outside the dispensation (bāhiraka) and one within the dispensation (sāsanika). Among them, a person outside the dispensation who is a proponent of kamma (kammavādī) is one of Right View through the knowledge of the ownership of kamma; but he is not one of Right View through the knowledge in conformity with the truths because of his adherence to the view of self (attadiṭṭhi). A person within the dispensation is one of Right View through both kinds of knowledge. A trainee is one of Right View through the fixed (niyata) Path-wisdom. One beyond training is through the wisdom of one beyond training.

In this sutta, however, a person endowed with the Right View of supramundane wholesome Path-wisdom, which is fixed and leads out of suffering (niyyānika), is intended as 'one of Right View.' For that very reason, He said: 'His view is straight; he is endowed with unwavering confidence in the Dhamma; he has arrived at this True Dhamma.' Indeed, only the Right View associated with supramundane wholesomeness is a straight view, because it proceeds in a straight manner without approaching the two extremes, and because it proceeds by completely cutting off all crookedness such as crookedness of body and so forth. A person endowed with that Path-wisdom is endowed with unwavering confidence—unshakeable confidence—in the ninefold supramundane Dhamma. Disentangling all thickets of views, abandoning all defilements, escaping from the cycle of birth, and bringing the practice to completion, he is called one who has arrived by the Noble Path at this True Dhamma (Saddhamma), which is taught by the Buddhas, which is the plunge into the Deathless, and which is known as Nibbāna.

'Yato kho' is a term defining time, meaning 'at which time.' 'He knows the unwholesome' means knowing the unwholesome known as the ten courses of unwholesome action (akusala-kammapatha).
201:
He understands the unwholesome in its various aspects. By means of the function of wisdom that takes Nibbāna as its object, he understands the unwholesome by penetrating it thus: "This is the Truth of Suffering." "He understands the unwholesome roots" means he understands the unwholesome roots which are the basic causes of that unwholesome state. In that same manner, he understands by penetrating thus: "This is the Truth of the Origin [of Suffering]." The same method applies to the wholesome and the wholesome roots. Just as the Truth of Suffering and so forth are understood here, so too in all subsequent sections, the understanding of the objects in their various aspects should be known by way of their function. By this much understanding of the unwholesome and so forth, he becomes one possessed of the supramundane right view of the kind described. With the right view of upright nature... [pe]... until reaching this True Dhamma which is Nibbāna, the teaching shown in brief is thus completed. Although this teaching is only in brief, for those monks, the proper attention in insight and the penetration by the Path should be understood as being in detail.

In the second section, however, the teaching is given in detail, and the proper attention and penetration should also be understood as being stated in detail. Between these two, the monks said: "In the brief teaching, the two lower Paths were taught; in the detailed teaching, the two higher Paths were taught." They said this because they clearly saw the words at the end of the detailed teaching: "Having abandoned all underlying tendencies of lust," and so forth. The Elder, however, said: "In the brief teaching, all four Paths were taught collectively; in the detailed teaching, it is the same." The investigation regarding the brief and detailed teachings revealed here should be understood in this same manner in all sections. Indeed, from here on, I shall only provide an explanation of new and obscure terms.

## Explanation of the Unwholesome Courses of Action

Among those sections, in the detailed teaching of the first section, in the passages such as "Taking life (pāṇātipāta), friends, is unwholesome," it should be understood as unwholesome because it arises from lack of skill (akosalla). Alternatively, it should be understood as unwholesome because it is the opposite of the wholesome which will be mentioned later. That unwholesome state should be understood by its characteristics as being blameworthy, having painful results, or being defiled. This is the explanation of the common terms here.

Among the specific terms, "pāṇātipāta" is the taking of the life of a living being. It means the killing of a being or the destruction of life. Here, "pāṇa" (living being) is a being in conventional terms, but in the ultimate sense, it is the life faculty (jīvitindriya). In that being, the intention to kill, which arises in either the door of body or the door of speech, and which produces the effort to cut off the life faculty of one perceived as a living being, is called "pāṇātipāta". That taking of life is of little blame in the case of small beings among those devoid of virtues such as animals.
202:
In the case of a large-bodied being, the blame is great. Why? Because of the greatness of the effort. Even when the effort is equal, the blame is great because of the greatness of the object (the physical body). Among humans and others who possess virtues, it is of little blame in the case of a being with few virtues, and of great blame in the case of a being with great virtues. When the body and virtues are equal, it should be understood that the blame is little due to the mildness of the defilements and the effort, and the blame is great due to their intensity. There are five factors for that taking of life: a living being, the perception of a living being, the thought of killing, the effort, and the death resulting from that effort. There are six kinds of effort: by one's own hand (sāhattika), by command (āṇattika), by missiles or weapons (nissaggiya), by permanent devices (thāvara), by magical arts (vijjāmaya), and by psychic power (iddhimaya). If this were to be elaborated here, it would be too extensive; therefore, we shall not elaborate on this or other similar matters. Those who desire it should consult and take it from the Vinaya Commentary called the Samantapāsādika.

Taking what is not given is "adinnādāna". It means the carrying away of another's property, theft, or stealing. In this context, "adinnā" (not given) refers to property possessed by another, where the owner would not be liable to punishment or reproach if they were to do as they pleased with it. In that property possessed by another, the intention to steal, which produces the effort to take it by one who perceives it as another's property, is called "adinnādāna". That taking of what is not given is of little blame in the case of the property of an inferior person, and of great blame in the case of the property of a superior person. Why? Because of the excellence of the object. Even when the objects are equal, the blame is great in the case of property belonging to those with superior virtues. In relation to those with superior virtues, the blame is little in the case of property belonging to those with fewer virtues. There are five factors for that taking of what is not given: property possessed by another, the perception of it as another's property, the thought of stealing, the effort, and the taking away by that effort. The efforts are the same as "sāhattika" and so forth. Those six kinds of effort occur by way of these five types of theft: theft by stealth (theyyāvahāra), theft by force (pasahyāvahāra), theft by concealment (paṭicchannāvahāra), theft by stratagem (parikappāvahāra), and theft by false weights/measures (kusāvahāra). This is the summary here. The detail is stated in the Samantapāsādika Commentary.

In the term "kāmesumicchācāra", "kāmesu" refers to sexual misconduct. "Micchācāra" is a low conduct that is utterly blameworthy. By its characteristic, the intention to transgress against prohibited persons, occurring in the door of the body with the desire for sexual misconduct, is called "kāmesumicchācāra".

In that regard, for men, the prohibited persons (agamanīya-ṭṭhāna) are first the ten types of women such as those protected by the mother (māturakkhitā), those protected by the father (piturakkhitā), those protected by both mother and father (mātāpiturakkhitā), those protected by a brother (bhāturakkhitā), those protected by a sister (bhaginirakkhitā), those protected by relatives (ñātirakkhitā), those protected by the clan (gottarakkhitā), those protected by fellow practitioners (dhammarakkhitā), those who are already protected (sārakkhā), and those under penalty (saparidaṇḍā).
203:
A woman bought with wealth (dhanakkītā), a woman living by mutual consent (chandavāsinī), a woman living for the sake of wealth (bhogavāsinī), a woman living for the sake of clothing (paṭavāsinī), a woman who becomes a wife by dipping her hands in a bowl of water (odapattakinī), a woman who has laid down her head-pad (obhaṭacumbaṭā), a woman who is both a slave and a wife (dāsī ca bhariyā ca), a woman who is both a worker and a wife (kammakārī ca bhariyā ca), a woman captured in war (dhajāhatā), and a temporary wife (muhuttikā)—these ten women, starting with the dhanakkītā, together with the ten mentioned previously, make twenty types of women. Among these, the two types—the woman protected by relatives and the woman protected by law—and the ten starting with the dhanakkītā, totaling twelve types of women, are known as forbidden objects (agamanīyaṭṭhāna) for other men.

This sexual misconduct (kāmesumicchācāra) is of lesser blame regarding a forbidden object devoid of virtue such as morality, and of greater blame regarding a forbidden object endowed with virtue such as morality. The four factors (sambhāra) of sexual misconduct are: being a forbidden object (agamanīyavatthu), the thought of engaging with it (sevanacitta), the effort to engage (sevanapayoga), and the acceptance of the union of the organs (maggena maggapappaṭipatti-adhivāsana). There is only one type of effort (payoga), which is personal effort (sāhatthika).

Falsehood (musā) refers to a verbal or bodily effort aimed at deceiving and destroying another's benefit. The volition (cetanā) that triggers the bodily or verbal effort to deceive another with the intent of deception is called false speech (musāvāda). Alternatively, musā is an untrue or false thing, and vāda is the act of making it known as true. Characteristically, the volition that triggers the communication of an untrue thing as true, by one who wishes to make another believe it as true, is musāvāda. The blame is lesser if the benefit destroyed by that false speech is small, and greater if it is large. Furthermore, for laypeople, saying "I do not have it" etc., because of a desire not to give one's own property, is of lesser blame; but speaking as a witness to destroy another's benefit is of greater blame. For monks, receiving a little oil or ghee and saying, "Today in the village, oil is flowing like a river," according to the ancient figurative style with the intent to joke, is of lesser blame; but saying one has seen what was not seen is of greater blame.

The four factors of false speech are: an untrue thing (atatha-vatthu), the intent to deceive (visamvādana-citta), the corresponding effort (tajjo vāyāmo), and the other person understanding the meaning (parassa tadatthavijānana). There is only one type of effort, which is personal effort (sāhatthika). This effort should be understood as performing the act of deception through the body, through objects connected to the body, or through speech. If the other person understands the meaning through that action, the kamma of false speech is completed at the very moment of the volition that triggered the action.

In the terms such as slanderous speech (pisuṇā vācā), the speech which, when spoken to someone, causes oneself to be loved and another to be hated in that person's heart, is called pisuṇā vācā. The speech which makes oneself and others harsh, and is itself harsh, being neither pleasant to the ear nor pleasant to the heart, is called harsh speech (pharusā vācā).
204:
That personal effort (sahatthika-payoga) should be understood as an act that causes deviation through the body, through objects connected to the body, or through speech. Through this deviating action, another person understands the intended meaning. The intention (cetanā) that produces this bodily and vocal effort is associated with the path of lying (musāvāda-kamma) at the very moment of that deviating utterance.

Regarding the terms such as malicious speech (pisuṇāvācā): the speech by which one makes oneself loved by another or causes another to be alienated from their love is called malicious speech. The speech by which one makes oneself or another harsh—which is itself harsh, unpleasant to the ear, and unpleasant to the mind—is called harsh speech (pharusāvācā). The state of mind (cittuppāda) by which one speaks useless words is called frivolous talk (samphappalāpa). The intention that is the root of these, such as malicious speech, also receives the name 'malicious speech,' and so on. In the context of vocal misconduct, it should be understood that this intention alone is what is intended.

Among these, the intention of one with a defiled mind that produces bodily and vocal effort for the purpose of breaking the affection of others or because of a desire to be loved is called malicious speech (pisuṇāvācā). This malicious speech is of small blame if the person whose affection is broken has few virtues, and of great blame if they have many virtues. Its four factors (aṅga) are: (1) another person to be divided; (2) the intent to divide, thinking 'These people shall be separated and alienated,' or the desire to be loved, thinking 'I shall be loved and trusted'; (3) the corresponding effort; and (4) the understanding of the meaning of that speech by the other person.

The truly harsh intention that produces bodily and vocal effort which cuts the affection of another is called harsh speech (pharusāvācā). To illustrate this, the following story is told: A boy went to the forest, disregarding his mother's words. The mother, unable to make him return, cursed him, saying, 'May a fierce buffalo cow pursue you!' Then, a buffalo cow actually appeared before him in that forest. The boy made an act of truth (saccakiriya): 'May what my mother said with her mouth not happen, but may what she thought in her heart happen!' The buffalo cow stood still as if tied there. Thus, even if there is an effort that cuts affection, it is not harsh speech if the mind is soft and gentle. For parents sometimes say to their children, 'May thieves cut you into pieces!' yet they do not wish even a lotus petal to fall upon them. Teachers and preceptors (ācariya-upajjhāya) also sometimes say to their pupils, 'Why do these shameless and fearless ones wander about? Drive them out!' yet they only desire their pupils' success in scriptural learning (āgama) and realization (adhigama). Just as it is not harsh speech when the mind is gentle, so too it is not non-harsh speech simply because the words are gentle. The words of one who wishes to kill, saying 'Let this person sleep happily,' are not non-harsh speech. Because of the harshness of the mind, such speech is indeed harsh speech. This harsh speech is of small blame if the person targeted has few virtues, and of great blame if they have many virtues. Its three factors are: (1) another person to be reviled; (2) an angry mind; and (3) the act of reviling.

The unwholesome intention that produces bodily and vocal effort which communicates what is useless is called frivolous talk (samphappalāpa). This frivolous talk is of small blame if the habit is slight, and of great blame if the habit is great. Its two factors are: (1) the intent for useless talk such as the Bharata war or the abduction of Sītā, and (2) the speaking of such talk.

The mental state that thinks with the aim of inclining another's property toward oneself is called covetousness (abhijjhā). The meaning is that it occurs by being directed toward another's property and inclining it to oneself. It has the characteristic of thinking directed at another's property, such as 'O, that this property of another were mine!' It is of small or great blame, similar to theft (adinnādāna). Its two factors are: (1) another's property and (2) the inclining of it toward oneself.
205:
It is called covetousness (abhijjhā) because it thinks by inclining towards the property of others. The meaning is that it occurs by being directed towards another's goods and inclining them towards oneself. That covetousness has the characteristic of longing for another's property in this way: "Oh, would that this were mine!" Like the taking of what is not given (theft), it may be of small or great blame. There are two factors for that covetousness: another's property and the inclination towards oneself. Indeed, even if greed arises regarding an object that is another's property, it does not yet constitute a path of action (kammapatha) as long as one does not incline it towards oneself, thinking, "Oh, would that this were mine!"

It is called ill will (byāpāda) because it destroys welfare and happiness. That ill will has the characteristic of malice of mind with the desire to destroy another's welfare. Like harsh speech, it may be of small or great blame. There are two factors for that ill will: another being and the thought of that being's destruction. Indeed, even if anger arises regarding an object that is another being, it does not yet constitute a path of action as long as one does not think of that person's destruction, thinking, "Oh, would that this person were cut off or destroyed!"

It is called wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) because it sees wrongly by not grasping according to reality. That wrong view has the characteristic of distorted seeing in such ways as "There is no result of giving," etc. Like frivolous talk, it may be of small or great blame. Furthermore, indefinite wrong view is of small blame, while definite wrong view (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi) is of great blame. There are two factors for that wrong view: the distorted nature of the way the object is grasped and the appearance of the object according to how it is grasped (contrary to reality).

The decision regarding these ten unwholesome paths of action (akusala-kammapatha) should be understood by way of five aspects: by nature (dhamma), by category (koṭṭhāsa), by object (ārammaṇa), by feeling (vedanā), and by root (mūla).

Among those five, "by nature" means that among these ten, seven in sequence are only the state of volition (cetanā). The three beginning with covetousness are states associated with volition.

"By category" means that the seven in sequence and wrong view—these eight—are only paths of action, not roots. Covetousness and ill will are both paths of action and roots. For covetousness, having reached the status of a root, is the unwholesome root of greed (lobha). Ill will is the unwholesome root of hatred (dosa).

"By object" means that killing (pāṇātipāta) has a formation (saṅkhāra) as its object because its object is the life faculty (jīvitindriya). Theft (adinnādāna) has either a being or a formation as its object. Sexual misconduct (micchācāra) has a formation as its object by way of the tangible object (phoṭṭhabba). Some teachers say it has a being as its object. False speech (musāvāda) has either a being or a formation as its object. Slander (pisuṇā-vācā) is the same. Harsh speech (pharusā-vācā) has only a being as its object. Frivolous talk (samphappalāpa), by way of what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized...
206:
...has either a being or a formation as its object. Covetousness is the same. Ill will has only a being as its object. Wrong view has a formation as its object by way of states belonging to the three planes of existence.

By way of feeling (vedanā): Killing is associated with painful feeling. For even if kings, upon seeing a thief, say laughingly, "Go and kill him," their decisive volition (sanniṭṭhāpaka-cetanā) is associated only with painful feeling. Theft is associated with all three feelings. Sexual misconduct is associated with two feelings—pleasant and neutral—but in the decisive mind, neutral feeling does not occur. False speech is associated with all three feelings; slander is the same. Harsh speech is associated only with painful feeling. Frivolous talk is associated with all three feelings. Covetousness is associated with two feelings—pleasant and neutral; wrong view is the same. Ill will is associated with painful feeling.

By way of root (mūla): Killing has two roots by way of hatred and delusion. Theft has two roots, either by way of hatred and delusion or by way of greed and delusion. Sexual misconduct has two roots by way of greed and delusion. False speech has two roots, either by way of hatred and delusion or by way of greed and delusion; slander and frivolous talk are the same. Harsh speech has two roots by way of hatred and delusion. Covetousness has a single root by way of delusion; ill will is the same. Wrong view has two roots by way of greed and delusion.

In the phrases such as "Greed is an unwholesome root," it is called greed (lobha) because it covets. It is called hatred (dosa) because it is malicious. It is called delusion (moha) because it is muddled. Among those three, greed is itself unwholesome in the sense of being blameworthy and having painful results. It is called an unwholesome root (akusala-mūla) because it is a root for these unwholesome acts like killing, etc., in the sense of being a productive state for some and a decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya) for others. This has also been said: "Friends, one who is lustful, overcome by greed, with a mind obsessed, kills even a living being," etc. The same method applies to the status of hatred and delusion as unwholesome roots.

## Explanation of the Wholesome Paths of Action

In the phrases such as "Abstinence from killing is wholesome," the terms like killing (pāṇātipāta), etc., have the meanings already stated. It is called abstinence (veramaṇī) because it discards enmity (vera); the meaning is that it abandons enmity. Or one abstains (viramati) by means of this as an instrument; it is called veramaṇī by changing the syllable 'vi' to 've'. This is the explanation by way of phrasing. By way of meaning, however, abstinence (veramaṇī) is the abstinence (virati) associated with a wholesome mind. That abstinence (virati) associated with a wholesome mind, which occurs for one abstaining from killing at that time, is of three kinds: spontaneous abstinence (sampatta-virati), abstinence by undertaking (samādāna-virati), and abstinence by eradication (samုccheda-virati). Among these three, spontaneous abstinence should be understood as the abstinence that arises in those who have not formally undertaken the precepts, but who, considering their own birth, age, and learning, etc., do not transgress against an object that has presented itself, thinking, "It is not proper for us to do such a thing." How? Like the abstinence of the lay follower Cakkana in the island of Sri Lanka. It is heard that when Cakkana Upāsaka was young, his mother fell ill.
207:
At that time, abstinence (virati) associated with a wholesome mind, which is described as 'abstaining from taking life,' is of three kinds: abstinence from things encountered (sampatta-virati), abstinence by undertaking (samādāna-virati), and abstinence by eradication (samuccheda-virati). Among these three, abstinence from things encountered should be understood as the abstinence that arises in those who have not yet undertaken the precepts, but who, reflecting on their own birth, age, and great learning, etc., think, 'It is not proper for us to do such a thing,' and thus do not transgress against the object that has come before them. This is like the abstinence of the lay devotee Cakkana in the island of Sīhaḷadīpa.

It is said that when Cakkana was still young, his mother fell ill. The physician said, 'It would be good if you could get fresh rabbit meat.' Then Cakkana's elder brother sent him, saying, 'Brother, go and wander through the fields.' He went there. At that time, a rabbit had come to eat the young crops; seeing him, it ran swiftly but became entangled in a creeper and cried out, 'Kiri kiri!' Cakkana went to the source of the sound, caught the rabbit, and thought, 'I will make medicine for my mother.' Then he thought again, 'It is not proper for me to deprive another of life for the sake of my mother's life.' Then he released it, saying, 'Go and eat grass and water with the other rabbits in the forest.' When his brother asked, 'Brother, did you get a rabbit?' he told him the whole story. His brother then rebuked and scolded him. Cakkana went to his mother and made an act of truth, saying, 'Since I was born, I do not recall ever intentionally depriving a living being of life.' At that very moment, his mother was freed from her illness and became healthy.

Furthermore, abstinence by undertaking should be understood as the abstinence that arises in those who have undertaken the precepts, who, in the course of undertaking the precepts and beyond, would even sacrifice their own lives rather than transgress against the object. This is like the abstinence of the lay devotee living on Uttaravaḍḍhamāna Mountain.

It is said that this lay devotee, having taken the precepts from the Elder Piṅgalabuddharakkhita who lived at Ambarīyavihāra, was plowing his field. Then his ox went missing, and while searching for it, he climbed Uttaravaḍḍhamāna Mountain, where a large snake caught him. He thought, 'I will cut off the snake's head with this sharp billhook.' Then he thought again, 'It is not proper for me to break the precepts after having taken them from my venerable teacher.' Having thought this up to three times, he decided, 'I will sacrifice my life, but I will not sacrifice the precepts,' and threw away the billhook that was in his hand. At that very moment, the large snake...
208:
Thinking, 'I shall sacrifice my life, but I will not sacrifice the precept,' he threw away the sharp-handled billhook he had placed on his shoulder into the forest. At that very moment, the great beast (the large snake) released him and went away.

Abstinence associated with the Noble Path (ariya-magga) should be understood as abstinence by eradication (samuccheda-virati). From the moment that Noble Path arises, even the thought 'I will kill a living being' no longer occurs to Noble Persons (ariya-puggala). This abstinence is called wholesome (kusala) because it is an occurrence of skillfulness. Alternatively, it is wholesome (kusala) because it cuts off (lunāti) bad conduct (dussīlya), which is called 'kusa' because it lies in a contemptible way (kucchita-sayana). Because it does not correspond (in gender and number) with the question 'What, friends, is the wholesome?' it is not called 'kusalā' (plural) but is stated as 'kusalam' (singular).

Just as with the unwholesome, the determination of these wholesome courses of action (kusala-kammapatha) should also be understood by way of five aspects: (1) by nature (dhamma), (2) by category (koṭṭhāsa), (3) by object (ārammaṇa), (4) by feeling (vedanā), and (5) by root (mūla).

Among these, by nature: the first seven in the sequence can be both volitions (cetanā) and abstinences (virati). The last three are only states associated with volition. By category: the first seven in the sequence are only courses of action (kammapatha), not roots. The last three are both courses of action and roots. For when non-covetousness (anabhijjhā) reaches the state of a root, it is the wholesome root of non-greed (alobha). Non-ill will (abyāpāda) is the wholesome root of non-hatred (adosa). Right view (sammādiṭṭhi) is the wholesome root of non-delusion (amoha).

By object: the objects of taking life and so forth are indeed the objects of these (wholesome states), for abstinence (veramaṇī) occurs precisely because of the object that is to be transgressed. Just as the Noble Path, which has Nibbāna as its object, abandons the defilements, so too these courses of action, which have the life faculty and so forth as their objects, should be understood to abandon immoralities such as taking life. By feeling: all wholesome courses of action are either pleasant feelings (sukha-vedanā) or neutral (upekkhā) feelings. There is no such thing as a painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā) in wholesome states. By root: for one who abstains with a mind associated with knowledge (ñāṇa-sampayutta), the first seven in the sequence have three roots by way of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion. For one who abstains with a mind dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇa-vippayutta), they have two roots. Non-covetousness, with a mind associated with knowledge...
209:
For one who abstains with a consciousness associated with knowledge (ñāṇasampayutta), there are two roots (non-hatred and non-delusion). For one who abstains with a consciousness dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇavippayutta), there is only one root. Non-greed (alobha) itself is not its own root; the same method applies to non-ill will (adosa). Right view (sammādiṭṭhi) should be understood as having two roots by virtue of non-greed and non-hatred.

In the passages beginning with "Non-greed is a wholesome root" (alobho kusalamūlaṃ), it is called non-greed because it is not greed; this name "non-greed" is a designation for the state that is the opposite of greed. The same method applies to non-hatred and non-delusion. Among those three, non-greed is itself wholesome (kusala); it is called a wholesome root (kusalamūla) because it is a root for other wholesome states such as abstinence from taking life, in the sense of being associated (sampayutta) with some wholesome states and in the sense of being a decisive support condition (upanissayapaccaya) for others. The same method applies to the nature of non-hatred and non-delusion as wholesome roots.

Now, wishing to conclude the entire meaning taught both in brief and in detail, he spoke the section on attainment (appanāvāra) beginning with "When, friends..." (yato khေါ āvuso). In that concluding passage, "thus he understands the unwholesome" (evaṃ akusalaṃ pajānāti) means understanding the unwholesome by virtue of the ten unwholesome courses of action (akusalakammapatha) already mentioned. The same method applies to the passages beginning with "thus the unwholesome root" (evaṃ akusalamūlaṃ). By this sequence of words, the liberation from the round of suffering up to Arahatship is taught by one method for the person practicing the meditation on the Four Noble Truths. 

How is it taught? In these courses of action, excluding covetousness (abhijjhā), the remaining unwholesome courses of action and the ten wholesome courses of action are the Truth of Suffering (dukkhasacca). These two states—covetousness and greed, which is the unwholesome root—are the Truth of the Origin (samudayasacca) in the direct sense (nippariyāyena). However, in the figurative sense (pariyāyena), all courses of action are the Truth of Suffering; all wholesome and unwholesome roots are the Truth of the Origin. Nibbāna, which is the non-occurrence of both suffering and origin, is the Truth of Cessation (nirodhasacca). The Noble Path, which fully understands suffering, abandons the origin, and realizes cessation, is the Truth of the Path (maggasacca). Thus, two truths are taught in their own form (sarūpa), and the other two truths should be understood by virtue of the mode of conveying a reversal (āvattahāra).

"Having entirely abandoned the underlying tendency to lust" (so sabbaso rāgānusayaṃ pahāya) means that the person, thus understanding the unwholesome and so forth, abandons the underlying tendency to lust in every way. "Having dispelled the underlying tendency to aversion" (paṭighānusayaṃ paṭivinodetvā) means having completely removed the underlying tendency to aversion in every way. By this much, the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmimagga) is taught. "Having uprooted the underlying tendency to the conceit and view 'I am'" (asmīti diṭṭhimānānusayaṃ samūhanitvā) means having completely uprooted the underlying tendency to conceit, which is similar to view, that occurs in the manner of grasping as a whole the five aggregates as "I am," without distinguishing any single state among them.

In that phrase, "the underlying tendency to conceit and view" (diṭṭhimānānusaya) means the underlying tendency to conceit which is like a view. Because this underlying tendency to conceit occurs as "I am," it is similar to view; therefore, it is so...
210:
...stated. One who wishes to know this conceit "I am" (asmimāna) in detail should look at the Khemaka Sutta in the Khandhavagga.

"Having abandoned ignorance" (avijjaṃ pahāya) means having abandoned ignorance, which is the root of the round of suffering. "Having given rise to true knowledge" (vijjaṃ uppādetvā) means having given rise to the knowledge of the Path of Arahatship (arahattamaggavijja) which utterly uproots that ignorance. By this much, the Path of Arahatship is taught. "In this very life, he becomes an end-maker of suffering" (diṭṭhe va dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti) means that in this very existence, he makes an end (makes a limit) to the suffering of the round. With the words "By this much, friends..." (ettāvatāpi kho āvuso), he concludes the teaching. It means that this is also by virtue of the penetration through wise attention (manasikāra) mentioned in this teaching on the courses of action. The remaining words are just as previously explained. Thus, he concluded the teaching with the Path of Non-returning and the Path of Arahatship.

## The Explanation of the Wholesome Courses of Action is Finished.

## The Explanation of the Section on Nutriment

"It is well, friend" (sādhāvuso) and so forth refers to one who has arrived at this True Dhamma. Thus, having heard the teaching on the Four Noble Truths based on the wholesome and unwholesome from the Venerable Sāriputta, those bhikkhus greatly rejoiced in the Venerable Sāriputta's words with the expression "It is well, friend." It means they approved with a mind that produced those words, accepted it with speech, and cherished it with the heart. Now, because the Elder is capable of teaching the Four Noble Truths in various ways (as the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, Sāriputta is capable of explaining and teaching the Four Noble Truths in detail"), or because he wished to teach further and said "By this much also," those bhikkhus, wishing to hear the teaching of the Truths by another method, asked the Venerable Sāriputta a further question. Therefore, beyond the question he himself asked and answered, they asked another additional question in this manner: "Friend, might there be another way (pariyāya), another reason?" or it means they asked concerning the higher part of the previous question. Then, the Elder, answering them, said "There might be, friends," and so forth.

In that passage, the explanation of the obscure terms is as follows: "Nutriment" (āhāra) means a condition (paccaya). A condition is called "nutriment" because it brings (āharati) its own fruit. In the terms "for those who have come to be or those seeking birth" (bhūtānaṃ vā sambhavesīnaṃ vā), "those who have come to be" (bhūta) are beings who have already been born (emerged from the mother's womb). "Those seeking birth" (sambhavesī) are beings who are searching for an existence (or a birth). Among the four types of birth, egg-born (aṇḍaja) and womb-born (jalābuja/gabbhaseyyaka) beings are called "seeking birth" as long as they have not yet broken through the eggshell or the membrane. When they break the eggshell or membrane and come out, they are called "come to be." Moisture-born (saṃsedaja) and spontaneously born (opapātika) beings are called "seeking birth" in the first moment of rebirth-consciousness, and from the second moment of consciousness onwards, they are called "come to be." Alternatively, they are called "seeking birth" as long as they have not yet changed from the first posture in which they were born, and after that, they are called "come to be." Or, "come to be" refers to beings who have fully emerged and grown; it refers to those who have clearly appeared and will not reach a new existence (i.e., the liberated).
211:
In the phrases such as "bhūtānaṃ vā sattānaṃ," the term "bhūta" refers to beings who have emerged from the mother's womb and have come into existence. "Sambhavesī" refers to beings who are seeking a new existence, birth, or arising. Among the four types of birth (yoni), egg-born (aṇḍaja) and womb-born (jalābuja) beings are called "sambhavesī" as long as they have not yet broken through the egg-shell (aṇḍakosa) or the membrane (vatthikosa). When they have broken the shell or membrane and emerged outside, they are called "bhūta." Moisture-born (saṃsedaja) and spontaneously born (opapātika) beings are called "sambhavesī" at the very first moment of rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi cittakkhaṇa), and from the second thought-moment onwards, they are called "bhūta." Alternatively, beings are called "sambhavesī" as long as they have not yet changed from the initial posture (iriyāpatha) in which they were born to another posture; after that, they are called "bhūta."

Alternatively, "bhūta" refers to beings who have already come into existence. Those who have already become and do not fall into the category of being born again in a future existence—this is a designation for Arahants. Those who seek a new existence are called "sambhavesī." Because they have not yet abandoned the fetters of existence (bhavasaṃyojana) and will seek arising in the future, this is a designation for learners (sekhas) and worldlings (puthujjanas). Thus, in all respects, these two terms encompass all living beings. Here, the word "vā" has the sense of a conjunction (and). Therefore, the meaning should be understood as "of those who have become (bhūtas) and of those seeking birth (sambhavesīs)."

"Ṭhitiyā" means for the purpose of maintenance (staying). "Anuggahāya" means for the purpose of support or favor. Although these are different linguistic expressions, the meaning of both terms is the same. Alternatively, "ṭhitiyā" is for the non-interruption of the states (dhamma) that have already arisen in various beings, by way of their continuous succession. "Anuggahāya" is for the arising of states that have not yet arisen. Both of these reasons should be understood as applying to both: for the maintenance and support of those who have become (bhūtas), and for the maintenance and support of those seeking birth (sambhavesīs). "Kabaḷīkāra āhāra" (edible food nutriment) is called nutriment because it is made into balls (kabaḷa) and swallowed. This is a designation for the nutritive essence (ojā) found in substances such as boiled rice, junket, etc. "Oḷārika" (gross) or "sukhuma" (subtle) is called gross because the substance (vatthu) that is the base of the nutritive essence is gross, and it is called subtle because the substance is subtle. By nature, however, because it is included within subtle matter (sukhumatā), edible food nutriment is indeed subtle. Its grossness or subtleness according to its substance should be understood by way of comparison.

For compared to the food of crocodiles, the food of peacocks is subtle. It is said that crocodiles swallow stones, and these stones dissolve as soon as they reach their stomachs. Peacocks eat creatures such as snakes and scorpions. Compared to the food of peacocks, the food of bears (taraccha) is subtle. It is said that they eat horns and bones that have been discarded for three years. These horns and bones, merely by being moistened with their saliva, become soft like roots...
212:
Compared to the food of bears, the food of elephants is subtle. They eat various kinds of tree branches. Compared to the food of elephants, the food of beings such as the gayal (gavaya), elk (gokaṇṇa), and deer is subtle. It is said that they eat various kinds of heartless tree leaves and such. Compared to the food of those beings, the food of cattle is subtle. They eat fresh and dry grass. Compared to the food of cattle, the food of rabbits is subtle. Compared to the food of rabbits, the food of birds is subtle. Compared to the food of birds, the food of humans living in the border regions (paccantadesa) is subtle. Compared to the food of those in the border regions, the food of village headmen (gāmabhojaka) is subtle. Compared to the food of village headmen, the food of the great ministers of kings is subtle. Compared to the food of those ministers, the food of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) is subtle. Compared to the food of a Universal Monarch, the food of the terrestrial and tree deities (bhumma and rukkha devas) is subtle. Compared to the food of terrestrial deities, the food of the Cātumahārājika devas is subtle. In this manner, the description should be expanded up to the food of the Paranimmitavasavatti devas; the food of those devas is the ultimate in subtlety.

In this context, in a gross substance, the nutritive essence (ojā) is small and weak; in a subtle substance, it is powerful. This is true: for one who drinks a full bowl of rice gruel (yāgu), hunger returns in a moment, and they wish to eat something else. But by drinking merely a handful of ghee, one may have no desire to eat for the whole day. Between these two, the substance (the matter excluding the nutritive essence) removes the physical fatigue of the body caused by hunger, but it is not able to sustain it. The nutritive essence (ojā) sustains it, but it is not able to remove the fatigue. When the two are combined, they can both remove fatigue and sustain the body.

'Contact (phassa) is the second nutriment' refers to the six types of contact, such as eye-contact (cakkhusamphassa). Among these four nutriments, it should be understood as the second nutriment. This is merely the method of the teaching (desanānaya). Therefore, one should not search for a reason here as to why it is the second or the third. 'Mental volition' (manosañcetanā) refers to volition (cetanā) itself. 'Consciousness' (viññāṇa) refers to any kind of mind (citta).

Here, a question arises: 'If the meaning of cause (paccaya) is the meaning of nutriment (āhāra), then why are only these four mentioned when there are other causes for beings?' It is said: Because they are the predominant causes in the continuity of beings. To elaborate: for the physical body (rūpakāya) of beings who eat edible food, edible food nutriment is the predominant cause.
