Similarly, contact (phassa) is the predominant cause for feeling (vedanā); mental volition (manosañcetanā) for consciousness (viññāṇa); and consciousness (viññāṇa) for mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa). This is the answer. It is just as He taught: 'Monks, just as this body stands because of nutriment, stands depending on nutriment, and cannot stand without nutriment; even so, monks, feeling arises because of contact, consciousness arises because of feeling, mind-and-matter arises because of consciousness. Monks, just as this body stands because of nutriment... even so, contact...'
213:
It is because they are specific causes within one's own continuity. Indeed, for beings who consume edible food, edible food is the specific cause for the physical body. In the mental group, contact is the specific cause for feeling; mental volition for consciousness; and consciousness for mind-and-matter.

As it was taught: "Monks, just as this physical body is sustained by nutriment, exists depending on nutriment, and cannot exist without nutriment; even so, feeling exists due to the cause of contact, consciousness exists due to the cause of formations, and mind-and-matter exists due to the cause of consciousness."

In this context, what is nutriment and what does it bring? Edible food brings the material groups with nutritive essence as the eighth (ojaṭṭhamakarūpa). Contact nutriment brings the three kinds of feeling. Mental volition nutriment brings the three realms of existence. Consciousness nutriment brings rebirth mind-and-matter.

How does it bring them? First, edible food, merely by being placed in the mouth, causes the eight material qualities to arise. Each morsel of rice, crushed by the teeth and being swallowed, certainly causes those eight material qualities to arise. Thus, it brings the material groups with nutritive essence as the eighth.

As for contact nutriment, when contact associated with pleasant feeling arises, it brings pleasant feeling. Likewise, contact associated with painful feeling brings pain, and contact associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling brings neither-pain-nor-pleasure. Thus, in every way, contact nutriment brings the three feelings.

Mental volition nutriment: kamma leading to the sense-sphere existence brings sense-sphere existence. Kammas leading to the fine-material and immaterial existences bring those respective existences. Thus, in every way, mental volition nutriment brings the three realms of existence.

As for consciousness nutriment, it is said to bring, by way of co-nascence and other conditions, the three aggregates associated with it at the moment of rebirth, as well as the thirty material qualities that arise by way of the three continuities (the body-decad, sex-decad, and heart-decad). Thus, consciousness nutriment brings rebirth mind-and-matter.

In this context, when it is said "mental volition nutriment brings the three realms of existence," it refers only to wholesome and unwholesome volitions that are objects of the taints (sāsava). When it is said "consciousness brings rebirth mind-and-matter," it refers only to rebirth-consciousness. However, generally speaking, these are to be understood as nutriments because they bring those states associated with them and those states produced by them.
214:
Among these four nutriments, edible food fulfills the function of nutriment only by supporting and strengthening. Contact fulfills it only by performing the act of touching; mental volition only by striving and accumulating; and consciousness only by cognizing through the power of awareness.

How does it fulfill it? Edible food, only by supporting and strengthening, sustains the physical body and thus serves for the stability of beings. Indeed, this physical body, though produced by kamma, being supported and strengthened by edible food, lasts for ten years, a hundred years, or for the full extent of the lifespan. For example, how? Just as a child born of a mother, when fed and nurtured with milk and so on by a nurse, lasts for a long time; and just as a house supported by a prop lasts. This was also said in the Milindapañha: "Great King, when a house is about to fall, people prop it up with another piece of wood; being propped up by another piece of wood, that house does not fall. Even so, Great King, this physical body is sustained by nutriment and exists depending on nutriment."

Thus, edible food, while supporting, fulfills the function of nutriment. Edible food, while so fulfilling, is a condition for two material continuities: nutriment-produced matter and clung-to matter. It is a condition by protecting kamma-born matter, and it is a condition by generating nutriment-produced matter.

Contact, however, only by touching the object which is the basis for pleasant feeling and so on, produces pleasant and other feelings, and thus serves for the stability of beings. Mental volition, only when striving by the power of wholesome and unwholesome kamma, serves for the stability of beings because it brings about the root of existence. Consciousness, only by cognizing, produces mind-and-matter and thus serves for the stability of beings.

In these four nutriments, which fulfill the function of nutriment by way of supporting and so on, four dangers should be seen. What are these dangers? In edible food, attachment (nikanti) itself is the danger; in contact, approaching/encountering is the danger; in mental volition, striving/accumulating is the danger; and in consciousness, falling into (abhinipāta) is the danger. For what reason should they be seen thus? To state the consequence: beings who have attachment to edible food, surrounded by cold and so on, perform tasks such as finger-counting and calculation for the sake of food, and thereby undergo immeasurable suffering. Some people in this Dispensation...
215: Even those who have gone forth in this Dispensation (Sāsanā) but seek nutriment through improper means (anesanā) such as practicing medicine are blameworthy even in the present life. In the future life as well, they become ascetic ghosts (samaṇapeta) according to the method taught in the Lakkhaṇa Saṃyutta, where it is said that their outer robes (saṃghāṭi) are ablaze and flaming. For this reason, it should be understood that attachment (nikanti) to edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra) is indeed a danger. Those who indulge in contact (phassa) and take delight in it commit offenses against the wives and property of others that are guarded and protected. The owners of the property seize them along with the goods, cut them into pieces, and discard them on rubbish heaps, or hand them over to the king. Then the king subjects them to various forms of torture. After the dissolution of the body, they can only expect to reach a miserable destination (duggati). Thus, all dangers of both the present life and the future life, which have delight in contact as their root, come upon them. For this reason, it should be understood that the approach to sense objects in the nutriment of contact (phassāhāra) is indeed a danger. Due to the accumulation of wholesome and unwholesome kamma, all dangers in the three realms of existence, which have that kamma as their root, come upon them. For this reason, it should be understood that the accumulation of kamma in the nutriment of mental volition (manosañcetanāhāra) is indeed a danger. Rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-viññāṇa) falls first into whatever place it may be; in that place, it arises by taking up rebirth-linking mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa). When that mind-and-matter arises, all dangers arise because they are rooted in it. For this reason, it should be understood that the falling into a new existence in the nutriment of consciousness (viññāṇāhāra) is indeed a danger. To end attachment to these nutriments which are accompanied by danger, the Fully Enlightened One taught the Puttamaṃsūpama Sutta (The Simile of the Son’s Flesh) regarding edible food, using the method beginning with, 'Bhikkhus, suppose there were a couple...' To end attachment to the nutriment of contact, He taught the Niccammagāvūpama Sutta (The Simile of the Flayed Cow) beginning with, 'Bhikkhus, suppose there were a flayed cow...' To end attachment to the nutriment of mental volition, He taught the Aṅgārakāsūpama Sutta (The Simile of the Pit of Glowing Coals) beginning with, 'Bhikkhus, suppose there were a pit of glowing coals...' To end attachment to the nutriment of consciousness, He taught the Sattisatahatūpama Sutta (The Simile of the Hundred Spears) beginning with, 'Bhikkhus, suppose there were a criminal...' In those similes, the brief explanation of the meaning, established upon the factual sense, is as follows: It is said that a couple, taking their son and a small amount of provisions, set out on a difficult journey of a hundred yojanas. When they reached fifty yojanas, their provisions were exhausted. Oppressed by hunger and thirst, they sat down at the foot of a tree with sparse shade. Then the husband said to the wife, 'Dear, within fifty yojanas around this place, there is neither village nor town. Therefore, although there are many tasks to be done by men, such as plowing and cattle-rearing, I can no longer perform any of them now. Kill this son, eat half of the flesh, and making the other half your provisions, cross the difficult journey with me.' The wife also said, 'Lord, although there are many tasks to be done by women, such as spinning, I can no longer perform any of them now. As for me...'
216: (The couple) traveled on the difficult road. When they had gone about fifty yojanas, their provisions were exhausted. Being oppressed by hunger and thirst, they sat in a place with sparse shade. Then the husband said to the wife, 'Dear... within fifty yojanas around here, there is neither village nor town. Therefore, I can no longer perform the many tasks that men must do, such as plowing and cattle-rearing. Come, kill me, eat half of my flesh, and making the other half your provisions, escape from this difficult journey with our son.' The woman replied, 'Lord... I can no longer perform the many tasks that women must do, such as spinning. Come, kill me, eat half of my flesh, and making the other half your provisions, escape from this difficult journey with our son.' Then the husband said to the wife, 'Dear... by the death of the woman, the death of both will occur. A tender child cannot survive without a mother. If we live, we may have another child. Come, let us now kill the young son, take his flesh, and escape from this difficult journey.' Then the mother said to the son, 'Dear son... go to your father.' The son went. Then the father said, 'Thinking that I would support my young son, I have endured immeasurable suffering through plowing, cattle-rearing, and so on. I cannot kill my son. You yourself kill your son,' and said, 'Dear son... go only to your mother.' The son went. Then the mother also said, 'Because I longed for a son, I have endured immeasurable suffering through practices like the cow-vow (govata), the dog-vow (kukkuravata), and praying to deities. What then need be said of my carrying him in my womb? I cannot kill my son,' and said, 'Dear son... go only to your father.' Thus, while the child was going back and forth between the two, he died. Seeing him, they wept, and then, taking the flesh as previously mentioned, they went on while eating it. To them, that nutriment of the son's flesh was repulsive for nine reasons; therefore, it was not for fun, not for intoxication, not for decoration, and not for beautifying the limbs, but only for the purpose of escaping the difficult journey. By what nine reasons was it repulsive? Because it was the flesh of one's own species, the flesh of a relative, the flesh of a son, the flesh of a beloved son, tender flesh, raw flesh, flesh without the taste of milk, the absence of salt, and because it was not smoked. Therefore, a monk [should view] edible food as being like the flesh of a son...
217:
(The monk who sees edible food as similar to a son's flesh) sees it thus; that monk exhausts craving for that nutriment. This is the application of the meaning in the first simile of the son's flesh.

In the simile of the flayed cow: Just as that cow, having had its skin flayed from neck to hoof and then released, wherever it stands leaning against a wall or the like, it is bitten by insects such as gnats, mosquitoes, flies, and red ants, and thus becomes a source of suffering; in the same way, contact (phassa) also, whatever base or object it depends on, becomes a source of the felt suffering that arises from that base and object. Therefore, the monk who sees the nutriment of contact as similar to a flayed cow exhausts craving for that nutriment of contact. This is the application of the meaning in the simile of the flayed cow.

In the simile of the pit of glowing embers: The three realms of existence should be understood as being like that pit of glowing embers because of their nature of intense burning. Mental volition (manosañcetanā) should be understood as being like the two men who, seizing one by the arms, drag him toward that pit of embers, because of its nature of dragging one into the realms of existence. Therefore, the monk who sees the nutriment of mental volition as similar to the men who drag one toward a pit of embers exhausts craving for that nutriment of mental volition. This is the application of the meaning in the simile of the pit of glowing embers.

In the simile of being struck by a hundred spears: That man is struck by a hundred spears in the morning; those spears make a hundred wounds in his body and, without stopping in between, pierce through and fall on the other side. The remaining two hundred spears are the same. Thus, the whole body becomes riddled with holes by the spears that pass through without falling where he fell. There is no measure to the suffering arising even from a single wound for that man; what need is there to speak of the suffering arising from three hundred wounds? In that simile, the time the spears strike is like the time the rebirth-linking consciousness arises. The production of wounds is like the production of the aggregates (khandhas). The arising of painful feeling in the wounds is like the arising of various sufferings rooted in the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) within the produced aggregates. Another way: The man who has committed a crime is like the rebirth-linking consciousness. The wounds produced in that man by the spear-strikes are like name-and-form (nāmarūpa) caused by consciousness. Just as the arising of harsh suffering for that man is caused by the wounds, the arising of various sufferings for consciousness—by way of the thirty-two punishments, ninety-eight diseases, and so on—caused by name-and-form should be understood. Therefore, the monk who sees the nutriment of consciousness as similar to being struck by a hundred spears exhausts craving for that nutriment of consciousness. This is the application of the meaning in the simile of being struck by a hundred spears.
218:
When that monk exhausts craving for these nutriments in this way, he also fully understands the four nutriments; when these things are fully understood, the entire object of the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca) is indeed fully understood. For this was said by the Blessed One:

"Monks, when the nutriment of edible food is fully understood, the lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure is fully understood. When the lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure is fully understood, there is no fetter bound by which a noble disciple would come back to this world. Monks, when the nutriment of contact is fully understood, the three feelings are fully understood. When the three feelings are fully understood, I say there is nothing further to be done by the noble disciple. Monks, when the nutriment of mental volition is fully understood, the three cravings are fully understood. When the three cravings are fully understood, I say there is nothing further to be done by the noble disciple. Monks, when the nutriment of consciousness is fully understood, name-and-form is fully understood. When name-and-form is fully understood, I say there is nothing further to be done by the noble disciple" (SN 2.63).

"With the arising of craving, there is the arising of nutriment" means that because of craving in a previous life, the arising of nutriments at the time of rebirth-linking occurs. How? At the moment of rebirth-linking, there is nutritive essence (ojā) produced within the thirty types of matter (rūpa) that arise by way of the three continuities: the decad of the body (kāya-dasaka), the decad of sex (bhāva-dasaka), and the decad of the physical base (vatthu-dasaka). This nutritive essence is the kamma-born edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra) that is 'clung-to' (upādinnaka), arising because of craving. Contact and volition associated with the rebirth-linking consciousness, and the consciousness itself—these kamma-born contact, mental volition, and nutriment of consciousness are called nutriments arising because of craving. Thus, first, the arising of nutriments at the time of rebirth-linking because of craving in a previous life should be understood.

Since in this Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta, both 'clung-to' (upādinnaka) and 'not-clung-to' (anupādinnaka) nutriments are taught in combination, the arising of 'not-clung-to' nutriments because of craving should also be understood in this way. For in the matter (rūpa) produced by the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed (lobha), there is nutritive essence; this nutritive essence is the 'not-clung-to' edible food arising because of conascent craving. Contact and volition associated with the consciousness accompanied by greed, and the consciousness itself—these 'not-clung-to' contact, mental volition, and nutriment of consciousness are called nutriments arising because of craving.
219:
In the statement, "With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of nutriment," the cessation of nutriment is evident through the cessation of craving, which is the cause of both clung-to (upādinnaka) and not clung-to (anupādinnaka) nutriments. The remaining text is as previously explained. The distinction in this section is that the Four Noble Truths are taught in their specific aspects (sarūpa). Just as the Truths are extracted in this section, so too should the Four Noble Truths be extracted in all subsequent sections. Therefore, one who is not confused in any section should extract the Truths. In all sections, the conclusion of the teaching, "Friends, to this extent also," should be applied according to the nature of the Dhamma taught in each respective section. The application (yojanā) in this section is as follows: "to this extent also" means also by the power of penetration through attention (manasikāra) as stated in this teaching on nutriment. This method applies to all sections.

## The Explanation of the Section on Nutriment is finished.

## Explanation of the Section on Truths

Now, having greatly rejoiced in and appreciated the Venerable Sāriputta's words according to the previous method, saying "Excellent, friend," those bhikkhus further asked a question. The Elder also answered them by another method. This method applies to all subsequent sections. Therefore, from here on, without examining such repetitive words, I shall only explain the meaning of the specific method by which he answers. In the brief teaching of this section, in the phrase "he also understands suffering," "suffering" refers to the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca). As for everything that should be said in the detailed teaching, it has already been stated in the Saccaniddesa of the Visuddhimagga.

## The Explanation of the Section on Truths is finished.

## Explanation of the Section on Aging and Death

From here on, the teaching proceeds by way of Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). In that section on aging and death, the phrase "of those, those [beings]" (tesaṃ tesaṃ) should be understood as a general designation (sādhāraṇa-niddesa) for many beings in brief. Indeed, if one were to speak all day long, saying "the aging of Devadatta, the aging of Somadatta," the beings...
220:
...would be exhausted (or the list would be endless). However, by these two words, no being is left out; all are included. Therefore, it is said, "This is a general designation for many beings in brief."

"In this or that" (tamhi tamhi) is a general designation for many groups (nikāya) by way of destiny (gati) and birth (jāti). The phrase "in the order of beings" (sattanikāye) is an illustration of the specific form designated by the general designation. Among the terms beginning with "aging, decaying" (jarā jīraṇatā), "aging" (jarā) is a designation of the nature (sabhāva-niddesa). "Decaying" (jīraṇatā) is a designation of the manner (ākāra-niddesa). Terms such as "brokenness" (khaṇ|ḍicca) are designations of the function (kicca-niddesa) that occurs with the passage of time. The last two are designations of the natural state (pakati-niddesa).

Indeed, because this aging is shown by its nature through the word "jarā," it is a designation of nature. Because it is shown by its manner through the word "jīraṇatā," it is a designation of manner. It is shown by the word "khaṇḍicca" (brokenness) because of the function of causing the breaking of teeth and nails when time has passed; by the word "pālicca" (grayness) because of the function of causing the hair of the head and body to turn gray; and by the word "valittacatā" (wrinkledness) because of the function of causing the flesh to wither and the skin to wrinkle. Therefore, these three, beginning with "khaṇḍicca," are designations of the function that occurs with the passage of time.

Through these terms, "evident aging" (pākaṭa-jarā) is shown, which becomes clear by observing these transformations. For example, the path taken by water, fire, or wind becomes evident through the breaking of grass and trees or by the charred remains, yet that path is not the water or fire itself. In the same way, the path taken by aging becomes evident in the teeth and so on by way of brokenness and such, and can be perceived just by opening the eyes; however, brokenness and the like are not aging itself. This is because aging is not an object perceivable by the eye.

By the phrases "decline of life" (āyuno saṃhāni) and "ripening of the faculties" (indriyānaṃ paripāko), the natural state is shown, known as the end of life and the ripening of the eye-faculty and so on, which becomes very evident only when time has passed. Therefore, these last two should be understood as designations of the natural state (pakati-niddesa).

In that context, since the life of one who has reached old age declines, aging is called "decline of life" by way of metonymy (phalūpacāra), attributing the effect to the cause. Furthermore, the faculties such as the eye, which in youth were very clear and capable of easily grasping even subtle objects, become over-ripe, disturbed, and unclear upon reaching old age, becoming incapable of grasping even gross objects. Therefore, it is also called "ripening of the faculties" (by way of metonymy).
221:
(Decay) is spoken of only by way of metonymy (phalūpacāra). All such decay thus pointed out is of two kinds: apparent decay (pākaṭajarā) and concealed decay (paṭicchannajarā).

Among those two, the decay that occurs in material phenomena (rūpadhamma) is called apparent decay because one can see the state of being broken in teeth and so on. In mental phenomena (arūpadhamma), however, it is called concealed decay because such alteration is not seen. Therein, the state of being broken in teeth and so on that is seen is merely the easily discernible appearance (vaṇṇa) of those teeth, etc. Having seen that appearance with the eye and reflecting upon it with the mind-door, one knows the decay, thinking, "These teeth have been struck by decay." This is like seeing the heads of oxen tied in a place where there is water and thereby knowing the existence of water below. Furthermore, decay is also of two kinds: continuous decay (avīcijarā) and intermittent decay (savīcijarā). Therein, the decay that occurs in gems, gold, silver, coral, the sun, and so on, as well as in the decades of decline (mandadasaka) of living beings, and in inanimate things such as flowers, fruits, and sprouts, is called continuous decay because the distinctions in appearance and so on at various intervals are difficult to discern; it means decay without interval. Apart from those, the decay in the aforementioned objects where the distinctions in appearance and so on at various intervals are easily discernible is to be known as intermittent decay (savīcijarā).

From here on, the phrases such as "tesaṃ tesaṃ" and so on should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. Among the terms such as cuti (falling away) and cavanatā (the state of falling away), cuti is spoken of by way of passing away; it is a general term for the one, four, or five aggregates. By the word cavanatā, which is an abstract noun, the characteristic is shown. Bhedo (breaking up) refers to the manifestation of the destruction of the aggregates at the moment of passing away. Antaradhānaṃ (disappearance) refers to the fact that the broken aggregates at passing away, like a broken pot, no longer exist in any way. Maccu maraṇaṃ is death known as 'Maccu' (the Killer). By that term, it excludes such things as 'death by cutting off' (samuccheda-maraṇa). Time (Kāla) is the King who makes an end; his action is called 'making an end of time' (kālakiriyā). By this term, death is shown according to worldly convention.

Now, in order to show it according to the ultimate sense (paramattha), he said "khandhānaṃ bhedo" (the breaking up of the aggregates) and so on. In the ultimate sense, only the aggregates break up; no being as such dies. However, when the aggregates are breaking up, there is the conventional usage that "a being dies," and when they have broken up, that "he is dead."

In this context, the breaking up of the aggregates occurs by way of the four-constituent existence (catu-vokāra), and the laying down of the carcass (kaḷevara) occurs by way of the one-constituent existence (eka-vokāra). Alternatively, it should be understood that the breaking up of the aggregates occurs by way of the four-constituent existence, and the laying down of the carcass occurs by way of the remaining two types of existence. Why? Because the carcass, known as the material body (rūpakāya), can exist in both types of existence. Or else, since in the realms of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājikā) and so on, the aggregates merely break up and they do not lay down anything, therefore for those devas...
222:
...(for those devas) it is death by way of the breaking up of the aggregates, while for humans and others, it is the laying down of the carcass. Here, the meaning should be understood thus: death is called "the laying down of the carcass" because the laying down of the carcass is the cause (or sign) of death.

Thus, taking both this decay and this death together, it is said, "Friends, this is called decay and death (jarāmaraṇa)." The rest is exactly as previously stated.

## The Explanation of the Section on Decay and Death is Finished.

## The Explanation of the Section on Birth

In the section on birth (jātivāra), among the terms "jāti sañjāti" and so on, it is called jāti (birth) in the sense of being born; that jāti is appropriate by way of incomplete bases (āyatana). It is called sañjāti (complete birth) in the sense of being fully born; that sañjāti is appropriate by way of complete bases. It is called okkanti (descent) in the sense of entering; that okkanti is appropriate by way of egg-born (aṇḍaja) and womb-born (jalābuja) beings. Indeed, those egg-born and womb-born individuals, when entering the egg-shell and the womb, take rebirth as if they were entering a house. It is called abhinibbatti (manifestation) in the sense of becoming manifest; that abhinibbatti is appropriate by way of moisture-born (saṃsedaja) and spontaneously born (opapātika) beings; indeed, those moisture-born and spontaneously born individuals are born by becoming manifest at once. This is first the conventional teaching (vohāra-desanā).

Now, the ultimate teaching (paramattha-desanā) is presented. Indeed, in the ultimate sense, only the aggregates become manifest, not a being. Therein, by the phrase "of the aggregates" (khandhānaṃ), it should be understood as taking one aggregate in the one-constituent existence, four in the four-constituent existence, and all five in the five-constituent existence. Pātubhāvo (manifestation) means arising. In the phrase "of the bases" (āyatanānaṃ), the inclusion should be understood only by way of the bases that are arising in those respective planes of existence. Paṭilābho (acquisition) is the very manifestation in the continuity (santati). Indeed, those bases are said to be acquired only when they become manifest. By the phrase "Friends, this is called birth (jāti)," he concludes the birth that has been taught both by way of convention and in the ultimate sense. In the phrase "bhava-samudayā" (from the origin of existence), however, the kamma-process existence (kammabhava) which is the condition for birth should be understood. The rest is exactly as previously stated.

## The Explanation of the Section on Birth is Finished.
223:
## Commentary on the Section on Existence (Bhava)

In the section on existence, 'sensual existence' (kāmabhava) consists of two types: karmic existence (kammabhava) and rebirth existence (upapattibhava). Among these, karmic existence refers to the kamma itself that leads to the sensual realm. Because that kamma is the cause of rebirth existence, it is called 'existence' by attributing the name of the effect to the cause, as in the scriptural passages: 'The arising of Buddhas is blissful' (Dhp. 194) and 'The accumulation of evil is painful' (Dhp. 117). Rebirth existence refers to the group of five aggregates of clinging (upādinnakkhandha) produced by that kamma. Since those five aggregates arise in that sensual realm, they are called 'existence.' Thus, in every respect, both this kamma and rebirth are referred to here as 'sensual existence.' The same method should be understood for fine-material existence (rūpabhava) and immaterial existence (arūpabhava). In the phrase 'upādānasamudayā' (with clinging as origin), clinging assists wholesome karmic existence only by way of natural decisive support (pakatūpanissaya). However, it assists unwholesome karmic existence both by way of natural decisive support and by way of conascence (sahajāta), etc. For all rebirth existence, it assists only by way of natural decisive support. The remaining terms are to be understood in the manner already described.

## Commentary on the Section on Clinging (Upādāna)

In the section on clinging, regarding 'clinging to sensuality' (kāmupādāna) and so forth, one clings to objective sensuality (vatthukāma) by means of this state, or it clings to that objective sensuality itself; therefore, it is called 'clinging to sensuality.' Alternatively, it is called 'clinging to sensuality' because it is both sensuality and clinging. Clinging (upādāna) refers to firm grasping. Here, the prefix 'upa' expresses the sense of firmness, as in 'upāyāsa' (intense despair) and 'upakaṭṭha' (very near). This 'clinging to sensuality' is a designation for the lust (rāga) that occurs in the five strands of sensual pleasure. This is the summary here. In detail, it should be understood according to the method stated: 'Among those, what is clinging to sensuality? It is the sensual desire (kāmacchanda) for sensual pleasures...' (Dhs. 1220; Vibh. 938).

Similarly, it is called 'clinging to views' (diṭṭhupādāna) because it is both a view and clinging. Alternatively, it is called 'clinging to views' because it clings to a view, or views are clung to by means of this state. Indeed, a subsequent view clings to a preceding view. And by that view, they cling to a view. As it is said: 'The self and the world are eternal; only this is true, anything else is futile' (M. Ni. 3.27), etc. This is a designation for all types of wrong views, excluding clinging to rules and observances (sīlabbatupādāna) and clinging to the doctrine of self (attavādupādāna). This is the summary here. In detail, it should be understood according to the method stated: 'Among those, what is clinging to views? It is the view that there is no merit in almsgiving...' (Dhs. 1220; Vibh. 938).
224:
Similarly, by means of that wrong view, associated states or individuals cling to rules and observances; or it clings to them itself. Because it is both a rule/observance and clinging, it is called 'clinging to rules and observances' (sīlabbatupādāna). Due to the adherence that 'purity comes through this' regarding cow-virtue, cow-vows, etc., clingings arise naturally. This is the summary here. In detail, this clinging to rules and observances should be understood according to the method stated: 'Among those, what is clinging to rules and observances? It is the belief of recluses and brahmins outside this Dispensation that purity comes through rules...'

Now, it is called 'doctrine' (vāda) because they speak by means of it. It is called 'clinging' (upādāna) because they cling by means of it. What do they speak of, or what do they cling to? They speak of or cling to a self (atta). Clinging to one's own doctrine of self is 'clinging to the doctrine of self' (attavādupādāna). Alternatively, it is called 'clinging to the doctrine of self' because one clings to the mere doctrine of self as 'self' by means of that view. This is a designation for identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) which has twenty bases. This is the summary here. In detail, this clinging to the doctrine of self should be understood according to the method stated: 'Among those, what is clinging to the doctrine of self? Here, an uninstructed worldling, who has no regard for the Noble Ones...'

In the phrase 'taṇhāsamudayā' (with craving as origin), craving is a condition for clinging to sensuality by way of natural decisive support (pakatūpanissaya), or by way of proximity (anantara), contiguity (samanantara), absence (natthi), disappearance (vigata), and repetition (āsevana). For the remaining types of clinging, it is a condition by way of conascence (sahajāta), etc. The remaining terms are to be understood in the manner already described.

## Commentary on the Section on Craving (Taṇhā)

In the section on craving, from 'craving for forms' (rūpataṇhā) to 'craving for mental objects' (dhammataṇhā), the craving that occurs in the javana process at the eye-door, etc., receives its name from its object, which is like a father, just as names like 'son of a wealthy man' or 'son of a brahmin' are given based on the father. Here, craving that has a form as its object, or craving for a form, is called 'craving for forms.' When that craving for forms arises enjoying the form through the nature of sensual lust, it is called 'sensual craving' (kāmataṇhā). When it arises enjoying the form as 'permanent, stable, eternal' through the nature of lust associated with the eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi), it is called 'craving for existence' (bhavataṇhā). When it arises enjoying the form as 'it will be annihilated, it will perish, it will not exist after death' through the nature of lust associated with the annihilationist view (ucchedadiṭṭhi), it is called 'craving for non-existence' (vibhavataṇhā). Thus, it is of three kinds. Just as craving for forms is of three kinds, so too are craving for sounds, etc. Thus, there are eighteen mental explorations of craving (taṇhā-vicarita). These are eighteen regarding internal forms, etc., and eighteen regarding external forms, etc., making thirty-six. Thus, there are thirty-six in the past, thirty-six in the future, and thirty-six in the present, totaling one hundred and eight. Based on one's own internal continuity, thinking 'I am'...
225:
There are eighteen modes of craving (taṇhā-vicarita) based on internal forms and so forth, such as 'it is in this way'. Or, there are eighteen modes of craving based on external forms and so forth, such as 'I am by this' or 'it is in this way by this'. Thus, there are thirty-six modes (18 internal and 18 external). In this way, there are thirty-six modes of craving in the past, thirty-six in the future, and thirty-six in the present. Thus, there are one hundred and eight modes of craving. Again, when summarized, there are only six groups of craving regarding the six objects such as forms, and only three types such as craving for sensual pleasures (kāma-taṇhā).

The wise should understand craving by way of the brief meaning in the Niddesa Pāḷi, by the detailed one hundred and eight modes of craving in that Niddesa, and again by way of summary.

In the phrase 'vedanā-samudayā' (from the arising of feeling), feeling refers to resultant feeling (vipāka-vedanā). If it is asked: how does that resultant feeling become a condition for craving in the six doors? It is because it is enjoyable. To explain further: beings, through enjoying pleasant feeling, cherish that feeling, give rise to craving for it, and becoming lustful with greed for feeling, they long only for desirable forms in the eye-door. When they obtain them, they enjoy those forms and show honor and hospitality to those who provide the objects, such as painters. Similarly, in the ear-door and so forth, they long for desirable sounds and so forth. When they obtain them, they enjoy them and show honor and hospitality to those who provide the objects, such as lute players, perfumers, cooks, weavers, and various performers of arts. For example, just as parents who cherish their son out of love for him show honor and hospitality to the nurse and feed the child only with suitable ghee, milk, and so forth. The rest is just as previously stated.

## Commentary on the Section on Feeling

In the section on feeling, 'vedanā-kāyā' means groups of feeling. The statement 'feeling born of eye-contact... (and so forth) feeling born of mind-contact' is the name for wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate feelings arising in the eye-door and so forth, because it is stated in the Vibhaṅga: 'Feeling born of eye-contact is wholesome, is unwholesome, is indeterminate.' Just as names like 'Sāriputta' or 'Mantāṇiputta' are given based on the mother, this name is given based on the object (contact) which is like a mother. Here, the word-definition is: feeling born due to the cause of eye-contact is 'feeling born of eye-contact' (cakkhu-samphassajā vedanā). This method is the same in all instances. This is the method here (of comprehensive inclusion).
226:
To speak by way of the comprehensive method, feelings should be understood by way of association with the two eye-consciousnesses, two mind-elements, and three mind-consciousness-elements in the eye-door by way of resultants. This method also applies to the ear-door and so forth. In the mind-door, however, only feelings associated with the mind-consciousness-element should be understood.

In the phrase 'phassa-samudayā' (from the arising of contact), for feelings based on the five bases such as the eye-sensitivity in the five doors, arising occurs due to the cause of co-nascent eye-contact and so forth. For the remaining feelings, eye-contact and so forth are conditions by way of decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya) and so forth. In the mind-door, it should be understood that for registration feelings (tadārammaṇa-vedanā) and for the door-freed feelings of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death (paṭisandhi-bhavaṅga-cuti-vedanā), arising occurs due to the cause of co-nascent mind-contact. The rest is just as previously stated.

## Commentary on the Section on Contact

In the section on contact, 'cakkhu-samphassa' (eye-contact) is contact in the eye-base. This method is the same in all instances. By this sequence of words from 'eye-contact' to 'body-contact', the ten types of contact based on the five bases, which are wholesome, unwholesome, and resultant, are spoken of. By the term 'mind-contact' (mano-samphassa), the remaining twenty-two types of contact associated with mundane resultant consciousness are taught. 'saḷāyatana-samudayā' (from the arising of the six bases) means that due to the arising of the six bases such as the eye, the arising of these six types of contact occurs. The rest is just as previously stated.

## Commentary on the Section on the Six Bases

In the section on the six bases, all that should be said regarding terms such as 'cakkhāyatana' (eye-base) is just as stated in the Visuddhimagga in the Description of the Aggregates (Khandha-niddesa) and the Description of the Bases (Āyatana-niddesa). In the phrase 'nāmarūpa-samudayā' (from the arising of name-and-form), whichever name, whichever form, or whichever name-and-form is a condition for whichever base, the arising of the six bases due to the arising of name-and-form should be understood by way of that name-and-form according to the method stated in the Visuddhimagga in the Description of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda-niddesa). The rest is just as previously described.

## Commentary on the Section on Name-and-Form

In the section on name-and-form, that which has the characteristic of inclining (namana-lakkhaṇa) towards an object is called 'name' (nāma). That which has the characteristic of being deformed (ruppana-lakkhaṇa) is called 'form' (rūpa). In the detailed section of that name-and-form, 'feeling' (vedanā) should be understood as the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-kkhandha), 'perception' (saññā) as the aggregate of perception (saññā-kkhandha), and 'volition, contact, and attention' (cetanā, phassa, manasikāra) as the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhāra-kkhandha). Indeed, there are also other states included in the aggregate of mental formations...
228:
...this is the name for the twenty types of bodily volition (kāyasañcetanā) arising from the eight types of sense-sphere wholesome (kāmāvacara kusala) and twelve types of unwholesome (akusala) consciousness occurring by way of movement (copana). "Vacīsaṅkhāra" means formations occurring because of the vocal door. This is the name for the twenty types of vocal volition (vacīsañcetanā) occurring by way of speech in the vocal door. "Cittasaṅkhāra" means formations occurring because of the mind. This is the name for the twenty-nine types of mental volition (manosañcetanā) by way of mundane wholesome and unwholesome consciousness occurring for one who sits in seclusion and thinks without making movements in the body or vocal doors. In the phrase "avijjāsamudayā," it should be understood that ignorance (avijjā) is a condition for wholesome formations by way of the decisive support condition (upanissaya), and for unwholesome formations by way of the conascence condition (sahajāta), etc. The rest is as previously stated.

## Description of the Section on Ignorance (Avijjāvāravaṇṇanā)

In the section on ignorance, "dukkhe aññāṇaṃ" means not knowing the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca); this is a name for delusion (moha). The same method applies to "samudaye aññāṇaṃ" (not knowing the origin), etc. In that context, not knowing the truth of suffering (ignorance) should be understood through four reasons: inclusion (antogadha), basis (vatthu), object (ārammaṇa), and concealment (paṭicchādana). This is true. Because it is included within the truth of suffering, it is "included" in suffering. The truth of suffering is also the "basis" (vatthu) for this ignorance by way of being a support condition (nissaya-paccaya), and it is the "object" (ārammaṇa) by way of being an object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya). This ignorance "conceals" the truth of suffering by preventing the penetration of its true nature and by not allowing knowledge (ñāṇa) to arise regarding this truth of suffering.

Not knowing the truth of the origin (samudaya-sacca) should be understood through three reasons: basis, object, and concealment. Not knowing the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca) and the truth of the path (magga-sacca) should be understood through only one reason: concealment. For in the truths of cessation and the path, ignorance only conceals by preventing the penetration of their true nature and by not allowing knowledge to arise regarding those truths. It is not "included" in those two truths because it is not comprised within them. Those two truths are not the "basis" (vatthu) for that ignorance because they do not arise together (not conascent). They are not the "object" because ignorance does not arise taking them as objects. The latter two truths (cessation and path) are difficult to see because they are profound; blind-like ignorance does not occur in these two truths. However, the former two truths (suffering and origin) are profound because their individual natures are difficult to see due to their deceptive nature; ignorance occurs in those two truths by way of perverted grasping.

Furthermore, by the word "dukkhe" (in suffering), ignorance is shown briefly, by way of basis, object, and function. By the word "dukkhasamudaye" (in the origin of suffering), by way of basis...
229:
(Avijjā) is shown by way of object and by way of function. In the context of the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering and the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering (the Truth of the Path), Avijjā is shown by way of function through these words. However, in a general sense without distinction, it should be understood that Avijjā is indicated by its nature through the term "Aññāṇa" (non-knowledge). In the phrase "Āsavasamudaya" (the origin of the taints), the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava) and the taint of existence (bhavāsava) assist Avijjā by way of conascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya) and so on. The taint of ignorance (avijjāsava) assists only by way of decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya). Here, the ignorance that arose previously should be understood as the "taint of ignorance." That previous ignorance assists the subsequent ignorance by way of decisive support condition. The remaining text is as previously explained.

## Explanation of the Section on Taints (Āsavavāra-vaṇṇanā)

In the section on taints, regarding the phrase "Avijjāsamudaya," ignorance assists the taint of sensual desire and the taint of existence by way of conascence condition and so on. It assists the taint of ignorance only by way of decisive support condition. Here, the ignorance that arises in succession should be understood as the "taint of ignorance." The ignorance that arose earlier assists the subsequent taint of ignorance by way of decisive support condition. The remaining text is as previously explained. This section is taught to show the causal condition of ignorance, which is the chief among the factors of Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). By this section thus taught, the beginninglessness of Saṃsāra is established. How is it established? Because of the arising of taints, there is the arising of ignorance; because of the arising of ignorance, there is also the arising of taints. Thus, by establishing that the taints assist ignorance and ignorance assists the taints, the prior limit of ignorance is not apparent. Since that prior limit is not apparent, the beginninglessness of Saṃsāra is proven.

Thus, in this Sutta, all sixteen sections are taught: the section on the course of action (kamma-patha), the section on nutriment (āhāra), the section on suffering (dukkha), the section on aging and death (jarā-maraṇa), the section on birth (jāti), the section on existence (bhava), the section on clinging (upādāna), the section on craving (taṇhā), the section on feeling (vedanā), the section on contact (phassa), the section on the sixfold sense base (saḷāyatana), the section on mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa), the section on consciousness (viññāṇa), the section on volitional formations (saṅkhāra), the section on ignorance (avijjā), and the section on taints (āsava).

Among these sixteen sections, when each section is analyzed in two ways—briefly and in detail—there are thirty-two instances. Thus, in this Sutta, the Four Noble Truths are taught in these thirty-two instances. In the sixteen instances taught in detail, the Fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala) is taught. According to the Elder's view, it should be understood that the Four Noble Truths and the Four Paths are taught in all thirty-two instances. Thus, in the entire Word of the Buddha contained in the five Great Nikāyas, there is no other Sutta besides this Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta where the Four Noble Truths are proclaimed thirty-two times and the Fruit of Arahantship is proclaimed thirty-two times.
230:
The Venerable Sāriputta said this. The Venerable Sāriputta taught the Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta, adorning it with sixty-four reasons: thirty-two ways of knowing the Four Noble Truths and thirty-two ways of knowing the Fruit of Arahantship. Those bhikkhus were delighted and rejoiced in the Venerable Sāriputta's words.

## The Explanation of the Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta in the Majjhima Nikāya Commentary
## named Papañcasūdanī is finished.

## 10. Explanation of the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta

'Thus have I heard' and so on is the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta. Therein, 'staying among the Kurus' (kurūsu viharati) means a certain district which is the dwelling place of the princes of the district named Kuru; it is called 'Kuru' by way of conventional usage (ruḷhī-sadda). It means (he was staying) in that Kuru district. The teachers of the Commentary, however, say this: In the time of King Mandhātu, the people of the three great islands heard that the island of Jambudīpa was the birthplace of supreme persons (uttama-purisa) such as Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, Great Disciples, and Wheel-turning Monarchs, and that it was a noble island, extremely delightful. Therefore, when the Wheel-turning Monarch Mandhātu traveled around the four great islands, placing the wheel-treasure (cakka-ratana) at the front, they followed along with the king. Then the king asked the advisor-treasure (pariṇāyaka-ratana), 'Is there any place more delightful than the human world?' 'Great King, why do you ask so? Do you not see the power of the moon and the sun? The place of those deities is much more delightful than this place,' he replied.

The king, placing the wheel-treasure at the front, went to that place. When the Four Great Kings heard that 'the Great King Mandhātu has arrived,' they thought, 'It is not possible to resist this king of great psychic power and majesty by war,' and they surrendered their kingdoms. After taking those kingdoms, the king asked again, 'Is there any place more delightful than this?' Then they told him about the Tāvatiṃsa heaven: 'Great King, the Tāvatiṃsa heaven is more delightful. There, in the presence of Sakka, the King of Gods, these Four Great Kings serve as gatekeepers. Sakka, the King of Gods, is of great psychic power and majesty. His places of enjoyment are the Vejayanta Palace, which is a thousand leagues (yojana) high; the Sudhammā Hall of the Gods, which is five hundred leagues high; the Vejayanta Chariot, which is one hundred and fifty leagues; and the elephant-king Erāvaṇa.'
